question_text:
A 78-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Ballarat, Victoria, after the practice nurse noticed an irregular pulse during a routine health assessment. She has had occasional palpitations for two months but no chest pain, syncope or breathlessness. She has hypertension treated with perindopril 5 mg daily and knee osteoarthritis, for which she takes paracetamol 1 g up to three times daily. She has no history of stroke, transient ischaemic attack, diabetes, heart failure, vascular disease or bleeding. She drinks one standard drink a week and has never smoked.

Her pulse is 84/min and irregularly irregular, and her blood pressure is 136/82 mmHg. She weighs 57 kg. The rest of the examination is unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 82/min. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart with no mitral stenosis and no prosthetic valve.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115–160)
- Platelets 245 × 10^9/L (150–400)
- Serum creatinine 118 µmol/L (45–90)
- Creatinine clearance (Cockcroft–Gault) 31 mL/min
- Liver function tests normal

After discussion, she agrees to start oral anticoagulation.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate regimen?
options: Apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily
Dabigatran 150 mg orally twice daily
Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily
Rivaroxaban 20 mg orally once daily
Aspirin 100 mg orally once daily
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily

---

Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 3: age 75 years or over scores 2 and hypertension scores 1. The 2018 NHFA/CSANZ Australian AF guideline dropped female sex from the score. A score of 2 or more means oral anticoagulation is recommended, and a NOAC (DOAC) is preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF. The Australian product information says to reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily only when at least TWO of these apply: age 80 years or over, weight 60 kg or less, serum creatinine 133 µmol/L or more. She meets only one (weight 57 kg). She is 78, and her creatinine of 118 µmol/L is below 133. So the standard 5 mg twice daily is correct. Her creatinine clearance of 31 mL/min is above the level where the Australian PI contraindicates apixaban (below 25 mL/min).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Use CHA2DS2-VA in Australia (no point for female sex). Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily only if 2 of these 3 apply: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 µmol/L or more.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation 2018 (MJA)", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2018/209/8/national-heart-foundation-australia-and-cardiac-society-australia-and-new"}
• {"name": "Eliquis (apixaban) Australian Product Information, sections 4.2 and 4.3", "url": "https://rss.medsinfo.com.au/bq/pi.cfm?product=bqpeliqu"}
• {"name": "Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG complete): Cardiovascular, atrial fibrillation (subscription)", "url": "https://www.tg.org.au"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Atrial fibrillation: choosing an anticoagulant and dose

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A common error: under-dosing because of low weight or reduced renal function alone. Only one dose-reduction criterion applies (weight 60 kg or less), and two are needed. Under-dosing apixaban gives less protection against stroke.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Dabigatran is contraindicated in Australia when CrCl is below 30 mL/min, and she is only just above that at 31 mL/min. It is also mostly cleared by the kidneys, and 110 mg twice daily is generally preferred at age 75 or over. 150 mg twice daily is not appropriate here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Rivaroxaban is a reasonable drug, but the dose is wrong. With CrCl 30–49 mL/min the AF dose is 15 mg once daily, not 20 mg.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF. It is much less effective than anticoagulation and its bleeding risk is not meaningfully lower in older people.

key_takeaways: Use CHA2DS2-VA in Australia (no point for female sex). Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily only if 2 of these 3 apply: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 µmol/L or more.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department of a Brisbane hospital with two days of left-sided chest pain. The pain is sharp, worse on deep inspiration and twisting, and started the morning after she moved house. She has no cough, haemoptysis, fever or leg symptoms. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and has no other medical history. She has not travelled, had surgery or been immobilised recently, and has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 92/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Firm pressure over the left sixth costochondral junction reproduces part of her pain. Heart sounds are normal, the chest is clear, and there is no calf swelling or tenderness. ECG shows sinus rhythm with no abnormality, and a chest X-ray is normal. Urine β-hCG is negative. The treating team judges that a musculoskeletal cause is more likely than pulmonary embolism.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with no further testing for pulmonary embolism
Measure a D-dimer level
Arrange a CT pulmonary angiogram
Arrange a ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) scan
Arrange bilateral lower-limb venous duplex ultrasound
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Measure a D-dimer level

---

Her pre-test probability is low. She scores 0 on the Wells score: no criteria are met, and PE is not the most likely diagnosis, so the +3 item does not apply. In a low-probability patient, the next question is whether she is PERC-negative, because a PERC-negative patient needs no further testing. PERC needs ALL eight criteria to be negative: age under 50, pulse under 100, SpO2 95% or more, no haemoptysis, no exogenous oestrogen, no previous VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, and no recent surgery or trauma. She uses the combined oral contraceptive pill (exogenous oestrogen), so she is PERC-positive. PE therefore cannot be ruled out clinically, and the next step is a D-dimer (age-adjusted where the local pathway uses this). A negative D-dimer excludes PE in a low-probability patient. A positive D-dimer leads to imaging.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
At low pre-test probability, PERC rules out PE only if all eight criteria are negative. Oestrogen use (e.g. the combined pill) makes her PERC-positive, so do a D-dimer.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation (ECI): Pulmonary thromboembolism evaluation pathway (Wells, PERC, age-adjusted D-dimer)", "url": "https://aci.health.nsw.gov.au/networks/eci/clinical/tools/respiratory/pe/pulmonary-thromboembolism-pe---evaluation-pathway"}
• {"name": "Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG complete): Cardiovascular, venous thromboembolism (subscription)", "url": "https://www.tg.org.au"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspected pulmonary embolism: pre-test probability, PERC and D-dimer

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This would be right only if she were PERC-negative. Oestrogen-containing contraception is one of the eight PERC criteria, so she cannot be discharged without a D-dimer.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: CTPA is for high (PE likely) pre-test probability or a positive D-dimer. Going straight to CTPA in a low-probability patient exposes her to unnecessary radiation, contrast and the risk of incidental findings.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A V/Q scan is an alternative to CTPA, for example in pregnancy, contrast allergy or renal impairment. It is still imaging, and imaging is not the next step before D-dimer at low pre-test probability.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Leg ultrasound can support a diagnosis of VTE when there are leg signs or CTPA is contraindicated. She has no leg symptoms, and a negative leg ultrasound would not exclude PE.

key_takeaways: At low pre-test probability, PERC rules out PE only if all eight criteria are negative. Oestrogen use (e.g. the combined pill) makes her PERC-positive, so do a D-dimer.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man is on the surgical ward of a regional hospital in New South Wales, 36 hours after an emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis. He has type 2 diabetes treated with empagliflozin/metformin 12.5 mg/1000 mg twice daily. He took his usual morning dose on the day he was admitted and went to theatre that evening. Since surgery he has eaten very little because of nausea. The nurse calls you because he has vomited three times, feels exhausted and is breathing quickly.

His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. His abdomen is soft, with appropriate port-site tenderness and no peritonism. His last HbA1c was 8.9% (74 mmol/mol).

Venous blood gas and biochemistry:
- pH 7.14 (7.35–7.45)
- pCO2 21 mmHg (35–45)
- Bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22–32)
- Base excess −19 mmol/L (−3 to +3)
- Lactate 1.4 mmol/L (<2.0)
- Glucose 11.2 mmol/L
- Capillary β-hydroxybutyrate (ketones) 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6)
- Sodium 138 mmol/L (135–145)
- Chloride 104 mmol/L (95–110)
- Potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Creatinine 96 µmol/L (60–110)

Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his acid–base disturbance?
options: Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis
Metformin-associated lactic acidosis
Starvation ketosis after fasting
Early postoperative sepsis with hypoperfusion
Hyperchloraemic acidosis from intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis

---

He has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis: anion gap 138 − (104 + 8) = 26. There is appropriate respiratory compensation (Winter's formula predicts pCO2 of about 20 ± 2), with marked ketonaemia (5.8 mmol/L) and a normal lactate. His glucose is only 11.2 mmol/L. The Australian Diabetes Society periprocedural alert defines presumed DKA as ketones above 1.0 mmol/L with base excess below −5, and presumed euglycaemic DKA as the same with glucose below 14 mmol/L. SGLT2 inhibitors cause this, especially with fasting, surgery, intercurrent illness or relative insulin deficiency (HbA1c above 9% raises risk further). He could not stop empagliflozin 3 days before surgery because it was an emergency. A near-normal glucose does not exclude DKA. Management is DKA treatment: IV fluids, IV insulin with added IV glucose once BGL is below about 15 mmol/L, potassium replacement, stopping the SGLT2 inhibitor, and escalation to the rapid response team/ICU with endocrinology input.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In a patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor who is unwell, check blood ketones and a blood gas even if glucose is near-normal. Ketones above 1.0 with base excess below −5 means DKA. With glucose below 14, it is euglycaemic DKA.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ADS/ADEA/ANZCA/NZSSD Alert Update (May 2023): Periprocedural DKA with SGLT2 inhibitor use in people with diabetes", "url": "https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/ADS-ADEA-ANZCA-NZSSD_DKA_SGLT2i_Alert_Ver-May-2023.pdf"}
• {"name": "ADS\u2013ANZCA Perioperative Diabetes and Hyperglycaemia Guidelines (Adults), Nov 2022", "url": "https://www.diabetessociety.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/ADS-ANZCA-Perioperative-Diabetes-and-Hyperglycaemia-Guidelines-Adults-November-2022-v2-Final-3.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis after surgery

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis needs a raised lactate, usually with renal impairment or hypoperfusion. Lactate is 1.4 mmol/L and creatinine is normal. Ketones explain the anion gap.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Starvation ketosis gives mild ketonaemia (the ADS notes up to about 1.7 mmol/L) with little or no acidosis. A pH of 7.14, bicarbonate of 8 and ketones of 5.8 are far beyond simple starvation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: He is tachycardic, but lactate is normal, he is afebrile and the abdomen is benign. Sepsis would raise lactate and would not explain ketones of 5.8 mmol/L. Sepsis can trigger DKA, but it is not the direct cause of this acidosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Saline-induced hyperchloraemic acidosis has a NORMAL anion gap and a high chloride. His chloride is normal and his anion gap is 26.

key_takeaways: In a patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor who is unwell, check blood ketones and a blood gas even if glucose is near-normal. Ketones above 1.0 with base excess below −5 means DKA. With glucose below 14, it is euglycaemic DKA.

question_text:
A 52-year-old Aboriginal man is brought to Katherine Hospital in the Northern Territory in February with three days of fever, cough and increasing breathlessness. He works as a community ranger and has spent the past week clearing flood debris and mud after heavy wet-season rain. He has type 2 diabetes (last HbA1c 10.2% [88 mmol/mol]) and stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and attends his community clinic regularly for his diabetes and kidney care. He has not been in hospital or had antibiotics in the past three months. At his request, the hospital's Aboriginal Liaison Officer is supporting him and has contacted his family.

His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse 124/min, blood pressure 84/50 mmHg after 1 L of intravenous crystalloid, respiratory rate 32/min and oxygen saturation 87% on room air. He is alert but anxious. There is bronchial breathing over the right upper zone. Chest X-ray shows dense right upper lobe consolidation. Lactate is 4.3 mmol/L and creatinine 162 µmol/L (60–110; his baseline is 140). Blood and sputum cultures have been collected. Retrieval to Royal Darwin Hospital ICU has been requested, and a noradrenaline infusion has been started.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?
options: Intravenous ceftriaxone plus intravenous azithromycin
Intravenous benzylpenicillin plus intravenous gentamicin
Intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam plus intravenous vancomycin
Intravenous meropenem plus intravenous azithromycin
Intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanate plus oral doxycycline
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Intravenous meropenem plus intravenous azithromycin

---

This is severe community-acquired pneumonia with septic shock and hypoxaemia in the tropical Top End during the wet season. He has major risk factors for melioidosis: diabetes, CKD, and heavy soil and water exposure after rain. Empirical therapy must cover Burkholderia pseudomallei as well as the usual CAP pathogens, including atypical organisms such as Legionella. The 2024 revised Darwin Melioidosis Treatment Guideline recommends meropenem (1 g IV 8-hourly, adjusted for renal function) for patients in ICU or with critical sepsis, and ceftazidime for less severe disease on the ward. In septic shock with augmented renal clearance it suggests 2 g 8-hourly as an extended infusion, and G-CSF may be considered. Therapeutic Guidelines pairs this with azithromycin for severe CAP in tropical northern Australia. If melioidosis is confirmed, the intensive IV phase lasts at least 14 days (at least 4 weeks for pneumonia needing ICU care). This is followed by at least 3 months of oral eradication therapy with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole plus folic acid. In remote NT clinics, the CARPA manual advises starting ceftriaxone or ceftazidime (with gentamicin) while retrieval is arranged, and the retrieval team gives meropenem. The very high burden of melioidosis in the Top End reflects environmental exposure and the high prevalence of diabetes and kidney disease. It is not explained by individual behaviour.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In severe CAP in tropical northern Australia (especially in the wet season, with diabetes, CKD, hazardous alcohol use or soil and water exposure), start meropenem plus azithromycin to cover melioidosis. Use ceftazidime for less severe melioidosis on the ward.

---

• {"name": "Meumann EM, Currie BJ. Approach to melioidosis. CMI Communications 2024;1:100008 (Charles Darwin University repository)", "url": "https://ris.cdu.edu.au/ws/portalfiles/portal/112385432/1-s2.0-S2950590924000088-main.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Severe community-acquired pneumonia in tropical northern Australia: melioidosis cover

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This is the standard empirical regimen for severe CAP in temperate Australia. Ceftriaxone does not reliably treat B. pseudomallei, so in the tropical wet season with his risk factors it could miss a highly lethal infection.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: An older severe-CAP combination for temperate regions. B. pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to gentamicin and penicillin, and gentamicin is best avoided with his worsening CKD.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Broad cover for hospital-acquired or MRSA-risk pneumonia. Piperacillin–tazobactam is not a recommended melioidosis agent, and he has no hospital-acquired or MRSA risk factors that would make vancomycin the priority.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Amoxicillin–clavulanate is a second-line oral eradication option for melioidosis only. It is inadequate as initial therapy for septic shock, and oral doxycycline is unreliable in a shocked patient.

key_takeaways: In severe CAP in tropical northern Australia (especially in the wet season, with diabetes, CKD, hazardous alcohol use or soil and water exposure), start meropenem plus azithromycin to cover melioidosis. Use ceftazidime for less severe melioidosis on the ward.

question_text:
A 71-year-old man is brought by ambulance to a metropolitan stroke centre in Adelaide. At 0730 hours he suddenly developed right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking while eating breakfast; his wife had seen him well at 0725. He arrives at 0915. He has hypertension, treated with amlodipine, and no history of bleeding, recent surgery, stroke or anticoagulant use.

He is alert, with expressive dysphasia, right facial droop, and dense right arm and moderate right leg weakness (NIHSS 14). His pulse is 78/min and regular, blood pressure 204/112 mmHg on repeated measurement, and capillary blood glucose 7.1 mmol/L. He weighs 80 kg.

Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct. CT angiography shows an occlusion of the proximal left middle cerebral artery (M1). The stroke team plans intravenous thrombolysis, and the endovascular clot retrieval team has been activated.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give tenecteplase 20 mg as an IV bolus now, then treat blood pressure after thrombolysis
Give aspirin 300 mg rectally now and withhold thrombolysis
Withhold thrombolysis because blood pressure exceeds 185/110 mmHg, and proceed to clot retrieval alone
Lower systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg with a glyceryl trinitrate infusion before any reperfusion therapy
Give IV labetalol to bring blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg, then give tenecteplase
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Give IV labetalol to bring blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg, then give tenecteplase

---

He has a disabling ischaemic stroke with large vessel occlusion, within 4.5 hours of last known well (about 1 h 50 min). He is eligible for IV thrombolysis and endovascular clot retrieval. The Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management recommend reducing blood pressure to below 185/110 mmHg BEFORE thrombolysis and keeping it there for the first 24 hours. The recommended agent is tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg), so 20 mg for 80 kg. Blood pressure above 185/110 is a reason to treat the blood pressure, not to abandon thrombolysis. Typical local protocols use IV labetalol 10–20 mg boluses, or alternatives such as hydralazine or a GTN infusion. If the target cannot be reached, thrombolysis is not given. Clot retrieval proceeds in parallel and should not be delayed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Before thrombolysis for ischaemic stroke, bring blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg and keep it there for 24 hours. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) is the preferred agent in the Australian living guideline.

---

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Acute ischaemic stroke: blood pressure before intravenous thrombolysis

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The dose is correct (0.25 mg/kg = 20 mg), but thrombolysing with blood pressure above 185/110 raises the risk of symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage. Blood pressure must be lowered first.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Aspirin is not given in the first 24 hours after thrombolysis, and choosing it instead of reperfusion withholds an effective treatment from an eligible patient.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Blood pressure that has NOT yet been treated is not a reason to withhold thrombolysis. He should get both thrombolysis and clot retrieval if blood pressure can be controlled.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Intensive lowering to systolic below 140 mmHg is not recommended in acute ischaemic stroke. It may reduce perfusion to the penumbra, and pursuing it delays reperfusion.

key_takeaways: Before thrombolysis for ischaemic stroke, bring blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg and keep it there for 24 hours. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) is the preferred agent in the Australian living guideline.

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman who was born in Vietnam and moved to Australia six years ago attends a general practice in Footscray, Melbourne. Three years ago her antenatal screening showed she was hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positive, but she did not attend follow-up. She feels well, drinks no alcohol and takes no regular medicines. Her mother died of liver cancer at 68. Examination is normal, with no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Investigations:
- HBsAg: positive
- HBeAg: negative
- Anti-HBe: positive
- Anti-HBc (total): positive
- IgM anti-HBc: negative
- HBV DNA: 850 IU/mL
- ALT: 16 U/L (female upper limit used by the laboratory: 19)
- Platelets 232 × 10^9/L; albumin and INR normal
- Liver transient elastography: 4.8 kPa
- Hepatitis C antibody, HIV and hepatitis D antibody: negative

Which one of the following best describes her current hepatitis B status?
options: Resolved past hepatitis B infection
HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis (immune escape phase)
HBeAg-negative chronic infection (immune control phase)
HBeAg-positive chronic infection (immune tolerance phase)
Acute hepatitis B infection in the window period
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. HBeAg-negative chronic infection (immune control phase)

---

HBsAg has been positive for more than 6 months (three years), so this is chronic infection. She is HBeAg-negative and anti-HBe-positive, with HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL, persistently normal ALT (using the lower female upper limit used in Australian guidance), and no fibrosis on elastography. That is the HBeAg-negative chronic infection (immune control, formerly 'inactive carrier') phase. Antiviral treatment is not indicated now. She needs lifelong monitoring: ALT about every 6 months and HBV DNA periodically (the ASHM toolkit suggests yearly) to detect reactivation into the immune escape phase. She also needs household and sexual contact tracing and vaccination of contacts. HCC surveillance is not yet indicated. The 2023 NHMRC-approved Australian guideline suggests considering 6-monthly ultrasound from age 50 for women of Asian background with chronic HBV, and from 10 years before the earliest family case where there is a family history. Her mother was diagnosed at 68 (which points to 58), so the family history does not bring the start age forward from 50.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
HBsAg-positive for more than 6 months, HBeAg-negative, HBV DNA below 2,000 IU/mL and normal ALT means immune control. Monitor for life; treatment is not needed now.

---

REFERENCES

question_text:
A 76-year-old woman comes to the emergency department in Geelong, Victoria, with five hours of severe, constant periumbilical pain that started suddenly. She has vomited twice and had one loose bowel motion. She has atrial fibrillation, normally treated with apixaban, which she stopped six days ago before a colonoscopy and polypectomy. She has not restarted it. She also has hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease.

She is distressed and needs repeated doses of IV fentanyl. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse 112/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Her abdomen is soft and only mildly tender, with no guarding or rebound. Bowel sounds are present. There are no hernias.

Investigations:
- White cell count 17.8 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- Haemoglobin 131 g/L (115–160)
- Venous lactate 1.9 mmol/L (<2.0)
- Lipase 32 U/L (<60)
- Creatinine 128 µmol/L (45–90), eGFR 36 mL/min/1.73 m²
- Troponin not raised
- ECG: atrial fibrillation, rate 110/min, no acute ischaemic changes

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Multiphase CT angiography of the abdomen
Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis to avoid contrast nephropathy
Erect chest X-ray and supine abdominal X-ray
Repeat venous lactate in two hours before deciding on imaging
Duplex ultrasound of the mesenteric arteries
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Multiphase CT angiography of the abdomen

---

Sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination, in a patient with AF whose anticoagulant has been stopped, suggests acute embolic superior mesenteric artery occlusion until proven otherwise. The leucocytosis supports this. Guidelines (e.g. ESVS 2025) recommend urgent multiphase CT angiography as the first-line test, with the suspicion of mesenteric ischaemia stated on the request. A normal lactate does NOT exclude acute mesenteric ischaemia: it rises late, once the bowel is infarcted, and single biomarkers should not be used to rule it out. Moderate renal impairment should not delay CTA in a condition where hours of delay mean bowel loss and death. The benefit far outweighs the small risk of contrast-associated kidney injury. Give IV hydration, start therapeutic heparin once the diagnosis is confirmed or strongly suspected, and refer urgently to vascular and general surgery.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Pain out of proportion to signs with AF (especially off anticoagulation) needs urgent CT angiography. Do not be reassured by a normal lactate, and do not delay for moderate CKD.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ESVS 2025 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Diseases of the Mesenteric and Renal Arteries and Veins (Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg)", "url": "https://www.ejves.com/article/S1078-5884(25)00516-7/fulltext"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Non-contrast CT cannot show arterial occlusion and may look normal in early ischaemia. Avoiding contrast because of eGFR 36 would be a dangerous trade-off here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Plain films are usually normal early and only show late signs (ileus, pneumatosis, free gas). They delay diagnosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Waiting for lactate to rise means waiting for bowel infarction. A normal lactate has poor negative predictive value in early mesenteric ischaemia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Duplex ultrasound depends on the operator, is limited by bowel gas in the acute abdomen, and cannot assess bowel viability. It is used mainly for chronic mesenteric ischaemia.

key_takeaways: Pain out of proportion to signs with AF (especially off anticoagulation) needs urgent CT angiography. Do not be reassured by a normal lactate, and do not delay for moderate CKD.

question_text:
An 84-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of a regional hospital in Queensland from her residential aged care facility after a fall. She was found on the floor with left hip pain and could not bear weight. She has moderate dementia (usually oriented to person only), hypertension, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease (baseline eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m²). She has no drug allergies and takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines.

Her left leg is shortened and externally rotated. The distal limb is neurovascularly intact. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the left femoral neck. The orthopaedic team plans a hemiarthroplasty on tomorrow's list.

An hour ago she was given oral paracetamol 1 g and two 2.5 mg doses of IV morphine. She still grimaces and calls out whenever she is moved, and her PAINAD score is 7/10. She is now drowsy between episodes of pain, with a respiratory rate of 12/min.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing her pain?
options: Further IV morphine 2.5 mg every five minutes until she is settled
Ultrasound-guided fascia iliaca block with local anaesthetic
Oral ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with regular paracetamol
Apply skin traction to the left leg to reduce muscle spasm
Intramuscular tramadol 100 mg once, with oral oxycodone as required
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Ultrasound-guided fascia iliaca block with local anaesthetic

---

The ACSQHC Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard (2023) expects early pain assessment (using a tool validated for cognitive impairment, such as PAINAD) and multimodal analgesia that includes a peripheral nerve block unless contraindicated. An ultrasound-guided fascia iliaca (or femoral nerve) block gives excellent analgesia for positioning and transfer and reduces opioid needs. That matters here: she is already drowsy with a respiratory rate of 12 after modest morphine doses, she has dementia (a delirium risk), and she has CKD (morphine metabolites accumulate). Surgery should ideally happen within 36 hours of presentation under the 2023 standard, and the block covers this period.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
The hip fracture standard calls for pain assessment with a dementia-appropriate tool and a nerve block (e.g. fascia iliaca) as part of multimodal analgesia, which limits opioid use in frail older people.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: NSAIDs are best avoided at eGFR 38 in an 84-year-old (risk of AKI and GI bleeding), and they would not give adequate analgesia on their own.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Routine preoperative skin traction is not recommended in hip fracture: it does not improve pain or outcomes and can cause skin injury.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold, is serotonergic and causes delirium in older people. The IM route is painful and absorption is unpredictable. It is not a substitute for a regional block.

question_text:
A 46-year-old man comes to the emergency department in Townsville with two days of severe colicky left loin-to-groin pain. Since this morning he has had rigors and feels much worse. He has had kidney stones before.

His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg after 1 L of IV crystalloid, and respiratory rate 22/min. He has marked left renal angle tenderness.

Investigations:
- White cell count 19.6 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- C-reactive protein 214 mg/L (<5)
- Creatinine 165 µmol/L (60–110; 85 six months ago)
- Lactate 2.8 mmol/L (<2.0)
- Urinalysis: leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 3+
- Non-contrast CT KUB: 7 mm calculus at the left vesicoureteric junction with moderate left hydronephrosis. Right kidney normal.

Blood and urine cultures have been taken, and IV antibiotics and further fluid resuscitation have started.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily as medical expulsive therapy, with analgesia
Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy to the stone within 24 hours
Continue IV antibiotics for 48 hours, then repeat the CT KUB
Urgent decompression with a ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy
Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy on the next elective list
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Urgent decompression with a ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy

---

This is an obstructed, infected kidney (pyonephrosis or obstructive pyelonephritis) with sepsis and AKI, a urological emergency. Antibiotics cannot sterilise an obstructed collecting system. Urgent drainage by retrograde ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy is needed alongside antibiotics and resuscitation. EAU urolithiasis guidelines regard both methods as equally effective, and the choice depends on local expertise and the patient's condition. Definitive stone treatment is DEFERRED until the sepsis has resolved and the course of antibiotics is complete.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
A fever with an obstructing stone is an emergency: decompress the kidney urgently (stent or nephrostomy) along with antibiotics, and delay definitive stone treatment.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "EAU Guidelines on Urolithiasis: decompression of the obstructed infected kidney", "url": "https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urolithiasis"}
• {"name": "Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG complete): Antibiotic, acute pyelonephritis; and Gastrointestinal/urological, renal colic (subscription)", "url": "https://www.tg.org.au"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Obstructed infected kidney from a ureteric stone

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Medical expulsive therapy is reasonable for an uncomplicated distal stone of 10 mm or less. It is contraindicated as the sole treatment when there is infection and obstruction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Shock wave lithotripsy in the presence of active infection and obstruction risks worsening sepsis, and does not give immediate drainage.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Waiting 48 hours with the kidney undrained risks septic shock, loss of the kidney and death. Antibiotics alone are inadequate when there is obstruction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Definitive stone treatment is not done during active sepsis because of the risk of urosepsis. A delay to an elective list also leaves the kidney undrained.

key_takeaways: A fever with an obstructing stone is an emergency: decompress the kidney urgently (stent or nephrostomy) along with antibiotics, and delay definitive stone treatment.

question_text:
A 67-year-old woman goes to a rural general practice in Mudgee, New South Wales, at 8 am. Since late last night she has had severe pain in her right eye with a right frontal headache, nausea and two episodes of vomiting. Before the pain started, she noticed coloured rings around the streetlights while driving home. She has always been long-sighted and wears reading glasses. Her medicines are amlodipine 5 mg daily, perindopril 4 mg daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily. Six days ago, she started oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for urge incontinence. She has no drug allergies and no history of asthma or chronic lung disease.

Her right visual acuity is 6/60 and her left is 6/9. The right eye is red with injection most marked around the limbus. The cornea is hazy, and the pupil is mid-dilated, oval and does not react to light. The globe feels firm to gentle palpation through the closed lid. When a penlight is shone from the side, the left anterior chamber appears shallow. The practice has a tonometer: right intraocular pressure is 58 mmHg and left is 18 mmHg. The nearest ophthalmologist is at a regional base hospital about three hours' drive away.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Dilate the right pupil with tropicamide to examine the optic disc, then decide on referral
Stop oxybutynin, give analgesia and an antiemetic, and review her in the practice tomorrow
Give intensive pilocarpine 2% drops to the right eye every 5 minutes as the sole treatment
Give topical prednisolone 1% drops and arrange routine ophthalmology outpatient review
Give acetazolamide, timolol and apraclonidine now, stop oxybutynin, and arrange same-day ophthalmology transfer
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Give acetazolamide, timolol and apraclonidine now, stop oxybutynin, and arrange same-day ophthalmology transfer

---

She has acute primary angle closure (acute angle-closure glaucoma): a painful red eye with halos, vomiting, reduced vision, a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated oval pupil and a very high IOP. The shallow anterior chamber in the other eye shows the anatomical predisposition. Hypermetropia and older age add to this, and the recently started anticholinergic (oxybutynin) is the likely trigger. This is sight-threatening, and lowering the IOP should start straight away, before and during transfer. RVEEH and NSW ACI guidance for non-ophthalmologists recommends: acetazolamide 500 mg (IV, or orally if she can keep it down), after checking for sulfonamide allergy and significant renal impairment; topical timolol 0.5% (check for asthma or COPD) and apraclonidine; pilocarpine 2% once the IOP starts to fall, because the ischaemic iris sphincter does not respond at very high pressure; lying supine; and analgesia and an antiemetic. Stop the precipitating drug. Refer urgently for same-day ophthalmology assessment and laser peripheral iridotomy. The fellow eye usually needs prophylactic iridotomy as well.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In acute angle closure, start IOP-lowering treatment immediately (acetazolamide, topical beta-blocker and alpha-agonist, then pilocarpine once pressure falls), stop any anticholinergic trigger, never dilate the pupil, and arrange same-day ophthalmology for laser iridotomy.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation. Eye Emergency Manual, 3rd edition (December 2023): acute angle closure glaucoma", "url": "https://aci.health.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0013/155011/ACI-Eye-Emergency-Manual.pdf"}
• {"name": "Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG complete): Eye, acute angle-closure glaucoma (subscription)", "url": "https://www.tg.org.au"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Stopping the precipitant is right but not enough. Waiting until tomorrow without lowering the pressure risks irreversible optic nerve damage within hours.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: At an IOP of 58 mmHg the iris sphincter is ischaemic and responds poorly to miotics. Pilocarpine is added once the pressure starts to fall, alongside aqueous suppressants, not used alone.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Topical steroids may be used by the ophthalmologist to reduce inflammation, but they do not lower the IOP. Routine outpatient review is unsafe for acute angle closure.

question_text:
A 29-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks and 2 days of gestation comes to the birth suite of a regional hospital in Toowoomba, Queensland, with six hours of frontal headache, flashing lights in her vision and epigastric discomfort. Her antenatal care has been uncomplicated, and her booking blood pressure was 112/70 mmHg.

On arrival her blood pressure was 172/114 mmHg, and 168/112 mmHg 15 minutes later. She was given oral immediate-release nifedipine, and 30 minutes later her blood pressure is 146/88 mmHg. Her pulse is 92/min, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Patellar reflexes are brisk, with three beats of ankle clonus. There is mild right upper quadrant tenderness. The cardiotocograph is normal.

Investigations:
- Urine protein:creatinine ratio 96 mg/mmol (<30)
- Platelets 92 × 10^9/L (150–400)
- ALT 118 U/L (<35)
- AST 140 U/L (<35)
- Creatinine 68 µmol/L (45–90)
- Haemoglobin 122 g/L (110–150)

The consultant obstetrician is present and plans to expedite birth once she is stabilised.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour infusion
Phenytoin 15 mg/kg IV loading dose for seizure prophylaxis
IV labetalol 20 mg bolus to lower blood pressure further
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart, before birth
Emergency caesarean section now, before any other treatment
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour infusion

---

She has pre-eclampsia with severe features: neurological symptoms and signs (headache, visual disturbance, hyperreflexia with clonus), liver involvement (epigastric/RUQ pain, transaminases above twice normal) and thrombocytopenia (partial HELLP picture). Her severe hypertension has been treated, and blood pressure is now within the target range (Queensland flowchart: sBP 130–150, dBP 80–90). The priority now is preventing eclampsia with magnesium sulfate, which is superior to phenytoin and diazepam: 4 g IV over 20 minutes via a controlled infusion device, then 1 g/hour, usually continued for 24 hours after birth. Monitor respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output (IDC), and have 10% calcium gluconate available as the antidote. Birth is the definitive treatment and follows maternal stabilisation.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In severe pre-eclampsia, control blood pressure, then give MgSO4 4 g IV over 20 min followed by 1 g/h (continued 24 h after birth). Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output, and keep calcium gluconate ready.

---

---

question_text:
A 44-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Hobart for the result of her cervical screening test. Eight years ago she had a kidney transplant for IgA nephropathy. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone 5 mg daily, and her graft function is stable. Her previous cervical screening test, three years ago, was clinician-collected, and oncogenic HPV was not detected. This time she chose to collect her own vaginal sample in the clinic.

The report states: 'Oncogenic HPV detected: HPV (not 16/18).'

She has no abnormal vaginal bleeding, postcoital bleeding or discharge. She is in a monogamous relationship and has two children.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Recall her for a clinician-collected cervical sample for liquid-based cytology
Repeat a self-collected HPV test in 12 months
Refer her directly for colposcopic assessment
Repeat an HPV test in 3 years on the immune-deficient screening schedule
Recall her in 6 weeks for a clinician-collected co-test (HPV and cytology)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Refer her directly for colposcopic assessment

---

A solid organ transplant recipient on immunosuppression counts as 'immune-deficient' under the National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines (2025). For immune-deficient participants, detection of ANY oncogenic HPV type, including HPV (not 16/18), means direct referral for colposcopic assessment (REC 7.15). If the sample was self-collected, LBC is taken at colposcopy, so she does not need a separate clinician-collected sample first. This differs from the general population, where HPV (not 16/18) on a self-collected sample means returning (ideally within 6 weeks) for a clinician-collected sample for reflex LBC, which then decides the risk category.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Immune-deficient people (e.g. transplant recipients, people living with HIV) screen 3-yearly. ANY oncogenic HPV detected, including on self-collection, means direct referral for colposcopy.

---

question_text:
A 3-year-old girl is admitted to the paediatric ward of a Melbourne hospital on the eighth day of fever (up to 39.8°C). Her general practitioner diagnosed a viral illness four days ago. Her parents describe her as the most irritable they have ever seen her. For the past five days her eyes have been red without discharge, and she has had a blotchy red rash on her trunk. She is fully immunised.

She is miserable but well perfused. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse 150/min, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg and respiratory rate 28/min. She has bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection that spares the limbus, red cracked lips and a polymorphous macular rash on her trunk. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy, and her hands and feet are normal. Heart sounds are normal with no murmur. There is no hepatosplenomegaly or meningism.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 98 g/L (105–135)
- White cell count 17.4 × 10^9/L (5.0–15.0)
- Platelets 552 × 10^9/L (150–450)
- C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (<5)
- ESR 74 mm/h (<20)
- Albumin 27 g/L (35–50)
- ALT 86 U/L (<30)
- Urine microscopy: 25 white cells/high-power field, culture negative
- Throat swab: no group A streptococcus. Respiratory PCR: rhinovirus detected. Blood culture: no growth at 48 hours.

The first available echocardiogram is tomorrow afternoon.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Await the echocardiogram before deciding whether to give IVIG
Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily alone, then echocardiography
High-dose aspirin 80–100 mg/kg/day alone until the fever settles
IV ceftriaxone for presumed occult bacterial infection, and review in 48 hours
IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin 5 mg/kg daily, started today
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin 5 mg/kg daily, started today

---

She has had fever for 4 days or more with only 3 of the 5 principal features (conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes, rash), so this is suspected INCOMPLETE Kawasaki disease. Under the AHA algorithm adopted by the RCH guideline, CRP of 30 mg/L or more and/or ESR of 40 mm/h or more with 3 or more supplementary laboratory criteria justifies treatment even before echocardiography. The supplementary criteria are anaemia for age, platelets of 450 or more after day 7, albumin of 30 g/L or less, raised ALT, WCC of 15 or more, and urine with 10 or more white cells/hpf. She meets all six. The RCH guideline states that the availability of an echo should not delay treatment. First-line therapy is IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 8–12 hours plus aspirin 5 mg/kg once daily, continued until cardiology review at about 6 weeks. Treatment within 10 days of fever onset reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysm. A positive respiratory virus PCR does not exclude KD: about one-third of children with KD have one.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In incomplete KD, CRP of 30 or more / ESR of 40 or more plus 3 or more supplementary laboratory criteria means giving IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin now. Do not wait for the echo, and a positive viral PCR does not exclude KD.

---

REFERENCES

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Corticosteroids are an ADD-ON (primary intensification) for children at high risk of coronary aneurysm or with IVIG resistance. They do not replace IVIG.

question_text:
An 8-year-old Aboriginal boy is brought to his community health clinic in Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, by his grandmother, who is one of his main carers. For three days his eyes have been puffy in the mornings and his urine has been 'dark like tea'. He also has a headache. Three weeks ago the clinic's Aboriginal Health Practitioner treated him for infected skin sores on both legs and scabies as part of the community's skin health program. He has not had a sore throat. There is no rash, joint pain or abdominal pain.

His blood pressure is 132/90 mmHg (above the 95th centile for his age and height). He has periorbital and ankle oedema and healing crusted lesions on both shins. There is no purpura. The rest of the examination is normal.

Urine dipstick: blood 3+, protein 2+. Microscopy at the regional laboratory shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts.

Blood results (from Royal Darwin Hospital):
- Creatinine 74 µmol/L (25–60)
- Albumin 33 g/L (35–50)
- C3 0.21 g/L (0.75–1.65)
- C4 0.24 g/L (0.14–0.54)
- Antistreptolysin O titre 150 IU/mL (<200)
- Anti-DNase B titre 1,150 U/mL (<240)
- Antinuclear antibody: negative

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: IgA nephropathy
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Lupus nephritis
IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura) nephritis
Minimal change disease
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

---

He has nephritic syndrome: haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, oedema and a mild rise in creatinine. It began about 3 weeks after group A streptococcal skin infection, which fits the typical 3–6 week latent period after impetigo (1–3 weeks after pharyngitis). Low C3 with normal C4 reflects alternative pathway activation, which is characteristic. A normal ASOT does NOT argue against the diagnosis: ASOT often does not rise after skin (as opposed to throat) infection, and anti-DNase B is the more useful marker here. In the NT most APSGN follows skin sores. The higher burden in some remote communities is driven by structural factors such as household crowding and limited access to working health hardware (washing facilities), not by individual or family behaviour. Management: supportive care (fluid and salt restriction, a loop diuretic for oedema or hypertension), benzathine benzylpenicillin for infected sores, public health notification with screening of household contacts, and follow-up C3/C4 at about 12 weeks to confirm normalisation. Plan care together with his grandmother and family and the Aboriginal Health Practitioner, who can support household skin checks and follow-up.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Nephritic syndrome 3–6 weeks after skin sores, with low C3 and normal C4, is APSGN. Anti-DNase B is more sensitive than ASOT after skin infection.

---

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Lupus nephritis typically lowers BOTH C3 and C4 and is ANA-positive. It is rare at this age.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: IgA vasculitis nephritis comes with palpable purpura (buttocks and legs), joint and abdominal pain, and normal complement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, albumin usually below 25 g/L, oedema) without red cell casts or hypertension, and complement is normal.

question_text:
You are the junior doctor on the postnatal ward of a hospital in Wollongong, New South Wales. A midwife asks you to review a boy who is 16 hours old. He was born at 39 weeks and 1 day by normal vaginal birth, weighing 3,420 g, with Apgar scores of 9 and 9. His mother is 27 years old, and this is her second baby. Her blood group is O RhD-positive and her antenatal red cell antibody screen was negative. Her first child needed phototherapy on the first day of life.

He is breastfeeding every 2–3 hours and has had two wet nappies and passed meconium. He is alert and pink, with a temperature of 36.9°C. The midwife has noticed yellow skin on his face and upper chest. There is no cephalhaematoma or bruising. The rest of the examination is normal. A transcutaneous bilirubin meter reads 128 µmol/L, which is below the phototherapy line for his age on the nomogram.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the transcutaneous bilirubin in 6 hours and plot the trend
Start phototherapy now and repeat the transcutaneous bilirubin in 6 hours
Encourage more frequent breastfeeds and review at 24 hours of age
Urgent total serum bilirubin with FBC, blood group and direct antiglobulin test
Conjugated bilirubin, liver function tests and abdominal ultrasound
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Urgent total serum bilirubin with FBC, blood group and direct antiglobulin test

---

Jaundice visible within the first 24 hours of life is pathological until proven otherwise, most often because of haemolysis. Here ABO incompatibility is likely: the mother is group O and her previous baby needed phototherapy on day 1. Queensland Clinical Guidelines (and other Australian neonatal guidelines) call for urgent measurement of total serum bilirubin (with conjugated and unconjugated fractions), plus FBC, the baby's blood group and a direct antiglobulin test (DAT), with escalation to the medical team. Transcutaneous bilirubin is intended for babies over 24 hours old and 35 weeks or more gestation. It should not be relied on in the first 24 hours, when bilirubin may be rising quickly. Treatment decisions are based on the serum level plotted on the gestation-specific nomogram and on the rate of rise.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Visible jaundice under 24 hours of age means urgent serum bilirubin plus FBC, blood group and DAT. Do not rely on a transcutaneous reading at this age.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Queensland Clinical Guidelines. Neonatal jaundice (guideline MN25.7)", "url": "https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/142038/g-jaundice.pdf"}
• {"name": "Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Jaundice in early infancy", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Jaundice_in_early_infancy/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: TcB is not recommended as the basis for decisions under 24 hours of age. Haemolytic jaundice can rise quickly, so waiting 6 hours for another estimate could miss a need for urgent treatment.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Phototherapy may well be needed, but without a serum bilirubin, DAT and FBC you cannot find the cause, set the threshold or assess the risk of exchange transfusion. TcB is also unreliable in the first 24 hours and once phototherapy has started.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Increasing feeds suits physiological or breastfeeding-related jaundice after 24 hours. Jaundice in the first 24 hours needs urgent investigation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This is the work-up for conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (e.g. biliary atresia), which is suspected in prolonged jaundice (beyond 14 days) or with pale stools and dark urine. The conjugated fraction is part of the urgent TSB request, but LFTs and imaging do not look for haemolysis, the likely problem here.

key_takeaways: Visible jaundice under 24 hours of age means urgent serum bilirubin plus FBC, blood group and DAT. Do not rely on a transcutaneous reading at this age.

question_text:
A 44-year-old woman is on the orthopaedic ward of a Perth hospital, 40 hours after open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture under general anaesthesia. The operation and anaesthetic were uneventful. She has major depressive disorder, well controlled for three years on sertraline 150 mg daily, which she has continued. Since surgery she has been charted tramadol 100 mg orally 6-hourly and ondansetron 4 mg as needed (four doses given), and she received a single dose of metoclopramide 10 mg yesterday. She drinks about two standard drinks a week.

Over the past six hours she has become restless, anxious and tremulous. She is sweating heavily and has had three episodes of diarrhoea. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse 122/min, blood pressure 162/94 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. She is alert and oriented. Her pupils are dilated and reactive, and her skin is flushed and moist. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. She has a coarse tremor and generalised hyperreflexia, more marked in the legs, with sustained inducible ankle clonus on both sides and intermittent horizontal ocular clonus. Tone is increased in the legs but normal in the arms. Creatine kinase is 380 U/L (<200).

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Serotonin toxicity
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Anticholinergic toxicity
Alcohol withdrawal syndrome
Malignant hyperthermia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Serotonin toxicity

---

She meets the Hunter serotonin toxicity criteria: she is taking serotonergic drugs (sertraline plus tramadol, and ondansetron to a lesser extent) and has inducible clonus with agitation and diaphoresis, ocular clonus, and tremor with hyperreflexia. Neuromuscular excitation worse in the lower limbs, rapid onset over hours, mydriasis, diarrhoea, hyperactive bowel sounds and autonomic instability all fit. Tramadol inhibits serotonin reuptake and is a common trigger when combined with an SSRI. Management: stop all serotonergic drugs (tramadol, ondansetron; review sertraline), give supportive care and benzodiazepines for agitation and neuromuscular hyperactivity, and use non-serotonergic analgesia. Consider cyproheptadine in moderate toxicity. Severe toxicity (temperature above 38.5°C with rising rigidity) needs ICU for cooling, sedation and paralysis.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Clonus (inducible, spontaneous or ocular) with hyperreflexia after adding a serotonergic drug such as tramadol to an SSRI is serotonin toxicity (Hunter criteria). NMS is slow, rigid and hyporeflexic.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Isbister GK, Buckley NA, Whyte IM. Serotonin toxicity: a practical approach to diagnosis and treatment. Med J Aust 2007;187(6):361\u20135", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2007/187/6/serotonin-toxicity-practical-approach-diagnosis-and-treatment"}
• {"name": "Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG complete): Toxicology and Toxinology, serotonin toxicity (subscription)", "url": "https://www.tg.org.au"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Serotonin toxicity from tramadol with an SSRI

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The single metoclopramide dose is a tempting clue, but NMS develops over days, with bradykinesia, generalised 'lead-pipe' rigidity, REDUCED reflexes, no clonus, and often a much higher CK and altered consciousness.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Anticholinergic toxicity gives DRY, hot skin, urinary retention, reduced bowel sounds and delirium, without clonus. She is sweating, has diarrhoea and has clonus.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Her alcohol intake is minimal, and withdrawal would not explain inducible and ocular clonus. Tremor, sweating and tachycardia overlap, but the neuromuscular findings point to serotonin excess.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Malignant hyperthermia happens during or soon after exposure to volatile agents or suxamethonium, with rigidity, hypercarbia and rapidly rising temperature. It does not start 40 hours after an uneventful anaesthetic with clonus.

key_takeaways: Clonus (inducible, spontaneous or ocular) with hyperreflexia after adding a serotonergic drug such as tramadol to an SSRI is serotonin toxicity (Hunter criteria). NMS is slow, rigid and hyporeflexic.

question_text:
A 27-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is an inpatient in an acute mental health unit in Brisbane. He is on day 18 of clozapine titration and currently takes 200 mg daily. His baseline ECG, troponin and C-reactive protein were normal, as were his weekly full blood counts and the week 1 and week 2 troponin and CRP. His resting pulse has been 95–100/min since the dose was increased.

This morning he says he feels 'like I've got the flu', with aching muscles, tiredness and a vague central chest discomfort. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse 126/min, blood pressure 104/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He is alert and oriented, with no rigidity or tremor. Heart sounds are normal, the chest is clear and the throat is not inflamed. A full blood count taken this morning shows a white cell count of 9.8 × 10^9/L and neutrophils of 6.4 × 10^9/L.

Which one of the following investigations is the most important to obtain now?
options: Plasma clozapine concentration
Respiratory virus PCR swab
Troponin and C-reactive protein
Serum creatine kinase level
Chest X-ray (PA and lateral)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Troponin and C-reactive protein

---

Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically appears between days 14 and 21 of treatment. The prodrome is non-specific and flu-like, with fever, a rise in heart rate above the patient's clozapine baseline, malaise, chest discomfort and breathlessness. The Queensland Health guideline for clozapine in mental health services (QH-GDL-437), which follows the Ronaldson protocol, requires baseline troponin and CRP, then weekly troponin and CRP for the first month (with ECG in weeks 1–4). Symptoms such as fever, chest pain, effort intolerance or a heart rate above 120/min (or 30/min above the patient's usual rate) prompt urgent testing and medical review. A troponin more than twice the upper limit of normal or a CRP above 100 mg/L means withholding clozapine and arranging urgent cardiology review and echocardiography. Smaller rises lead to daily repeat testing. His neutrophil count is normal today, so agranulocytosis is already excluded as the cause of the fever. That leaves myocarditis as the life-threatening diagnosis to exclude immediately.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Fever, tachycardia and flu-like symptoms 2–3 weeks into clozapine treatment mean checking troponin and CRP to exclude myocarditis. Withhold clozapine and get urgent cardiology review if troponin is more than twice the ULN or CRP is above 100 mg/L.

---

---

question_text:
A 44-year-old man attends his general practitioner in Canberra to ask about bowel cancer screening. His mother was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 57. She was treated with surgery and is well six years later. Her tumour showed normal (proficient) mismatch repair protein expression. No other first- or second-degree relatives on either side of the family have had bowel, endometrial or other cancers.

He has no rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, abdominal pain or weight loss. He has no personal history of polyps or inflammatory bowel disease. Examination is normal, and a recent full blood count and iron studies were normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate screening recommendation for him?
options: Immunochemical FOBT every two years from age 45 through the NBCSP
Colonoscopy every five years, starting at age 47
Colonoscopy now, then every five years
Colonoscopy every five years, starting at age 50
Referral for germline genetic testing for Lynch syndrome
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Colonoscopy every five years, starting at age 47

---

The 2023 NHMRC-approved Clinical practice guidelines for the prevention, early detection and management of colorectal cancer (family history chapter) moved the cut-off from 55 to 60 years. One first-degree relative diagnosed BEFORE age 60 now places a person in Category 2 (moderately increased risk, at least 2–4 times average). For Category 2 the guideline recommends offering colonoscopy every five years, starting 10 years younger than the earliest age of diagnosis in a first-degree relative or at age 50, whichever is EARLIER, until age 74. 57 − 10 = 47, which is earlier than 50, so colonoscopy starts at 47. Low-dose aspirin (100 mg daily) should also be considered from age 45 to 70 after discussing benefits and harms.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Under the 2023 Australian guideline, one first-degree relative diagnosed with CRC before 60 is Category 2: colonoscopy 5-yearly from 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis, or from 50 if that is earlier.

---

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Starting at 44 has no basis in the guideline. The start age is 10 years before the relative's diagnosis (47), or 50 if that is earlier.

His mother's tumour was mismatch repair proficient, and a single relative diagnosed at 57 does not meet criteria.

question_text:
A 36-year-old emergency physician sees her general practitioner in Melbourne. For three months she has had low mood, poor sleep, reduced enjoyment and difficulty concentrating after a relationship breakdown. She has had no suicidal thoughts and does not use alcohol or other drugs to excess. Her PHQ-9 score is 16. Two weeks ago, on her own initiative, she arranged four weeks of leave because she felt she was 'not at her best'. No clinical errors or complaints have been raised, and she describes no near-misses.

She is keen to start treatment. She agrees to a mental health treatment plan, psychology sessions and sertraline, and to review with the GP every two weeks. She says she will not return to work until she and her GP agree she is well enough. She has also contacted the Victorian Doctors' Health Program. She asks whether the GP is obliged to report her to Ahpra.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate response?
options: Make a mandatory notification to Ahpra because she has a mental illness that affects concentration
Advise her to self-notify the Medical Board before starting treatment
Contact her hospital's director of medical services to arrange supervised practice
Make a voluntary notification to Ahpra as a precaution while treatment starts
Continue treatment and document the risk assessment; no notification is needed now
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Continue treatment and document the risk assessment; no notification is needed now

---

Under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law (as amended in 2020) and Ahpra's mandatory notification guidelines, a TREATING practitioner must notify impairment only if they reasonably believe the practitioner-patient is placing the public at SUBSTANTIAL risk of harm. This is a deliberately high threshold, so that health practitioners seek care. The relevant factors are the nature and severity of the impairment, the patient's insight and willingness to engage with treatment, the steps already taken to limit risk (here, voluntary leave and a return-to-work plan agreed with the GP), and the effectiveness of treatment. She has moderate depression, good insight, has removed herself from practice and is fully engaged with care, so the threshold is not met. The GP should keep her confidentiality, document the risk assessment, review regularly and reconsider if the risk changes (e.g. she returns to work while impaired or disengages from treatment).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
A treating practitioner notifies Ahpra about a doctor-patient's impairment only if there is a reasonable belief of SUBSTANTIAL risk of harm to the public. Insight, treatment and voluntary leave lower that risk.

---

question_text:
A 31-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy sees her general practitioner in western Sydney. The local public health unit rang her this morning: four days (about 96 hours) ago she sat in an emergency department waiting room at the same time as a person with confirmed infectious measles. She was born in 1995 overseas and has no vaccination records. Her parents think she 'had all her needles'. Her antenatal bloods at 9 weeks showed she was rubella IgG-positive, hepatitis B surface antigen-negative, HIV-negative and syphilis-negative. Measles serology was not done. She is well, with no fever, cough, conjunctivitis or rash. She weighs 62 kg and is not immunocompromised. The public health unit is available to advise.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Give MMR vaccine today
Reassure her that rubella immunity implies measles immunity
Advise no prophylaxis, as more than 72 hours have passed
Urgent measles IgG, then NHIG 0.2 mL/kg IM if non-immune
NHIG 0.5 mL/kg IM today without checking serology
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Urgent measles IgG, then NHIG 0.2 mL/kg IM if non-immune

---

She has no documented evidence of measles immunity (no records of two MMR doses and no measles serology), and she was born after 1966. The Australian Immunisation Handbook (adapted from the CDNA measles guidelines) says that a susceptible pregnant contact should have measles IgG checked if time allows, and normal human immunoglobulin (NHIG) 0.2 mL/kg IM (maximum 15 mL) if not immune, within 6 days (144 hours) of exposure, in consultation with the public health unit. At 96 hours there is still time for an urgent IgG result before giving NHIG (62 kg × 0.2 = 12.4 mL). MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy. She should also avoid contact with other susceptible or vulnerable people and seek care (phoning ahead) if symptoms develop during the incubation period. MMR should be given after birth, and at least 5 months after NHIG.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Measles PEP: MMR within 72 h for non-pregnant, non-immune contacts. For pregnant non-immune contacts, give NHIG 0.2 mL/kg IM (max 15 mL) within 144 h, checking IgG first if time allows.

---

question_text:
A 64-year-old man is brought by ambulance to the emergency department of a regional hospital in Toowoomba, Queensland, with 90 minutes of central crushing chest pain and sweating. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. The paramedics gave aspirin 300 mg orally and one 400 microgram spray of sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 15 minutes ago. Soon after the spray he became light-headed and nauseated.

His pulse is 56/min and regular, blood pressure 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. He is pale and clammy but alert. The jugular venous pressure is raised at 6 cm above the sternal angle, the chest is clear to auscultation and there is no peripheral oedema.

The 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with 3 mm ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF (greater in III than II) and ST depression in I and aVL. A right-sided lead V4R shows 1.5 mm ST elevation. The on-site cardiac catheterisation laboratory has been activated for primary percutaneous coronary intervention and the team will be ready in 20 minutes.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate management of his hypotension?
options: Furosemide 40 mg intravenously to relieve congestion
Sodium chloride 0.9% 250 mL IV bolus, repeated if needed
Glyceryl trinitrate IV infusion at 5 micrograms/min
Metoprolol 5 mg intravenously over 2 minutes
Morphine 2.5 mg intravenously for pain and anxiety
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Sodium chloride 0.9% 250 mL IV bolus, repeated if needed

---

This is an inferior STEMI with right ventricular (RV) involvement. ST elevation greater in III than II, reciprocal change in I/aVL and ST elevation of 1 mm or more in V4R point to a proximal right coronary artery occlusion. The triad of hypotension, raised JVP and clear lung fields, made worse by a nitrate, is typical of RV infarction. The ischaemic RV depends on preload, so venodilators (nitrates, morphine) and diuretics can cause profound hypotension. While reperfusion by primary PCI is arranged, the immediate treatment is cautious IV crystalloid in small boluses (for example 250 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride), reassessing blood pressure, JVP and lungs after each bolus. If he stays hypotensive after adequate filling, inotropes are the next step. Bradycardia or heart block, common with inferior infarcts, may need atropine or pacing. Nitrates should be withheld.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In inferior STEMI, record V4R. Hypotension with a raised JVP and clear lungs means RV infarction: give cautious fluid boluses, avoid nitrates, morphine and diuretics, and reperfuse urgently.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NHFA/CSANZ Comprehensive Australian Clinical Guideline for Diagnosing and Managing Acute Coronary Syndromes 2025 (Heart Foundation)", "url": "https://www.heartfoundation.org.au/for-professionals/acs-guideline"}
• {"name": "2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes (European Heart Journal)", "url": "https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/44/38/3720/7243210"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Inferior STEMI with right ventricular infarction: hypotension after nitrate

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A raised JVP can tempt a clinician to diurese, but the lungs are clear. The JVP is high because the RV is failing, not because of fluid overload. A diuretic cuts preload further and will worsen the shock.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Nitrates are relatively contraindicated in RV infarction and in hypotension (systolic below 90 mmHg). The sublingual dose has probably already caused this deterioration.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Beta-blockers are avoided in the acute phase when there is hypotension, bradycardia or signs of low cardiac output. His pulse is 56/min and he is shocked.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Opioids venodilate and can drop blood pressure further in a preload-dependent patient. Analgesia matters, but it is not the treatment for his hypotension and would be given very cautiously, if at all, until the pressure improves.

key_takeaways: In inferior STEMI, record V4R. Hypotension with a raised JVP and clear lungs means RV infarction: give cautious fluid boluses, avoid nitrates, morphine and diuretics, and reperfuse urgently.

question_text:
A 67-year-old woman attends the heart failure clinic at a Hobart hospital. Eight months ago she was diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy. Her left ventricular ejection fraction on repeat echocardiography last week was 30%. She becomes breathless after walking about 200 m on the flat (NYHA class II–III) and has had no hospital admissions in the past 6 months.

Her medicines are perindopril 10 mg each morning at 0800 hours, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily and furosemide 20 mg daily. She has no history of angioedema. Her pulse is 64/min and regular, and blood pressure 118/70 mmHg. There is no peripheral oedema and the chest is clear.

Investigations:
- Sodium 138 mmol/L (135–145)
- Potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Creatinine 88 µmol/L (45–90)
- eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73 m²

The cardiologist decides to replace perindopril with sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily. She took her perindopril at 0800 hours today, and the clinic appointment is at 1100 hours.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate instruction for starting sacubitril/valsartan?
options: Stop perindopril now and take the first dose at 2000 hours tonight
Stop perindopril now and take the first dose at 0800 hours tomorrow
Halve perindopril to 5 mg daily and take both medicines together for 2 weeks
Stop perindopril now and take the first dose at 2000 hours tomorrow
Swap perindopril for candesartan for 4 weeks, then start the new medicine
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Stop perindopril now and take the first dose at 2000 hours tomorrow

---

Sacubitril/valsartan (an angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor, ARNI) is recommended in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB in patients with HFrEF who remain symptomatic on an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) and a beta-blocker. It lowers mortality and heart failure hospitalisation. Because combined ACE and neprilysin inhibition greatly increases the risk of angioedema, the Australian product information contraindicates co-administration and requires at least 36 hours between the last ACE inhibitor dose and the first sacubitril/valsartan dose. Her last perindopril was at 0800 today, so the earliest safe first dose is 2000 hours tomorrow (36 hours later). She should continue bisoprolol, spironolactone, dapagliflozin and furosemide. Check potassium, renal function and blood pressure 1–2 weeks after starting and after each up-titration.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
ACE inhibitor to sacubitril/valsartan: stop the ACE inhibitor and wait at least 36 hours before the first ARNI dose. No washout is needed when switching from an ARB.

---

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This is 24 hours after the last perindopril dose, still inside the 36-hour washout.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: ACE inhibitors and sacubitril/valsartan must not be taken together at any dose, because the combination increases the risk of angioedema.

question_text:
A 19-year-old Aboriginal man from a remote community in the Kimberley, Western Australia, is flown to Broome Hospital with five days of a painful, swollen right knee. For the past two days he has also felt hot and unwell. He remembers a sore throat about three weeks ago and has had infected skin sores on his legs this year. He has no known history of acute rheumatic fever and is not on any regular medicines. He has not injured the knee and has no urethral discharge. An Aboriginal Liaison Officer is present, at his request.

His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse 104/min and blood pressure 122/70 mmHg. The right knee is warm and swollen with a moderate effusion and painful restriction of movement. No other joint is swollen or tender. There is no rash, no subcutaneous nodules and no abnormal movements. Heart sounds are normal with no murmur.

Investigations:
- Knee aspirate: turbid; white cells 16 × 10^9/L, mostly neutrophils; Gram stain negative; no crystals; culture negative at 48 hours
- C-reactive protein 72 mg/L (<5)
- ESR 58 mm/h (<15)
- Anti-streptolysin O titre 820 IU/mL (reference upper limit 200) and anti-DNase B raised
- ECG: sinus rhythm, PR interval 240 ms
- Echocardiogram (performed by an experienced sonographer and reviewed by a cardiologist): structurally normal heart, no pathological regurgitation

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these findings?
options: Definite acute rheumatic fever, first episode
Probable acute rheumatic fever, as there is a single major manifestation
Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis, not acute rheumatic fever
Culture-negative septic arthritis until proven otherwise
Possible acute rheumatic fever, as monoarthritis counts as a minor manifestation
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Definite acute rheumatic fever, first episode

---

He belongs to a high-risk population: Aboriginal people living in rural or remote Australia. The Australian criteria (2020 guideline, retained in the 2025 third edition) use a different set of criteria for high-risk groups. In high-risk groups, aseptic monoarthritis is a MAJOR manifestation. The minor manifestations for high-risk groups include fever of 38°C or higher, ESR of 30 mm/h or more (or CRP of 30 mg/L or more), and a prolonged PR interval for age (when carditis is not already counted as major). An initial episode of ARF needs evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection plus either two major manifestations, or one major and two minor. He has one major (aseptic monoarthritis), three minor (fever 38.3°C, raised ESR/CRP, PR 240 ms) and raised streptococcal serology. That meets the criteria for definite ARF. Management includes notification (ARF is notifiable in WA), registration with the jurisdictional RHD control program, benzathine benzylpenicillin G secondary prophylaxis, NSAIDs for the arthritis once the diagnosis is secure, and repeat echocardiography. This should be done in partnership with the patient, his family and Aboriginal health staff.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In high-risk Australian populations, aseptic monoarthritis is a major ARF criterion, and fever of 38°C or more, ESR/CRP of 30 or more and a prolonged PR interval are minor criteria. One major plus two minor with streptococcal evidence equals definite ARF.

---
