The 2020 Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease (MJA 2021)", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2021/214/5/2020-australian-guideline-prevention-diagnosis-and-management-acute-rheumatic"}
• {"name": "RHDAustralia/CSANZ: Australian ARF/RHD Guideline, 3rd edition (2025)", "url": "https://www.csanz.edu.au/Common/Uploaded%20files/Smart%20Suite/Smart%20Library/862f5626-c013-4299-bf8b-dae2d8c7f554/Australian-ARF-RHD-Guideline-2025.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Acute rheumatic fever in a high-risk population: applying the Australian criteria

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 'Probable ARF' is used when the criteria are not quite met (one minor manifestation short or no streptococcal evidence) but ARF is still the most likely diagnosis. He meets the full criteria, so 'probable' under-calls the diagnosis and may lead to less certain follow-up.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis is a diagnosis to be very cautious about in high-risk Australian populations. The guideline advises that people in high-risk groups who meet the ARF criteria be diagnosed and managed as ARF, because missing ARF risks progressive rheumatic heart disease.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Septic arthritis must be considered in any acute monoarthritis, and it was appropriately excluded by aspiration (Gram stain and culture negative). With strong streptococcal serology and supporting criteria, ARF is the unifying diagnosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Monoarthritis is a MINOR manifestation only in low-risk populations. In high-risk populations it is a MAJOR manifestation, and monoarthralgia (pain without swelling) is the minor one.

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Wollongong, New South Wales, for a cardiovascular risk assessment. She has chronic kidney disease secondary to childhood reflux nephropathy and is followed by a nephrologist. She does not have diabetes, has never smoked and does not identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. There is no family history of premature cardiovascular disease and she has no history of atrial fibrillation. Her only medicine is irbesartan 150 mg daily.

Her blood pressure is 134/80 mmHg and her body mass index 26 kg/m².

Investigations:
- eGFR 43 mL/min/1.73 m² (five months ago: 41 mL/min/1.73 m²)
- Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 2.8 mg/mmol (<3.5 in women)
- Total cholesterol 5.6 mmol/L; HDL cholesterol 1.4 mmol/L; LDL cholesterol 3.5 mmol/L
- HbA1c 5.4% (36 mmol/mol)

The practice nurse has entered her details into the online Australian CVD risk calculator, which reports a 5-year cardiovascular risk of 3%.

Which one of the following best describes her cardiovascular risk?
options: Low risk, based on the calculated 5-year risk of 3%
Intermediate risk, after reclassifying upward for reduced eGFR
Unable to be classified until the urine albumin is repeated twice
Intermediate risk, because age over 55 with CKD adds 5%
High risk, clinically determined without using the calculator
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. High risk, clinically determined without using the calculator

---

The 2023 Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk starts by identifying people at CLINICALLY DETERMINED high risk. For them the calculator is not used. Only two conditions now qualify: moderate-to-severe CKD and familial hypercholesterolaemia. Moderate-to-severe CKD is defined as a sustained eGFR below 45 mL/min/1.73 m², or a persistent uACR above 25 mg/mmol in men or above 35 mg/mmol in women. Her eGFR has been below 45 on two occasions more than 3 months apart, so she is automatically high risk (equivalent to 10% or more over 5 years). The calculator result of 3% is invalid for her. High risk means she should be offered lipid-lowering therapy (a statin) alongside her renin–angiotensin blockade and lifestyle advice, unless contraindicated or declined after shared decision-making.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
2023 Australian CVD risk guideline: sustained eGFR below 45, or uACR above 25 (men) / above 35 (women) mg/mmol, or familial hypercholesterolaemia means clinically determined high risk. Do not use the calculator for these people.

---

---

question_text:
A 27-year-old man sees a general practitioner in Canberra for a repeat prescription of salbutamol. He has had asthma since childhood. Over the past three months he has used salbutamol 2–3 times a week for wheeze and chest tightness, mostly when cycling in cold weather or during pollen season. He wakes with asthma symptoms about once a month. He has not needed oral corticosteroids or emergency care in the past two years. Two years ago he was prescribed a daily inhaled corticosteroid preventer, but he stopped it after a few weeks because he felt well and kept forgetting it. He says he is unlikely to take any inhaler every day.

He does not smoke or vape. His inhaler technique is good. Examination is normal. Spirometry today shows FEV1 88% predicted with a 9% (230 mL) improvement after bronchodilator.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
options: Continue salbutamol as needed and add montelukast 10 mg nightly
Continue salbutamol as needed with no additional treatment
Replace salbutamol with budesonide/formoterol 200/6 microg, 1 inhalation as needed
Budesonide/formoterol 200/6 microg, 2 inhalations twice daily plus as needed
Fluticasone propionate 100 microg twice daily plus salbutamol as needed
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Replace salbutamol with budesonide/formoterol 200/6 microg, 1 inhalation as needed

---

He has mild asthma: symptoms less than daily, night waking less than weekly and no recent flare-ups, but he still needs a treatment that reduces flare-up risk. The Australian Asthma Handbook no longer recommends SABA-only treatment for adults and adolescents, because relying on SABA alone increases the risk of severe flare-ups and asthma death. For adults and adolescents with mild asthma, as-needed low-dose budesonide–formoterol (anti-inflammatory reliever, 'AIR-only') is a preferred option. It is as effective as a daily ICS for preventing severe flare-ups and much better than SABA alone. It suits people who will not use a daily preventer. He takes 1 inhalation of 200/6 microg whenever he has symptoms, with no more than 6 inhalations on one occasion and up to 12 in a day. His written asthma action plan should be updated and he should be reviewed in 1–3 months.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Adults with mild asthma should not be on SABA alone. As-needed budesonide–formoterol 200/6 (1 inhalation per dose, maximum 12 per day) is a preferred option, especially when daily preventer use is unlikely.

---

question_text:
A 76-year-old man is admitted to a Perth hospital with worsening breathlessness. He has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 25%) from ischaemic heart disease. For the first three days he received intravenous furosemide 80 mg twice daily and lost 4 kg. His orthopnoea and leg oedema have improved, but a chest X-ray still shows a moderate right pleural effusion and a small left effusion. He has no fever, cough, weight loss or chest pain, and he stopped smoking 20 years ago. A diagnostic pleural aspiration is done on day 4.

Investigations (day 4):
- Serum total protein 64 g/L; pleural fluid protein 33 g/L (ratio 0.52)
- Serum LDH 210 U/L (laboratory upper limit 250); pleural fluid LDH 115 U/L (ratio 0.55)
- Serum albumin 31 g/L; pleural fluid albumin 16 g/L
- Pleural fluid: straw-coloured; pH 7.46; glucose 6.8 mmol/L; white cells 0.6 × 10^9/L (80% lymphocytes); Gram stain negative
- NT-proBNP 6800 ng/L (on admission 11 200 ng/L)
- Pleural fluid cytology: pending

Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for his pleural effusion?
options: Transudate from heart failure, altered by diuresis
Uncomplicated parapneumonic exudate
Malignant pleural effusion from occult lung cancer
Tuberculous pleuritis with lymphocytic exudate
Exudate caused by pulmonary embolism
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Transudate from heart failure, altered by diuresis

---

By Light's criteria this fluid is only just an exudate. The protein ratio is 0.52 (above 0.5). The LDH ratio is 0.55 (below 0.6), and pleural LDH of 115 U/L is below two-thirds of the serum upper limit (about 167 U/L). So only one criterion is met, and only barely. Light's criteria are sensitive for exudates but misclassify about a quarter of transudates as exudates, especially after diuretics, which concentrate pleural protein. In this situation the serum-to-pleural albumin gradient helps. A gradient above 12 g/L suggests a transudate; here it is 31 − 16 = 15 g/L. (A serum-to-pleural protein gradient above 31 g/L is an alternative test; here it is exactly 31, which is borderline.) Together with bilateral effusions, a high NT-proBNP, lymphocyte-predominant low-cell fluid, normal pH and glucose, and recent intensive diuresis, this is a heart-failure transudate mislabelled as an exudate. Management is to optimise heart failure treatment. Cytology results should still be followed up.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Diuretics can make a heart-failure transudate meet Light's criteria. If the fluid is only borderline exudative in a diuresed patient, a serum-to-pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L supports a transudate.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Light RW et al. Pleural effusions: the diagnostic separation of transudates and exudates (Ann Intern Med 1972), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/4642731/"}
• {"name": "British Thoracic Society Guideline for pleural disease 2023 (Thorax)", "url": "https://thorax.bmj.com/content/78/Suppl_3/s1"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A parapneumonic effusion would usually come with fever, cough and consolidation, and the fluid would be neutrophil-predominant. He has none of these features, and the pH and glucose are normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Malignancy has to be considered in any unexplained exudate in an ex-smoker, and the cytology will be followed up. However, the albumin gradient shows a transudate, and bilateral effusions with a very high NT-proBNP fit heart failure better.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: TB effusions are lymphocytic exudates, usually with a clearly high protein and high adenosine deaminase, often with fever and weight loss. The fluid here is only borderline exudative and the gradient points to a transudate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: PE-related effusions are usually small, unilateral and often bloodstained, with pleuritic pain or hypoxaemia. Nothing here points to PE.

question_text:
A 62-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Geelong, Victoria, because of breathlessness that has slowly worsened over 18 months. She now becomes breathless climbing one flight of stairs, and she has a cough with white sputum most mornings. She has smoked 20 cigarettes a day since she was 18 (about 44 pack-years). She had no asthma or hay fever as a child and has had no weight loss or haemoptysis. She was treated with antibiotics for a 'chest infection' twice last winter.

She has scattered expiratory wheeze and a prolonged expiratory phase, but no clubbing. Oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. A chest X-ray shows hyperinflated lungs with no mass or consolidation.

At the practice, the nurse performs spirometry WITHOUT giving a bronchodilator. The results are FEV1 1.52 L (64% predicted), FVC 2.35 L (82% predicted) and FEV1/FVC 0.65. The report states that the manoeuvres were acceptable and repeatable.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?
options: Diagnose COPD from these results and start a long-acting antimuscarinic
Arrange high-resolution CT of the chest
Arrange measurement of gas transfer (DLCO) and lung volumes
Repeat spirometry before and after an inhaled bronchodilator
Ask her to keep a twice-daily peak expiratory flow diary for 2 weeks
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Repeat spirometry before and after an inhaled bronchodilator

---

COPD is diagnosed by showing persistent airflow limitation: a POST-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 in a person with suitable symptoms and exposure. A pre-bronchodilator ratio can overestimate obstruction. Part of the limitation may reverse (as in asthma or asthma–COPD overlap), and some people with a low pre-bronchodilator ratio have a normal post-bronchodilator ratio. COPD-X and GOLD therefore require post-bronchodilator spirometry to confirm the diagnosis and grade severity. Measuring the bronchodilator response also gives information about possible asthma. Once COPD is confirmed, she should get smoking cessation support (the most effective intervention), vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation referral and inhaled bronchodilator therapy under the COPD-X stepwise plan.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
COPD needs a POST-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7. Pre-bronchodilator spirometry alone cannot confirm the diagnosis.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "COPD-X Plan: C. Case finding and confirm diagnosis", "url": "https://copdx.org.au/copd-x-plan/confirm-diagnosis/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Full lung function tests are useful when spirometry is uncertain or another disease is suspected. They are not the first step to confirm airflow limitation, which is done with post-bronchodilator spirometry.

question_text:
A 59-year-old Torres Strait Islander man sees his general practitioner at a community-controlled health service in Cairns, Queensland, for his diabetes review. He has had type 2 diabetes for 8 years. He takes metformin XR 1000 mg twice daily, perindopril 10 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. He has no history of heart failure, myocardial infarction or stroke, and he has had no genital infections. He works as a boat mechanic.

His blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg and his body mass index 31 kg/m². Foot examination is normal.

Investigations:
- HbA1c 7.6% (60 mmol/mol)
- eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m² (stable over 12 months)
- Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 38 mg/mmol (on three samples over 6 months)
- Potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- LDL cholesterol 1.7 mmol/L

Which one of the following is the most appropriate addition to his treatment?
options: Gliclazide MR 30 mg daily
Empagliflozin 10 mg daily
Sitagliptin 50 mg daily
Irbesartan 150 mg daily
Insulin glargine 10 units at night
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Empagliflozin 10 mg daily

---

He has type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease: eGFR 52 with persistent albuminuria (uACR 38 mg/mmol, which is macroalbuminuria). He is already on a maximum-dose ACE inhibitor. Australian guidance (the ADS type 2 diabetes algorithm and the Kidney Health Australia CKD guidance) recommends adding an SGLT2 inhibitor for people with type 2 diabetes and CKD, regardless of HbA1c. SGLT2 inhibitors slow the decline in eGFR, reduce progression to kidney failure, and lower heart failure and cardiovascular events. Empagliflozin can be started at an eGFR of 20 or more (dapagliflozin at 25 or more), although its glucose-lowering effect weakens below an eGFR of about 45. He should be counselled about sick-day rules (withhold during acute illness, fasting or surgery because of the risk of euglycaemic DKA), genital hygiene and hydration. A small initial dip in eGFR is expected. Metformin can continue at his eGFR, with dose review below 45.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In type 2 diabetes with albuminuric CKD, add an SGLT2 inhibitor (on top of maximum-tolerated ACE inhibitor/ARB) for kidney and heart protection whatever the HbA1c. Empagliflozin can be started at an eGFR of 20 or more.

---

• {"name": "Medicine Today: Preventing diabetic kidney disease progression \u2013 a 2025 update", "url": "https://medicinetoday.com.au/mt/supplements/feature-article/preventing-diabetic-kidney-disease-progression-2025-update"}

---

question_text:
A 41-year-old woman sees her general practitioner on the Sunshine Coast, Queensland, with two weeks of pain in the front of her neck that spreads to both ears and her jaw, and palpitations. Four weeks ago she had an upper respiratory tract infection. She has lost 2 kg. She last gave birth 3 years ago, is not breastfeeding, and has had no iodinated contrast in the past year. She takes no medicines or supplements.

Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 108/min and regular, and blood pressure 134/76 mmHg. The thyroid is firm, mildly enlarged and exquisitely tender, with no discrete nodule. There is a fine tremor. She has no eye signs or pretibial myxoedema.

Investigations:
- TSH <0.01 mIU/L (0.4–4.0)
- Free T4 38 pmol/L (10–20)
- Free T3 9.5 pmol/L (3.0–6.0)
- ESR 78 mm/h (<20); CRP 45 mg/L (<5)
- TSH-receptor antibody: negative
- White cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- Technetium-99m thyroid scan: diffusely and markedly reduced uptake

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Graves disease (autoimmune hyperthyroidism)
Toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer disease)
Painless (silent) lymphocytic thyroiditis
Acute suppurative thyroiditis
Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis

---

She has thyrotoxicosis with a painful, tender goitre after a viral illness, a markedly raised ESR/CRP, negative TSH-receptor antibodies and LOW radionuclide uptake. Low uptake shows the thyrotoxicosis comes from leakage of preformed hormone from an inflamed gland, not from overproduction. Pain, tenderness and high inflammatory markers identify subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis. The typical course is thyrotoxic (weeks), then hypothyroid (weeks to months), then usually back to normal. Treatment is symptomatic: an NSAID for pain (prednisolone if severe or NSAID-resistant) and a beta-blocker for adrenergic symptoms. Antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, propylthiouracil) have no role because hormone synthesis is not increased. Check thyroid function every 4–6 weeks to detect the hypothyroid phase.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Thyrotoxicosis plus a tender thyroid, high ESR/CRP and low radionuclide uptake means subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis. Treat with an NSAID (or prednisolone) and a beta-blocker, not carbimazole.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Ross DS et al. 2016 American Thyroid Association Guidelines for diagnosis and management of hyperthyroidism and other causes of thyrotoxicosis (Thyroid)", "url": "https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/10.1089/thy.2016.0229"}
• {"name": "StatPearls: De Quervain thyroiditis (NCBI Bookshelf)", "url": "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK526066/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Toxic multinodular goitre shows patchy INCREASED uptake in autonomous nodules, is painless and usually affects older people.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Painless (silent) thyroiditis also shows low uptake, but by definition the gland is NOT tender and inflammatory markers are normal or only mildly raised. It often occurs post partum (within 12 months of delivery), which does not apply here.

question_text:
A 44-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Adelaide, South Australia, after routine blood tests for a life-insurance application showed a high calcium. He feels well and has no history of kidney stones, fractures, abdominal pain, polyuria or mood change. He takes no medicines or supplements, including no lithium or thiazides. His 47-year-old sister was 'found to have a high calcium' several years ago and had a neck exploration in Melbourne, but no parathyroid adenoma was found and her calcium stayed high afterwards.

Examination is normal. His blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg.

Investigations (repeated twice, fasting samples taken without prolonged tourniquet):
- Albumin-adjusted calcium 2.76 mmol/L and 2.78 mmol/L (2.10–2.60)
- Parathyroid hormone 7.4 pmol/L (1.6–6.9)
- Phosphate 0.82 mmol/L (0.75–1.50)
- Magnesium 1.02 mmol/L (0.70–1.10)
- 25-hydroxyvitamin D 72 nmol/L (>50)
- Creatinine 84 µmol/L; eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m²

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Technetium-99m sestamibi scan to localise an adenoma
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of spine, hip and forearm
24-hour urine calcium with calcium/creatinine clearance ratio
Ultrasound of the neck for parathyroid localisation
Ultrasound of the renal tract for nephrocalcinosis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. 24-hour urine calcium with calcium/creatinine clearance ratio

---

He has PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia (raised calcium with an inappropriately high PTH). The main differential is primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) versus familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH), usually due to an inactivating CASR variant. FHH is benign and does not need surgery, and parathyroidectomy does not cure it. His sister's failed neck exploration with persistent hypercalcaemia is a strong clue to a familial condition. The Australian position statement on PHPT recommends measuring the calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR) from a 24-hour urine collection with paired serum values before localisation or surgery. A CCCR below 0.01 strongly suggests FHH; above 0.02 favours PHPT; 0.01–0.02 overlaps and needs CASR genetic testing. The test should be done when vitamin D is replete (as here, because vitamin D deficiency lowers urine calcium) and off thiazides or lithium. CASR (and AP2S1/GNA11) gene testing confirms FHH, and cascade testing can be offered to relatives.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Before localising a parathyroid adenoma, exclude FHH. A calcium/creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 (vitamin D replete, off thiazides) suggests FHH, and a relative with a failed parathyroidectomy is a red flag.

---

question_text:
A 46-year-old man sees his general practitioner on the Gold Coast, Queensland, for blood pressure review. Hypertension was diagnosed 2 years ago and is not controlled despite amlodipine 10 mg daily and perindopril 10 mg daily. Home readings average 158/96 mmHg. He takes no diuretics, NSAIDs, liquorice or other supplements, drinks two standard drinks a week and does not snore. He has mild muscle cramps. His father had a stroke at 52.

His blood pressure is 162/98 mmHg in both arms and his body mass index 25 kg/m². There are no cushingoid features or renal bruits.

Investigations:
- Sodium 144 mmol/L (135–145)
- Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Bicarbonate 31 mmol/L (22–32)
- Creatinine 82 µmol/L
- Fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L
- ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria

You suspect primary aldosteronism.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in his investigation?
options: CT of the adrenal glands with fine cuts
Correct potassium, then measure aldosterone and renin on current medicines
Arrange a seated saline suppression test
Stop both antihypertensives for 4 weeks, then measure aldosterone and renin
Collect a 24-hour urine for fractionated metanephrines
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Correct potassium, then measure aldosterone and renin on current medicines

---

He has several reasons to screen for primary aldosteronism (PA): uncontrolled hypertension on two drugs, spontaneous hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis, early LVH and a family history of early stroke. The screening test is the plasma aldosterone concentration with renin (aldosterone-to-renin ratio, ARR). Hypokalaemia suppresses aldosterone secretion and can give a falsely negative result, so potassium should be corrected first. The 2025 Endocrine Society guideline (co-authored by the Australian PA expert Stowasser) supports initial screening while patients stay on most antihypertensives, including ACE inhibitors and dihydropyridine CCBs. These drugs tend to RAISE renin, so a positive screen on them strongly suggests PA; a negative result in a high-suspicion patient can be repeated after adjusting medicines. Blood should be taken mid-morning after at least 2 hours upright and 5–15 minutes seated. A positive screen leads to endocrinology referral for confirmatory testing, adrenal CT and adrenal venous sampling.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Screen for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone–renin ratio after correcting hypokalaemia. Most antihypertensives can be continued for the initial screen; a positive result on an ACE inhibitor or CCB is strongly suggestive.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Adler GK, Stowasser M et al. Primary aldosteronism: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline (2025): guideline page", "url": "https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/primary-aldosteronism-2"}
• {"name": "Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine: Interpreting the 2025 Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism guideline", "url": "https://www.ccjm.org/content/93/9/515"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspected primary aldosteronism: preparing for aldosterone–renin screening

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Adrenal imaging comes AFTER biochemical confirmation. Non-functioning adrenal incidentalomas are common, and CT cannot tell unilateral from bilateral PA (that needs adrenal venous sampling).
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Confirmatory (suppression) testing follows a positive screening ARR. It is not the first test, and the 2025 guideline allows it to be skipped when spontaneous hypokalaemia, suppressed renin and clearly raised aldosterone coexist.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Stopping both drugs would leave a man with LVH and BP of 160/98 exposed to dangerously uncontrolled hypertension. Full withdrawal is not needed for initial screening, and the hypokalaemia would still be uncorrected. If withdrawal is later needed, substitute drugs (for example verapamil SR, prazosin, hydralazine or moxonidine) are used.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Phaeochromocytoma screening is for paroxysmal symptoms, labile or crisis hypertension, or an adrenal incidentaloma. Hypokalaemic alkalosis with steady hypertension points to aldosterone excess.

key_takeaways: Screen for primary aldosteronism with the aldosterone–renin ratio after correcting hypokalaemia. Most antihypertensives can be continued for the initial screen; a positive result on an ACE inhibitor or CCB is strongly suggestive.

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Newcastle, New South Wales. Five years ago she was found to have osteoporosis (lumbar spine T-score −3.0) after a low-trauma wrist fracture. She has since had denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months (10 injections), with calcium and vitamin D supplements. She has had no further fractures. Her last injection was exactly 6 months ago.

A DXA scan last week showed a lumbar spine T-score of −2.1 and a total hip T-score of −1.9. She has read about osteonecrosis of the jaw and, now that her 'bones are better', wants to stop denosumab. After a full discussion of the benefits and risks, she has firmly decided to stop.

She has no dental problems and saw her dentist last month. There is no history of reflux or oesophageal disease.

Investigations:
- Albumin-adjusted calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10–2.60)
- 25-hydroxyvitamin D 84 nmol/L (>50)
- eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m²

Which one of the following is the most appropriate plan?
options: Stop denosumab and give zoledronic acid 5 mg IV now, at the due date
Stop denosumab and repeat DXA in 2 years as a planned drug holiday
Delay the next denosumab injection by 6 months, then reassess her wishes
Stop denosumab and continue calcium and vitamin D supplements alone
Stop denosumab and start raloxifene 60 mg daily in 12 months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Stop denosumab and give zoledronic acid 5 mg IV now, at the due date

---

Denosumab's effect wears off quickly. When it is stopped or delayed, bone turnover rebounds above baseline, the BMD gained is lost within about 12–24 months, and there is a well-documented risk of multiple vertebral fractures. The TGA has strengthened warnings about this, and the 2024 RACGP/Healthy Bones Australia guideline advises that denosumab should not be stopped without follow-on antiresorptive therapy. The recommended approach is to switch to a bisphosphonate, most often IV zoledronic acid, given about 6 months after the last denosumab dose (that is, when the next injection would be due). Continue calcium and vitamin D. Some specialists check bone turnover markers and repeat zoledronic acid if needed. Her eGFR of 68 and normal calcium and vitamin D make zoledronic acid suitable. A drug holiday is a bisphosphonate concept and does not apply to denosumab.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Do not stop denosumab without a transition plan: give a bisphosphonate (usually zoledronic acid) about 6 months after the last injection to prevent rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "2024 RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia guideline for osteoporosis management and fracture prevention (MJA 2025)", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2025/222/9/2024-royal-australian-college-general-practitioners-and-healthy-bones-australia"}
• {"name": "TGA safety update: Strengthened warnings for fracture risk after discontinuation of denosumab (Prolia and biosimilars)", "url": "https://www.tga.gov.au/news/safety-updates/strengthened-warnings-fracture-risk-after-discontinuation-denosumab-prolia-and-biosimilars"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Stopping denosumab: preventing rebound vertebral fractures

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab does not stay bound in bone. A 'holiday' after denosumab leads to rapid bone loss and a high risk of multiple vertebral fractures.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Delaying a dose by more than about 4 weeks already starts the rebound. Waiting a further 6 months exposes her to the same fracture risk as stopping without cover.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Calcium and vitamin D alone do not prevent the rebound increase in bone resorption after denosumab.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Waiting 12 months leaves her unprotected during the period of highest rebound risk. Raloxifene is also a weak antiresorptive with little evidence for preventing post-denosumab bone loss, and it increases VTE risk.

key_takeaways: Do not stop denosumab without a transition plan: give a bisphosphonate (usually zoledronic acid) about 6 months after the last injection to prevent rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures.

question_text:
A 78-year-old man is admitted to a hospital in Bendigo, Victoria, with three days of diarrhoea and vomiting after a family gathering where several relatives also became unwell. He has hypertension and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. His regular medicines are perindopril 5 mg daily and furosemide 40 mg daily. Ten days ago he started ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, bought at a pharmacy, for knee osteoarthritis. He has kept taking all his medicines during the illness.

His pulse is 104/min, blood pressure 102/60 mmHg lying and 84/50 mmHg standing, and temperature 37.2°C. His mucous membranes are dry and the jugular venous pressure is not visible. There is no rash. A bladder scan after voiding shows 40 mL.

Investigations:
- Creatinine 245 µmol/L (60–110; baseline 105 two months ago)
- Urea 24.1 mmol/L (3.0–8.0)
- Potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Urine sodium 12 mmol/L; fractional excretion of sodium 0.6%
- Urinalysis: specific gravity 1.028; no blood, protein or leucocytes; microscopy shows occasional hyaline casts
- Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis

Which one of the following is the most likely mechanism of his acute kidney injury?
options: Acute interstitial nephritis caused by ibuprofen
Ischaemic acute tubular necrosis after dehydration
Bilateral renal artery stenosis unmasked by perindopril
Bladder outlet obstruction from prostatic enlargement
Prerenal AKI from volume loss and the 'triple whammy'
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Prerenal AKI from volume loss and the 'triple whammy'

---

This is haemodynamic (prerenal) AKI. Volume depletion from gastroenteritis was made much worse by the 'triple whammy': an ACE inhibitor (efferent arteriolar dilatation), a diuretic (further volume loss) and an NSAID (afferent vasoconstriction by blocking prostaglandins). Together these remove the kidney's ability to autoregulate GFR. The urine picture confirms intact tubular function: urine sodium below 20 mmol/L, FENa below 1%, concentrated urine, bland sediment with only hyaline casts, a raised urea-to-creatinine ratio, and postural hypotension. Management is to stop ibuprofen, withhold perindopril and furosemide during the acute illness (sick-day rules), give careful IV fluid while watching his HFpEF, treat the hyperkalaemia, and monitor creatinine. The medicines are reviewed on recovery, and he should be counselled to avoid NSAIDs.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID ('triple whammy') plus volume depletion causes prerenal AKI with urine sodium below 20 and FENa below 1%. Stop the NSAID and follow sick-day rules for the others.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Kidney Health Australia: Chronic Kidney Disease Management in Primary Care handbook, 5th edition (2024), including medicines and sick-day guidance", "url": "https://kidney.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/KHA-CKD-Handbook-5th-Ed-July2024.pdf"}
• {"name": "bpacnz: Avoiding the triple whammy in primary care (2018)", "url": "https://bpac.org.nz/2018/triple-whammy.aspx"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Acute kidney injury from the 'triple whammy' (ACE inhibitor, diuretic, NSAID) with volume depletion

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: NSAID-induced AIN usually causes sterile pyuria, white cell casts, sometimes eosinophiluria, and often proteinuria (NSAIDs can also cause minimal change disease). FENa is usually above 1%. The bland urine and low FENa here do not fit.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Established ATN causes loss of tubular sodium reabsorption: urine sodium above 40 mmol/L, FENa above 2%, isosthenuric urine and muddy brown granular casts. His tubules are still conserving sodium avidly.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Renovascular disease can cause AKI after starting an ACE inhibitor, but he has been on perindopril long-term with a stable baseline creatinine. The acute trigger is clearly the illness plus the new NSAID.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A post-void residual of 40 mL and no hydronephrosis exclude clinically significant obstruction.

key_takeaways: ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID ('triple whammy') plus volume depletion causes prerenal AKI with urine sodium below 20 and FENa below 1%. Stop the NSAID and follow sick-day rules for the others.

question_text:
A 69-year-old woman is admitted to a hospital in Mackay, Queensland, after her daughter noticed she had been confused and unsteady for two days. Three weeks ago her general practitioner started sertraline 50 mg daily for depression after her husband's death. She also takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. She takes no diuretics. She has not had vomiting or diarrhoea, and she says she has been drinking 'plenty of water and tea' because she read it is good for her.

Her pulse is 78/min, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg lying and 136/82 mmHg standing. Her mucous membranes are moist, the jugular venous pressure is normal, and there is no oedema or ascites. She is disoriented to time but has no focal neurological signs. She has not had a seizure.

Investigations:
- Sodium 121 mmol/L (135–145); one month ago 138 mmol/L
- Potassium 4.0 mmol/L
- Urea 2.8 mmol/L (3.0–8.0)
- Creatinine 58 µmol/L
- Glucose 5.6 mmol/L
- Serum osmolality 254 mOsm/kg (275–295)
- Uric acid 0.16 mmol/L (0.15–0.40)

Which one of the following is the most useful next investigation to establish the cause of her hyponatraemia?
options: CT scan of the brain without contrast
Serum lipids and total protein
Plasma copeptin concentration
Spot urine osmolality and urine sodium
Fluid restriction to 1 L a day and repeat sodium at 48 hours
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Spot urine osmolality and urine sodium

---

She has hypotonic hyponatraemia (serum osmolality 254) and is clinically euvolaemic. The key next step is to measure urine osmolality and urine sodium on a spot sample taken at the same time as the serum sample, before treatment. A urine osmolality below 100 mOsm/kg means maximally dilute urine, pointing to excess water intake (primary polydipsia) or low solute intake ('tea and toast'). Her reported heavy fluid intake makes this a real possibility. A urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg with urine sodium above 30 mmol/L in a euvolaemic patient not on diuretics fits SIADH, here plausibly caused by the SSRI. This distinction changes management: fluid restriction treats SIADH, whereas polydipsia responds to reduced intake and carries a high risk of rapid overcorrection once water diuresis begins. Hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency must also be excluded (TSH, morning cortisol) before SIADH is diagnosed. She has moderate symptoms, so correction should be monitored closely, with a limit of about 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In hypotonic, euvolaemic hyponatraemia, measure paired urine osmolality and urine sodium before treatment. Urine osmolality below 100 suggests polydipsia or low solute intake; above 100 with urine sodium above 30 suggests SIADH (after excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "RACGP Australian Family Physician: The suspect \u2013 SIADH (2017)", "url": "https://www.racgp.org.au/afp/2017/september/the-suspect-siadh"}
• {"name": "Spasovski G et al. Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia (European Journal of Endocrinology 2014), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24569125/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Hypotonic hyponatraemia in a euvolaemic older woman: next investigations

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Imaging may be needed if she has a fall or focal signs, but her confusion is explained by acute hyponatraemia. A CT will not identify its cause.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Lipids and protein are checked when pseudohyponatraemia is suspected, that is, when measured serum osmolality is NORMAL. Her osmolality is low, confirming true hypotonic hyponatraemia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Copeptin is a specialist test with limited routine availability and uncertain value in the routine hyponatraemia work-up. It is not the next step.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Starting fluid restriction before the urine studies may be wrong (for example if urine osmolality is low) and changes the urine results, making them harder to interpret. Investigate first.

key_takeaways: In hypotonic, euvolaemic hyponatraemia, measure paired urine osmolality and urine sodium before treatment. Urine osmolality below 100 suggests polydipsia or low solute intake; above 100 with urine sodium above 30 suggests SIADH (after excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency).

question_text:
A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of Rockhampton Hospital, Queensland, with tingling around his mouth and painful spasms of his hands. Over the past month he has had two episodes of palpitations. He has gastro-oesophageal reflux disease treated with esomeprazole 40 mg daily for 5 years, heart failure treated with furosemide 40 mg daily, and hypertension. He drinks one standard drink a day. He has had no neck surgery or radiation. Two weeks ago his general practitioner started oral potassium chloride and calcium carbonate supplements for low levels, but his symptoms have worsened.

He has a positive Trousseau sign. His pulse is 92/min and irregular, and blood pressure 132/78 mmHg.

Investigations:
- Albumin-adjusted calcium 1.84 mmol/L (2.10–2.60)
- Potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Magnesium 0.28 mmol/L (0.70–1.10)
- Phosphate 1.10 mmol/L (0.75–1.50)
- Parathyroid hormone 3.2 pmol/L (1.6–6.9)
- 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (>50)
- Creatinine 96 µmol/L
- ECG: sinus rhythm with frequent ventricular ectopics; QTc 492 ms

Which one of the following best explains his biochemical abnormalities?
options: Primary hypoparathyroidism
Vitamin D–deficient osteomalacia
Hypomagnesaemia from long-term proton pump inhibitor use
Gitelman syndrome presenting late in life
Hypokalaemia from furosemide causing secondary hypocalcaemia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Hypomagnesaemia from long-term proton pump inhibitor use

---

Severe hypomagnesaemia (0.28 mmol/L) is the unifying cause. Magnesium is needed for PTH secretion and for end-organ responsiveness to PTH, so severe deficiency causes hypocalcaemia with an inappropriately NORMAL or low PTH (functional hypoparathyroidism). Magnesium deficiency also causes renal potassium wasting through ROMK channels, which is why his potassium and calcium did not respond to oral replacement. Long-term PPI use (usually more than a year) is a recognised cause, through reduced intestinal magnesium absorption via TRPM6/7. The TGA and Australian Prescriber have highlighted it, and the loop diuretic makes it worse. Treatment is IV magnesium sulfate with cardiac monitoring (a typical adult regimen is about 10 mmol over 1–2 hours, then an infusion), followed by repletion of calcium and potassium, and review of the PPI indication (step down, H2 antagonist or stop if possible). Magnesium usually falls again if the PPI is continued.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia with inappropriately normal PTH: check magnesium. Long-term PPIs (worse with diuretics) are a common cause. Replace magnesium first and review the PPI.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber: Proton pump inhibitor-associated hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/proton-pump-inhibitor-associated-hypomagnesaemia-and-hypocalcaemia.html"}
• {"name": "TGA: Product Information safety updates \u2013 January 2023", "url": "https://www.tga.gov.au/news/safety-updates/product-information-safety-updates-january-2023"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Refractory hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia from PPI-induced hypomagnesaemia

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: True primary hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical, autoimmune) would not explain the severe hypomagnesaemia or the refractory hypokalaemia, and he has had no neck surgery. His inappropriately normal PTH is caused by the low magnesium.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: His vitamin D is replete. Vitamin D deficiency causes secondary hyperparathyroidism (HIGH PTH) and low phosphate, neither of which is present.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Gitelman syndrome causes hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, metabolic alkalosis and HYPOcalciuria, but usually normal serum calcium. It usually presents in adolescence or young adulthood. A 5-year PPI history offers a far more likely acquired cause.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Furosemide causes hypokalaemia and magnesium loss, but hypokalaemia does not cause hypocalcaemia. Loop diuretics increase urinary calcium but rarely cause symptomatic hypocalcaemia on their own.

key_takeaways: Refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia with inappropriately normal PTH: check magnesium. Long-term PPIs (worse with diuretics) are a common cause. Replace magnesium first and review the PPI.

question_text:
A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department of Mount Isa Hospital, Queensland, at 0700 hours. He passed one black, tarry, offensive stool overnight and another this morning. For three weeks he has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for a shoulder injury. He has not vomited blood and has not fainted or felt light-headed. He has no history of liver disease, heart failure or previous bleeding and takes no other medicines. He drinks about 10 standard drinks a week. He feels well and asks to go home because he works a fly-in fly-out roster and is due to fly out tomorrow.

His pulse is 88/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, with no postural drop. He has mild epigastric tenderness. Digital rectal examination confirms melaena.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 136 g/L (130–180)
- Urea 8.4 mmol/L (3.0–8.0)
- Creatinine 82 µmol/L (60–110)
- Platelets 260 × 10^9/L
- INR 1.0

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of his bleeding risk?
options: Glasgow-Blatchford score 4; not low risk, so admit for endoscopy
Glasgow-Blatchford score 1; low risk, suitable for outpatient endoscopy
Glasgow-Blatchford score 0; low risk, suitable for discharge today
Glasgow-Blatchford score 9; high risk, needs endoscopy within 2 hours
Score is unreliable until haemoglobin is repeated at 6 hours
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Glasgow-Blatchford score 4; not low risk, so admit for endoscopy

---

The Glasgow-Blatchford score (GBS) predicts the need for intervention (transfusion, endoscopic therapy, surgery) or death in upper GI bleeding. His points: urea 8.4 mmol/L falls in the 8.0–9.9 band, which scores 3. Melaena scores 1. Haemoglobin 136 g/L in a man (130 or more) scores 0. Systolic BP 128 scores 0. Pulse below 100 scores 0. No syncope, liver disease or heart failure. Total GBS = 4. International guidelines (ESGE 2021, ACG 2021) accept a GBS of 0–1 as low risk for outpatient management. A score of 4 is not low risk. He should be admitted, have a PPI started, and have endoscopy within 24 hours. Urea rises because blood proteins are digested and absorbed in the upper GI tract, and it is often the first abnormal result before the haemoglobin falls. His wish to travel should be explored respectfully, but flying out with an untreated NSAID-related bleed would be unsafe.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Glasgow-Blatchford: urea is weighted heavily (6.5–7.9 = 2, 8.0–9.9 = 3, 10–24.9 = 4, 25 or more = 6) and melaena adds 1. Only a GBS of 0–1 is low risk for outpatient care, even if the patient looks well with a normal haemoglobin.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Gralnek IM et al. ESGE Guideline: Endoscopic diagnosis and management of nonvariceal upper GI haemorrhage \u2013 update 2021 (Endoscopy), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33567467/"}
• {"name": "Laine L et al. ACG Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding (2021)", "url": "https://www.darmzentrum-bern.ch/fileadmin/darmzentrum/Education/Bible_Class/2022/upper_GI_bleeding/ACG_-_Upper_GI_Bleed_2021.pdf"}

---

subtopic: Upper GI bleeding risk stratification: Glasgow-Blatchford score in a well-looking patient

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This miscounts the urea, which scores 3 points in the 8.0–9.9 mmol/L band. Only a GBS of 0–1 is considered low risk.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A score of 0 needs a urea below 6.5 mmol/L and no melaena. Both are present here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A score of 9 is not supported by his data. International guidelines also advise against very urgent (under 6 hours) endoscopy even in higher-risk patients once they are resuscitated; within 24 hours is standard.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: The GBS is designed for use at presentation. A normal haemoglobin does not make it unreliable; the urea and melaena already carry the risk signal.

key_takeaways: Glasgow-Blatchford: urea is weighted heavily (6.5–7.9 = 2, 8.0–9.9 = 3, 10–24.9 = 4, 25 or more = 6) and melaena adds 1. Only a GBS of 0–1 is low risk for outpatient care, even if the patient looks well with a normal haemoglobin.

question_text:
A 29-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Albany, Western Australia, with tiredness. Blood tests show iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 104 g/L, ferritin 6 µg/L). For two years she had bloating and loose stools. Four months ago, after reading about gluten online, she started a strict gluten-free diet and her bowel symptoms settled. Her sister has type 1 diabetes. She has heavy periods only occasionally and eats red meat three times a week.

Last week her GP requested tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA), which was negative, with a normal total IgA level. She is relieved, feels much better on the diet and says she is 'very reluctant' to eat gluten again unless it is truly necessary. Examination is normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step to clarify whether she has coeliac disease?
options: Accept the negative tTG-IgA as excluding coeliac disease
Refer for duodenal biopsies while she stays gluten-free
Measure deamidated gliadin peptide IgG antibodies now
Measure faecal calprotectin to look for intestinal inflammation
Arrange HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping from a blood sample
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Arrange HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping from a blood sample

---

Coeliac serology and duodenal histology depend on gluten being eaten. After four months gluten-free, a negative tTG-IgA (even with normal total IgA) does not exclude coeliac disease, and biopsies may already have healed. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping is not affected by diet. About 99% of people with coeliac disease carry HLA-DQ2 and/or DQ8, so a NEGATIVE result effectively excludes it and spares her a gluten challenge. A positive result does not diagnose coeliac disease (about 30–40% of the population carry these genes). If she is positive, she would need a gluten challenge (Coeliac Australia suggests at least 3–6 g gluten a day, about 4 slices of wheat bread, for at least 6 weeks) followed by serology and gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies. Her unexplained iron deficiency also needs investigating in its own right, and a gastroenterologist may recommend endoscopy regardless of the coeliac result.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
If a patient is already gluten-free, serology and biopsy are unreliable. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing can exclude coeliac disease if negative; if positive, a gluten challenge (about 4 slices of bread daily for at least 6 weeks) is needed before testing.

---

question_text:
A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought to the emergency department of North West Regional Hospital, Burnie, Tasmania, by his partner. For two days he has had vague generalised abdominal discomfort and has been 'not himself', sleeping during the day and muddled at night. He stopped drinking alcohol 8 months ago. His medicines are spironolactone 100 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily and propranolol 10 mg twice daily. He has no vomiting, haematemesis or melaena, and his bowels opened yesterday.

His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse 96/min and blood pressure 108/64 mmHg. He is jaundiced, drowsy but rousable and has asterixis. The abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and mild diffuse tenderness, without guarding or rigidity.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 118 g/L; white cells 11.8 × 10^9/L; platelets 72 × 10^9/L
- INR 1.7
- Bilirubin 64 µmol/L; albumin 26 g/L
- Sodium 131 mmol/L; creatinine 118 µmol/L (baseline 85)
- Urinalysis: no leucocytes or nitrites
- Chest X-ray: no consolidation

Which one of the following is the most important next investigation?
options: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
Diagnostic paracentesis for cell count and culture
Serum ammonia concentration
Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler of the portal vein
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy within 12 hours
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Diagnostic paracentesis for cell count and culture

---

Any patient with cirrhosis and ascites admitted to hospital, especially with fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy or worsening kidney function, needs a diagnostic paracentesis to look for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). SBP is often subtle and has high mortality. An ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm³ confirms SBP and should be treated straight away with an IV third-generation cephalosporin (for example ceftriaxone), without waiting for culture. Ascitic fluid should be inoculated into blood culture bottles at the bedside to improve culture yield. The procedure is safe despite his INR and platelet count; routine correction of clotting is not recommended. Because his creatinine has risen, IV albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3) reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome and death. SBP is a common precipitant of his hepatic encephalopathy, which also needs treatment (lactulose).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Cirrhosis with ascites and fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy or AKI: do a diagnostic paracentesis. An ascitic neutrophil count above 250/mm³ means SBP; treat with a third-generation cephalosporin and give IV albumin if renal function is impaired.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of patients with decompensated cirrhosis (J Hepatol 2018), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29653741/"}
• {"name": "MSD Manual Professional: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis", "url": "https://www.msdmanuals.com/professional/hepatic-and-biliary-disorders/approach-to-the-patient-with-liver-disease/spontaneous-bacterial-peritonitis-sbp"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Cirrhosis with ascites, fever and confusion: diagnostic paracentesis for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: CT may be needed if secondary (surgical) peritonitis is suspected, for example from a very high ascitic neutrophil count, multiple organisms or peritonism. It is not the first test, and IV contrast is best avoided with his rising creatinine.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis. A high ammonia supports it but does not change management or find the precipitant. A normal ammonia makes the diagnosis less likely.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Portal vein thrombosis can cause decompensation, and Doppler ultrasound is reasonable later. It does not address the most dangerous treatable cause of fever and encephalopathy here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: There is no evidence of GI bleeding (no haematemesis or melaena, stable haemoglobin). Endoscopy is not the priority.

question_text:
A 66-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis sees her rheumatologist in Toowong, Brisbane, because of increasing tiredness and breathlessness climbing stairs. Her arthritis has flared over the past 3 months, with swelling of several small joints of both hands. She takes methotrexate 20 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly and naproxen 500 mg twice daily. Her periods stopped at 51. She has no overt GI bleeding and eats a mixed diet including red meat.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115–160)
- MCV 77 fL (80–100); MCH 24 pg (27–32)
- Platelets 468 × 10^9/L (150–400)
- White cells 7.2 × 10^9/L
- Ferritin 85 µg/L (30–300)
- Serum iron 5 µmol/L (10–30)
- Transferrin 3.4 g/L (2.0–3.6)
- Transferrin saturation 9% (15–45)
- C-reactive protein 38 mg/L (<5)
- Blood film: hypochromic microcytic red cells with pencil cells

Which one of the following is the most likely interpretation of her anaemia?
options: Anaemia of inflammation alone, with adequate iron stores
Beta-thalassaemia trait unmasked by active arthritis
Methotrexate-induced marrow suppression
Iron deficiency, with ferritin raised by inflammation
Sideroblastic anaemia related to methotrexate and folate antagonism
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Iron deficiency, with ferritin raised by inflammation

---

Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant. During active inflammation (CRP 38) it rises and can hide iron deficiency. A ferritin below 30 µg/L confirms iron deficiency, but with inflammation a ferritin up to about 100 µg/L can still be consistent with it, especially with a transferrin saturation below 20%. Other features point to true iron deficiency rather than anaemia of inflammation alone: marked microcytosis and hypochromia with pencil cells, reactive thrombocytosis, and a high-normal transferrin (in anaemia of inflammation transferrin is typically LOW). The likely cause is occult GI blood loss from a long-term NSAID. She needs GI evaluation (gastroscopy and colonoscopy, given her age and the coexisting iron deficiency), review of the NSAID, and iron replacement (IV iron is often preferred when inflammation reduces oral iron absorption through hepcidin). Her arthritis control also needs attention.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Ferritin is an acute-phase protein: with inflammation, a ferritin up to about 100 µg/L plus transferrin saturation below 20% still suggests iron deficiency. Look for a source (for example NSAID-related GI loss).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Zhang GD et al. Updating the diagnosis and management of iron deficiency in the era of routine ferritin testing of blood donors by Australian Red Cross Lifeblood (MJA 2024)", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2024/221/7/updating-diagnosis-and-management-iron-deficiency-era-routine-ferritin-testing"}
• {"name": "Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Diagnosis and investigation of iron deficiency anaemia", "url": "https://www.lifeblood.com.au/health-professionals/clinical-practice/clinical-indications/iron-deficiency-anaemia/diagnosis-investigation"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Interpreting iron studies in inflammation: iron deficiency with ferritin in the 'normal' range

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: In pure anaemia of inflammation, transferrin is usually low or low-normal, microcytosis is mild, and ferritin is often well above 100. A transferrin saturation of 9% with a high-normal transferrin and pencil cells points to coexisting absolute iron deficiency.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Thalassaemia trait causes marked microcytosis with a NORMAL or high red cell count and normal iron studies, and it does not cause a low transferrin saturation. It is also not 'unmasked' by inflammation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Methotrexate toxicity causes macrocytosis or pancytopenia (especially with renal impairment or interacting drugs), not isolated microcytic anaemia with thrombocytosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Sideroblastic anaemia (for example from alcohol, isoniazid, copper deficiency or MDS) gives high ferritin and HIGH transferrin saturation with ring sideroblasts in the marrow. Her saturation is low.

key_takeaways: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein: with inflammation, a ferritin up to about 100 µg/L plus transferrin saturation below 20% still suggests iron deficiency. Look for a source (for example NSAID-related GI loss).

question_text:
A 71-year-old woman is on the orthopaedic ward of a private hospital in Gosford, New South Wales, 7 days after an elective right total knee replacement. She was started on enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily after surgery. She had no heparin exposure in the past year. Today her right calf is swollen and painful, and duplex ultrasound shows a right popliteal and femoral vein thrombosis. She weighs 70 kg.

Investigations:
- Platelets: day 0, 280 × 10^9/L; day 7, 110 × 10^9/L
- Haemoglobin 112 g/L
- INR 1.0; APTT normal
- Creatinine 68 µmol/L (eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m²)
- No other cause of thrombocytopenia identified

Her 4Ts score is 8. The medical registrar sends a heparin/PF4 immunoassay, which is pending.

In addition to stopping enoxaparin, which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Start warfarin today, overlapping with enoxaparin until INR is 2–3
Start therapeutic unfractionated heparin by IV infusion
Start therapeutic-dose fondaparinux subcutaneously once daily
Transfuse platelets and withhold anticoagulation until results return
Insert an inferior vena cava filter and withhold anticoagulation
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Start therapeutic-dose fondaparinux subcutaneously once daily

---

She has a high 4Ts score: a platelet fall of more than 50% (2 points), onset between day 5 and 10 (2), new thrombosis (2) and no other cause (2), total 8. HIT is highly likely. Management should not wait for the immunoassay. All heparin (including LMWH and heparin flushes) must be stopped, and a therapeutic dose of a non-heparin anticoagulant started, because HIT is strongly prothrombotic. Suitable options include fondaparinux (weight-based: 7.5 mg daily for 50–100 kg, with normal renal function), argatroban or bivalirudin, or a DOAC in selected stable patients (ASH 2018). Warfarin should NOT be started until the platelet count has recovered (usually above 150 × 10^9/L), because early warfarin lowers protein C and can cause venous limb gangrene. Platelet transfusion is avoided unless there is bleeding or a high-risk procedure. HIT should be recorded as an adverse drug reaction. In Australia no anticoagulant is registered for HIT, so fondaparinux use is off-label; the THANZ consensus (MJA 2019) names fixed-dose fondaparinux as the simpler option for clinically stable patients with adequate renal function, with haematology input.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected HIT with an intermediate or high 4Ts score: stop all heparin and start a therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulant (for example fondaparinux, argatroban or a DOAC) without waiting for results. No warfarin until platelets recover, and no platelet transfusion.

---

---

question_text:
A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency department of Fiona Stanley Hospital, Perth, with 3 days of headache, tiredness and bruising on her legs. This morning her partner noticed she was briefly muddled and could not find words for about 20 minutes. She has no diarrhoea. She takes no regular medicines apart from the combined oral contraceptive pill. She is not pregnant.

Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse 104/min and blood pressure 132/84 mmHg. She has scattered petechiae on both shins. Neurological examination is now normal.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 78 g/L (115–160)
- Platelets 14 × 10^9/L (150–400)
- Reticulocytes 6% (0.5–2.5)
- Blood film: numerous schistocytes
- Lactate dehydrogenase 1650 U/L (120–250)
- Bilirubin 42 µmol/L (unconjugated)
- Haptoglobin undetectable
- Direct antiglobulin test negative
- INR 1.1; APTT 30 s; fibrinogen 3.2 g/L
- Creatinine 96 µmol/L (45–90)
- Urine β-hCG negative

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis and immediate treatment?
options: Evans syndrome; start prednisolone and IV immunoglobulin
Immune TTP; start urgent plasma exchange and corticosteroids
Disseminated intravascular coagulation; give platelets and cryoprecipitate
Atypical HUS; give eculizumab and avoid plasma therapy
Immune thrombocytopenia; give a platelet transfusion and IV immunoglobulin
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Immune TTP; start urgent plasma exchange and corticosteroids

---

She has microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, raised LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, negative DAT) with severe thrombocytopenia, normal coagulation, fluctuating neurological signs, and only mild renal impairment. This is typical of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), a medical emergency that is fatal in most untreated cases. Her PLASMIC score is high (platelets below 30, haemolysis, no active cancer, no transplant, MCV and INR not raised, creatinine below 177 µmol/L). An ADAMTS13 activity sample should be collected before plasma is given, but treatment must not wait for the result: urgent haematology referral, therapeutic plasma exchange, and corticosteroids. Caplacizumab and rituximab are usually added for immune TTP (ISTH 2020). Platelet transfusion should be avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding, because it may worsen thrombosis.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
MAHA (schistocytes, high LDH, DAT negative) + severe thrombocytopenia + normal coagulation ± neurological signs = TTP until proven otherwise. Take an ADAMTS13 sample, then start plasma exchange and steroids urgently; avoid platelet transfusion.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Zheng XL et al. ISTH guidelines for treatment of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (J Thromb Haemost 2020), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32914526/"}
• {"name": "Zheng XL et al. ISTH good practice statements for the clinical care of patients with TTP (J Thromb Haemost 2020), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32914535/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Thrombotic microangiopathy: recognising immune TTP and its urgent treatment

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Evans syndrome (autoimmune haemolysis with ITP) is DAT POSITIVE and has spherocytes rather than schistocytes.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: DIC causes a prolonged INR/APTT and low fibrinogen, usually with an obvious trigger such as sepsis. Her coagulation is normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Atypical HUS is dominated by acute kidney injury and is usually diagnosed after TTP is excluded (ADAMTS13 above 10%). Plasma exchange is the right first step while results are pending.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: ITP does not cause haemolysis or schistocytes. Platelet transfusion in TTP may worsen microvascular thrombosis.

key_takeaways: MAHA (schistocytes, high LDH, DAT negative) + severe thrombocytopenia + normal coagulation ± neurological signs = TTP until proven otherwise. Take an ADAMTS13 sample, then start plasma exchange and steroids urgently; avoid platelet transfusion.

question_text:
A 79-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Orange, New South Wales, for a routine INR check. He takes warfarin for non-valvular atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VA score 4: age, hypertension and coronary disease). His doctors chose warfarin over a DOAC because of severe chronic kidney disease (creatinine clearance about 22 mL/min). He also takes aspirin 100 mg daily, prescribed by his cardiologist after a coronary stent 8 months ago, plus metoprolol, atorvastatin and pantoprazole. Five days ago he started a course of roxithromycin for a chest infection. His last INR, two weeks ago, was 2.6.

Today's point-of-care INR is 7.4, confirmed at 7.3 on a venous sample. He has no bleeding, bruising, black stools or blood in his urine, and has had no falls. Haemoglobin is 128 g/L and platelets 190 × 10^9/L. He has no planned procedures. His pulse is 76/min and irregular, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Withhold one warfarin dose, then restart at a lower dose and recheck the INR in a week
Continue warfarin at a reduced dose and recheck the INR in 3 days
Withhold warfarin and give vitamin K 5–10 mg intravenously
Withhold warfarin and give four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
Withhold warfarin, give vitamin K 1–2 mg orally, and recheck the INR in 24 hours
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Withhold warfarin, give vitamin K 1–2 mg orally, and recheck the INR in 24 hours

---

Under the Australasian warfarin reversal consensus (Tran et al., MJA 2013; reaffirmed for non-bleeding patients in the 2025 update), an INR of 4.5–10 without bleeding is managed by stopping warfarin and restarting at a lower dose once the INR is in range. Vitamin K is usually unnecessary. However, if the patient has a HIGH bleeding risk, vitamin K 1–2 mg orally (or 0.5–1 mg IV) should be given and the INR checked within 24 hours. The consensus lists concurrent antiplatelet therapy as a high-risk feature, along with major bleeding within 4 weeks, major surgery within 2 weeks, thrombocytopenia (platelets below 50) and liver disease. He is on aspirin, so vitamin K is recommended. Low-dose vitamin K lowers the INR without causing warfarin resistance, which matters for his high stroke risk. The trigger for the rise (a macrolide antibiotic that reduces warfarin metabolism) should be noted, and closer INR monitoring arranged until the course ends. The need for aspirin alongside anticoagulation more than 6 months after a stent is also worth raising with his cardiologist.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
INR 4.5–10 without bleeding: cease warfarin; add vitamin K 1–2 mg orally (INR within 24 hours) only if bleeding risk is high. High risk includes concurrent antiplatelet therapy, recent major bleed or surgery, platelets below 50 and liver disease.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Tran HA et al. An update of consensus guidelines for warfarin reversal (MJA 2013)", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2013/198/4/update-consensus-guidelines-warfarin-reversal"}
• {"name": "Updated recommendations for warfarin reversal in the setting of four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (MJA 2025)", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2025/222/1/updated-recommendations-warfarin-reversal-setting-four-factor-prothrombin"}

---

subtopic: Supratherapeutic INR without bleeding: effect of concurrent antiplatelet therapy on vitamin K use

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This would suit an INR of 4.5–10 WITHOUT high bleeding risk (the consensus advises withholding warfarin until back in range). His concurrent aspirin puts him in the high-risk group, where low-dose vitamin K and an INR check within 24 hours are advised.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Dose reduction alone is appropriate for an INR above range but below 4.5 without bleeding. It is inadequate at an INR of 7.4 with an antiplatelet.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: High-dose IV vitamin K (5–10 mg) is for clinically significant bleeding. In a non-bleeding patient it over-corrects and can cause warfarin resistance for days, leaving him unprotected against stroke.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The 2025 MJA update suggests 4F-PCC outside surgery only for an INR above 10 in high-risk patients, or for bleeding. It is not indicated at an INR of 7.4 without bleeding.

key_takeaways: INR 4.5–10 without bleeding: cease warfarin; add vitamin K 1–2 mg orally (INR within 24 hours) only if bleeding risk is high. High risk includes concurrent antiplatelet therapy, recent major bleed or surgery, platelets below 50 and liver disease.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer, known to have bone metastases, presents to the emergency department of Wagga Wagga Base Hospital, New South Wales, at 2100 hours. For 3 weeks he has had worsening mid-back pain that is worse lying flat and keeps him awake. Over the last 2 days his legs have felt heavy and 'wobbly', and today he stumbled twice. He has had no incontinence but has noticed some hesitancy passing urine. He is on androgen deprivation therapy with goserelin. He has no diabetes or history of peptic ulcer.

Examination shows tenderness over the T9–T10 spinous processes. Power is 4/5 in hip flexion bilaterally, with brisk knee reflexes and upgoing plantars. He has reduced pinprick sensation below the umbilicus. Anal tone is normal. Post-void bladder scan shows 150 mL. Oral morphine has been given for pain.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Give dexamethasone 16 mg now and arrange urgent whole-spine MRI
Arrange thoracic spine X-ray and bone scan in the morning
Give dexamethasone and arrange outpatient spinal radiotherapy
Arrange CT of the thoracic spine and refer to physiotherapy
Arrange MRI of the thoracic spine within the next week
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Give dexamethasone 16 mg now and arrange urgent whole-spine MRI

---

Back pain in a patient with known bone metastases, plus progressive leg weakness, upper motor neuron signs and a sensory level around T10, is metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) until proven otherwise. It is an oncological emergency: neurological function at the time of treatment is the strongest predictor of whether he will walk again. eviQ recommends dexamethasone 16 mg (orally or IV) as soon as MSCC is suspected, with PPI cover, and an MRI of the WHOLE spine urgently (ideally within 24 hours, sooner with neurological deficit). The whole spine is imaged because compression is often multilevel. He should be nursed flat (spinal precautions) if there is pain or instability, and discussed urgently with radiation oncology and spinal surgery. Definitive treatment is radiotherapy and/or surgical decompression.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected MSCC (known cancer + back pain + neurological signs): dexamethasone 16 mg immediately, urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours, and early oncology/spinal referral.

---

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman with stage IV melanoma presents to the emergency department of a Melbourne metropolitan hospital. She had her second cycle of combination ipilimumab and nivolumab 3 weeks ago. For 4 days she has had watery diarrhoea, now 8–9 times a day (her usual is once daily), with crampy lower abdominal pain and some nocturnal stools. There is no blood in the stool. She has not travelled, and nobody at home is unwell. She took loperamide at home without benefit.

Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse 102/min and blood pressure 112/70 mmHg. The abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness and no peritonism.

Investigations:
- White cells 10.2 × 10^9/L; haemoglobin 128 g/L
- C-reactive protein 64 mg/L
- Potassium 3.2 mmol/L; creatinine 88 µmol/L
- Stool: multiplex PCR and C. difficile toxin sent
- Abdominal X-ray: no colonic dilatation

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue immunotherapy, advise oral fluids and increase the loperamide dose
Withhold immunotherapy and start oral budesonide 9 mg daily as an outpatient
Start infliximab 5 mg/kg IV today, before any corticosteroid
Withhold immunotherapy, admit and give IV methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg daily
Start empirical oral metronidazole and review when stool results return
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Withhold immunotherapy, admit and give IV methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg daily

---

Diarrhoea of 7 or more stools a day above baseline, with abdominal pain and interference with daily life, is grade 3 immune-related colitis (CTCAE). It is common with combined anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1 therapy. eviQ guidance for grade 3–4 colitis: withhold the checkpoint inhibitor, admit, give IV fluids and electrolyte replacement, and start IV methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day (after sending stool tests for infection, but without waiting for results). Early gastroenterology input and flexible sigmoidoscopy are advised. If there is no improvement after about 48–72 hours of IV steroids, add infliximab 5 mg/kg (or vedolizumab). Steroids are tapered slowly over at least 4–6 weeks once symptoms improve. Antidiarrhoeals such as loperamide can mask worsening colitis and raise the risk of toxic megacolon, so they are avoided in moderate to severe ICI colitis.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
ICI colitis grade 3 (7 or more stools/day above baseline): withhold the ICI, admit, IV methylprednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day; infliximab if no response in 48–72 hours. Avoid loperamide.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "Schneider BJ et al. Management of immune-related adverse events in patients treated with ICI therapy: ASCO guideline update (J Clin Oncol 2021), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34724392/"}

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Budesonide may have a role in mild colitis, but grade 3 disease with tachycardia and a high CRP needs admission and IV corticosteroids.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Infliximab is second-line, used for steroid-refractory colitis (no response after 48–72 hours) or sometimes early in selected severe cases. It is not given instead of corticosteroids.

question_text:
A 34-year-old accountant sees his general practitioner in Devonport, Tasmania, 10 days after an emergency department visit. At home, his wife saw him have a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes, followed by 20 minutes of confusion. He had slept normally the night before, drinks 2–3 standard drinks a week, uses no recreational drugs and takes no medicines. He has had no previous seizures, head injury or central nervous system infection. There is no family history of epilepsy.

In the emergency department his blood glucose, electrolytes, calcium and magnesium were normal. He has since had an MRI brain and a sleep-deprived EEG, both normal. The neurologist has not started antiseizure medication. He holds a private (car) licence only and drives to work daily. He asks when he can drive again.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice about driving?
options: He may drive now, because his MRI and EEG are both normal
He may drive after a 4-week stand-down if he remains well
He should not drive until at least 6 months seizure-free
He should not drive until at least 12 months seizure-free
He should not drive until 5 years seizure-free, off medication
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. He should not drive until at least 6 months seizure-free

---

Under the Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive' standards, a person with a first unprovoked seizure should not drive a private vehicle for at least 6 months. A conditional licence may then be considered by the licensing authority on the advice of the treating doctor, provided there has been no further seizure. Normal investigations do not shorten this non-driving period for private drivers. Commercial drivers face much longer restrictions (generally at least 5 years seizure-free for a first unprovoked seizure, subject to specialist review). The doctor should document the advice. The legal responsibility to notify the driver licensing authority rests with the driver, but the doctor may report in the interests of public safety if the patient continues to drive against advice (in South Australia and the Northern Territory, health professionals have mandatory reporting obligations). Other safety advice includes supervision when swimming or bathing and care with heights and machinery.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Austroads: first unprovoked seizure means no private driving for at least 6 months seizure-free (conditional licence possible), and much longer (about 5 years) for commercial drivers. The patient is responsible for notifying the licensing authority.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive \u2013 Neurological conditions: Seizures and epilepsy", "url": "https://austroads.gov.au/publications/assessing-fitness-to-drive/ap-g56/neurological-conditions/seizures-and-epilepsy"}
• {"name": "Epilepsy Foundation (Australia): Driving and epilepsy", "url": "https://epilepsyfoundation.org.au/managing-epilepsy/living-with-epilepsy/driving/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Normal MRI and EEG lower but do not remove the risk of recurrence (highest in the first 6 months). There is no immediate return to driving under Austroads.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A 4-week stand-down does not apply to a first unprovoked seizure in a private driver.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Twelve months applies to other scenarios, such as established epilepsy for private drivers. For a first unprovoked seizure the standard is 6 months.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This long period relates to commercial vehicle standards, not a private licence.
