question_text:
A 46-year-old man is admitted to the medical ward at Townsville University Hospital, Queensland. For 5 days he has had tingling in his feet and hands, and over the past 2 days he has had increasing difficulty climbing stairs and getting out of a chair. Three weeks ago he had a diarrhoeal illness. He has no bladder or bowel symptoms.

On examination he has symmetrical weakness: 4/5 proximally in the legs and 4+/5 in the arms. Reflexes are absent throughout, with reduced vibration sense at the toes. Neck flexion power is mildly reduced. His voice and swallow are normal. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, respiratory rate 16/min, pulse 92/min and blood pressure 146/88 mmHg. Nerve conduction studies are pending, and neurology has recommended IV immunoglobulin.

Which one of the following is the most important bedside measurement to monitor him for impending respiratory failure?
options: Continuous pulse oximetry with a target saturation of 94–98%
Peak expiratory flow rate measured four times a day
Arterial blood gas measured every 12 hours
Respiratory rate recorded with routine observations
Serial forced vital capacity and mouth pressures
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Serial forced vital capacity and mouth pressures

---

About 20–30% of people with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) develop respiratory failure needing ventilation. Deterioration from diaphragmatic weakness can be sudden. Serial forced vital capacity (FVC), ideally with maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures, measured several times a day, is the standard bedside monitor. The '20/30/40 rule' flags high risk: FVC below 20 mL/kg, maximal inspiratory pressure weaker than −30 cmH2O, or maximal expiratory pressure below 40 cmH2O. A falling FVC (for example a 30% drop) should prompt ICU review and consideration of elective intubation. Neck flexion weakness, bulbar weakness, rapid progression and inability to lift the head or elbows are further red flags (the EGRIS score helps predict ventilation risk). Autonomic instability (arrhythmias, labile BP) also needs cardiac monitoring.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
GBS: monitor serial FVC (± MIP/MEP) several times a day. Use the 20/30/40 rule (FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30, MEP <40 cmH2O) to trigger ICU review. Saturation and blood gases deteriorate late.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Leonhard SE et al. Diagnosis and management of Guillain\u2013Barr\u00e9 syndrome in ten steps (Nat Rev Neurol 2019), PMC", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6821638/"}
• {"name": "van Doorn PA et al. EAN/PNS guideline on management of Guillain-Barr\u00e9 syndrome (2023), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37814552/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Guillain-Barré syndrome: bedside monitoring for impending respiratory failure

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Oxygen saturation falls LATE in neuromuscular respiratory failure, often only just before arrest. Normal saturation is falsely reassuring.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Peak flow reflects airway obstruction and effort and depends on facial and bulbar muscle seal. It is not a validated measure of neuromuscular ventilatory reserve.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Hypercapnia and hypoxaemia on ABG are late findings. Waiting for them delays safe elective intubation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Respiratory rate is useful but insensitive; patients can maintain a normal rate until close to decompensation.

key_takeaways: GBS: monitor serial FVC (± MIP/MEP) several times a day. Use the 20/30/40 rule (FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30, MEP <40 cmH2O) to trigger ICU review. Saturation and blood gases deteriorate late.

question_text:
A 44-year-old woman presents to the emergency department of a regional hospital in Shepparton, Victoria, at 0200 hours. At 1600 hours yesterday, while lifting a heavy box, she had a sudden, severe occipital headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds; she describes it as 'the worst headache of my life'. She vomited once. There was no loss of consciousness or seizure. She has no history of migraine. She is a smoker and takes no medicines.

She is alert, GCS 15, temperature 36.8°C and blood pressure 152/90 mmHg. She has mild neck stiffness and no focal neurological signs. Fundi are normal.

A non-contrast CT brain was performed at 0200 hours, 10 hours after onset, and is reported by a consultant radiologist as normal. The hospital's policy is that CT angiography is not the first-line test after a normal CT. Her headache has eased to 4/10 with paracetamol and she wants to go home.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage?
options: Discharge her, as a normal CT within 12 hours excludes haemorrhage
Perform a lumbar puncture from 12 hours after onset, for xanthochromia
Perform a lumbar puncture now, for red cell count
Arrange outpatient MRI brain in the next 2 weeks and review
Repeat the non-contrast CT brain at 24 hours after onset
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Perform a lumbar puncture from 12 hours after onset, for xanthochromia

---

A normal non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset of a thunderclap headache, read by an experienced radiologist on a modern scanner, is highly sensitive for subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH), and many pathways (for example the Ottawa SAH approach) accept it as ruling out SAH in neurologically intact patients. Her CT was done 10 hours after onset, so this rule does not apply: CT sensitivity falls as blood is cleared. The next step is a lumbar puncture. The LP should be done at least 12 hours after headache onset (from 0400 hours here). It takes that long for red cells to break down into bilirubin, producing xanthochromia (detected by spectrophotometry), which separates true SAH from a traumatic tap. The NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation emergency care pathway describes this CT-then-delayed-LP approach. CT angiography is an alternative in some centres, but it detects incidental aneurysms and the stem states it is not first-line locally. If the LP is positive, she needs CT angiography and neurosurgical referral.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Thunderclap headache: CT within 6 hours (neurologically intact, experienced reader) can rule out SAH. After 6 hours, a normal CT needs an LP at least 12 hours after onset for xanthochromia (or CTA as per local pathway).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation (ECI): Subarachnoid haemorrhage \u2013 clinical tool", "url": "https://aci.health.nsw.gov.au/networks/eci/clinical/tools/neurology/headache/subarachnoid-heamorrhage"}
• {"name": "Perry JJ et al. Sensitivity of computed tomography performed within six hours of onset of headache for diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage (BMJ 2011), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21768192/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Thunderclap headache with normal CT more than 6 hours after onset: timing of lumbar puncture

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The rule-out applies to CT within 6 hours of onset, not 12. At 10 hours, SAH is not excluded by a normal CT.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: An LP before 12 hours may be falsely negative for xanthochromia, and red cells alone cannot distinguish SAH from a traumatic tap.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A delayed outpatient scan risks missing a sentinel bleed. Aneurysmal rebleeding carries high mortality and usually occurs early.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Repeat non-contrast CT becomes LESS sensitive with time as blood clears; it adds nothing here.

key_takeaways: Thunderclap headache: CT within 6 hours (neurologically intact, experienced reader) can rule out SAH. After 6 hours, a normal CT needs an LP at least 12 hours after onset for xanthochromia (or CTA as per local pathway).

question_text:
A 31-year-old man who has sex with men attends a sexual health clinic in Darlinghurst, Sydney, for his routine 3-monthly HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) review. He is well and has no rash, genital or anal ulcers, or neurological, visual or hearing symptoms. Two years ago he was treated for secondary syphilis with benzathine benzylpenicillin. Since then his RPR has fallen and stayed at 1:2 on 5 consecutive checks, most recently 3 months ago. He has had 4 new male partners in the past 3 months, with inconsistent condom use.

Examination, including the genitals, anus, mouth and skin, is normal.

Investigations today:
- Syphilis EIA (treponemal): reactive (as before)
- TPPA: reactive (as before)
- RPR: 1:32
- HIV antigen/antibody: negative
- Pharyngeal, rectal and urine gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT: pending

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and management?
options: Reinfection; benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 million units IM, single dose
Serofast state after treatment; no treatment, repeat serology in 3 months
Likely false-positive RPR; repeat the RPR in 4 weeks before any treatment
Tertiary syphilis; benzathine benzylpenicillin weekly for 3 weeks
Neurosyphilis until proven otherwise; admit for IV benzylpenicillin
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Reinfection; benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 million units IM, single dose

---

Treponemal tests (EIA, TPPA) usually stay reactive for life after syphilis, so they cannot distinguish past from new infection. The non-treponemal RPR titre is used to monitor treatment and detect reinfection. A sustained fourfold (two-dilution) or greater rise in RPR indicates reinfection or treatment failure. His RPR has risen from a stable 1:2 (including 3 months ago) to 1:32, a 16-fold rise, in the setting of ongoing risk. He has no signs, so this is early latent syphilis: a new infection acquired within the last 2 years (in fact within 3 months). The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 million units IM as a single dose for early syphilis (primary, secondary or early latent). Syphilis is notifiable, partner notification is needed for the past 3 months (plus symptom duration), and the RPR should be followed to confirm a fourfold fall. No neurological, ocular or otic symptoms means an LP is not routinely needed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Treponemal tests stay positive for life; follow the RPR. A fourfold or greater rise after previous treatment means reinfection. Early (less than 2 years) syphilis: benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM once; late latent: weekly for 3 weeks.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian STI Management Guidelines for Use in Primary Care (ASHM): Syphilis", "url": "https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/syphilis/"}
• {"name": "NSW Health: Syphilis control guideline / fact sheet", "url": "https://www.health.nsw.gov.au/Infectious/factsheets/Pages/syphilis.aspx"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Syphilis serology after previous treatment: distinguishing reinfection from serofast state

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A serofast state is a LOW, stable titre after treatment, which is what he had until now. A jump to 1:32 is not serofast.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: False-positive RPRs are usually low titre with NEGATIVE treponemal tests. Delaying treatment of infectious syphilis risks onward transmission.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Weekly doses for 3 weeks are used for late latent syphilis (over 2 years or unknown duration). His infection is clearly recent, and he has no features of tertiary syphilis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: IV benzylpenicillin is for neurosyphilis or ocular/otic syphilis. He has no neurological, visual or hearing symptoms.

key_takeaways: Treponemal tests stay positive for life; follow the RPR. A fourfold or greater rise after previous treatment means reinfection. Early (less than 2 years) syphilis: benzathine benzylpenicillin 2.4 MU IM once; late latent: weekly for 3 weeks.

question_text:
A 27-year-old man presents to a general practice in Maryborough, Queensland, with 6 days of high fevers, sweats, severe frontal headache and aching muscles. For 2 days he has had a dry cough and mild breathlessness. He moved from New Zealand 5 months ago and works on the slaughter floor of a local abattoir processing cattle and goats. He has had no vaccines since arriving. He has not waded in floodwater or kept birds, has not travelled overseas recently, and drinks only pasteurised milk.

His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He has fine crackles at the left base, mild tender hepatomegaly, no rash, no conjunctival suffusion and no lymphadenopathy.

Investigations:
- White cells 6.8 × 10^9/L; platelets 96 × 10^9/L
- ALT 186 U/L; ALP 160 U/L; bilirubin 18 µmol/L
- Creatinine 84 µmol/L
- Chest X-ray: patchy left lower lobe consolidation

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Leptospirosis
Brucellosis
Psittacosis
Q fever
Legionnaires' disease
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Q fever

---

Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, spread by inhaling contaminated dust or aerosols from cattle, sheep and goats (especially birth products). Abattoir workers are a classic high-risk group. His recent arrival from New Zealand, where Q fever is essentially absent, means he is likely to be non-immune and unvaccinated. Acute Q fever typically causes a flu-like illness with high fever, marked headache and myalgia, often with atypical pneumonia and/or granulomatous hepatitis, and thrombocytopenia. Diagnosis is by serology (phase II antibodies, repeated at 2–4 weeks) and PCR on early blood. Treatment should start on clinical suspicion: doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days. It is notifiable in Queensland. He should be followed up for chronic Q fever (especially endocarditis in people with valve disease) and post-Q fever fatigue syndrome. Abattoir co-workers need pre-vaccination screening (skin test and serology) and vaccination with Q-VAX.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Abattoir or farm worker (unvaccinated, often recently arrived) with fever, severe headache, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis and thrombocytopenia = acute Q fever. Treat with doxycycline 100 mg bd for 14 days; it is notifiable, and co-workers need screening and vaccination.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Queensland Health: Q fever (disease control)", "url": "https://www.health.qld.gov.au/disease-control/conditions/q-fever"}
• {"name": "CDNA National Guidelines for Public Health Units: Q fever", "url": "https://www.cdc.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/q-fever-cdna-national-guidelines-for-public-health-units_0.pdf"}
• {"name": "Australian Immunisation Handbook: Q fever", "url": "https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/q-fever"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Occupational zoonosis in an abattoir worker: acute Q fever

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Leptospirosis also causes fever, myalgia, hepatitis and thrombocytopenia in Queensland, but is linked to floodwater, mud and rodent or cattle urine. Conjunctival suffusion and renal impairment are common. His exposure and pneumonia fit Q fever better.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Brucellosis (in Australia mainly Brucella suis from feral pig hunting; B. abortus has been eradicated from cattle) causes undulant fever with joint and testicular involvement. Consolidation is uncommon.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Psittacosis is caught from birds such as parrots and poultry. He has no bird exposure.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Legionella causes severe pneumonia with hyponatraemia and GI upset, usually from cooling towers or potting mix. It would not explain his occupational exposure, prominent hepatitis and thrombocytopenia as well as Q fever.

key_takeaways: Abattoir or farm worker (unvaccinated, often recently arrived) with fever, severe headache, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis and thrombocytopenia = acute Q fever. Treat with doxycycline 100 mg bd for 14 days; it is notifiable, and co-workers need screening and vaccination.

question_text:
A 63-year-old man is admitted to Geraldton Regional Hospital, Western Australia, with fever and rigors. He has type 2 diabetes and had an infected blister on his left heel 2 weeks ago. Two sets of blood cultures taken on admission, 48 hours ago, grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). He was started on IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours, and he is now afebrile.

He has no prosthetic valve, pacemaker or intravascular device, no previous endocarditis and no history of injecting drug use. Examination shows a healing heel ulcer with mild surrounding erythema, no heart murmur, and no embolic or vasculitic skin lesions. His ECG is normal (PR interval 160 ms).

Repeat blood cultures were collected this morning. X-ray of the heel shows no bone changes. The infectious diseases team is consulted by phone from Perth.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Transoesophageal echocardiography as the first cardiac imaging test
Serum C-reactive protein repeated daily until normal
Transthoracic echocardiography during this admission
Whole-body PET-CT to look for a metastatic focus
MRI of the lumbar spine to exclude discitis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Transthoracic echocardiography during this admission

---

Every patient with S. aureus bacteraemia (SAB) needs echocardiography, because infective endocarditis is common and changes the duration and route of therapy. Australian guidance (for example the WA Therapeutic Advisory Group and Hunter New England SAB guidelines) recommends transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for all patients, with TOE when the TTE is non-diagnostic or abnormal or the risk is high. High-risk features include a prosthetic valve or cardiac device, previous endocarditis, injecting drug use, persistent bacteraemia (positive cultures after 72 hours of treatment), a new murmur, embolic phenomena, or a new conduction abnormality. He has none of these, and his repeat cultures are already collected. Other key SAB bundle elements are: a source search (the heel), infectious diseases consultation, IV flucloxacillin (or cefazolin), and at least 14 days of IV therapy for uncomplicated SAB from the first negative culture, longer if complicated.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
All S. aureus bacteraemia: repeat blood cultures, ID consult, source control and echocardiography. TTE for all; TOE if high risk (prosthetic valve/device, IVDU, persistent bacteraemia, emboli) or if the TTE is non-diagnostic.

---

question_text:
A 26-year-old man presents to the emergency department of a Melbourne hospital at 1400 hours on a Sunday. About 30 hours ago he had receptive anal intercourse without a condom with a casual male partner he met through a dating app. He does not know the partner's HIV status and cannot contact him. He is not on PrEP. He had a negative HIV test 5 months ago. He has no symptoms. He takes no medicines and has no known kidney or liver disease or hepatitis B.

Examination is normal. Rapid point-of-care HIV testing is not available; blood is taken for HIV antigen/antibody, hepatitis B and C serology, syphilis serology, creatinine and liver function tests. Urine, pharyngeal and rectal swabs are taken for gonorrhoea and chlamydia.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Start tenofovir DF/emtricitabine plus dolutegravir for 28 days
Start PrEP daily and continue indefinitely, without a PEP course
Start tenofovir DF/emtricitabine once daily for 28 days
Await the HIV result and start PEP if the test is negative
No PEP; the risk is too low with a partner of unknown status
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Start tenofovir DF/emtricitabine once daily for 28 days

---

He had receptive anal intercourse, the highest-risk sexual exposure, with a partner from a population with higher HIV prevalence (a man who has sex with men) whose status is unknown. He presented well within the 72-hour window. The ASHM Australian PEP guidelines recommend PEP in this situation, and for an unknown-status source a 2-drug regimen (tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg/emtricitabine 200 mg once daily) is recommended. A 3-drug regimen (adding dolutegravir 50 mg daily) is reserved for exposures where the source is KNOWN to have HIV with a detectable or unknown viral load, or where resistance is suspected. PEP should be started as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours of assessment, without waiting for the baseline HIV result. It is taken for 28 days, with follow-up HIV testing at about 6 and 12 weeks. This is also a good opportunity to discuss transitioning to PrEP ('PEP-in-PrEP') after completing the course if the HIV test at the end is negative.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
ASHM PEP: receptive anal sex with an unknown-status MSM partner within 72 hours needs 2-drug PEP (TDF/FTC daily for 28 days). Three drugs only if the source is known HIV-positive with a detectable or unknown viral load. Start without waiting for results.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ASHM: National PEP Guidelines \u2013 When to prescribe PEP", "url": "https://hiv.guidelines.org.au/pep-guidelines/when-to-prescribe-pep/"}
• {"name": "ASHM: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis after Non-Occupational and Occupational Exposure to HIV \u2013 National Guidelines (2025, PDF)", "url": "https://hiv.guidelines.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ASHM-PEP-guidelines-2025_FA_20251024.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Non-occupational HIV post-exposure prophylaxis: choosing a 2-drug versus 3-drug regimen

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A 3-drug regimen is for a source known to have HIV with a detectable or unknown viral load, or suspected resistance. For an unknown-status partner, ASHM recommends 2 drugs; adding dolutegravir adds cost and side effects without clear benefit.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: PrEP taken now does not treat an exposure 30 hours ago in the way a full PEP course does. The usual approach is a 28-day PEP course, then transition to PrEP.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Delaying PEP until results return wastes the time-critical window; PEP works best when started early. A baseline test is taken, but PEP starts immediately.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Receptive anal intercourse with an unknown-status MSM partner meets the ASHM threshold for recommending PEP.

key_takeaways: ASHM PEP: receptive anal sex with an unknown-status MSM partner within 72 hours needs 2-drug PEP (TDF/FTC daily for 28 days). Three drugs only if the source is known HIV-positive with a detectable or unknown viral load. Start without waiting for results.

question_text:
A 48-year-old market gardener presents to a general practice in Bunbury, Western Australia, 6 hours after stepping on a rusty garden fork. The tines went through his work boot, leaving a deep puncture wound in the sole of his right foot contaminated with soil and manure. He has HIV infection, diagnosed 9 years ago, and takes bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. His viral load is undetectable and his CD4 count 3 months ago was 610 cells/µL.

His records show he completed a primary course of tetanus-containing vaccine as a child and had a booster (dTpa) 7 years ago. He has no allergies. The wound is irrigated and debrided and is not showing signs of infection.

In addition to wound care, which one of the following is the most appropriate tetanus prophylaxis?
options: dTpa booster alone, as his last dose was over 5 years ago
Oral metronidazole for 7 days instead of vaccine or immunoglobulin
No vaccine or immunoglobulin, as his last dose was within 10 years
Tetanus immunoglobulin 500 IU IM, without vaccine
dTpa booster and tetanus immunoglobulin 250 IU IM
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. dTpa booster and tetanus immunoglobulin 250 IU IM

---

A deep puncture wound contaminated with soil and manure is tetanus-prone. According to the Australian Immunisation Handbook, a tetanus-prone wound in a person with at least 3 previous doses needs a tetanus-containing vaccine booster if the last dose was more than 5 years ago. He received his 7 years ago, so a booster is needed (dTpa or ADT). Tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) is also recommended for tetanus-prone wounds in people with humoral immune deficiency, including HIV infection, regardless of the time since the last dose, because they may not mount an adequate antibody response. This applies even if HIV is well controlled. The TIG dose is 250 IU IM if given within 24 hours of injury (500 IU if more than 24 hours), given at a different site from the vaccine with a separate syringe. Antibiotics are used only for clinical wound infection, not to prevent tetanus.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Tetanus-prone wound: booster if last dose more than 5 years ago (3 or more prior doses). Add TIG (250 IU if within 24 hours, 500 IU if later) for fewer than 3 doses or unknown history, OR for any HIV/humoral immunodeficiency, regardless of time since last dose.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Immunisation Handbook: Guide to tetanus prophylaxis in wound management (table)", "url": "https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/resources/tables/table-guide-to-tetanus-prophylaxis-in-wound-management"}
• {"name": "Australian Immunisation Handbook: Tetanus", "url": "https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/tetanus"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Tetanus prophylaxis for a tetanus-prone wound in a person with HIV

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The booster is needed, but the Handbook also recommends TIG for tetanus-prone wounds in people with HIV, regardless of how recently they were vaccinated.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Antibiotics do not replace active or passive immunisation for tetanus prevention.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The 10-year interval applies to clean minor wounds. For tetanus-prone wounds the booster interval is 5 years, and HIV adds TIG.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: TIG 500 IU is for presentations more than 24 hours after injury; he is at 6 hours. It is also given ALONGSIDE, not instead of, the booster he is due for.

key_takeaways: Tetanus-prone wound: booster if last dose more than 5 years ago (3 or more prior doses). Add TIG (250 IU if within 24 hours, 500 IU if later) for fewer than 3 doses or unknown history, OR for any HIV/humoral immunodeficiency, regardless of time since last dose.

question_text:
A 74-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Coffs Harbour, New South Wales, on a Friday afternoon. For 3 weeks she has had a new, persistent right-sided temporal headache, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, and aching and stiffness of her shoulders in the mornings. Over the past week her jaw has ached after chewing for a few minutes. She has lost 3 kg. She has no visual disturbance, double vision or transient loss of vision. She has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin, and osteopenia.

Her temperature is 37.5°C and blood pressure 138/82 mmHg. The right temporal artery is thickened and tender, with a reduced pulse. Visual acuity, visual fields and fundoscopy are normal. The shoulders are tender with painful movement.

Point-of-care and same-day laboratory results:
- C-reactive protein 86 mg/L
- ESR 78 mm/h
- Haemoglobin 112 g/L; platelets 486 × 10^9/L
- Blood glucose 8.4 mmol/L

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Arrange temporal artery biopsy first, then start prednisolone if giant cell arteritis is confirmed
Start prednisolone 40–60 mg today, then arrange urgent temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy
Start prednisolone 15 mg daily for likely polymyalgia rheumatica and review in a week
Start IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days, then arrange urgent temporal artery biopsy
Arrange urgent MRI brain and a neurology review for a new-onset headache in an older adult
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Start prednisolone 40–60 mg today, then arrange urgent temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy

---

She has typical features of giant cell arteritis (GCA): age over 50, new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, an abnormal temporal artery, polymyalgic symptoms and raised inflammatory markers. Untreated GCA can cause sudden, permanent blindness. Guidelines (for example BSR 2020) advise starting high-dose glucocorticoids IMMEDIATELY on clinical suspicion, without waiting for confirmation: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily for GCA without visual or ischaemic symptoms. She should be referred urgently (same day or next day) to a rheumatology or fast-track GCA service for confirmation with temporal artery ultrasound and/or biopsy, ideally within a week of starting steroids. Diagnostic yield falls only slowly with treatment. Other steps: monitor and treat her glucose on steroids, bone protection (calcium, vitamin D and an antiresorptive given her osteopenia), and consider PPI cover. Low-dose aspirin is no longer routinely recommended.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected GCA: start prednisolone 40–60 mg immediately (IV methylprednisolone if visual symptoms), then arrange urgent ultrasound/biopsy within a week. Do not wait for confirmation before treating.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Mackie SL et al. British Society for Rheumatology guideline on diagnosis and treatment of giant cell arteritis (Rheumatology 2020)", "url": "https://academic.oup.com/rheumatology/article/59/3/e1/5714024"}
• {"name": "BSR 2020 GCA recommendations (summary PDF, hosted by PMRGCA Scotland)", "url": "https://pmrgcascotland.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/BSR-2020-Recommendations-for-the-management-of-GCA.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspected giant cell arteritis without visual loss: steroid before confirmatory testing

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Delaying steroids until biopsy risks irreversible visual loss. Biopsy remains diagnostic for 1–2 weeks after steroids are started.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Prednisolone 15 mg treats PMR alone. Jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and an abnormal temporal artery mean GCA, which needs 40–60 mg.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: IV methylprednisolone pulses are recommended for GCA with visual loss or amaurosis fugax. She has no visual symptoms, so oral prednisolone is appropriate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Her clinical picture is typical of GCA, not an intracranial lesion. Delaying steroids to pursue neuroimaging is inappropriate.

key_takeaways: Suspected GCA: start prednisolone 40–60 mg immediately (IV methylprednisolone if visual symptoms), then arrange urgent ultrasound/biopsy within a week. Do not wait for confirmation before treating.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry sees his general practitioner in Chatswood, Sydney. He has had 4 attacks of gout in the past year, affecting his big toe and ankle, and has tophi on two fingers. His serum urate is 0.58 mmol/L. He has hypertension and stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m²). He takes amlodipine and irbesartan. He does not drink alcohol. His current attack settled a month ago on colchicine.

You agree that he needs long-term urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol, started at a low dose and gradually increased to a target serum urate below 0.30 mmol/L because of his tophi. He asks whether anything should be tested before he starts.

Which one of the following tests should be offered before starting allopurinol?
options: HLA-B*58:01 genotyping
HLA-B27 genotyping
Thiopurine methyltransferase activity
HLA-B*15:02 genotyping
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. HLA-B*58:01 genotyping

---

Allopurinol is a leading cause of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR), including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) and Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis, which can be fatal. The HLA-B*58:01 allele greatly increases this risk. It is common in people of Han Chinese, Thai and Korean ancestry (especially with CKD). The RCPA and Australian Prescriber recommend HLA-B*58:01 testing before starting allopurinol in people from these higher-risk groups. If he carries HLA-B*58:01, allopurinol should be avoided and an alternative such as febuxostat considered. If negative, allopurinol can be started at a low dose (for example 50 mg daily with eGFR 48) and increased gradually, with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis (colchicine) for the first months. His CKD adds to the SCAR risk, but CKD alone is not a reason to avoid gradual dose titration to target.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Before allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean ancestry (especially with CKD), test for HLA-B*58:01; if positive, avoid allopurinol. HLA-B*15:02 is for carbamazepine.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "RCPA: Pharmacogenomic indications in Australia \u2013 Allopurinol (HLA-B*58:01)", "url": "https://www.rcpa.edu.au/Library/Practising-Pathology/Pharmacogenomic-Indications-in-Australia/Recommended/Allopurinol"}
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber: Using pharmacogenomics to personalise drug therapy \u2013 which drugs, when and how", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/using-pharmacogenomics-to-personalise-drug-therapy-which-drugs-when-and-how.html"}
• {"name": "MJA 2023: Avoiding severe drug hypersensitivity reactions \u2013 the case for HLA genotyping", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2023/218/10/avoiding-severe-drug-hypersensitivity-reactions-case-hla-genotyping-risk"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Pharmacogenomic screening before urate-lowering therapy in a patient of Han Chinese ancestry

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: HLA-B27 is associated with spondyloarthritis, not with drug hypersensitivity to allopurinol.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: TPMT activity guides azathioprine and mercaptopurine dosing. It is relevant because allopurinol interacts with azathioprine, but it is not a pre-allopurinol screen.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: HLA-B*15:02 predicts carbamazepine (and phenytoin/oxcarbazepine)-induced SJS/TEN, especially in South-East Asian ancestry. It is not the allele relevant to allopurinol.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: G6PD deficiency matters for drugs like primaquine, dapsone and rasburicase. It does not predict allopurinol hypersensitivity.

key_takeaways: Before allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean ancestry (especially with CKD), test for HLA-B*58:01; if positive, avoid allopurinol. HLA-B*15:02 is for carbamazepine.

question_text:
A 69-year-old man presents to the emergency department of Dubbo Base Hospital, New South Wales, with a 2-day history of a painful, swollen left knee. He cannot bear weight. He has had 3 previous attacks of gout in his big toes, the last a year ago, and takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and metformin for type 2 diabetes. He is not on urate-lowering therapy. He had a left knee steroid injection for osteoarthritis 3 weeks ago. He has no rash, urethral discharge or recent diarrhoea.

His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse 104/min and blood pressure 128/76 mmHg. The left knee is hot, red and swollen with a large effusion, and any movement is very painful. There are no other swollen joints and no tophi.

Investigations:
- White cells 15.2 × 10^9/L (neutrophils 12.8)
- C-reactive protein 164 mg/L
- Serum urate 0.52 mmol/L (0.20–0.42)
- Creatinine 96 µmol/L
- Blood cultures: 2 sets taken
- X-ray of the knee: effusion, degenerative changes, no fracture

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start oral colchicine and review the knee in 24 hours
Start IV flucloxacillin, then aspirate the knee tomorrow
Arrange MRI of the knee to look for osteomyelitis
Aspirate the knee for Gram stain, culture and crystals, then start IV antibiotics
Give an intra-articular corticosteroid injection after aspirating the effusion
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Aspirate the knee for Gram stain, culture and crystals, then start IV antibiotics

---

An acute hot, swollen joint with fever is septic arthritis until proven otherwise, even in someone with known gout. The two can coexist, and a raised serum urate does not prove gout (urate may be normal or high in either). His recent intra-articular steroid injection, diabetes, fever and high inflammatory markers all increase the likelihood of infection. The key investigation is urgent joint aspiration for synovial white cell count, Gram stain, culture (ideally also inoculated into blood culture bottles) and crystal microscopy. This should be done BEFORE antibiotics if it does not cause significant delay, because antibiotics reduce culture yield. Blood cultures are already taken. Empirical IV antibiotics (for example flucloxacillin, adjusted for local MRSA risk) should then start immediately, with orthopaedic review for washout if the aspirate suggests infection.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Hot swollen joint + fever = septic arthritis until proven otherwise, even with known gout. Aspirate for Gram stain, culture and crystals before antibiotics (if no delay), then start empirical IV antibiotics.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Ravn C et al. Guideline for management of septic arthritis in native joints (SANJO), J Bone Jt Infect 2023, PMC", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9901514/"}
• {"name": "Healthdirect: Septic arthritis", "url": "https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/septic-arthritis"}

---

subtopic: Acute hot swollen knee with fever in a patient with known gout: joint aspiration before antibiotics

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Treating as gout without aspiration risks missing septic arthritis, which can destroy the joint within days and cause sepsis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Antibiotics are needed urgently, but aspirating first (without delay) gives the best chance of identifying the organism. Postponing aspiration to tomorrow is inappropriate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: MRI is not needed to diagnose septic arthritis and would delay aspiration and treatment.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Injecting a steroid into a possibly infected joint is dangerous. Infection must be excluded first.

key_takeaways: Hot swollen joint + fever = septic arthritis until proven otherwise, even with known gout. Aspirate for Gram stain, culture and crystals before antibiotics (if no delay), then start empirical IV antibiotics.

question_text:
A 24-year-old woman of Samoan heritage with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), diagnosed 2 years ago, sees her rheumatologist in Logan, Queensland. She takes hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily but admits she stopped it 4 months ago because she felt well. For 3 weeks she has had ankle swelling, frothy urine, joint pains and mouth ulcers. She is not pregnant.

Her blood pressure is 158/96 mmHg. She has pitting oedema to the mid-shins, synovitis of several finger joints and two painless palatal ulcers.

Investigations:
- Creatinine 124 µmol/L (6 months ago: 68)
- Urine microscopy: >100 × 10^6/L dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts
- Urine protein:creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol (<15)
- Albumin 28 g/L
- Anti-dsDNA 420 IU/mL (<10), up from 60
- C3 0.38 g/L (0.9–1.8); C4 0.04 g/L (0.1–0.4)
- Anti-phospholipid antibodies negative
- Renal ultrasound: normal-sized kidneys

Which one of the following is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?
options: Minimal mesangial lupus nephritis (class I)
Advanced sclerosing lupus nephritis (class VI)
Membranous lupus nephritis (class V) alone
Proliferative lupus nephritis (class III or IV)
Thrombotic microangiopathy from antiphospholipid syndrome
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Proliferative lupus nephritis (class III or IV)

---

She has an active nephritic picture: dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts, rising creatinine, hypertension and heavy proteinuria. This is accompanied by strongly positive and rising anti-dsDNA and very low C3 and C4, indicating immune-complex-driven disease. These features most strongly predict proliferative (focal class III or diffuse class IV) lupus nephritis, the most common and most serious class, with a high risk of progression to kidney failure. Renal biopsy is still needed to confirm the class and assess activity and chronicity before treatment. Treatment of class III/IV disease (KDIGO 2024) is glucocorticoids plus induction with mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide, often with belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor, along with hydroxychloroquine, renin-angiotensin blockade and BP control. Stopping hydroxychloroquine is a common trigger for flares. Pacific Islander and Māori patients have higher rates of severe lupus nephritis.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
SLE with an active sediment (red cell casts), rising creatinine, heavy proteinuria, high dsDNA and low complement suggests proliferative (class III/IV) lupus nephritis. Biopsy confirms it before induction therapy.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Lupus Nephritis (Kidney International), PubMed", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38182286/"}
• {"name": "Arthritis Australia / Lupus Australia: Lupus and your kidneys (patient information)", "url": "https://arthritisaustralia.com.au/types-of-arthritis/lupus/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Systemic lupus erythematosus with active urinary sediment: predicting lupus nephritis class

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Class I has normal glomeruli by light microscopy with only mesangial deposits. It does not cause an active sediment, rising creatinine or nephrotic-range proteinuria.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Class VI (over 90% sclerosed glomeruli) causes chronic kidney failure with small kidneys and little active sediment. Her kidneys are normal in size and her decline is recent.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Pure membranous lupus nephritis presents mainly with nephrotic syndrome, often with a bland sediment, and anti-dsDNA and complement may be relatively normal. Red cell casts and rapidly rising creatinine favour proliferative disease.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: TMA from APS causes haemolysis and thrombocytopenia with a bland sediment. Her antiphospholipid antibodies are negative.

key_takeaways: SLE with an active sediment (red cell casts), rising creatinine, heavy proteinuria, high dsDNA and low complement suggests proliferative (class III/IV) lupus nephritis. Biopsy confirms it before induction therapy.

question_text:
A 76-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is brought to the emergency department of a hospital in Ballarat, Victoria, with 4 days of painful mouth ulcers, tiredness and a fever. She has taken methotrexate 15 mg once weekly (every Monday) with folic acid 5 mg weekly for 6 years, with stable blood tests. Ten days ago her GP started trimethoprim 300 mg daily for a urinary tract infection, which she is still taking because 'the chemist said to finish the box'. She also takes perindopril and paracetamol. She confirms she takes methotrexate once weekly only.

Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse 108/min and blood pressure 110/68 mmHg. She has extensive oral ulceration and mucositis and a few petechiae on her legs.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 92 g/L (6 months ago 124); MCV 104 fL
- White cells 1.4 × 10^9/L; neutrophils 0.4 × 10^9/L
- Platelets 38 × 10^9/L
- Creatinine 98 µmol/L (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m²; baseline eGFR 60)
- ALT 64 U/L
- Chest X-ray: clear

Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for her presentation?
options: Methotrexate toxicity potentiated by trimethoprim
Myelodysplastic syndrome unmasked by infection
Vitamin B12 deficiency from long-term folate supplementation
Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia from trimethoprim
Felty syndrome from long-standing rheumatoid arthritis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Methotrexate toxicity potentiated by trimethoprim

---

She has pancytopenia with macrocytosis, severe mucositis and neutropenic fever: the typical picture of methotrexate toxicity. The trigger is the recent addition of trimethoprim, which is an antifolate (dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor) and reduces renal excretion of methotrexate. This interaction is additive and well documented, and the product information warns against the combination. Older age and mildly reduced renal function (worsened by dehydration and an ACE inhibitor) add to the risk. Management: treat as febrile neutropenia (take cultures and give empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately per sepsis guidelines), stop methotrexate and trimethoprim, give folinic acid (calcium folinate) rescue, provide hydration and mouth care, and consider G-CSF and transfusion as needed. Her methotrexate level may be measured, although it can be low after weekly dosing. Patients on methotrexate should avoid trimethoprim and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and pharmacists and GPs should check for this interaction.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Methotrexate + trimethoprim (or co-trimoxazole) can cause life-threatening marrow suppression and mucositis, especially in older patients with reduced renal function. Stop both, give folinic acid, and treat febrile neutropenia.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "Case series: Methotrexate and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole interaction (PMC)", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3994806/"}
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber: Methotrexate (safety, interactions)", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/methotrexate.html"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Pancytopenia in a patient on methotrexate: interaction with trimethoprim

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: MDS can cause macrocytic pancytopenia in older adults, but it would not appear abruptly with mucositis after an interacting antifolate, with previously stable counts.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Folic acid does not cause B12 deficiency (it can mask the anaemia), and B12 deficiency does not cause acute mucositis with neutropenic fever.

question_text:
A 52-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Mandurah, Western Australia, because his wife noticed a mole on his upper back had changed. He is a fair-skinned former surveyor with extensive past sun exposure. He has had two basal cell carcinomas removed. There is no family history of melanoma.

On examination there is a 7 mm pigmented lesion on the left upper back with an irregular border and uneven colours (brown, black and a grey area). His wife's photographs from 6 months ago show a smaller, more uniform lesion. Dermoscopy shows an atypical pigment network, irregular dots and globules, and a blue-white veil. There is no palpable axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy. The lesion is on flat skin that can be closed easily.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Shave biopsy of the most raised part of the lesion
Wide local excision with a 1 cm margin
Excisional biopsy with a 2 mm clinical margin
Punch biopsy of the darkest area and review
Repeat photography and dermoscopy in 3 months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Excisional biopsy with a 2 mm clinical margin

---

The lesion is suspicious for melanoma: it is changing, asymmetric in colour and border, and shows several dermoscopic melanoma features. Australian melanoma guidelines (Cancer Council Australia) recommend complete EXCISIONAL biopsy with a 2 mm clinical margin and a cuff of subcutaneous fat as the preferred first step. This gives the pathologist the whole lesion to measure Breslow thickness accurately, which determines staging, re-excision margins and whether sentinel lymph node biopsy is discussed. Excising with a narrow margin, closed along the line of lymphatic drainage, preserves accurate lymphatic mapping if sentinel node biopsy is needed later. Once the diagnosis and thickness are known, definitive wide excision follows (for example 5–10 mm for in situ disease, 1 cm for melanoma 1 mm or less thick, 1–2 cm for more than 1 mm up to 4 mm, and 2 cm for more than 4 mm).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected melanoma: excisional biopsy with a 2 mm clinical margin (and some fat) for accurate Breslow thickness. Definitive wide excision margins are set after histology.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of melanoma \u2013 biopsy", "url": "https://www.cancer.org.au/clinical-guidelines/skin-cancer/melanoma"}
• {"name": "Cancer Council NSW: Melanoma skin cancer \u2013 guide for medical practitioners (2023, PDF)", "url": "https://www.cancercouncil.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/melanoma-skin-cancer-guide-for-medical-practitioners.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspicious changing pigmented lesion: optimal initial biopsy technique

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Shave biopsies can transect the lesion and underestimate Breslow thickness, compromising staging.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Wide excision before diagnosis is not recommended. It may be unnecessary and can disrupt lymphatic drainage for later sentinel node mapping; margins are chosen after histology.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Partial (punch or incisional) biopsy risks sampling error and inaccurate thickness. It is reserved for large lesions or cosmetically sensitive sites where full excision is impractical.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: A changing lesion with multiple dermoscopic melanoma features should not be monitored; it needs excision now.

key_takeaways: Suspected melanoma: excisional biopsy with a 2 mm clinical margin (and some fat) for accurate Breslow thickness. Definitive wide excision margins are set after histology.

question_text:
A 61-year-old man is being treated through Royal Darwin Hospital's Hospital-in-the-Home service with IV vancomycin for MRSA vertebral osteomyelitis. He is in his fourth week of therapy, with vancomycin troughs in the target range. For 3 days he has had fever and an itchy rash that started on his face and upper trunk and has spread to most of his body. His face is swollen. He has no mouth, eye or genital soreness. He takes no other new medicines.

His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse 104/min and blood pressure 124/74 mmHg. He has a confluent, morbilliform red rash covering about 60% of his body surface area, with marked facial oedema. There are no blisters, pustules or skin detachment, and Nikolsky sign is negative. Mucous membranes are normal. He has tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy.

Investigations:
- White cells 16.4 × 10^9/L; eosinophils 2.8 × 10^9/L (<0.5)
- Blood film: atypical (reactive) lymphocytes
- ALT 412 U/L; ALP 210 U/L; bilirubin 22 µmol/L
- Creatinine 132 µmol/L (baseline 80)

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)
Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)
Vancomycin infusion reaction (vancomycin flushing syndrome)
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

---

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction. It typically starts 2–8 weeks after a new drug and causes fever, a widespread morbilliform rash (often more than 50% of the body surface) with facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and/or atypical lymphocytes, and internal organ involvement, most often the liver, then the kidneys. Vancomycin is one of the commonest causes of DRESS, along with allopurinol, anticonvulsants and sulfonamides. The RegiSCAR score helps confirm the diagnosis; he scores highly. Management: stop the culprit drug immediately (switch to a structurally unrelated anti-MRSA agent, for example daptomycin, with ID advice), admit, give supportive care, and start systemic corticosteroids for significant organ involvement. Document the allergy clearly as a severe reaction. Monitor for late complications, including thyroiditis and diabetes months later.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
DRESS: 2–8 weeks after a new drug, with fever, widespread rash and facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia/atypical lymphocytes and organ involvement (liver, kidney). Vancomycin is a common cause. Stop the drug and give steroids for organ involvement.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "DermNet: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)", "url": "https://dermnetnz.org/topics/drug-hypersensitivity-syndrome"}
• {"name": "ASCIA: Drug allergy \u2013 severe cutaneous adverse reactions (health professional information)", "url": "https://www.allergy.org.au/hp/papers/drug-allergy"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Delayed drug hypersensitivity during outpatient IV antibiotic therapy: recognising DRESS

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: SJS causes painful mucosal erosions (two or more sites) and blistering with less than 10% skin detachment. He has no mucosal involvement or blisters.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: TEN has more than 30% epidermal detachment, a positive Nikolsky sign and mucosal involvement. None of these is present.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: AGEP appears within days of a new drug (often beta-lactams), with hundreds of small sterile pustules on a red background, and resolves rapidly after stopping the drug. It is not associated with weeks of latency and marked eosinophilia with hepatitis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Vancomycin flushing syndrome (formerly 'red man syndrome') occurs during or soon after the infusion, is rate-related, affects the face, neck and upper trunk, and does not cause fever, eosinophilia or organ injury.

key_takeaways: DRESS: 2–8 weeks after a new drug, with fever, widespread rash and facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia/atypical lymphocytes and organ involvement (liver, kidney). Vancomycin is a common cause. Stop the drug and give steroids for organ involvement.

question_text:
A 54-year-old Aboriginal woman from a remote community in Central Australia is admitted to Alice Springs Hospital, Northern Territory, with a 2-month history of thick, scaly, crusted skin on her hands, elbows, buttocks and feet. Her itch is mild. She has type 2 diabetes and stage 3 chronic kidney disease and had a fall at home 3 weeks ago. Her grandchildren, who live with her, have had itchy rashes and several have had skin sores treated at the community clinic.

On examination she has thick, grey-yellow, fissured crusts over the hands, wrists, elbows, buttocks and soles, with nail thickening. There are some areas of impetiginised skin. Skin scrapings show numerous Sarcoptes scabiei mites and eggs. Her temperature is 37.4°C. She is admitted with an Aboriginal Liaison Officer involved, and the treating team has graded her crusted scabies as grade 2 using the NT grading tool.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment plan?
options: Topical permethrin 5% repeated in 7 days, and discharge to community follow-up
Multi-dose oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg with permethrin and keratolytic cream
A single dose of oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg, and treat household contacts
Oral prednisolone for eczema and flucloxacillin for skin infection, then review
Topical benzyl benzoate 25% daily for 7 days, with no need for oral treatment
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Multi-dose oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg with permethrin and keratolytic cream

---

Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is a severe form with a massive mite burden. It is highly contagious and a reservoir for recurrent scabies, impetigo, and downstream complications (for example acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and possibly rheumatic heart disease) in remote communities. Secondary bacterial sepsis carries significant mortality. NT Health guidance recommends admission and a combined approach: repeated oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg (with food), with the number of doses set by the severity grade (grade 1: 3 doses on days 0, 1 and 7; grade 2: 5 doses adding days 8 and 14; grade 3: 7 doses adding days 21 and 28). This is combined with topical permethrin 5% and a keratolytic cream (for example urea with lactic acid) to break down crusts. Crusted scabies is notifiable in the NT. Household and community contacts need simultaneous treatment, with environmental measures (washing bedding and clothing). Care should be culturally safe and involve Aboriginal Health Practitioners or Liaison Officers, family and the community clinic. Her possible immune compromise (diabetes, CKD) should also be considered, and HTLV-1 serology is often checked in Central Australia.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Crusted scabies: admit; oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg in 3, 5 or 7 doses by grade, plus permethrin 5% and a keratolytic. It is notifiable in the NT; treat contacts and involve Aboriginal health staff and the community clinic.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NT Health: Scabies (public health, including crusted scabies)", "url": "https://health.nt.gov.au/public-health-notifiable-diseases/scabies"}
• {"name": "NT Health: Crusted scabies \u2013 clinical guideline (NT Health Digital Library)", "url": "https://digitallibrary.health.nt.gov.au/nthealthserver/api/core/bitstreams/c91ad290-ef58-4379-b428-48c4bb6297ad/content"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Crusted scabies in a remote-community patient: inpatient multi-dose ivermectin and public health response

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Topical treatment alone cannot penetrate thick crusts and fails in crusted scabies. Early discharge also risks ongoing community transmission.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A single ivermectin dose (repeated in 7–14 days) suits ordinary scabies. Crusted scabies needs multiple doses by grade plus topical and keratolytic therapy, and contacts need treatment too.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This is scabies, not eczema. Steroids would worsen infestation. The impetigo needs antibiotics, but the underlying infestation must be treated.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Topical therapy alone, without oral ivermectin and keratolytics, is inadequate for crusted scabies.

key_takeaways: Crusted scabies: admit; oral ivermectin 200 microgram/kg in 3, 5 or 7 doses by grade, plus permethrin 5% and a keratolytic. It is notifiable in the NT; treat contacts and involve Aboriginal health staff and the community clinic.

question_text:
An 84-year-old man is in his third day on the medical ward at South West Healthcare, Warrnambool, Victoria, after admission with cellulitis of the left leg, now improving on IV cefazolin. Overnight he became agitated and disoriented, tried to climb out of bed, and pulled at his cannula. The day before, he was lucid. He has mild cognitive impairment and benign prostatic hyperplasia. His medicines include amitriptyline 25 mg at night (for nerve pain), oxycodone 5 mg as needed (taken 4 times in the last 24 hours), and paracetamol. Nursing staff report he has been passing small amounts of urine frequently and had no bowel action for 3 days.

His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse 94/min, blood pressure 142/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He is inattentive (cannot count backwards from 20) and restless, without focal neurological signs. The leg erythema is receding. He has lower abdominal fullness that is dull to percussion, and he groans when this is palpated.

Investigations this morning:
- White cells 9.1 × 10^9/L (admission 15.2)
- Sodium 138 mmol/L; creatinine 118 µmol/L (admission 92)
- Capillary glucose 7.2 mmol/L

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step to identify the cause of his delirium?
options: Non-contrast CT scan of the brain
Urine dipstick and culture
Bladder scan for residual urine volume
Electroencephalogram (EEG) this morning
Serum ammonia and thyroid function
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Bladder scan for residual urine volume

---

He has new, fluctuating inattention and agitation, which is hyperactive delirium. The most likely precipitant is acute urinary retention: benign prostatic hyperplasia, an anticholinergic drug (amitriptyline), opioid use and constipation all predispose to it. Frequent small voids (overflow), a dull, tender suprapubic mass and a rising creatinine support this. The ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard asks clinicians to identify and treat the underlying causes. A bedside bladder scan is quick and non-invasive and immediately confirms retention, which should then be relieved by catheterisation. Other steps: review and deprescribe amitriptyline and minimise opioids, treat constipation, use non-drug strategies (orientation, family involvement, sleep hygiene), and avoid physical restraint and routine antipsychotics.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In older inpatients with delirium, look for retention and constipation (especially with BPH, anticholinergics and opioids). A bedside bladder scan is a quick first step; avoid blaming a positive dipstick.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard (2021)", "url": "https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/standards/clinical-care-standards/delirium-clinical-care-standard"}
• {"name": "Queensland Health: Residential aged care clinical pathway \u2013 new or worsened confusion", "url": "https://www.health.qld.gov.au/clinical-practice/guidelines-procedures/clinical-pathways/residential-aged-care-clinical-pathways/all-pathways/new-or-worsened-confusion"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Hyperactive delirium in an older inpatient on anticholinergic medication: bedside search for urinary retention

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: He has no head injury or focal neurological signs and has a clear alternative cause. CT is not the first step here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Dipstick testing in older adults is unreliable because asymptomatic bacteriuria is common; a positive result could lead to wrongly blaming a UTI and missing retention. Retention should be confirmed first.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: EEG is reserved for suspected non-convulsive status epilepticus. It is not a first-line delirium investigation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: There is no liver disease or thyroid history to suggest these, and they would not explain his suprapubic findings.

question_text:
An 81-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease (eGFR 8 mL/min/1.73 m²) has chosen conservative (non-dialysis) kidney management. He is receiving end-of-life care at home in Launceston, Tasmania, supported by the community palliative care team. Five days ago, for painful bone metastases from prostate cancer, he was started on a continuous subcutaneous infusion of morphine 10 mg/24 hours via a syringe driver, with morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously as needed (he has used 3 breakthrough doses a day).

His wife reports he has become increasingly drowsy and muddled over 2 days, sees 'insects on the walls' and has jerking of his arms and legs. His pain is well controlled. On examination he is drowsy but rousable and oriented to person only, respiratory rate 14/min, pupils 3 mm, with multifocal myoclonus. He has no fever, and his bowels opened yesterday. His goals of care are comfort at home, and there is an advance care directive.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Increase the morphine infusion to 15 mg/24 hours for better comfort
Give naloxone 400 microgram IV bolus and stop the opioid
Add subcutaneous midazolam and continue the morphine unchanged
Switch to subcutaneous fentanyl at a reduced equianalgesic dose
Change to oral tramadol, which is less sedating than morphine
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Switch to subcutaneous fentanyl at a reduced equianalgesic dose

---

He has opioid-induced neurotoxicity: drowsiness, delirium with hallucinations, and myoclonus, with good pain control. In severe kidney impairment, morphine's active metabolites (morphine-3-glucuronide and morphine-6-glucuronide) accumulate and cause these effects. Management is to rotate to an opioid that is safer in kidney failure. Fentanyl is metabolised in the liver to inactive metabolites and is preferred in end-stage kidney disease. A conservative starting dose (reduced from the calculated equianalgesic dose to allow for incomplete cross-tolerance) is used, with breakthrough fentanyl doses and advice from the palliative care team. Other supportive measures: hydration if consistent with goals of care, reviewing other contributing drugs, and treating reversible causes such as constipation and urinary retention. Midazolam can help distressing myoclonus but does not treat the cause.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Opioid neurotoxicity (drowsiness, hallucinations, myoclonus) on morphine in severe CKD: rotate to fentanyl (hepatic metabolism, no active metabolites) at a reduced equianalgesic dose. Avoid morphine, codeine and tramadol in ESKD.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Eastern Palliative Care Victoria (EPCVic) / Palliative Care Victoria: Opioid Conversion Workbook (August 2024)", "url": "https://www.epcvic.org.au/uploads/778/64/Opioid-Conversion-Workbook-August-2024.pdf"}
• {"name": "WA Cancer and Palliative Care Network: Evidence-based clinical guidelines for adults in the terminal phase (2nd edition)", "url": "https://ahs.health.wa.gov.au/~/media/Files/Corporate/general-documents/Health-Networks/WA-Cancer-and-Palliative-Care/Palliative-care/Evidencebasedclinicalguidelinesforadultsintheterminalphase-2nd-Ed.pdf"}

---

subtopic: Opioid neurotoxicity in end-stage kidney disease on conservative care: opioid rotation

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: His respiratory rate is 14/min, so there is no opioid-induced respiratory depression. A full 400 microgram bolus in an opioid-tolerant patient in pain would precipitate severe pain and withdrawal. If ever needed, naloxone is given in small titrated doses.

question_text:
A 34-year-old man weighing 68 kg is brought to the emergency department of Cairns Hospital, Queensland, by ambulance. Two hours ago, after an argument, he swallowed 32 tablets of modified-release paracetamol 665 mg (for arthritis, from his mother's supply). He took nothing else and has not drunk alcohol. He is alert, cooperative and not vomiting. He says he regrets taking them.

His observations are normal and GCS 15. Examination is normal. Baseline blood tests have been sent, including a paracetamol concentration, liver function tests, INR, electrolytes and creatinine. The mental health liaison team has been contacted, and he is under appropriate supervision.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management of the overdose?
options: Activated charcoal, then start acetylcysteine if the 4-hour level is above the nomogram line
Activated charcoal, start acetylcysteine now and complete the full 20-hour course
Start acetylcysteine now with the second bag doubled to 200 mg/kg over 16 hours
No charcoal; take a 4-hour level and treat according to the nomogram line
Start acetylcysteine now, then stop it if two levels 4 hours apart are below the line
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Activated charcoal, start acetylcysteine now and complete the full 20-hour course

---

He has taken 32 × 665 mg = about 21.3 g of modified-release (MR) paracetamol, which is about 313 mg/kg. Under the 2020 ANZ paracetamol poisoning guidelines (Chiew et al., MJA), MR ingestions of 10 g or more, or 200 mg/kg or more (whichever is less), need specific management because absorption is delayed and prolonged: (1) Activated charcoal 50 g should be offered up to 4 hours after ingestion to a cooperative, awake patient. (2) Acetylcysteine should be started immediately, and a full 20-hour course given regardless of the serum paracetamol concentration. The nomogram cannot be used to decide on treatment after MR ingestion. (3) Two paracetamol concentrations 4 hours apart (the first at least 4 hours after ingestion) are used to guide dose and duration. The second bag is doubled (200 mg/kg over 16 hours) if either concentration is more than double the nomogram line, or if the ingestion is 30 g or more or 500 mg/kg or more. His 21 g (about 313 mg/kg) does not automatically qualify. ALT and paracetamol are rechecked near the end of the infusion. The standard two-bag regimen is 200 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours, with adult doses based on actual weight rounded up to the nearest 10 kg (70 kg here). A psychosocial assessment is needed once he is medically stable.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
MR paracetamol of 10 g or more or 200 mg/kg or more: charcoal up to 4 hours, and start acetylcysteine immediately and complete the full 20-hour course regardless of levels. Double the second bag if 30 g or more/500 mg/kg or more, or a level above double the line.

---

REFERENCES

question_text:
A 39-year-old cotton farmer is brought to the emergency department of Moree District Hospital, New South Wales, at 1500 hours. At 1330 hours, while moving irrigation pipes, he felt a sharp pain on his left ankle and saw a brown snake moving away. His co-worker applied an elasticised pressure bandage over the whole leg and a splint, and the ambulance crew kept him still. He has had no headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, collapse, blurred vision or bleeding.

On arrival he is well, with pulse 78/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg and normal neurological examination (no ptosis, diplopia or weakness). The pressure bandage and splint are in place. There are two small scratch marks on the ankle without ongoing bleeding. The hospital stocks antivenom.

Baseline investigations (taken on arrival, 1500 hours):
- INR 1.0; APTT 29 s; fibrinogen 3.1 g/L; D-dimer normal
- CK 140 U/L
- Full blood count and creatinine normal

According to NSW guidance, which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Remove the bandage in a critical care area; repeat bloods at 1 hour, then 6 and 12 hours
Swab the bite site for a venom detection kit to choose the correct antivenom
Give one vial of brown snake antivenom now, before removing the pressure bandage
Leave the pressure bandage on until 12 hours after the bite, then repeat the bloods
Remove the bandage, and discharge him if bloods are normal at 6 hours after the bite
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Remove the bandage in a critical care area; repeat bloods at 1 hour, then 6 and 12 hours

---

The NSW Health Snake and Spider Bites Clinical Management guideline (GL2024_007) says that if baseline blood tests are normal and there is no clinical envenomation, the pressure bandage with immobilisation (PBI) can be removed in a critical care area under medical direction, with antivenom available. Envenomation usually becomes evident within about an hour of removal, because the bandage acts as a 'dam' slowing lymphatic spread of venom. Serial coagulation studies (INR, APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) and CK are then repeated at 1 hour after PBI removal, 6 hours after the bite and 12 hours after the bite. All patients with suspected snakebite must be observed for 12 hours from the time of the bite. Discharge is appropriate only if tests at 6 and 12 hours are normal and the patient is well. Abnormal results (for example venom-induced consumption coagulopathy) or neurotoxicity at any stage mean he is envenomed and needs antivenom.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected snakebite, normal baseline tests and no symptoms: remove the PBI in a critical care area, then take coagulation studies and CK at 1 hour after removal and at 6 and 12 hours after the bite. Observe for 12 hours; no venom detection kit.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NSW Health Guideline GL2024_007: Snake and Spider Bites Clinical Management (June 2024)", "url": "https://www1.health.nsw.gov.au/pds/ActivePDSDocuments/GL2024_007.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspected snakebite with normal baseline tests: pressure bandage removal and serial blood testing

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: NSW guidance states that venom detection kits are no longer recommended, and swabbing the wound is not advised. Antivenom choice relies on geography, clinical syndrome and toxicology advice.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Antivenom is given only for clinical or laboratory evidence of envenomation. Empirical antivenom in a well patient with normal tests exposes him to anaphylaxis risk without benefit.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Leaving the PBI on unnecessarily for 12 hours delays detection of envenomation and risks limb ischaemia and discomfort. It is removed once baseline tests are normal and the patient is well.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: A single normal 6-hour set is insufficient; observation for 12 hours after the bite with a 12-hour set of bloods is required before discharge.

key_takeaways: Suspected snakebite, normal baseline tests and no symptoms: remove the PBI in a critical care area, then take coagulation studies and CK at 1 hour after removal and at 6 and 12 hours after the bite. Observe for 12 hours; no venom detection kit.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of Hervey Bay Hospital, Queensland, 20 minutes after eating prawns at a restaurant. She developed generalised hives, lip swelling, wheeze, dizziness and vomiting within 10 minutes. She has no known allergies and takes no regular medicines, including no beta-blockers. Paramedics gave adrenaline 0.5 mg IM into the thigh, and a second 0.5 mg IM dose 5 minutes later. She has since received 2 L of IV 0.9% sodium chloride, lying flat, with high-flow oxygen.

Now her pulse is 128/min, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min and oxygen saturation 93% on high-flow oxygen. She has widespread wheeze but is talking in phrases, with no stridor. She is alert. Cardiac monitoring shows sinus tachycardia. The emergency physician has called for senior and ICU help.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: IV hydrocortisone 200 mg and IV promethazine 25 mg
IV adrenaline 1 mg bolus, repeated every 3–5 minutes
Nebulised salbutamol and observe for 30 minutes
IV glucagon 1 mg bolus followed by an infusion
IV adrenaline infusion with continuous monitoring
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. IV adrenaline infusion with continuous monitoring

---

She has refractory anaphylaxis: persisting hypotension after 2 appropriate doses of IM adrenaline and fluid resuscitation. ASCIA and the ANZCOR refractory anaphylaxis algorithm recommend starting an IV adrenaline infusion (by clinicians experienced in its use, with continuous cardiac and blood pressure monitoring) when there is inadequate response to 2 or more IM doses. IM adrenaline can be continued every 5 minutes while the infusion is set up. More fluid boluses (for example a further 20 mL/kg) should be given, with early ICU and airway expert involvement. If hypotension persists despite the adrenaline infusion, a second vasopressor (for example noradrenaline or vasopressin) may be added. Glucagon is considered for patients on beta-blockers. Corticosteroids and antihistamines are not first-line: they do not treat hypotension or airway obstruction.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Anaphylaxis still hypotensive after 2 IM adrenaline doses plus fluids: start an IV adrenaline infusion with monitoring and call ICU. No IV 1 mg boluses unless in cardiac arrest; glucagon only with beta-blockers.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ASCIA: Acute management of anaphylaxis guidelines", "url": "https://www.allergy.org.au/hp/papers/acute-management-of-anaphylaxis-guidelines"}
• {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.10: Refractory anaphylaxis algorithm (July 2026)", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/assets/ANZCOR-Guidelines-/GL-11/GL-11-10-Flowcharts/GL-11.10-Refractory-anaphylaxis-algorithm-July-2026.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Refractory anaphylaxis despite two IM adrenaline doses and fluids: next step

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Steroids and antihistamines have no role in reversing shock. Promethazine is also a sedating antihistamine that can worsen hypotension; ASCIA does not recommend it in anaphylaxis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A 1 mg IV bolus is a cardiac arrest dose. In a patient with a pulse it risks severe hypertension, arrhythmia and myocardial ischaemia. IV adrenaline in anaphylaxis with a pulse is given as a titrated infusion.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Salbutamol may help bronchospasm as an add-on, but it does not treat shock. Observation alone would be unsafe.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Glucagon is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis in patients taking beta-blockers. She takes none, and adrenaline has not yet been given IV.

key_takeaways: Anaphylaxis still hypotensive after 2 IM adrenaline doses plus fluids: start an IV adrenaline infusion with monitoring and call ICU. No IV 1 mg boluses unless in cardiac arrest; glucagon only with beta-blockers.
