question_text:
A 64-year-old woman comes to the emergency department of a hospital in Wagga Wagga, New South Wales, with two days of colicky central abdominal pain, abdominal distension and vomiting. She has not passed flatus for 24 hours. She had an open appendicectomy at the age of 19 and an abdominal hysterectomy at 45. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine.

Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg and respiratory rate 18/min. Her abdomen is distended and tympanic, with mild diffuse tenderness but no guarding or rebound. There is no hernia, and bowel sounds are high-pitched.

Investigations:
- White cell count 10.8 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (<5)
- Venous lactate 1.3 mmol/L (<2.0)
- Sodium 134 mmol/L (135–145)
- Potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Creatinine 96 µmol/L (45–90)
- CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast: dilated small bowel loops up to 38 mm with a single transition point in the right lower quadrant and collapsed distal ileum. No closed loop, normal bowel wall enhancement, no mesenteric oedema, no free fluid and no free gas.

A nasogastric tube has drained 900 mL of bilious fluid. IV fluids with potassium replacement have been started, and the surgical registrar has reviewed her.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Emergency midline laparotomy and adhesiolysis today
Laparoscopic adhesiolysis on the next available emergency list
Water-soluble oral contrast via the nasogastric tube, then an abdominal X-ray
Continue nasogastric decompression and IV fluids for 5 days before reassessing
Barium small bowel follow-through to define the level of obstruction
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Water-soluble oral contrast via the nasogastric tube, then an abdominal X-ray

---

This is adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO) without CT signs of strangulation or ischaemia (no closed loop, normal wall enhancement, no free fluid, normal lactate) and without peritonism, so non-operative management is appropriate. The WSES Bologna guidelines (2017 update) recommend a water-soluble contrast agent (e.g. diatrizoate/Gastrografin), given orally or via the nasogastric tube, followed by an abdominal X-ray, usually at up to 24 hours. Contrast in the colon predicts resolution, so the patient can be fed. If contrast has not reached the colon by 24 hours, non-operative management is likely to fail and surgery should be considered. The contrast is also mildly therapeutic: it shortens time to resolution and hospital stay. Non-operative management should not usually continue beyond about 72 hours without resolution. Surgery is needed at any point if signs of strangulation, peritonitis or clinical deterioration appear.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In adhesive SBO without CT or clinical signs of strangulation, give water-soluble contrast and X-ray at up to 24 hours. Contrast in the colon predicts resolution; its absence predicts failure of non-operative care.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ten Broek RPG et al. Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO): 2017 update of the WSES guidelines. World J Emerg Surg 2018;13:24", "url": "https://wjes.biomedcentral.com/counter/pdf/10.1186/s13017-018-0185-2.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Adhesive small bowel obstruction: water-soluble contrast challenge

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Immediate laparotomy is for strangulation, peritonitis, closed-loop obstruction or ischaemia on CT. None is present, and most ASBO settles without surgery.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Laparoscopic adhesiolysis is an option in selected patients who need surgery, but she has not yet had a trial of non-operative management, which is first line here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The Bologna guidelines advise against prolonged non-operative management: failure to resolve within about 72 hours should prompt surgery. Leaving out the contrast challenge also loses its diagnostic and therapeutic value.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Barium should be avoided in suspected obstruction because it can inspissate and cause barium peritonitis if there is a perforation. CT has already defined the level.

key_takeaways: In adhesive SBO without CT or clinical signs of strangulation, give water-soluble contrast and X-ray at up to 24 hours. Contrast in the colon predicts resolution; its absence predicts failure of non-operative care.

question_text:
A 47-year-old woman was admitted to a public hospital in Hobart three days ago with severe epigastric pain radiating to her back and vomiting. Her lipase on admission was 3800 U/L (<60). She has no history of alcohol use disorder and takes no regular medicines.

Admission ultrasound showed multiple small gallstones, a gallbladder wall of normal thickness, and a common bile duct of 5 mm with no duct stone seen. She received IV fluids and analgesia and did not need oxygen, vasopressors or renal support. Her pain has now settled and she is eating a low-fat diet without pain.

Today her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse 76/min and blood pressure 124/78 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness.

Investigations (admission → today):
- Bilirubin 28 → 12 µmol/L (<20)
- ALT 310 → 84 U/L (<35)
- ALP 160 → 118 U/L (30–110)
- White cell count 13.1 → 8.2 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- Creatinine 70 → 62 µmol/L (45–90)
- C-reactive protein 95 → 60 mg/L (<5)

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission
Discharge and arrange elective cholecystectomy in 6 to 8 weeks
ERCP with sphincterotomy before discharge
Discharge with ursodeoxycholic acid and a low-fat diet
CT abdomen at 72 hours to exclude necrosis before any surgery
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission

---

She has mild acute biliary pancreatitis by the revised Atlanta classification: no organ failure and no local or systemic complications, with clinical resolution. International guidelines (IAP/APA, and the 2023 MANCTRA acute biliary pancreatitis bundle) recommend cholecystectomy during the index admission for mild biliary pancreatitis. The PONCHO trial showed that same-admission cholecystectomy roughly halved readmission for recurrent gallstone-related complications (recurrent pancreatitis, cholangitis, colic) compared with interval surgery, with no increase in operative difficulty. Her liver tests are falling, the duct is not dilated and there is no cholangitis, so routine ERCP is not indicated. Intraoperative cholangiography can assess the duct at surgery if needed. Delayed cholecystectomy is reserved for severe pancreatitis with peripancreatic collections, when surgery waits until inflammation settles or collections resolve (commonly after about 6 weeks).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Mild gallstone pancreatitis: cholecystectomy in the same admission. Delay surgery only for severe pancreatitis with collections. ERCP only for cholangitis or persistent obstruction.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Podda M et al. The 2023 MANCTRA Acute Biliary Pancreatitis Care Bundle. Ann Surg 2023 (open access, PMC)", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10782931/"}
• {"name": "AGA: Diagnosis and management of acute pancreatitis (Gastroenterology, 2024)", "url": "https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(24)04916-3/fulltext"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Mild gallstone pancreatitis: timing of cholecystectomy

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Interval cholecystectomy exposes her to a significant risk of a recurrent biliary event while waiting. It is the strategy for severe pancreatitis, not mild disease.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: ERCP is for cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. It does not prevent recurrent pancreatitis as well as cholecystectomy, and it carries a risk of post-ERCP pancreatitis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Ursodeoxycholic acid does not reliably prevent recurrent gallstone pancreatitis and is not a substitute for cholecystectomy in a fit patient.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Routine CT is not needed in mild pancreatitis that is resolving clinically. CT is for diagnostic doubt or failure to improve (usually after 72–96 hours).

key_takeaways: Mild gallstone pancreatitis: cholecystectomy in the same admission. Delay surgery only for severe pancreatitis with collections. ERCP only for cholangitis or persistent obstruction.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man is admitted under the general surgical team at a hospital in Ipswich, Queensland, with 18 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal. He has had three similar but shorter episodes in the past year. He has no fever or rigors, and his urine is a normal colour. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin.

His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse 88/min and blood pressure 138/84 mmHg. He is not jaundiced. He is tender in the right upper quadrant with a negative Murphy's sign.

Investigations:
- White cell count 9.6 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- Bilirubin 42 µmol/L (<20)
- ALT 220 U/L (<40)
- GGT 310 U/L (<60)
- ALP 190 U/L (30–110)
- Lipase 45 U/L (<60)
- Abdominal ultrasound: multiple gallstones, gallbladder wall 2 mm, no pericholecystic fluid. Common bile duct 8 mm. The distal duct is obscured by bowel gas and no duct stone is seen.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen
Repeat liver function tests in 6 weeks
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)

---

The ASGE 2019 guideline stratifies suspected choledocholithiasis. HIGH risk (go straight to ERCP) means any of: a duct stone seen on ultrasound or CT, clinical ascending cholangitis, or bilirubin above 4 mg/dL (about 68 µmol/L) together with a dilated duct. INTERMEDIATE risk means abnormal liver tests, age over 55, or a dilated duct on ultrasound without high-risk features. He has a dilated duct (8 mm), abnormal liver tests and is over 55, but his bilirubin is 42 µmol/L (about 2.5 mg/dL), no stone is seen and he has no cholangitis. So he is intermediate risk. Intermediate-risk patients should have confirmatory imaging with MRCP or EUS (or intraoperative cholangiography/laparoscopic ultrasound at cholecystectomy) before ERCP. This avoids diagnostic ERCP and its risks (pancreatitis, bleeding, perforation) in the many patients whose stone has already passed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
ASGE 2019: stone on imaging, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL (~68 µmol/L) with a dilated duct → ERCP. Otherwise abnormal LFTs, age >55 or dilated duct → MRCP/EUS first.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ASGE guideline on the role of endoscopy in the evaluation and management of choledocholithiasis (Gastrointest Endosc 2019)", "url": "https://www.asge.org/docs/default-source/guidelines/asge-guideline-on-the-role-of-endoscopy-in-the-evaluation-and-management-of-choledocholithiasis-2019-june-gie.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspected choledocholithiasis: risk stratification before ERCP

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: ERCP is for high-risk patients. Using it diagnostically in intermediate-risk patients exposes many people with no duct stone to post-ERCP pancreatitis and other complications.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A HIDA scan assesses cystic duct patency in suspected acute cholecystitis. It does not show duct stones or anatomy well enough to plan ERCP.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: CT has poor sensitivity for non-calcified duct stones and adds radiation. It is not the preferred confirmatory test.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: He has a dilated duct and obstructive liver tests now. Waiting 6 weeks risks cholangitis or pancreatitis from a retained stone.

key_takeaways: ASGE 2019: stone on imaging, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL (~68 µmol/L) with a dilated duct → ERCP. Otherwise abnormal LFTs, age >55 or dilated duct → MRCP/EUS first.

question_text:
A 79-year-old man is on the orthopaedic ward of a hospital in Bendigo, Victoria, four days after an elective right total knee replacement. Since day 2 he has had progressive abdominal distension with little pain. He has passed small amounts of flatus but no stool. He has been taking oxycodone for analgesia. He has hypertension and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

CT on day 2 showed gross dilatation of the caecum, ascending and transverse colon to the splenic flexure, with a caecal diameter of 10.5 cm. There was no transition point, no mass, no volvulus, no pneumatosis and no free gas. Since then he has been nil by mouth with a nasogastric tube and a rectal tube, oxycodone has been replaced with paracetamol and regional techniques, and his potassium and magnesium have been corrected. He has been mobilised as far as possible.

Today, 48 hours later, his temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 76/min and regular, and blood pressure 134/80 mmHg. His abdomen is tensely distended and tympanic but soft and non-tender. ECG shows sinus rhythm. Potassium is 4.2 mmol/L, magnesium 0.9 mmol/L and lactate 1.1 mmol/L. An abdominal X-ray shows a caecal diameter of 12 cm.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Emergency right hemicolectomy
IV neostigmine with cardiac monitoring and atropine at the bedside
Continue current conservative management and add IV metoclopramide
Percutaneous radiological caecostomy
Phosphate enema and oral macrogol to stimulate the colon
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. IV neostigmine with cardiac monitoring and atropine at the bedside

---

This is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome): massive colonic dilatation without mechanical obstruction, typically after orthopaedic surgery in older patients, worsened by opioids. The first 24–48 hours of supportive care (bowel rest, decompression, stopping opioids and anticholinergics, correcting electrolytes, mobilising) has failed, and the caecum has grown to 12 cm. The risk of ischaemia and perforation rises with caecal diameter above about 12 cm and with duration. The ASCRS 2021 guideline strongly recommends IV neostigmine when supportive care fails and there is no mechanical obstruction, ischaemia or perforation. Give it (commonly 2 mg IV slowly) with continuous cardiac monitoring and atropine immediately available, because bradycardia is the main risk. Mild COPD is a relative caution, not a contraindication. Colonoscopic decompression is the next step if neostigmine fails or is contraindicated. Surgery is reserved for perforation, ischaemia or failure of these measures.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Ogilvie syndrome: supportive care first; if it fails (or caecum is enlarging towards ~12 cm) give IV neostigmine with cardiac monitoring and atropine ready. Colonoscopic decompression next, surgery last.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ASCRS Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Colonic Volvulus and Acute Colonic Pseudo-Obstruction (2021)", "url": "https://www.ascrsu.com/ascrs/view/ASCRS-Evidence-Based-Guidelines-and-Expert-Consensus/3982019/all/Management_of_Colonic_Volvulus_and_Acute_Colonic_Pseudo_Obstruction__2021_"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) after failed conservative care

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Surgery is for perforation, ischaemia or peritonitis, or failure of medical and endoscopic treatment. It carries high mortality in this group and is not indicated with a soft, non-tender abdomen.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Supportive care has already failed at 48 hours and the caecum is enlarging. Metoclopramide has no proven role in colonic pseudo-obstruction and delay increases the risk of perforation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Caecostomy is a salvage option for patients who fail medical and endoscopic decompression and are unfit for surgery. It is not the next step.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Stimulant or osmotic laxatives can worsen distension and are not recommended in acute colonic pseudo-obstruction.

key_takeaways: Ogilvie syndrome: supportive care first; if it fails (or caecum is enlarging towards ~12 cm) give IV neostigmine with cardiac monitoring and atropine ready. Colonoscopic decompression next, surgery last.

question_text:
A 66-year-old man is on the colorectal ward of a tertiary hospital in Perth, five days after a laparoscopic high anterior resection with a primary stapled anastomosis and no defunctioning stoma, for a sigmoid adenocarcinoma. He was eating a light diet on day 3 but since yesterday has felt bloated, has vomited once and has vague lower abdominal pain. This morning the nurse noticed a fast, irregular pulse. He has no chest pain, cough or diarrhoea. He has no previous cardiac history.

His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse 128/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. His abdomen is mildly distended with tenderness in the left iliac fossa and suprapubic region, but no generalised guarding. Port sites look clean. Bowel sounds are sparse. The chest is clear.

Investigations:
- ECG: atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate 125/min, no ischaemic change
- White cell count 15.9 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- C-reactive protein: day 3, 72 mg/L; today (day 5), 246 mg/L (<5)
- Lactate 2.1 mmol/L (<2.0)
- Creatinine 104 µmol/L (baseline 80)
- Potassium 4.1 mmol/L, magnesium 0.8 mmol/L
- Chest X-ray: clear lungs, no free subdiaphragmatic gas

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Prolonged postoperative ileus
Clostridioides difficile colitis
Primary postoperative atrial fibrillation
Colorectal anastomotic leak
Hospital-acquired pneumonia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Colorectal anastomotic leak

---

An anastomotic leak typically presents around days 3–7 after colorectal resection, often subtly: return of ileus after initial recovery, fever, tachycardia, localised tenderness near the anastomosis, rising inflammatory markers and early organ dysfunction. New atrial fibrillation after colorectal surgery is a recognised early warning sign of an intra-abdominal septic complication, especially a leak, and should not be treated as a primary cardiac event. A CRP that rises between day 3 and day 5 (here 72 to 246 mg/L) is a strong signal: a low or falling CRP on day 3–4 has high negative predictive value for a leak, whereas a rising CRP should prompt imaging. Free gas on a chest X-ray is not expected and cannot exclude a leak after laparoscopy. The next steps are resuscitation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, rate control and urgent CT abdomen and pelvis with IV (and ideally rectal) contrast, with early senior surgical review.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Days 3–7 after colorectal anastomosis: new AF, return of ileus, fever or a rising CRP means anastomotic leak until proven otherwise. Get an urgent contrast CT.

---

question_text:
A 68-year-old man is referred to the emergency department of Mackay Base Hospital, Queensland, by his GP. For three weeks he has felt full after a few mouthfuls and has vomited large volumes of partly digested food, often several hours after eating, sometimes food he ate the day before. The vomit is not bile-stained. He has lost 8 kg. He has taken naproxen for back pain for several years and had a 'stomach ulcer' treated 5 years ago. He takes no diuretics or other regular medicines.

He looks dehydrated. His pulse is 108/min, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg lying and 88/58 mmHg sitting, and respiratory rate 12/min. The upper abdomen is distended, and a succussion splash is heard when the abdomen is shaken. There is no peritonism.

Investigations:
- Venous blood gas: pH 7.54, pCO2 50 mmHg, bicarbonate 42 mmol/L
- Sodium 131 mmol/L (135–145)
- Potassium 2.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Chloride 78 mmol/L (95–110)
- Urea 14.2 mmol/L (2.5–8.0)
- Creatinine 132 µmol/L (60–110; baseline 85)
- Glucose 5.8 mmol/L
- Spot urine: pH 5.0, sodium 12 mmol/L, chloride under 10 mmol/L

Which one of the following best explains his acid–base and urine findings?
options: Gastric acid loss causing chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis, with paradoxical aciduria
Mineralocorticoid excess causing chloride-resistant metabolic alkalosis with renal chloride wasting
Chronic respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation, with appropriate renal compensation
Metabolic alkalosis combined with a high anion gap acidosis from starvation ketosis
Occult diuretic use causing metabolic alkalosis with inappropriate renal chloride loss
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Gastric acid loss causing chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis, with paradoxical aciduria

---

Vomiting of old food, early satiety, weight loss and a succussion splash in a man with long-term NSAID use and previous peptic ulcer indicate gastric outlet obstruction (from a pyloric/duodenal ulcer stricture, or gastric cancer, which must be excluded). Loss of gastric HCl causes a metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.54, bicarbonate 42) with appropriate respiratory compensation (expected pCO2 ≈ 0.7 × 42 + 20 ≈ 49 mmHg). The anion gap is normal: 131 − (78 + 42) = 11. Volume depletion activates aldosterone, so the kidney avidly reabsorbs sodium. With low chloride available and marked potassium depletion, sodium is reabsorbed in exchange for H+ as well as K+, so the urine is inappropriately ACIDIC (paradoxical aciduria) despite a systemic alkalosis. A urine chloride below about 20 mmol/L identifies a chloride-responsive (saline-responsive) alkalosis; urine sodium can be misleading in alkalosis, which is why urine chloride is the better marker. Treatment is IV 0.9% sodium chloride with generous potassium replacement, nasogastric decompression, IV proton pump inhibitor, and endoscopy with biopsy once resuscitated.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Gastric outlet obstruction: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Low urine chloride = saline-responsive; acidic urine = paradoxical aciduria from volume and K+ depletion. Treat with saline and potassium.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "StatPearls. Gastric Outlet Obstruction (NCBI Bookshelf)", "url": "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557826/"}
• {"name": "Metabolic alkalosis pathogenesis, diagnosis, and treatment: Core Curriculum 2022. Am J Kidney Dis (PMC)", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10947768/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Mineralocorticoid excess gives a chloride-RESISTANT alkalosis with a high urine chloride (above 20–40 mmol/L), usually with hypertension. He is hypotensive with a very low urine chloride.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The pH is alkalaemic (7.54), so the primary process cannot be an acidosis. The raised pCO2 is compensation for the metabolic alkalosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The anion gap is normal (11), so there is no additional high anion gap acidosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Active diuretic use causes renal chloride loss, so urine chloride would be HIGH. His urine chloride is under 10 mmol/L and he takes no diuretics.

key_takeaways: Gastric outlet obstruction: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Low urine chloride = saline-responsive; acidic urine = paradoxical aciduria from volume and K+ depletion. Treat with saline and potassium.

question_text:
A 52-year-old man is brought by ambulance to the emergency department of a hospital in Geelong, Victoria, at 2 am. After a night of heavy drinking at a wedding, he vomited forcefully several times and then developed sudden, severe pain behind the lower sternum radiating to his back and left shoulder. The pain is worse on swallowing and deep breathing. He has not vomited blood. He has no cardiac history and takes no regular medicines.

He is sweaty and distressed. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 106/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. There is crepitus over the left supraclavicular fossa. Breath sounds are reduced at the left base. The upper abdomen is tender with some guarding.

Investigations:
- ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST-segment changes
- High-sensitivity troponin 6 ng/L (<14)
- Lipase 40 U/L (<60)
- White cell count 16.2 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0)
- Erect chest X-ray: small left pleural effusion and a thin lucent line along the left heart border; no free subdiaphragmatic gas

IV fluids, analgesia and oxygen have been started and he has been made nil by mouth.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Urgent flexible upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Barium swallow
CT pulmonary angiogram
CT chest and abdomen with oral water-soluble contrast
Transthoracic echocardiogram
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. CT chest and abdomen with oral water-soluble contrast

---

Forceful vomiting followed by severe retrosternal pain, subcutaneous emphysema (Mackler's triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema), a left effusion and probable pneumomediastinum on chest X-ray indicate spontaneous oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome). The typical site is the left posterolateral wall of the distal oesophagus. Mortality rises steeply with delay, so rapid confirmation is essential. The WSES 2019 guideline on oesophageal emergencies recommends CT (ideally with oral water-soluble contrast, i.e. CT oesophagography) as the investigation of choice: it confirms extraluminal gas or contrast leak, shows mediastinal and pleural contamination, and helps plan management. At the same time he needs broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and antifungal cover, nil by mouth, and urgent upper GI/thoracic surgical referral.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Vomiting then chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema = Boerhaave until proven otherwise. Confirm with CT using oral water-soluble contrast; avoid barium and avoid endoscopy as the first test.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Chirica M et al. Esophageal emergencies: WSES guidelines. World J Emerg Surg 2019;14:26", "url": "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13017-019-0245-2"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspected spontaneous oesophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome): imaging

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Endoscopy can miss small tears and insufflation may enlarge a perforation and worsen mediastinal contamination. It is not the first diagnostic test, although it may be used later by experienced teams (e.g. for stenting).
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Barium causes a severe inflammatory mediastinitis if it leaks. When a contrast swallow is used, a water-soluble agent is used first, and CT has largely replaced fluoroscopic studies.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A CTPA is timed for the pulmonary arteries and is not designed to detect a leak of oral contrast. The history, crepitus and chest X-ray point to the oesophagus, not pulmonary embolism.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: There is no clinical or ECG evidence of pericardial or cardiac disease, and echocardiography does not assess the oesophagus.

key_takeaways: Vomiting then chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema = Boerhaave until proven otherwise. Confirm with CT using oral water-soluble contrast; avoid barium and avoid endoscopy as the first test.

question_text:
A 29-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Fremantle, Western Australia, because she found a lump in her left breast in the shower three weeks ago. It is not painful and has not changed with her menstrual cycle. She has no nipple discharge or skin changes. She has never been pregnant and takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. Her maternal aunt had breast cancer at the age of 61. No other relatives have had breast or ovarian cancer, and she has no Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry.

On examination there is a 2 cm smooth, firm, rubbery and very mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. There is no skin tethering, nipple change or axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The right breast is normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Bilateral diagnostic mammography
Ultrasound of the left breast and axilla
MRI of both breasts
Core needle biopsy of the lump before any imaging
Referral to a familial cancer clinic for BRCA testing
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Ultrasound of the left breast and axilla

---

Every new breast lump needs the triple test: clinical examination, imaging and non-surgical biopsy. The lump is likely to be a fibroadenoma, but that cannot be assumed. Cancer Australia's guide to investigating a new breast symptom recommends ultrasound as the first imaging test for women under 35, because young breast tissue is dense and mammography is less sensitive. Mammography is added in younger women if clinical or ultrasound findings are suspicious or indeterminate. If ultrasound shows a solid lesion, a core biopsy (usually ultrasound-guided) completes the triple test. The triple test is only negative if all three components are benign; any suspicious or indeterminate component needs specialist referral.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
New breast lump: triple test. Under 35, start with ultrasound; add mammography if findings are suspicious or indeterminate.

---

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: MRI is not a first-line test for a palpable lump. It is used for specific indications such as high-risk screening, occult primary or assessing extent of known cancer.

question_text:
A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department of a hospital in Wollongong, New South Wales, five weeks after the vaginal birth of her first baby, whom she is exclusively breastfeeding. Six days ago she developed a painful red area in her right breast with fever. Her GP diagnosed lactational mastitis and started oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily. She has taken it as prescribed for 4 days. The redness has become more localised, but she now has a very tender swelling and her fever has returned. She has no drug allergies.

Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse 104/min and blood pressure 118/72 mmHg. In the upper outer quadrant of the right breast there is a 3 cm tender, fluctuant swelling with overlying erythema. The skin is intact and not necrotic. There is tender right axillary lymphadenopathy.

Bedside ultrasound shows a 3.2 cm unilocular fluid collection. White cell count is 14.2 × 10^9/L (4.0–11.0).

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Incision and drainage under general anaesthesia, with breastfeeding stopped on the right side
Continue oral flucloxacillin alone and review in one week
Stop breastfeeding and start cabergoline to suppress lactation
Change to IV vancomycin and avoid any drainage procedure
Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, continued antibiotics and continued breastfeeding
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, continued antibiotics and continued breastfeeding

---

Worsening localised pain, a fluctuant mass and recurrent fever despite antibiotics suggest a breast abscess, confirmed on ultrasound. First-line treatment is ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (repeated if needed) or small-incision drainage, together with antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus, guided by the culture of the aspirate. Aspiration has better cosmetic results than open incision and makes it easier to keep breastfeeding. Australian guidance (RACGP, Australian Breastfeeding Association) is to continue breastfeeding or expressing from the affected breast: effective milk removal helps resolution, and the milk is safe for a healthy term baby. Open incision and drainage is kept for large or multiloculated abscesses, abscesses that fail repeated aspiration, or skin necrosis.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Lactational breast abscess: ultrasound-guided aspiration plus anti-staphylococcal antibiotics, and keep breastfeeding or expressing from the affected side.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "Australian Breastfeeding Association. Breast abscess", "url": "https://www.breastfeeding.asn.au/resources/breast-abscess"}

---

subtopic: Lactational breast abscess

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Open drainage is not first line for a small unilocular abscess with intact skin, and there is no need to stop breastfeeding from the affected side.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: An established abscess rarely resolves with antibiotics alone. It needs drainage.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Stopping breastfeeding abruptly worsens milk stasis and is not needed. Lactation suppression is not part of abscess treatment.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: IV antibiotics may be needed if she is systemically unwell or MRSA is suspected, but antibiotics without drainage will not treat the abscess.

key_takeaways: Lactational breast abscess: ultrasound-guided aspiration plus anti-staphylococcal antibiotics, and keep breastfeeding or expressing from the affected side.

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Toowoomba, Queensland, for the result of her surveillance ultrasound for an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm found incidentally four years ago. She has no abdominal, back or groin pain. She is an ex-smoker (30 pack-years, stopped 6 years ago) with hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and stage 2 chronic kidney disease. She takes perindopril, atorvastatin and aspirin. She walks 5 km most days, cares for her grandchildren and has no symptoms of heart failure or angina.

Her blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg. There is a pulsatile, non-tender abdominal mass.

Serial maximum anteroposterior aortic diameters (same accredited vascular laboratory):
- 4 years ago: 4.2 cm
- 2 years ago: 4.5 cm
- 12 months ago: 4.8 cm
- This week: 5.1 cm

The report says 'Growth 0.3 cm in 12 months. Recommend clinical correlation.'

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of this result?
options: Below the repair threshold; continue 6-monthly ultrasound until it reaches 5.5 cm
Growth of 0.3 cm/year is rapid and is the main reason to refer for repair
At the diameter where elective repair should be considered in a woman; refer to vascular surgery
Below the repair threshold; repeat the ultrasound in 12 months
Refer for repair when symptoms develop, whatever the diameter
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. At the diameter where elective repair should be considered in a woman; refer to vascular surgery

---

Thresholds for elective AAA repair are lower in women. The ESVS 2024 guideline suggests considering elective repair at a maximum diameter of 5.5 cm or more in men and 5.0 cm or more in women (and advises against elective repair below these sizes). Women have smaller aortas, rupture at smaller diameters, and have a higher rupture risk at any given diameter, so applying the male 5.5 cm threshold to her would leave her at unnecessary risk. She is 5.1 cm, asymptomatic, active and apparently fit, so she should be referred to a vascular surgeon to assess for elective repair (CT angiography for anatomy and EVAR suitability, cardiorespiratory and renal assessment, and shared decision-making). The other indication for referral regardless of diameter is growth of 1 cm or more per year, or symptoms (pain or tenderness), which need urgent assessment.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Elective AAA repair is considered at 5.5 cm in men but 5.0 cm in women (ESVS 2024), or with growth of 1 cm/year or more, or symptoms.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Wanhainen A et al. ESVS 2024 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-Iliac Artery Aneurysms. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2024", "url": "https://www.ejves.com/article/S1078-5884(23)00889-4/fulltext"}
• {"name": "Vascular News. ESVS 2024 AAA guidelines: what's new?", "url": "https://vascularnews.com/esvs-2024-clinical-practice-guidelines-on-the-management-of-abdominal-aortoiliac-artery-aneurysms-whats-new/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Growth of 0.3 cm in a year is not rapid. The growth-based referral trigger is 1 cm or more per year. The reason to refer is her diameter, given her sex.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Annual scans suit small aneurysms (around 3.0–3.9 cm) in most schedules. At 5.1 cm in a woman, she needs referral, not routine surveillance.

question_text:
A 61-year-old Aboriginal man attends an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service in Mparntwe (Alice Springs), Northern Territory, with the Aboriginal Health Practitioner who has been dressing his foot. He has had an ulcer on the tip of his left great toe for six weeks that is not healing despite offloading footwear and regular dressings. He has had type 2 diabetes for 18 years (HbA1c 8.6% [70 mmol/mol]), stage 4 chronic kidney disease, and peripheral neuropathy. He smoked until 3 years ago. He walks only short distances because of knee pain and has not noticed calf pain.

The ulcer is 1 cm across with a pale, sloughy base and no probe-to-bone contact. There is no spreading erythema, warmth or discharge. His feet are cool with shiny, hairless skin. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses cannot be felt on either side. Monofilament sensation is absent to mid-shin.

A handheld Doppler shows monophasic signals at both left ankle arteries. The cuff could not compress the ankle arteries at 240 mmHg, and the ankle-brachial index is recorded as 1.45 on the left.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to assess perfusion of his left foot?
options: Repeat ankle-brachial index in 3 months
Toe systolic pressure and toe-brachial index
Digital subtraction angiography of the left leg
Treadmill exercise ankle-brachial index
Plain X-ray of the left foot
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Toe systolic pressure and toe-brachial index

---

In diabetes and CKD, medial arterial calcification makes ankle arteries incompressible and gives a falsely high or normal ankle-brachial index (ABI). An ABI above 1.3–1.4 (or incompressible arteries) is not reassuring. His non-healing ulcer, absent pulses and monophasic Doppler signals strongly suggest peripheral artery disease. The 2021 Australian evidence-based guideline on PAD in diabetes-related foot disease recommends combining pedal Doppler waveforms with ABI AND toe-brachial index (TBI), as no single bedside test excludes PAD. Digital arteries are usually spared from calcification, so toe pressure and TBI are more reliable here. A TBI below 0.70 suggests PAD, and a low toe pressure (e.g. below about 30 mmHg) predicts poor healing and supports urgent vascular imaging and referral for revascularisation. In this setting, telehealth and outreach vascular review with the ACCHS team, and planning around renal care and travel to Adelaide or Darwin, are important to culturally safe care.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In diabetes or CKD, an ABI above ~1.3 or incompressible arteries is unreliable. Use pedal Doppler waveforms plus toe pressure and toe-brachial index (TBI <0.70 suggests PAD).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Chuter V et al. Australian guideline on diagnosis and management of peripheral artery disease: part of the 2021 Australian evidence-based guidelines for diabetes-related foot disease (J Foot Ankle Res 2022)", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9254685/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Angiography may be needed to plan revascularisation, but it is invasive, uses contrast in a man with advanced CKD, and is not the next bedside test to establish perfusion.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Exercise ABI helps when resting ABI is normal in someone with claudication. It still depends on compressible ankle arteries, and he cannot walk far.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: An X-ray looks for osteomyelitis, gas or foreign body. The question asks about perfusion, and the ulcer does not probe to bone.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Orange, New South Wales, four days after an episode in which 'a curtain came down' over the vision of his left eye for about five minutes and then fully cleared. He had no weakness, speech disturbance or headache. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hypercholesterolaemia, and smokes 10 cigarettes a day. He was already taking aspirin 100 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, metformin and ramipril.

The GP arranged same-week investigations through the local TIA pathway. His blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg and pulse 72/min and regular. Neurological and fundal examination are normal.

Investigations:
- ECG and 24-hour Holter: sinus rhythm throughout
- MRI brain: no infarct
- Carotid duplex ultrasound: 80–99% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery; less than 50% on the right
- CT angiography: confirms about 85% stenosis at the origin of the left internal carotid artery, with no tandem lesion

He is independent, walks daily and has no symptoms of angina or heart failure. He is keen to reduce his risk of stroke.

In addition to optimising medical therapy and smoking cessation, which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue medical therapy alone and repeat carotid duplex in 6 months
Replace aspirin with warfarin
Elective carotid endarterectomy in 3 months once risk factors are controlled
Carotid artery stenting as the first-choice procedure
Urgent vascular referral for carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of symptoms
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Urgent vascular referral for carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of symptoms

---

Amaurosis fugax is a retinal TIA and counts as a symptomatic event in the territory of the left internal carotid artery. He has a symptomatic 70–99% stenosis. The Australian and New Zealand Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management recommend carotid endarterectomy for recent non-disabling stroke or TIA with ipsilateral 70–99% stenosis, performed as soon as possible and ideally within 2 weeks of the event, by a surgical team with audited low complication rates. The benefit of surgery is greatest in the first two weeks, when the risk of recurrent stroke is highest, and falls away quickly with delay. Medical therapy (antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, blood pressure and diabetes control, stopping smoking) is continued alongside surgery.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Symptomatic (including amaurosis fugax) 70–99% carotid stenosis: carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of the event, plus best medical therapy.

---

question_text:
A 19-year-old man comes to the emergency department of Dubbo Base Hospital, New South Wales, at 11 pm. Three hours ago he was woken by sudden, severe pain in his left testicle, which has spread to the left lower abdomen. He has vomited twice. He has no urinary symptoms, urethral discharge or recent trauma, and he has not been sexually active for six months. He had a similar but brief episode of pain a month ago that settled on its own.

His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse 104/min and blood pressure 132/78 mmHg. The left testis is swollen, exquisitely tender, high-riding and lies horizontally. The left cremasteric reflex is absent. Lifting the testis does not relieve the pain. The right testis is normal. Urinalysis shows no leucocytes or nitrites.

The on-call general surgeon is in the hospital and an operating theatre is available. Formal ultrasound is not available until the morning.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate scrotal exploration in theatre
Transfer to a tertiary centre for urgent colour Doppler ultrasound
Manual detorsion in the emergency department and discharge if pain settles
Ceftriaxone and doxycycline for epididymo-orchitis, with urine NAAT
Admit for analgesia and formal ultrasound in the morning
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Immediate scrotal exploration in theatre

---

Sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting, a high-riding horizontal testis, an absent cremasteric reflex and a previous self-resolving episode (suggesting intermittent torsion) make torsion highly likely. Testicular salvage depends on time: it is high if detorted within about 6 hours and falls sharply after that. The RACS 2022 guideline on acute scrotal pain and suspected testicular torsion states that suspected torsion is a surgical emergency and that imaging should not delay exploration, because ultrasound can be falsely reassuring. The surgeon on site should explore the scrotum immediately, detort, assess viability, and fix the testis (orchidopexy), with fixation of the contralateral testis because the 'bell-clapper' anomaly is often bilateral. A non-viable testis is removed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis: explore immediately. Do not let ultrasound or transfer delay surgery when a surgeon can operate.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation (ECI). Acute scrotum", "url": "https://aci.health.nsw.gov.au/networks/eci/clinical/tools/acute-scrotum"}

---

question_text:
A 67-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Mandurah, Western Australia, because he has twice noticed red urine over the past fortnight, each time lasting a day. He has no dysuria, frequency, loin pain or fever. He has no recent trauma or vigorous exercise. He smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 40 years and stopped 5 years ago. He worked as a painter and decorator. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine and takes no anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicine.

His blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg. Abdominal and genital examination is normal. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, mildly enlarged prostate.

Investigations:
- Urine dipstick today: blood 2+, protein trace, leucocytes negative, nitrites negative
- Urine microscopy: red cells 150 × 10^6/L (<13), no casts or dysmorphic red cells; culture: no growth
- Creatinine 84 µmol/L (60–110), eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m²
- Full blood count normal

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
options: Repeat urinalysis in 3 months and investigate if haematuria persists
Urine cytology alone
Serum prostate-specific antigen and review
CT urogram and referral for flexible cystoscopy
Renal tract ultrasound alone
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. CT urogram and referral for flexible cystoscopy

---

Painless visible (macroscopic) haematuria in an adult, once infection is excluded, needs investigation for urothelial and renal cancer, even if it is intermittent. His risk is high: age over 60, a heavy smoking history, and occupational exposure (painters are exposed to aromatic amines and solvents). Standard practice in Australia, following guidelines endorsed by USANZ (such as the EAU guidelines) and the Cancer Council optimal care pathway for bladder cancer, is to evaluate both the upper tract and the bladder: CT urography (the most sensitive imaging test for upper tract urothelial cancer and renal masses) and cystoscopy (the standard for detecting bladder cancer, which imaging can miss). Refer to urology. Glomerular causes are unlikely: renal function is normal and there are no casts, dysmorphic red cells or significant proteinuria.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Painless visible haematuria in a high-risk adult (age, smoking, occupation): CT urogram plus cystoscopy. Intermittent bleeding is not reassuring.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand (USANZ). Position statements and guidelines", "url": "https://usanz.org.au/info-resources/position-statements-guidelines"}
• {"name": "RACGP (AFP/AJGP). Macroscopic haematuria", "url": "https://www.racgp.org.au/getattachment/2713edc1-efd1-4a74-b9d1-6e8963e86f3d/Macroscopic-haematuria.aspx"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Cytology has poor sensitivity for low-grade urothelial tumours. It can complement but not replace cystoscopy and imaging.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A mildly enlarged prostate can bleed, but BPH is a diagnosis of exclusion in visible haematuria. PSA does not evaluate the urinary tract for urothelial cancer.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Ultrasound may be used in lower-risk patients or when CT contrast is contraindicated, but it misses small upper tract urothelial tumours, and on its own it leaves out cystoscopy.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man is admitted under urology at a hospital in Rockhampton, Queensland, with increasing confusion, lower abdominal distension and dribbling incontinence for several weeks. He has benign prostatic hyperplasia but stopped his tamsulosin a year ago. A urethral catheter was inserted in the emergency department at 1400 and drained 1.8 L of urine. His creatinine was 312 µmol/L (baseline 95 µmol/L six months ago), and renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis with a thick-walled bladder.

He is now more alert and drinking to thirst. He has had no IV fluids and no diuretics. His hourly urine output since the initial drainage has been:
- 1500–1600: 320 mL
- 1600–1700: 350 mL
- 1700–1800: 310 mL
- 1800–1900: 290 mL

At 1900 his pulse is 90/min, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg lying and 112/68 mmHg sitting, and his mucous membranes are slightly dry. The urine is clear.

Investigations at 1900:
- Sodium 142 mmol/L (135–145)
- Potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Creatinine 268 µmol/L
- Glucose 6.2 mmol/L
- Urine osmolality 290 mOsm/kg

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and plan?
options: Central diabetes insipidus; give desmopressin and restrict fluids
Hyperglycaemic osmotic diuresis; start an insulin infusion
Post-obstructive diuresis; monitor closely and replace part of the output
Post-obstructive diuresis; replace every millilitre of urine output with IV 0.9% sodium chloride
Normal physiological response; no monitoring beyond standard ward observations is needed
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Post-obstructive diuresis; monitor closely and replace part of the output

---

Post-obstructive diuresis is usually defined as urine output above 200 mL/h for 2 consecutive hours, or more than 3 L in 24 hours, after relief of obstruction. It is most common after relief of high-pressure chronic retention with renal impairment, as here. It has a physiological component (excretion of retained urea, salt and water) and sometimes a pathological component (a tubular concentrating defect), which can cause dehydration, hypotension and electrolyte disturbance. His near-isotonic urine (290 mOsm/kg), normal glucose and high-normal sodium fit this picture, and he is starting to show a postural drop. Management: hourly urine output and fluid balance, daily or twice-daily weights, 12-hourly (or more frequent) electrolytes, encourage oral intake if he can, and if IV fluids are needed replace a proportion (commonly about 50–75%) of the previous hour's output, rather than chasing the output mL for mL, which can perpetuate the diuresis. The catheter should not be clamped.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After relieving high-pressure chronic retention, >200 mL/h for 2 hours = post-obstructive diuresis. Monitor closely; replace part of the output (not mL for mL); do not clamp the catheter.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "StatPearls. Postobstructive Diuresis (NCBI Bookshelf)", "url": "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459387/"}
• {"name": "LITFL. Post-obstructive diuresis", "url": "https://litfl.com/post-obstructive-diuresis/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: High-pressure chronic retention: post-obstructive diuresis after catheterisation

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Central diabetes insipidus produces dilute urine (low osmolality) with a high sodium. His urine is near-isotonic and there is an obvious cause for the diuresis. Desmopressin and fluid restriction could cause harm.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: His glucose is 6.2 mmol/L, which cannot drive an osmotic diuresis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Replacing all output tends to keep the diuresis going and can lead to fluid and sodium overload. Partial replacement, guided by haemodynamics and electrolytes, is preferred.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Part of the diuresis is physiological, but he already has a postural drop and dry mucous membranes. He needs close monitoring of fluid balance and electrolytes.

key_takeaways: After relieving high-pressure chronic retention, >200 mL/h for 2 hours = post-obstructive diuresis. Monitor closely; replace part of the output (not mL for mL); do not clamp the catheter.

question_text:
A 44-year-old man comes to a general practice in Canberra the morning after playing indoor netball. As he pushed off to run, he felt as if someone had kicked him hard in the back of his right lower leg, and he heard a snap. He could not continue playing and has been walking with a limp since. He has no previous injury to this leg. He had a course of ciprofloxacin for prostatitis two months ago.

He walks with a flat-footed gait and cannot stand on tiptoe on the right. Lying prone, he can plantarflex his right ankle against gravity, although more weakly than on the left. There is swelling and tenderness about 5 cm above the right heel. A gap is difficult to feel because of swelling. With both knees flexed to 90 degrees, the right foot hangs in slightly more dorsiflexion than the left. The ankle is not tender over the malleoli, navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal.

Which one of the following examination findings would most strongly support the suspected diagnosis?
options: Active plantarflexion against resistance is preserved
Positive anterior drawer test of the right ankle
Pain when the Ottawa ankle criteria are applied
Tenderness over the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus
No plantarflexion of the foot when the calf is squeezed
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. No plantarflexion of the foot when the calf is squeezed

---

The history (sudden 'kick' or snap on push-off, a middle-aged recreational athlete, recent fluoroquinolone use) strongly suggests an acute Achilles tendon rupture. The Simmonds (Thompson) calf squeeze test is the key clinical test: with the patient prone and the feet over the end of the bed, squeezing the calf normally causes passive plantarflexion. No movement indicates a complete rupture. Other supportive findings are an increased resting angle of dorsiflexion with knees flexed (a lost 'angle of declination', as here) and a palpable gap. Diagnosis is clinical; ultrasound is used if in doubt. Many Achilles ruptures are missed because the patient can still actively plantarflex using tibialis posterior, the long toe flexors and the peroneal muscles.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected Achilles rupture: perform the Simmonds (Thompson) calf squeeze test and check the angle of declination. Preserved active plantarflexion does not exclude rupture.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "British Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (BOFAS) Hyperbook: Achilles tendon acute rupture", "url": "https://www.bofas.org.uk/hyperbook/trauma/achilles-tendon-acute-rupture"}
• {"name": "Achilles tendon rupture: how to avoid missing the diagnosis. Br J Gen Pract 2015;65:668", "url": "https://bjgp.org/content/65/641/668"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The anterior drawer test assesses the anterior talofibular ligament in lateral ankle sprain. It does not assess the Achilles tendon.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The Ottawa ankle rules decide whether an ankle X-ray is needed to exclude fracture. They are not designed to diagnose tendon rupture.

question_text:
A 23-year-old man is on the orthopaedic ward of a hospital in Newcastle, New South Wales, eight hours after admission with a closed, displaced fracture of the right tibial shaft from a motorbike crash. His leg was placed in an above-knee plaster backslab, elevated on two pillows, and he is waiting for intramedullary nailing on tomorrow's trauma list. He has a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump.

The nurse calls you because his pain has become much worse over the past two hours despite frequent PCA use. He says his leg feels 'tight' and 'like it's bursting'. His pulse is 108/min and blood pressure 126/70 mmHg. When the bandage over the backslab is loosened, the anterior leg is tense and swollen. Passive plantarflexion of the toes causes severe pain. He reports reduced sensation between the first and second toes. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and capillary refill in the toes is 2 seconds.

The orthopaedic registrar measures anterior compartment pressure at 52 mmHg.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Raise the leg higher to reduce swelling and reassess in one hour
Increase the PCA bolus dose and repeat the compartment pressure in two hours
Split dressings to skin and arrange emergency four-compartment fasciotomy
Arrange urgent CT angiography of the right leg
Proceed to intramedullary nailing first, then reassess compartments afterwards
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Split dressings to skin and arrange emergency four-compartment fasciotomy

---

He has acute compartment syndrome: escalating pain out of proportion to the injury despite opioids, pain on passive stretch of the anterior compartment muscles, a tense compartment and early deep peroneal nerve dysfunction (first web-space numbness). The measured pressure supports it: his delta pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) is 70 − 52 = 18 mmHg, and a delta below 30 mmHg indicates inadequate perfusion. An absolute pressure above 40 mmHg is also concerning. Palpable pulses do NOT exclude compartment syndrome: arterial pressure far exceeds compartment pressure until very late. The BOAST guideline (2025) says that once compartment syndrome is diagnosed, all circumferential dressings and casts must be split to skin, the limb kept at heart level, and decompression by fasciotomy performed as an emergency (target within 1 hour of the decision). For the leg, this means two-incision fasciotomy of all four compartments.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Compartment syndrome is clinical: pain out of proportion and on passive stretch. Pulses are usually present. Delta pressure <30 mmHg supports it. Split dressings to skin, limb at heart level, emergency fasciotomy.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "British Orthopaedic Association. BOAST: Diagnosis and management of compartment syndrome of the limbs (September 2025)", "url": "https://www.boa.ac.uk/static/d0432d40-5d99-4b64-9952f6eb1b60c166/BOASTCompartmentSyndromeSeptember-2025.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Acute compartment syndrome after tibial fracture with palpable pulses

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Elevating the limb above heart level lowers arterial inflow pressure and worsens compartment perfusion. The limb should be kept at heart level.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Increasing analgesia masks the main symptom, and waiting two hours with established compartment syndrome risks irreversible muscle and nerve necrosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The pulses and capillary refill are normal, so there is no sign of an arterial injury. Imaging would delay decompression.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Fracture fixation is done at the same operation, but fasciotomy is the priority. Nailing first without decompression would worsen compartment pressure.

question_text:
A 42-year-old woman comes to the emergency department of Townsville University Hospital, Queensland, with worsening low back pain and pain down both legs for three days. She has had intermittent back pain for years, and an MRI two years ago showed an L4/5 disc bulge. Since yesterday she has noticed numbness 'down below' when she wipes after going to the toilet, and she has had to strain to pass urine this morning. She has no fever, weight loss, cancer history or injecting drug use.

Her temperature is 36.8°C. Straight leg raising is limited to 40 degrees on both sides. Ankle reflexes are reduced bilaterally. Power is 5/5 except for 4/5 plantarflexion on the left. There is reduced pinprick sensation over the perianal area and the posterior upper thighs. A bladder scan after she tries to void shows a residual volume of 420 mL.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
CT of the lumbar spine without contrast
Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
Urgent outpatient neurosurgical review with MRI within 2 weeks
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine

---

She has red flags for cauda equina syndrome (CES): bilateral sciatica, saddle (perianal) numbness, new urinary hesitancy and a raised post-void residual volume, on a background of a known L4/5 disc. She has incomplete CES with retention developing (CES-I/early CES-R). Outcomes, especially bladder and sexual function, depend on decompression before the syndrome is complete. The investigation is an emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine. Pathways such as the national suspected CES pathway (GIRFT, England) set a target of MRI within about 4 hours of request, at the presenting hospital, without waiting for a spinal surgical opinion first. If MRI confirms compression, she needs urgent referral to spinal surgery for decompression.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia and bladder symptoms or a raised post-void residual = suspected cauda equina: emergency MRI the same day, then urgent spinal decompression.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "GIRFT (NHS England). National Suspected Cauda Equina Syndrome Pathway (updated March 2026)", "url": "https://gettingitrightfirsttime.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/National-Suspected-Cauda-Equina-Pathway-March-2026.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspected cauda equina syndrome

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: CT is less sensitive for disc herniation and neural compression. It is used only when MRI is contraindicated or truly unavailable, often with myelography.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: X-rays do not show the disc or cauda equina and would only delay diagnosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Suspected CES needs emergency imaging. A 2-week delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Neurophysiology is not used to diagnose acute cord or cauda equina compression and would delay treatment.

key_takeaways: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia and bladder symptoms or a raised post-void residual = suspected cauda equina: emergency MRI the same day, then urgent spinal decompression.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man is on the orthopaedic ward of Royal Hobart Hospital, Tasmania, 30 hours after a motorbike crash in which he sustained a closed, displaced fracture of the left femoral shaft. He is in skin traction awaiting intramedullary nailing, which was postponed because of emergency theatre demand. He has had no other injuries, no surgery and no blood transfusion. He is taking oxycodone for pain and enoxaparin prophylaxis was started 12 hours ago.

The nurse calls because he has become restless and confused over the past 2 hours. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse 128/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min and oxygen saturation 85% on room air, rising to 93% on 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask. His GCS is 13 (E3 V4 M6), with no focal neurological signs and pupils 4 mm, equal and reactive. There are fine petechiae in both axillae, across the upper chest and in the conjunctivae. Chest auscultation reveals scattered fine crackles.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 108 g/L (admission 139 g/L)
- Platelets 92 × 10^9/L (admission 240)
- White cell count 13.1 × 10^9/L
- Arterial blood gas on oxygen: pH 7.47, pCO2 30 mmHg, pO2 68 mmHg
- Chest X-ray: bilateral diffuse patchy opacities
- CT brain: normal
- CT pulmonary angiogram: no filling defects; diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pulmonary thromboembolism
Fat embolism syndrome
Hospital-acquired pneumonia with sepsis
Transfusion-related acute lung injury
Opioid-induced respiratory depression
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Fat embolism syndrome

---

Fat embolism syndrome (FES) typically appears 24–72 hours after a long bone (especially femoral) or pelvic fracture, more often when fixation is delayed. The classic triad is respiratory insufficiency (hypoxaemia, diffuse bilateral opacities), cerebral involvement (confusion, reduced GCS) and a petechial rash in non-dependent areas (axillae, upper chest, conjunctivae, oral mucosa), which is the most specific sign. He meets Gurd and Wilson's criteria: major criteria (petechiae, respiratory insufficiency, cerebral involvement) and minor criteria (tachycardia, fever, unexplained fall in haemoglobin, thrombocytopenia). A CTPA without filling defects and a normal CT brain support the diagnosis (MRI brain may show a 'starfield' pattern of small lesions). Treatment is supportive: oxygen and ventilatory support as needed, ICU review, and early fracture stabilisation, which also reduces the risk of FES.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
24–72 hours after a femoral fracture: hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae in the axillae/conjunctivae = fat embolism syndrome. Support and fix the fracture early.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "StatPearls. Fat Embolism (NCBI Bookshelf)", "url": "https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499885/"}
• {"name": "Radiopaedia. Fat embolism syndrome", "url": "https://radiopaedia.org/articles/fat-embolism-syndrome"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Fat embolism syndrome after femoral shaft fracture

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: PE is a key differential in an immobile trauma patient, but the CTPA shows no filling defects. PE would not explain petechiae, thrombocytopenia or a fall in haemoglobin.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Pneumonia with sepsis could cause fever, hypoxia and confusion, but not an abrupt onset at 30 hours with axillary and conjunctival petechiae and diffuse ground-glass change.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: TRALI occurs within 6 hours of transfusion of a blood product. He has not been transfused.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Opioid toxicity causes a LOW respiratory rate, a raised pCO2 and small pupils. He has tachypnoea, a low pCO2 and normal pupils.

key_takeaways: 24–72 hours after a femoral fracture: hypoxaemia, confusion and petechiae in the axillae/conjunctivae = fat embolism syndrome. Support and fix the fracture early.

question_text:
A 36-year-old man with epilepsy is brought to the emergency department of a hospital in Darwin, Northern Territory, by his partner. Overnight he had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in bed. He had run out of levetiracetam two days earlier. This morning he has severe pain in his right shoulder and cannot use his arm. There was no fall.

He is alert and oriented. He holds his right arm against his body in internal rotation. The front of the shoulder looks flattened and the coracoid process is prominent. He cannot externally rotate the arm, even passively. Sensation over the lateral upper arm is normal, and radial pulse and hand function are normal.

A single anteroposterior shoulder X-ray has been reported by the overnight junior doctor as 'no fracture, joint congruent'. On review, the humeral head looks symmetrically rounded, and the normal overlap of the humeral head with the posterior glenoid rim is lost.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)
Acute rotator cuff tear
Anterior glenohumeral dislocation
Posterior glenohumeral dislocation
Acromioclavicular joint dislocation
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Posterior glenohumeral dislocation

---

Seizures (and electric shocks) are the classic causes of posterior shoulder dislocation, because the powerful internal rotators overpower the external rotators. The clinical signs are an arm locked in adduction and internal rotation with a block to external rotation, flattening of the anterior shoulder and a prominent coracoid. On an AP view the internally rotated humeral head looks symmetrical (the 'light bulb' sign), and the normal half-moon overlap with the glenoid is lost; the AP film can look almost normal, which is why 50% or more of these injuries are missed at first presentation. An axillary or scapular Y view (or CT) confirms the diagnosis and shows any reverse Hill-Sachs lesion or fracture. It needs reduction and orthopaedic review, and his epilepsy management needs attention.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After a seizure, a shoulder locked in internal rotation with no external rotation is a posterior dislocation until proven otherwise. The AP film can look nearly normal: get an axillary or Y view.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Posterior dislocation of the shoulder: the light-bulb sign (PMC)", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10679799/"}
• {"name": "Neglected posterior dislocation of the shoulder: a systematic literature review (PMC)", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5982360/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Posterior shoulder dislocation after a seizure

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Frozen shoulder develops over weeks to months with global loss of movement. It does not start suddenly after a seizure with abnormal X-ray signs.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A cuff tear causes weakness and painful active movement, but passive movement is usually preserved. A mechanical block to passive external rotation suggests dislocation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Anterior dislocation (the commonest type) holds the arm in slight abduction and external rotation, with a squared-off shoulder and a humeral head that lies below the coracoid on the AP view.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: AC joint injury gives a step at the top of the shoulder and localised tenderness, usually after a fall onto the shoulder. It does not lock the arm in internal rotation.

key_takeaways: After a seizure, a shoulder locked in internal rotation with no external rotation is a posterior dislocation until proven otherwise. The AP film can look nearly normal: get an axillary or Y view.

question_text:
An 82-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of John Hunter Hospital, Newcastle, New South Wales, by her daughter two hours after tripping on a rug at home and hitting her forehead on a door frame. She did not lose consciousness, and she remembers the whole event. She has not vomited and has only a mild headache. She has atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban 5 mg twice daily (last dose 3 hours ago), hypertension and osteoarthritis. She lives independently.

Her GCS is 15. Her pulse is 78/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure 148/84 mmHg. There is a 3 cm bruise and swelling over the right forehead without laceration. There are no signs of a base-of-skull fracture. Pupils are equal and reactive, and there is no focal neurological deficit. There is no neck pain or midline cervical tenderness, and she moves her neck freely.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Non-contrast CT of the brain now
Observe for 4 hours in the emergency department, with CT if she deteriorates
Discharge home with written head injury advice and her daughter
Skull X-ray to exclude a fracture
Withhold apixaban for 48 hours and arrange GP review, without imaging
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Non-contrast CT of the brain now

---

She has a mild head injury (GCS 15, no loss of consciousness or amnesia) but is taking an anticoagulant and is over 65. The NSW Health guideline on initial management of closed head injury in adults classes anticoagulation or known coagulopathy as a high-risk feature that needs early CT brain, even with a GCS of 15 and no other symptoms. Anticoagulated older patients have a substantially higher risk of intracranial haemorrhage, and early symptoms can be minimal. If CT shows haemorrhage, apixaban should be reversed (e.g. andexanet alfa where available or prothrombin complex concentrate, according to local protocol) and neurosurgery consulted. If CT is normal, a period of observation is usual; local pathways vary on whether a repeat CT is needed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Head injury in a patient taking an anticoagulant (including a DOAC) needs early CT brain, even with GCS 15 and no symptoms.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "NSW Health Policy Directive PD2012_013: Closed Head Injury in Adults \u2013 Initial Management", "url": "https://www1.health.nsw.gov.au/pds/ActivePDSDocuments/PD2012_013.pdf"}

---

subtopic: Minor head injury in an older person taking a DOAC

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Observation without imaging is inappropriate for an anticoagulated patient. Deterioration from an expanding haematoma may be late and catastrophic.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Discharge without imaging ignores the anticoagulant, which is a high-risk feature on all major head injury rules.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Skull X-rays have no role in adult head injury assessment. A normal X-ray does not exclude intracranial bleeding.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Stopping apixaban without imaging leaves her unprotected from stroke and does not exclude an existing haemorrhage.

question_text:
A 38-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of The Alfred, Melbourne, after a high-speed car crash on the freeway. She was the restrained driver, the airbags deployed, and she was able to get out of the car herself. She complains of neck pain. She has no other medical history.

Her primary survey is normal: GCS 15, pulse 88/min, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She has a seatbelt abrasion across the left chest and lower abdomen, but not the neck. She has midline tenderness at the mid-cervical spine. Neurological examination of the limbs and cranial nerves is normal. There is no Horner syndrome, no carotid bruit, no neck haematoma and no epistaxis.

Trauma CT (non-contrast head, cervical spine; contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen and pelvis):
- CT brain: normal
- CT cervical spine: undisplaced fracture of the right C4 lateral mass extending into the right transverse foramen; alignment is normal, with no subluxation
- CT chest, abdomen and pelvis: no injury

She is comfortable in a cervical collar, and the spinal team plans non-operative management.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: MRI of the cervical spine to assess the ligaments
CT angiography of the head and neck vessels
Flexion–extension X-rays of the cervical spine
Duplex ultrasound of the carotid and vertebral arteries
No further imaging; discharge in a hard collar
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. CT angiography of the head and neck vessels

---

A cervical spine fracture extending into the transverse foramen puts the vertebral artery (which runs through the foramina from C6 to C1) at risk of blunt cerebrovascular injury (BCVI): dissection, intimal flap, pseudoaneurysm or occlusion. BCVI is often asymptomatic at first, and presents hours to days later with posterior circulation stroke. Screening finds it before a stroke, so that antithrombotic therapy can be started (in discussion with the trauma and spinal teams). The EAST 2020 practice management guideline strongly recommends CT angiography screening for patients with high-risk cervical spine injuries, specifically including fractures into the transverse foramen, subluxation and C1–C3 fractures. These are also expanded Denver criteria. A normal neurological examination does not remove the indication, which is why this is a common miss.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Cervical fracture into the transverse foramen, subluxation or C1–C3 fracture = high risk of blunt cerebrovascular injury: screen with CT angiography even if neurologically intact.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "EAST Practice Management Guideline: Evaluation and management of blunt cerebrovascular injury (2020)", "url": "https://www.east.org/Content/documents/practicemanagementguidelines/evaluation_and_management_of_blunt_cerebrovascular_injury.pdf"}
• {"name": "Radiopaedia. Denver criteria for blunt cerebrovascular injury", "url": "https://radiopaedia.org/articles/denver-criteria-for-blunt-cerebrovascular-injury-1"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Blunt cerebrovascular injury screening after a cervical fracture into the transverse foramen

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: MRI assesses ligaments, discs and cord. The CT already shows the fracture with normal alignment, and MRI does not answer the vascular question (MR angiography is a less preferred alternative).
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Flexion–extension films are not recommended in the acute phase and do not assess the vertebral artery.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Duplex ultrasound cannot image the vertebral artery reliably within the bony foramina, and misses many BCVIs. It is not an adequate screening test.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Discharging her without vascular screening leaves a possible vertebral artery injury undetected, with a risk of delayed stroke.
