question_text:
A 48-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Brisbane because he woke two days ago with his left ear feeling 'blocked' and muffled, with a high-pitched ringing. He has no ear pain, discharge, vertigo or recent upper respiratory infection, and no history of noise exposure, head injury or ear surgery. He has hypertension treated with candesartan.

Otoscopy shows normal, mobile tympanic membranes on both sides with no wax. Cranial nerve examination is otherwise normal, and there is no nystagmus or ataxia.

Tuning fork tests (512 Hz):
- Rinne test: air conduction louder than bone conduction on both sides
- Weber test: the sound is heard in the right ear

A whispered voice test shows reduced hearing on the left.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these findings?
options: Left conductive hearing loss from otitis media with effusion
Right conductive hearing loss
Right sensorineural hearing loss
Left sensorineural hearing loss needing same-day or next-day ENT assessment
Normal hearing with left Eustachian tube dysfunction
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Left sensorineural hearing loss needing same-day or next-day ENT assessment

---

In a unilateral sensorineural loss, Rinne is positive (air louder than bone) on both sides, because the affected cochlea hears both air and bone conduction less, in the normal ratio. Weber lateralises to the BETTER (unaffected) ear. In a conductive loss, Rinne is negative on the affected side and Weber lateralises TO the affected ear. So a Weber heard on the right with bilateral positive Rinne and poor left hearing means a left sensorineural loss. Sudden onset over less than 72 hours with no obvious cause is sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL), which is an otological emergency. The AAO-HNS 2019 guideline recommends audiometry as soon as possible to confirm it, offering systemic corticosteroids within 2 weeks of onset (earlier is better), and MRI of the internal auditory meati to exclude retrocochlear causes such as vestibular schwannoma. Many patients describe SSNHL as a 'blocked ear' and are wrongly treated for wax or congestion.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Weber goes TO a conductive loss and AWAY from a sensorineural loss. A sudden unilateral sensorineural loss needs urgent audiometry, steroids within 2 weeks and later MRI.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Chandrasekhar SS et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Sudden Hearing Loss (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2019 (AAO-HNS)", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31369359"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: interpreting tuning fork tests

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Middle ear effusion would give a negative Rinne on the left, Weber lateralising to the left, and usually an abnormal tympanic membrane. His drums are normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A right conductive loss would also lateralise Weber to the right, but it would give a negative Rinne on the right and poor hearing on the right. His hearing is worse on the left.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Weber lateralises away from a sensorineural loss. A right sensorineural loss would send Weber to the left.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Eustachian tube dysfunction usually causes a retracted drum or conductive features. It does not explain objective left-sided hearing loss with Weber lateralising away from that ear.

key_takeaways: Weber goes TO a conductive loss and AWAY from a sensorineural loss. A sudden unilateral sensorineural loss needs urgent audiometry, steroids within 2 weeks and later MRI.

question_text:
A 34-year-old concreter is brought by a workmate to a general practice in Katherine, Northern Territory, ten minutes after wet cement splashed into his right eye while he was pouring a slab. He rinsed it briefly with a water bottle at the site. He has severe pain, watering and cannot open the eye. He wears no contact lenses.

He is distressed and holding his eye closed. The eyelids are red and there is grey cement paste visible in the lower fornix. The left eye is normal. The practice has sterile saline, Hartmann's solution, topical anaesthetic drops, litmus (pH) paper, fluorescein and a Snellen chart. The nearest ophthalmologist is in Darwin, over 300 km away.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate first step?
options: Measure visual acuity in both eyes to document a baseline
Instil fluorescein and examine the cornea with a blue light
Instil chloramphenicol ointment and apply an eye pad
Check the pH of the tears with litmus paper to confirm an alkali
Instil topical anaesthetic and irrigate the eye copiously straight away
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Instil topical anaesthetic and irrigate the eye copiously straight away

---

Cement and lime are alkalis. Alkalis saponify cell membranes and penetrate deeply into the cornea and anterior chamber, causing limbal ischaemia, corneal opacification and blindness. Damage continues until the chemical is removed. Immediate, copious irrigation takes priority over everything else, including visual acuity, history and detailed examination. This is the one situation in ophthalmology where acuity is measured after treatment. The Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital referral guidelines advise irrigating immediately with saline, Hartmann's or water. Topical anaesthetic helps the patient open the eye. Evert the lids and sweep the fornices to remove particles of cement. Check the pH about 5 minutes after pausing irrigation, and continue until it is neutral (about 7–7.5). Then assess acuity and the cornea with fluorescein and arrange urgent ophthalmology review (via telehealth and transfer to Darwin as needed).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Chemical eye injury, especially alkali (cement, lime): irrigate immediately and copiously, before acuity or examination, and continue until the pH is neutral. Remove particles from the fornices.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Royal Victorian Eye and Ear Hospital. Primary Care Referral Guidelines \u2013 Ophthalmology (July 2026)", "url": "https://eyeandear.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Primary-Care-Referral-Guidelines-Ophthalmology-July-2026.pdf"}
• {"name": "AJGP 2024 (RACGP). Chemical eye injury in remote and urgent care clinics", "url": "https://www1.racgp.org.au/ajgp/2024/supplement-december/chemical-eye-injury-in-remote-and-urgent-care-clin"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Alkali (wet cement) chemical eye injury: first action

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Measuring acuity first is the usual rule in eye injuries, but chemical burns are the exception. Every minute of delay allows more alkali penetration.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Fluorescein examination comes after irrigation, once the pH is neutral.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Covering the eye traps the alkali against the cornea. Antibiotic ointment is not first-line treatment.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: pH testing guides how long to irrigate. It is done after irrigation starts, not before, and the history already tells you it is an alkali.

key_takeaways: Chemical eye injury, especially alkali (cement, lime): irrigate immediately and copiously, before acuity or examination, and continue until the pH is neutral. Remove particles from the fornices.

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman comes to the emergency department of University Hospital Geelong, Victoria. She has had a blocked nose, facial pressure and purulent nasal discharge for 6 days. For the past 2 days her right upper and lower eyelids have become increasingly swollen and red, and since this morning she has had double vision and pain when she moves her right eye. She has no history of trauma, insect bite or skin lesions around the eye. She is otherwise well and takes no regular medicines.

Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse 102/min and blood pressure 118/74 mmHg. The right eyelids are swollen, tense and red, and she can open the eye only with help. The right eye is displaced forward compared with the left. Abduction and upgaze of the right eye are restricted and painful. Visual acuity is 6/9 right and 6/6 left. Pupils are equal and reactive, with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Sensation over the forehead and cheeks is normal. The left eye is normal. She has no neck stiffness and is alert.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis
Acute dacryocystitis
Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis
Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Allergic angioedema
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis

---

Features that point to infection behind the orbital septum are proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), diplopia, reduced visual acuity or colour vision, and a relative afferent pupillary defect. She has proptosis, restricted and painful movements with diplopia, and slightly reduced acuity, after several days of sinusitis (ethmoid sinusitis is the usual source). This is orbital cellulitis. It needs urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits and sinuses (to look for a subperiosteal or orbital abscess), IV antibiotics, and urgent ophthalmology and ENT review. Vision, pupils and colour vision should be checked frequently, because an abscess or optic nerve compression may need surgical drainage.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Eyelid swelling plus proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, or reduced vision = orbital cellulitis: urgent CT orbits/sinuses, IV antibiotics, ophthalmology and ENT.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "StatPearls. Orbital Cellulitis (NCBI Bookshelf)", "url": "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507901/"}
• {"name": "Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis (paediatric; distinguishing features apply to adults)", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Periorbital_and_orbital_cellulitis/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis complicating sinusitis in an adult

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Preseptal cellulitis causes lid swelling and redness, but eye movements are full and painless, the eye is not proptosed and vision is normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Dacryocystitis causes a tender swelling at the medial canthus over the lacrimal sac, not proptosis with ophthalmoplegia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a rarer, more severe complication. It often becomes bilateral, with multiple cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, VI), reduced sensation in V1/V2, and a very unwell patient. She has unilateral signs and normal facial sensation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Angioedema is usually afebrile, itchy or painless, and does not cause proptosis, ophthalmoplegia or reduced vision.

key_takeaways: Eyelid swelling plus proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, or reduced vision = orbital cellulitis: urgent CT orbits/sinuses, IV antibiotics, ophthalmology and ENT.

question_text:
A 34-year-old man weighing 70 kg is brought to the emergency department of Fiona Stanley Hospital, Perth, after a gas barbecue exploded at 1400. He arrives at 1600. Paramedics cooled the burns with running water for 20 minutes and gave him 1000 mL of Hartmann's solution through two large-bore cannulas on the way.

He is alert and talking in full sentences with no hoarseness, stridor, carbonaceous sputum or singed nasal hair. His pulse is 118/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Carboxyhaemoglobin is 2%.

The burns have been mapped on a Lund and Browder chart:
- Deep dermal and full-thickness burns to the front of the trunk and both arms: 30% of total body surface area (TBSA)
- Erythema only (superficial burn) over the face and neck: 5% TBSA

A urinary catheter has been inserted. The team plans fluid resuscitation using the Emergency Management of Severe Burns (EMSB) formula.

At what hourly rate should Hartmann's solution be infused from 1600 until 2200?
options: 358 mL/h
394 mL/h
446 mL/h
525 mL/h
533 mL/h
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. 358 mL/h

---

The ANZBA EMSB course uses the modified Parkland formula for adults with burns over 20% TBSA: 3 mL Hartmann's × body weight (kg) × %TBSA burn over 24 hours, timed from the time of the BURN, not from arrival. Erythema (superficial epidermal burn) is NOT counted in the %TBSA. So %TBSA = 30. Total for 24 hours = 3 × 70 × 30 = 6300 mL. Half (3150 mL) is given in the first 8 hours after the burn (1400–2200). He has already received 1000 mL, so 2150 mL remains for the 6 hours from 1600 to 2200: 2150 ÷ 6 ≈ 358 mL/h. The remaining 3150 mL is given over the next 16 hours. The formula is only a starting point: titrate to a urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (about 35 mL/h here) to avoid both under-resuscitation and 'fluid creep'. He meets ANZBA criteria for transfer to a burns unit.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
EMSB adult burns >20% TBSA: 3 mL × kg × %TBSA (exclude erythema), half in the first 8 hours from the time of burn, minus fluid already given. Titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Tasmanian Health Service. Tasmanian Burns Service \u2013 Fluid Resuscitation (modified Parkland formula, 3 mL/kg/%TBSA)", "url": "https://www.health.tas.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-12/Fluid_Resuscitation_DoHTasmania2021.pdf"}
• {"name": "ANZBA/British Burn Association. EMSB Course Manual, 19th edition (2024, UK edition of the ANZBA course)", "url": "https://www.britishburnassociation.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/2024-EMSB-Manual-UK_19ed.pdf"}
• {"name": "ANZBA. Management of burns and referral criteria", "url": "https://www.anzba.org/quality-care/management-of-burns/"}

---

subtopic: Major burn: calculating fluid resuscitation (modified Parkland, EMSB)

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 446 mL/h results from counting the 5% erythema (35% TBSA: 7350 mL; half = 3675; minus 1000 = 2675 over 6 hours). Erythema is excluded from the calculation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 525 mL/h = 3150 mL over 6 hours. This correctly uses the time of burn but forgets to subtract the 1000 mL already given.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: 533 mL/h uses the older 4 mL/kg/%TBSA figure (8400 mL; half = 4200; minus 1000 = 3200 over 6 hours). Current EMSB teaching uses 3 mL/kg/%TBSA for adults, to reduce over-resuscitation.

question_text:
A 22-year-old man is having an elective arthroscopic anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction at a private hospital in Adelaide. He is fit and well, takes no regular medicines and has had no previous anaesthetic. His family history is not known because he was adopted. Anaesthesia was induced with propofol, fentanyl and rocuronium, and maintained with sevoflurane in oxygen and air through a circle system with a fresh CO2 absorbent.

Forty minutes into the operation, the anaesthetist notices that end-tidal CO2 has risen from 38 to 64 mmHg despite doubling the minute ventilation. Inspired CO2 is 0 mmHg. His heart rate has risen from 70 to 132/min with occasional ventricular ectopics, and blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. His nasopharyngeal temperature has risen from 36.4°C to 38.4°C over 15 minutes, and his jaw and limbs are rigid. The absorbent canister feels hot.

Arterial blood gas:
- pH 7.16 (7.35–7.45)
- pCO2 72 mmHg (35–45)
- pO2 210 mmHg (FiO2 0.5)
- Bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22–32)
- Lactate 4.2 mmol/L (<2.0)
- Potassium 6.0 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)

Which one of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Sepsis from contamination of the surgical field
Thyroid storm
Inadequate depth of anaesthesia
Exhausted CO2 absorbent causing rebreathing
Malignant hyperthermia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Malignant hyperthermia

---

A rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 that does not respond to increased ventilation is the most sensitive early sign of malignant hyperthermia (MH), a pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium in people with susceptibility variants (usually RYR1). Other features here are tachycardia with arrhythmia, muscle rigidity, rising temperature (often a later sign), a hot absorbent (from increased CO2 production), and a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia. A normal previous anaesthetic history is uninformative, as this is his first. The MHANZ (Malignant Hyperthermia Australia and New Zealand) resource kit steps are: call for help and the MH kit, stop the volatile agent, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen at high flow, give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV (repeated until the hypermetabolism resolves), switch to TIVA, cool actively, treat hyperkalaemia and arrhythmias, and finish or abandon surgery quickly. He and his relatives will later need referral to an MH diagnostic unit.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Unexplained rising end-tidal CO2 despite increased ventilation under volatile anaesthesia = malignant hyperthermia until proven otherwise. Stop the trigger, 100% O2, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg.

---

question_text:
A 46-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of Toowoomba Hospital, Queensland, after his motorbike hit a kangaroo at 90 km/h. He was wearing a helmet. The trauma team is carrying out the primary survey.

- Airway: talking, cervical collar in place
- Breathing: respiratory rate 26/min, oxygen saturation 97% on high-flow oxygen, equal air entry, eFAST shows no pneumothorax
- Circulation: pulse 132/min, blood pressure 80/50 mmHg after 1 L of warmed crystalloid; peripheries cold; no external bleeding; eFAST shows no free fluid in the abdomen or pericardium
- Disability: GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6), pupils equal and reactive
- Exposure: bruising over the lower abdomen, perineum and scrotum; no long bone deformity; blood at the urethral meatus

Chest X-ray is normal. Pelvic X-ray shows widening of the pubic symphysis to 4 cm with disruption of the right sacroiliac joint. The massive haemorrhage protocol has been activated, two units of O-negative red cells are running, and 1 g of IV tranexamic acid has been given.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Emergency laparotomy to control intra-abdominal bleeding
Apply a pelvic binder centred over the greater trochanters
Transfer to CT for contrast-enhanced imaging of the abdomen and pelvis
Apply a pelvic binder centred over the iliac crests
Give a further 2 L crystalloid bolus and reassess the blood pressure
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Apply a pelvic binder centred over the greater trochanters

---

He has haemorrhagic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, cold peripheries, poor response to fluid) with an open-book pelvic fracture (symphysis diastasis and sacroiliac disruption). eFAST is negative for abdominal free fluid and the chest is clear, so the pelvis is the likely source. Pelvic bleeding is mostly venous and from fracture surfaces. In EMST/ATLS teaching, the immediate step in circulation (C) is mechanical stabilisation with a pelvic binder, which reduces pelvic volume, tamponades venous bleeding and stabilises clot. The binder must be centred over the greater trochanters (at the level of the symphysis), not the iliac crests. This goes alongside damage control resuscitation (blood products in balanced ratios, tranexamic acid, permissive hypotension, avoiding large crystalloid volumes). If he remains unstable, definitive haemorrhage control is by angioembolisation and/or preperitoneal packing and external fixation, depending on local resources, with early discussion with the retrieval service and a major trauma centre. Blood at the meatus means no urethral catheter until the urethra is imaged.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Shock with an open-book pelvic fracture and negative eFAST: apply a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters, resuscitate with blood and TXA, then arrange angioembolisation or packing.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "Sydney HEMS / NSW Ambulance. Clinical practice standard: Pelvic trauma", "url": "https://sydneyhems.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ao.cli_.-07-pelvic-trauma.pdf"}

---

subtopic: Haemodynamically unstable pelvic fracture: EMST circulation priorities

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Laparotomy is for intra-abdominal bleeding. eFAST shows no free fluid, and opening the abdomen can release the tamponade of a pelvic haematoma and worsen bleeding.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A patient in shock who is not responding to resuscitation should not go to CT before bleeding is controlled. CT is for patients who have been stabilised.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A binder over the iliac crests is too high. It does not close the pelvic ring effectively and can even widen some fractures.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Large-volume crystalloid dilutes clotting factors, worsens acidosis and hypothermia, and raises blood pressure enough to disrupt clot. Resuscitation should be with blood products.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department of a hospital in Cairns, Queensland, with a painful, swollen right hand. Two days ago he punched another man in the mouth during an argument. He has a small cut over his knuckle that he cleaned himself. Since yesterday the hand has become more swollen and he cannot make a full fist. He is right-handed and works as a chef. His tetanus vaccination is up to date. He has no drug allergies.

His temperature is 37.9°C and pulse 96/min. There is a 5 mm ragged wound over the dorsum of the right fourth metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, with a little cloudy discharge. The dorsum of the hand is swollen and red, with erythema extending 3 cm proximally. Movement of the fourth MCP joint is very painful, and he cannot fully flex or extend the ring finger. Sensation and capillary refill are normal.

X-ray of the hand shows no fracture and no radio-opaque foreign body. White cell count is 13.8 × 10^9/L and CRP 64 mg/L.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Primary closure of the wound and oral amoxicillin–clavulanate
Oral flucloxacillin and review in the fracture clinic in 1 week
Oral amoxicillin–clavulanate at home with review in 48 hours
Admission for IV antibiotics and urgent surgical exploration and washout
Wound dressing and tetanus booster, with no antibiotics
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Admission for IV antibiotics and urgent surgical exploration and washout

---

A wound over the MCP joint after punching someone in the mouth is a clenched-fist (fight bite) injury until proven otherwise. With the fist clenched, a tooth can penetrate skin, extensor tendon and joint capsule; when the fingers straighten, the tendon slides and seals the tract, so the wound looks trivial. Mouth flora (streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, anaerobes and Eikenella corrodens) cause septic arthritis, tenosynovitis and osteomyelitis. He presented late with signs of established infection: fever, discharge, spreading cellulitis, painful joint movement and raised inflammatory markers. NSW ACI guidance on human bites recommends surgical consultation for suspected joint or tendon involvement, and admission for IV antibiotics for infected hand bites. He needs admission, elevation, IV antibiotics covering mouth flora (according to local guidance), and urgent hand surgery review for exploration, joint washout and debridement. The wound should be left open.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Knuckle wound after punching a mouth = fight bite. If infected or over the joint, admit for IV antibiotics and hand-surgical exploration and washout; never close primarily.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "Remote Primary Health Care Manuals. Bites \u2013 animal or human (CARPA)", "url": "https://remotephcmanuals.org.au/document/35645.html"}
• {"name": "Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG complete): Antibiotic, bite wound infections (subscription)", "url": "https://www.tg.org.au"}

---

subtopic: Infected clenched-fist (fight bite) injury over the MCP joint

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Bite wounds on the hand should not be closed primarily; closure traps bacteria. Oral antibiotics are not enough for an established deep infection.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Flucloxacillin does not cover Eikenella corrodens or anaerobes, and a week's delay risks joint destruction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Oral amoxicillin–clavulanate is right for prophylaxis of an early, uninfected bite, but not for an established infection with probable joint involvement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Tetanus is already covered. An infected fight bite needs antibiotics and surgical assessment.

key_takeaways: Knuckle wound after punching a mouth = fight bite. If infected or over the joint, admit for IV antibiotics and hand-surgical exploration and washout; never close primarily.

question_text:
A 54-year-old woman attends the pre-admission clinic of a public hospital in Canberra. She is booked for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 10 days for recurrent biliary colic. She has type 2 diabetes and obesity (BMI 38 kg/m²). She takes metformin 1 g twice daily and subcutaneous semaglutide 1 mg once weekly, which she injects every Sunday. Her HbA1c is 7.1% (54 mmol/mol) and she has lost 14 kg on semaglutide over the past year. She has no nausea, vomiting, bloating or reflux, and no other medical problems. Her surgery is scheduled for a Thursday morning.

She has read online that she should stop semaglutide before surgery and asks what she should do.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop semaglutide now and restart it 1 week after surgery
Withhold semaglutide for 3 weeks before surgery and bridge with insulin
Continue semaglutide, clear fluids the day before, then fast from 6 hours before surgery
Continue semaglutide and follow the standard 6-hour fast, as she has no gastrointestinal symptoms
Skip the Sunday dose before surgery and follow the standard 6-hour fast
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Continue semaglutide, clear fluids the day before, then fast from 6 hours before surgery

---

GLP-1 receptor agonists slow gastric emptying, and retained gastric contents have been found at endoscopy and anaesthesia despite standard fasting, raising aspiration risk. The 2025 ADS/ANZCA/GESA/NACOS clinical practice recommendations (updated April 2025) advise that GLP-1 RAs and dual GLP-1/GIP agonists should be CONTINUED around procedures, because stopping them worsens glucose control and weight management and no safe cessation period has been established. Instead, all patients taking these drugs should have a 24-hour clear fluid diet on the day before the procedure, followed by the standard 6-hour preoperative fast (clear fluids allowed in limited amounts until 2 hours before). The absence of gastrointestinal symptoms cannot be used to identify low risk. If the 24-hour clear fluid diet has not been followed, the anaesthetist should use risk mitigation (e.g. gastric ultrasound, prokinetics such as IV erythromycin, a modified anaesthetic technique) or defer the procedure. Metformin and other diabetes medicines are managed according to the ADS–ANZCA perioperative diabetes guideline.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
ANZ 2025: continue GLP-1 RAs (and GLP-1/GIP agonists) before procedures; 24-hour clear fluid diet the day before, then a standard 6-hour fast. GI symptoms do not stratify risk.

---

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman in her first pregnancy sees her general practitioner in Cabramatta, Sydney, for the results of her first antenatal blood tests at 9 weeks' gestation. She was born in Vietnam and moved to Australia at the age of 12. Her partner, whose family is from southern China, is well. She feels well apart from mild nausea. Her diet includes red meat several times a week.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 112 g/L (115–160)
- Mean cell volume (MCV) 68 fL (80–100)
- Mean cell haemoglobin (MCH) 21 pg (27–33)
- Ferritin 85 µg/L (30–200)
- Haemoglobin HPLC: HbA2 2.6% (2.0–3.5), HbF 0.4% (<1.0), no variant haemoglobin detected
- Blood group O Rh D positive, antibody screen negative
- Rubella immune; HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis serology negative

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start oral iron and repeat the full blood count in 6 weeks
Reassure her that the normal HbA2 excludes a clinically important haemoglobinopathy
Arrange full blood count, ferritin and haemoglobin studies for her partner now
Offer chorionic villus sampling at 11–13 weeks
Offer non-invasive prenatal testing (cfDNA) to screen the fetus for thalassaemia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Arrange full blood count, ferritin and haemoglobin studies for her partner now

---

She has microcytosis (MCV below 80 fL, MCH below 27 pg) with a normal ferritin, so iron deficiency does not explain it. A normal HbA2 makes beta-thalassaemia trait unlikely but does NOT exclude alpha-thalassaemia trait, which is common in people of Southeast Asian and southern Chinese background and cannot be diagnosed by HPLC. The key question in pregnancy is whether the couple is at risk of a severe fetal haemoglobinopathy, in particular haemoglobin Bart's hydrops fetalis (when both partners carry alpha-zero deletions such as --SEA, which is common in both their populations). RACGP genomics guidance on haemoglobinopathies advises that when a pregnant woman has a low MCV/MCH with normal iron studies, her partner should be tested promptly, and DNA testing for alpha-thalassaemia should be arranged for both partners when it cannot be excluded. Testing the partner early is time-critical so that an at-risk couple can be referred to genetics/fetal medicine and offered prenatal diagnosis (CVS at 11–13 weeks) in time.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Low MCV/MCH with normal ferritin in pregnancy: test the partner now. A normal HbA2 does not exclude alpha-thalassaemia; DNA testing is needed if it cannot be excluded.

---

• {"name": "O&G Magazine (RANZCOG). Thalassaemia and haemoglobinopathy screening in pregnancy (2024)", "url": "https://www.ogmagazine.org.au/24/1-24/thalassaemia-and-haemoglobinopathy-screening-in-pregnancy/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A normal HbA2 does not exclude alpha-thalassaemia trait, which is likely given her indices and ancestry.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: CVS is offered only once the couple is shown to be at risk. It carries a small miscarriage risk and is premature before partner testing.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Standard cfDNA screening is for chromosomal aneuploidy. It is not a routine screening test for fetal thalassaemia.

key_takeaways: Low MCV/MCH with normal ferritin in pregnancy: test the partner now. A normal HbA2 does not exclude alpha-thalassaemia; DNA testing is needed if it cannot be excluded.

question_text:
A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department of Mount Isa Hospital, Queensland, with 2 days of left iliac fossa pain and light vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She works as a cook on a cattle station 380 km away, reached by an unsealed road that often becomes impassable after rain. There is no mobile phone reception at the station. She plans to return there in two days. She has had one previous vaginal birth and has no medical problems. She is not breastfeeding.

Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse 82/min and blood pressure 118/74 mmHg. She has mild left iliac fossa tenderness without guarding.

Investigations:
- Serum β-hCG 1800 IU/L; repeat at 48 hours 1950 IU/L
- Haemoglobin 128 g/L
- Liver and renal function normal
- Blood group A Rh D positive
- Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus; 2.4 cm inhomogeneous left adnexal mass separate from the ovary, with no yolk sac or fetal heart; small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas; right tube and ovary normal

She would like to have more children in future.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m² and β-hCG on days 4 and 7
Expectant management with β-hCG every 48 hours
Intravenous methotrexate infusion because β-hCG is rising
Laparoscopic left salpingectomy
Laparoscopic left salpingostomy
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Laparoscopic left salpingectomy

---

She has a stable, unruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy with a plateauing β-hCG below 3000 IU/L, a mass under 3.5 cm and no fetal heart activity. On biochemical and ultrasound grounds she would be a candidate for methotrexate. But medical management needs reliable follow-up for weeks (serial β-hCG until it is undetectable, often 4–6 weeks or longer, with ready access to emergency care in case of rupture). The Queensland Clinical Guideline on early pregnancy loss lists geographic isolation and inability to take part in prolonged follow-up as contraindications to methotrexate. Rupture 380 km from hospital without phone access could be fatal. So laparoscopic surgery is safest. With a healthy contralateral tube, salpingectomy is preferred to salpingostomy: subsequent intrauterine pregnancy rates are similar, and salpingectomy avoids persistent trophoblast and the need for β-hCG follow-up.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy needs reliable follow-up. Geographic isolation or inability to attend is a contraindication: offer laparoscopic salpingectomy if the other tube is healthy.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Queensland Clinical Guidelines. Early pregnancy loss (guideline and flowchart)", "url": "https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0033/139947/g-epl.pdf"}
• {"name": "RANZCOG. Miscarriage, recurrent miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy (C-Gyn 38)", "url": "https://www.ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Miscarriage-Ectopic-Pregnancy.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy: geographic isolation as a contraindication to methotrexate

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Her β-hCG, mass size and lack of fetal heart would suit IM methotrexate, but follow-up is not feasible and she lives far from emergency care. This is exactly the situation the guideline warns against.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Expectant management is for a low and falling β-hCG (e.g. below 1500 IU/L at presentation) in a woman who can attend follow-up. Her β-hCG is above that and not falling, and follow-up is not possible.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The Queensland protocol uses IV methotrexate when β-hCG is above 3000 IU/L. Hers is below that, and the same follow-up problem applies whatever the route.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Salpingostomy conserves the tube but needs weekly β-hCG follow-up for persistent trophoblast (about 1 in 10–20). It is considered when the other tube is damaged. Her other tube is normal and follow-up is the problem.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman in her second pregnancy comes to an early pregnancy assessment service in Adelaide at 8 weeks and 2 days by dates. Yesterday evening she had one episode of light, bright red vaginal spotting that soaked half a panty liner and stopped within an hour. She has had no pain and no further bleeding. There was no trauma or intercourse beforehand. Her first pregnancy ended in an uncomplicated vaginal birth 3 years ago, after which she received Rh D immunoglobulin.

She is well, with pulse 74/min and blood pressure 112/70 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Speculum examination shows a closed cervix with a small amount of old blood and no active bleeding.

Investigations:
- Transvaginal ultrasound: single intrauterine pregnancy, crown–rump length consistent with 8 weeks 1 day, fetal heart rate 162/min, no subchorionic haematoma
- Blood group O Rh D negative; antibody screen negative

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management regarding Rh D immunoglobulin?
options: No Rh D immunoglobulin is needed for this episode
Give Rh D immunoglobulin 250 IU IM within 72 hours
Give Rh D immunoglobulin 625 IU IM within 72 hours
Perform a Kleihauer test to determine the Rh D immunoglobulin dose
Start routine antenatal prophylaxis now instead of waiting until 28 weeks
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. No Rh D immunoglobulin is needed for this episode

---

This is a threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks: a single episode of light, painless bleeding with a viable intrauterine pregnancy and a closed cervix. The National Blood Authority guideline on prophylactic Rh D immunoglobulin in pregnancy care (2021), which RANZCOG's C-Obs 6 statement refers Fellows to, states there is insufficient evidence that threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks needs Rh D immunoglobulin. It may be given at the clinician's discretion when bleeding is repeated or heavy, or associated with abdominal pain or significant pelvic trauma. None of these applies here. This differs from actual pregnancy loss or procedures in the first trimester: Australian guidance still recommends Rh D immunoglobulin (250 IU up to 12 weeks) for miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, chorionic villus sampling, and abortion (RANZCOG: after 10 weeks). She should have routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks, and should return if bleeding recurs, becomes heavy or is accompanied by pain, when the decision can be revisited.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks with light, painless bleeding: Rh D immunoglobulin is not routinely needed (NBA 2021). Consider it if bleeding is heavy or repeated, with pain, or after trauma; give it for actual miscarriage, ectopic or procedures.

question_text:
A 30-year-old woman in her third pregnancy presents to the maternity unit of Broken Hill Hospital, New South Wales, at 31 weeks' gestation with a sudden episode of painless, bright red vaginal bleeding that woke her from sleep. She estimates about 200 mL of blood loss, which has now slowed to light spotting. She has had two previous caesarean births. She booked late at 26 weeks after moving from interstate and missed her morphology ultrasound, so she has not yet had a scan in this pregnancy. She reports normal fetal movements. She has no pain, contractions or leakage of fluid, and no recent intercourse or trauma.

Her pulse is 92/min and blood pressure 116/72 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender between palpations, the uterus is not irritable, fundal height is 31 cm, and the fetus is in a transverse lie. CTG shows a baseline of 140 bpm with normal variability, accelerations and no decelerations. Blood group is O Rh D positive. IV access has been obtained and blood sent for full blood count, coagulation and group and hold.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in assessment?
options: Digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
Ultrasound to locate the placenta before any vaginal examination
Kleihauer test to quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage
Discharge home if the CTG remains normal for a further 2 hours
Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Ultrasound to locate the placenta before any vaginal examination

---

Painless bright red bleeding in the third trimester with a non-tender uterus and an abnormal lie (transverse) suggests placenta praevia until proven otherwise. Her two previous caesareans increase the risk of both praevia and placenta accreta spectrum. Her placental site is unknown because she has had no scan. A digital vaginal examination must not be done until placenta praevia has been excluded, because it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage (RCOG Green-top 63 and Australian local APH guidelines such as SESLHD). The next step is ultrasound to locate the placenta. Transvaginal ultrasound is safe in suspected praevia and is more accurate than transabdominal scanning. A gentle speculum examination can then be used to assess the cervix and bleeding. She will also need antenatal corticosteroids (at 31 weeks, with risk of preterm birth), admission, and plans for transfer to a tertiary unit with accreta expertise if praevia is confirmed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
APH with unknown placental site: no digital vaginal examination until ultrasound excludes placenta praevia. Transvaginal ultrasound is safe and more accurate.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "South Eastern Sydney LHD. Antepartum haemorrhage (APH) clinical guideline (2020)", "url": "https://www.seslhd.health.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/antepartumhaemorrhage-aph2020.pdf"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: She is Rh D positive, so a Kleihauer test to guide Rh D immunoglobulin dosing is not needed. It does not diagnose the cause of bleeding.

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman gave birth vaginally 20 minutes ago at a hospital in Bundaberg, Queensland, after an induction of labour at 38 weeks for pre-eclampsia. Her blood pressure has been controlled with oral labetalol. She has moderate asthma treated with budesonide/formoterol. She received oxytocin 10 IU IM with delivery of the anterior shoulder, and the placenta and membranes were delivered complete 10 minutes later.

She is now bleeding heavily, with an estimated blood loss of 1100 mL. Her pulse is 116/min and blood pressure 108/66 mmHg (it was 152/98 mmHg before birth). The uterus is soft and boggy and rises above the umbilicus; it firms briefly with fundal massage and bimanual compression. The bladder has been emptied by catheter. A rapid inspection shows no significant genital tract trauma. The PPH emergency has been called. Two large-bore cannulas are in place, bloods (including fibrinogen) have been sent, and she has been given oxytocin 5 IU IV twice, 5 minutes apart. An oxytocin infusion has been started. Bleeding continues.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate medication to give now?
options: Ergometrine 250 micrograms IV
Carboprost 250 micrograms IM
Recombinant activated factor VII IV
Misoprostol 200 micrograms orally
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes

---

This is a major primary PPH from uterine atony (tone), continuing despite oxytocin boluses, an infusion and uterine massage. The Queensland Clinical Guideline on primary PPH recommends tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible after the onset of PPH, ideally within 3 hours, in addition to uterotonics. The WOMAN trial showed that early TXA reduces death from bleeding, with no increase in thromboembolic events. A second 1 g dose can be given if bleeding continues after 30 minutes. Her other uterotonic options are limited: ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia and severe hypertension, and carboprost (a prostaglandin F2α) can cause bronchospasm and should be avoided or used with great caution in asthma. Alongside TXA, she needs continued bimanual compression, blood products and fibrinogen replacement guided by results, and early transfer to theatre for balloon tamponade or surgical measures if bleeding continues.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In PPH, give tranexamic acid 1 g IV early (within 3 hours) alongside uterotonics. Ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia or hypertension; carboprost is a problem in asthma.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "RANZCOG. Management of postpartum haemorrhage (C-Obs 43)", "url": "https://www.ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Management-Postpartum-Haemorrhage.pdf"}

---

question_text:
A 33-year-old woman in her second pregnancy is in spontaneous labour at 39 weeks and 4 days at a hospital in Ballarat, Victoria. Her first baby was born by lower segment caesarean section for breech presentation 3 years ago, and she has chosen a planned vaginal birth after caesarean. Labour was augmented with an oxytocin infusion 4 hours ago because of slow progress, and she has an effective epidural. Continuous CTG monitoring is in place. At the last examination, 1 hour ago, the cervix was 8 cm dilated with the vertex at station 0.

She now calls the midwife because of sudden, severe, constant lower abdominal pain that is breaking through her epidural, with pain in her right shoulder. There is fresh vaginal bleeding of about 150 mL. Her pulse has risen from 88 to 124/min and her blood pressure has fallen from 124/76 to 96/58 mmHg. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration to 70 bpm lasting 4 minutes, and the tocograph shows that contractions have become weak and irregular. On vaginal examination the vertex is now at station −3 and easily pushed up.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Uterine rupture
Placental abruption
Uterine tachysystole caused by oxytocin
Umbilical cord prolapse
Ruptured vasa praevia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Uterine rupture

---

Uterine rupture is the key risk of labour after caesarean (about 0.5–0.7% after one lower segment incision, higher with induction or augmentation). The most common and often earliest sign is an abnormal fetal heart rate pattern, especially a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia. Other features are new constant abdominal pain (including pain breaking through an epidural), shoulder-tip pain from haemoperitoneum, vaginal bleeding, maternal tachycardia and hypotension, a change in the contraction pattern (contractions weaken or stop), and loss of station of the presenting part as the fetus moves out of the uterus. She has all of these. Management is immediate: stop the oxytocin, call for help, resuscitate, and perform a category 1 caesarean (laparotomy) with neonatal team present. RANZCOG C-Obs 38 (Birth after previous caesarean) advises continuous fetal monitoring in labour for this reason.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In labour after caesarean: prolonged deceleration or bradycardia with new constant pain, shoulder-tip pain, bleeding, maternal shock, weaker contractions and loss of station = uterine rupture. Immediate laparotomy.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "RANZCOG. Birth After Caesarean (C-Obs 38), updated 2025", "url": "https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Birth-After-Caesarean.pdf"}
• {"name": "StatPearls. Uterine Rupture (NCBI Bookshelf)", "url": "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559209/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Labour after previous caesarean: recognising uterine rupture

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Abruption also causes pain, bleeding and fetal compromise, but the uterus becomes tense and hypertonic with frequent contractions. It does not cause loss of station, and contractions do not fade.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Tachysystole means more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes. Her contractions have become weaker, and tachysystole does not cause shoulder-tip pain, maternal shock or loss of station.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Cord prolapse causes fetal bradycardia, but it needs ruptured membranes with a cord felt or seen. It does not cause maternal pain, bleeding or shock.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Vasa praevia bleeding is fetal blood, typically at membrane rupture, causing a sinusoidal pattern or bradycardia with a well mother. It does not cause maternal shock, pain or loss of station.

key_takeaways: In labour after caesarean: prolonged deceleration or bradycardia with new constant pain, shoulder-tip pain, bleeding, maternal shock, weaker contractions and loss of station = uterine rupture. Immediate laparotomy.

question_text:
A 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy sees her general practitioner in Geelong, Victoria, at 27 weeks' gestation for the result of her routine 75 g pregnancy oral glucose tolerance test, done at 26 weeks. She is of South Asian background, her BMI before pregnancy was 27 kg/m², and her mother has type 2 diabetes. Her first-trimester HbA1c was 5.4% (36 mmol/mol). The pregnancy has been uncomplicated, and fundal height is 27 cm. Her previous GP had told her she was 'likely to get gestational diabetes' because of her risk factors.

75 g pregnancy OGTT (venous plasma glucose), taken in September 2026:
- Fasting 5.2 mmol/L
- 1 hour 10.3 mmol/L
- 2 hours 8.8 mmol/L

Which one of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this result?
options: Gestational diabetes on each of the three values; refer for diabetes education and monitoring
Gestational diabetes on the fasting value alone
Overt diabetes in pregnancy; start insulin
Does not meet the criteria for gestational diabetes; continue routine antenatal care
Borderline result; repeat the OGTT at 32 weeks
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Does not meet the criteria for gestational diabetes; continue routine antenatal care

---

In 2025 the Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society (ADIPS) raised the diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes on the 75 g pregnancy OGTT. GDM is now diagnosed if ANY of: fasting 5.3–6.9 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.6 mmol/L or more, or 2-hour 9.0–11.0 mmol/L. The previous (IADPSG/WHO 2013-based) thresholds were 5.1, 10.0 and 8.5 mmol/L. Her values (5.2, 10.3, 8.8) would have met all three OLD criteria but meet NONE of the new ones, so she does not have GDM. Victorian public and private pathology services changed to the new criteria on 4 August 2025. Overt diabetes in pregnancy is fasting 7.0 or more, 2-hour 11.1 or more, or HbA1c 6.5% or more. She should continue routine care with healthy eating and activity advice, and a repeat OGTT is not routinely recommended without a new clinical indication.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
ADIPS 2025 GDM thresholds (75 g POGTT): fasting ≥5.3, 1-hour ≥10.6, 2-hour ≥9.0 mmol/L. The old 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5 cut-offs are superseded.

---

• {"name": "Safer Care Victoria. New gestational diabetes guideline from ADIPS (16 Sep 2025)", "url": "https://www.safercare.vic.gov.au/news/new-gestational-diabetes-guideline-from-the-australian-diabetes-in-pregnancy-society-adips"}

question_text:
A 36-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Darwin at 11 weeks and 4 days of her second pregnancy, confirmed by a dating scan. She has had essential hypertension for 4 years, treated with perindopril 5 mg daily, and her blood pressure has been well controlled. She did not plan the pregnancy. Her first pregnancy, 5 years ago, was complicated by pre-eclampsia at 35 weeks. She takes no other medicines, does not smoke, and eats little dairy (she estimates under 1 serve a day).

Her blood pressure is 134/86 mmHg on repeated measurement. Her BMI is 31 kg/m². Urinalysis shows no proteinuria. Renal function, liver function, platelets and urine protein:creatinine ratio are normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue perindopril until 20 weeks, then change to labetalol
Change perindopril to labetalol and start aspirin 150 mg daily now
Change perindopril to methyldopa and start aspirin 100 mg daily now
Change perindopril to labetalol and start aspirin 150 mg daily from 20 weeks
Stop perindopril without a replacement, as blood pressure falls in the second trimester
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Change perindopril to labetalol and start aspirin 150 mg daily now

---

ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) should be stopped as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, because they are fetotoxic in the second and third trimesters (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia). They should be replaced with a pregnancy-compatible drug such as labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa. She is at high risk of pre-eclampsia (chronic hypertension and previous pre-eclampsia, plus age and BMI). The SOMANZ 2023 hypertension in pregnancy guideline strongly recommends aspirin 150 mg daily for women at high risk, started before 16 weeks and stopped between 34 weeks and birth. Because her dietary calcium intake is low (under 1 g/day), SOMANZ also recommends calcium supplementation (e.g. 1–1.5 g/day). Her BP target on treatment is around 110–140/80–85 mmHg; stopping all treatment would risk uncontrolled hypertension.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Chronic hypertension in pregnancy: stop ACE inhibitors/ARBs now, switch to labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa. High pre-eclampsia risk: aspirin 150 mg daily started before 16 weeks, plus calcium if intake is low (SOMANZ 2023).

---

• {"name": "A summary of the 2023 SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline. Med J Aust 2024;220(11)", "url": "https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2024/220/11/summary-2023-society-obstetric-medicine-australia-and-new-zealand-somanz"}

---

question_text:
A 24-year-old woman sees a pharmacist-referred general practitioner in Bunbury, Western Australia, on a Friday afternoon. She had unprotected vaginal intercourse on Monday night, about 90 hours ago, when a condom broke. Her last menstrual period started 13 days ago, and her cycles are regular at 28 days. This was the only episode of unprotected sex this cycle. She wants emergency contraception and would also like to start the combined oral contraceptive pill for ongoing contraception. She has a strong fear of pelvic procedures and declines an intrauterine device after discussion.

She weighs 92 kg (BMI 33 kg/m²) and her blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg. She has no migraine, no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, does not smoke and takes no other medicines. A urine pregnancy test is negative.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg now and start the combined pill today
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg now and start the combined pill today
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg now and start the combined pill 5 days later, with condoms meanwhile
Levonorgestrel 3 mg now and start the combined pill today
No emergency contraception needed, as ovulation has probably already occurred
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Ulipristal acetate 30 mg now and start the combined pill 5 days later, with condoms meanwhile

---

The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception (up to 120 hours, unaffected by weight), but she has declined it. Of the oral options, ulipristal acetate (UPA) is more effective than levonorgestrel (LNG), particularly beyond 72 hours and in women with a higher BMI. LNG is licensed in Australia up to 72 hours (with some efficacy to 96 hours), while UPA is licensed up to 120 hours. She is at 90 hours, mid-cycle, with a BMI of 33, so UPA is the best oral choice. UPA is a progesterone receptor modulator: progestogens taken in the following days can reduce its ability to delay ovulation. Australian guidance (e.g. Australian Prescriber; Sexual Health and Family Planning Australia) is to wait 5 days after UPA before starting hormonal contraception, using condoms or abstinence in the meantime and then for the first 7 days of active combined pills. A pregnancy test is advised 3–4 weeks after UPSI if the next period is delayed or unusual.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Emergency contraception: copper IUD is most effective. If declined, UPA beats LNG beyond 72 hours and at higher BMI. After UPA, wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "Sexual Health and Family Planning Australia. Statement on emergency contraception", "url": "https://www.fpnsw.org.au/sites/default/files/assets/shfpa_ec.pdf"}
• {"name": "RACGP (AFP 2017). Emergency contraception: oral and intrauterine options", "url": "https://www.racgp.org.au/afp/2017/october/emergency-contraception-oral-and-intrauterine-opti"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: LNG can be started with the pill immediately, but at 90 hours it is outside its licensed window and less effective than UPA, especially at a BMI of 33.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Some guidelines suggest a double LNG dose for higher weight, but this is off-label, the evidence is weak, and at 90 hours UPA is more effective anyway.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: She is on day 13 of a 28-day cycle, the time of highest pregnancy risk. Ovulation may not have occurred, and emergency contraception is clearly indicated.

question_text:
A 26-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Wollongong, New South Wales, to start contraception. She has been using condoms but would like something more reliable and has read about the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has 'sick headaches' three or four times a year that last most of a day and make her lie down in a dark room. She takes ibuprofen for them. She has no other medical history and takes no regular medicines. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, and her BMI is 23 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 114/70 mmHg. She had a normal cervical screening test 2 years ago.

Before deciding whether the combined pill is suitable, which one of the following is the most important additional information to obtain?
options: Whether she smokes cigarettes
Whether any relative has had breast cancer
Whether she has ever had a sexually transmitted infection
Whether she has had a previous ectopic pregnancy
Whether her headaches are preceded by visual or sensory symptoms
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Whether her headaches are preceded by visual or sensory symptoms

---

Her headaches sound like migraine. The key question is whether she has migraine WITH aura (e.g. spreading zig-zag lines, scotoma, unilateral tingling or numbness developing over minutes before the headache). Migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4 (unacceptable health risk) for combined hormonal contraception at any age, because oestrogen further increases the already raised risk of ischaemic stroke. Migraine without aura is category 2 for starting the pill under 35. This single question changes her options most. If she has aura, suitable alternatives include progestogen-only methods (implant, LNG-IUD, progestogen-only pill, DMPA) and the copper IUD. Australian clinicians commonly use the UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC), as recommended in Australian contraception resources.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Before prescribing combined hormonal contraception to a woman with migraine, ask about aura. Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 at any age: offer progestogen-only or copper IUD methods.

---

question_text:
A 23-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Hobart because of heavy periods. Her periods have been heavy since they started at 12: she bleeds for 8 days, changes a super tampon and pad every 1–2 hours on the heaviest days, passes large clots and has had to leave work because of flooding. Her cycles are regular at 28 days. She has frequent nosebleeds that sometimes last 20 minutes, bruises easily, and needed a return visit to the dentist for bleeding after a wisdom tooth extraction. Her mother had very heavy periods and a hysterectomy at 38. She is not sexually active and has never been pregnant. She takes no medicines, including no NSAIDs or supplements.

Examination shows scattered bruises on her shins. Abdominal examination is normal. She declines a pelvic examination.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115–160), MCV 74 fL (80–100)
- Platelets 268 × 10^9/L (150–400)
- Ferritin 6 µg/L (30–200)
- TSH normal
- Urine β-hCG negative

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: VWF antigen and activity, factor VIII and coagulation studies
Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound on days 5–10 of the cycle
Endometrial biopsy
Serum FSH, LH and oestradiol
Cervical screening test
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. VWF antigen and activity, factor VIII and coagulation studies

---

She has heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche with iron deficiency anaemia, AND a personal bleeding history (prolonged nosebleeds, easy bruising, bleeding after dental extraction) and a family history suggestive of heavy bleeding. This strongly suggests an inherited bleeding disorder, most often von Willebrand disease, which is present in a meaningful proportion of women with HMB and is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. The Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Clinical Care Standard (ACSQHC 2024) says testing for bleeding disorders, thyroid function, cervical screening and ultrasound are not routine for everyone, but should be arranged based on history and presentation. Here, the history makes bleeding disorder testing the priority: von Willebrand factor antigen and activity (e.g. VWF:GP1bM or ristocetin cofactor), factor VIII, full blood count and a coagulation screen, ideally with haematology input. She also needs iron replacement (probably IV given her ferritin and symptoms) and treatment for the bleeding (e.g. tranexamic acid or hormonal options) while results are awaited.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
HMB since menarche plus a personal or family bleeding history: test for von Willebrand disease and other bleeding disorders. Ultrasound and other tests are not routine; choose them by history.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "METEOR (AIHW). Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Clinical Care Standard 2024 indicators", "url": "https://meteor.aihw.gov.au/content/788514"}

---

question_text:
A 52-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Cairns, Queensland, because of severe hot flushes and night sweats for a year, waking her four or five times a night. Her last menstrual period was 14 months ago. She has tried layered clothing, reducing alcohol and cognitive behavioural therapy with little benefit, and would like hormone therapy. She has not had a hysterectomy.

She has obesity (BMI 36 kg/m²), migraine without aura and hypertriglyceridaemia. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, breast cancer, stroke or heart disease, and she does not smoke. Her blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg. Breast examination is normal and her screening mammogram 8 months ago was normal. Cervical screening is up to date.

Fasting lipids: total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 3.2 mmol/L (<2.0), HDL 1.1 mmol/L, LDL 2.8 mmol/L.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate regimen?
options: Oral conjugated oestrogens with oral medroxyprogesterone acetate daily
Transdermal oestradiol alone
Oral oestradiol with oral dydrogesterone daily
Transdermal oestradiol with oral micronised progesterone 100 mg nightly
Vaginal oestriol cream alone
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Transdermal oestradiol with oral micronised progesterone 100 mg nightly

---

She is under 60 and within 10 years of menopause with troublesome vasomotor symptoms, so MHT is appropriate and its benefits are likely to outweigh the risks. Because she has a uterus, she needs a progestogen to protect the endometrium. Being more than 12 months after her last period, a continuous combined regimen is appropriate (e.g. micronised progesterone 100 mg nightly). Transdermal oestrogen is preferred in her case: the Australasian Menopause Society notes that transdermal oestradiol at standard doses does not increase venous thromboembolism risk (important with obesity), avoids the first-pass hepatic effect that raises triglycerides with oral oestrogen, and is generally preferred in migraine. Micronised progesterone (or dydrogesterone) appears to carry less breast cancer and VTE risk than older synthetic progestogens such as medroxyprogesterone acetate. Micronised progesterone should be taken orally; transdermal progesterone creams do not protect the endometrium.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
MHT with a uterus needs a progestogen. Choose transdermal oestradiol in obesity/VTE risk, hypertriglyceridaemia or migraine, and prefer oral micronised progesterone (continuous if >12 months after the last period).

---

question_text:
A 29-year-old woman and her 31-year-old husband see a general practitioner in Parramatta, Sydney, because they have not conceived after 14 months of regular unprotected intercourse. She has had irregular periods since her teens, with cycles of 45–90 days, and she has excess hair on her chin and abdomen. She has no pelvic pain, no history of pelvic infection or abdominal surgery, and has never been pregnant. She does not smoke and drinks rarely. Her BMI is 27 kg/m² and blood pressure 118/76 mmHg.

Investigations:
- Pelvic ultrasound: more than 20 follicles per ovary, ovarian volume 12 mL bilaterally, normal uterus
- Total testosterone 2.4 nmol/L (<1.7), SHBG low
- TSH and prolactin normal
- 75 g OGTT: normal
- Rubella immune, cervical screening up to date, folic acid started
- Husband's semen analysis: normal by WHO criteria

They would like to start treatment.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?
options: Clomiphene citrate
Letrozole
Metformin alone
Gonadotrophin injections
Referral for in vitro fertilisation
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Letrozole

---

She meets the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS (oligo-ovulation, clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology), and her infertility is anovulatory, with a normal semen analysis and no risk factors for tubal disease. The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS (led from Australia by Monash University) recommends letrozole as the first-line pharmacological treatment for ovulation induction in anovulatory infertility with PCOS and no other infertility factors, because it gives higher ovulation, pregnancy and live birth rates than clomiphene. Letrozole is used off-label for this indication in Australia, which should be discussed with the couple. Lifestyle measures and preconception care continue alongside. Cycle monitoring (ultrasound) is advised to reduce the risk of multiple pregnancy.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Anovulatory infertility with PCOS: letrozole is first-line (2023 international guideline), off-label in Australia. Clomiphene and metformin are alternatives; gonadotrophins and IVF come later.

---

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Ballarat, Victoria, because of 3 months of abdominal bloating, early satiety and needing to pass urine more often. Her last period was at 51. She has not used hormone therapy. She has no family history of ovarian, breast or bowel cancer. Abdominal examination shows mild fullness in the lower abdomen, with no palpable mass and no shifting dullness.

Investigations:
- Transvaginal ultrasound: 7 cm left adnexal cystic mass with multiple locules (thick septations) and a 1.5 cm solid area with internal blood flow; right ovary normal; no ascites; no peritoneal deposits seen
- CA-125 30 U/mL (<35)
- Full blood count, liver and renal function normal

Which one of the following is the most accurate interpretation?
options: RMI 90: low risk; repeat the ultrasound in 6 weeks
RMI 30: low risk; reassure her because CA-125 is normal
RMI 270: high risk; refer urgently to a gynaecological oncologist
RMI cannot be used because CA-125 is within the normal range
RMI 270, but laparoscopic cystectomy by a general gynaecologist is appropriate
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. RMI 270: high risk; refer urgently to a gynaecological oncologist

---

The risk of malignancy index (RMI) = U × M × CA-125 (U/mL). U (ultrasound score) is 0 for no features, 1 for one feature and 3 for two to five features, where the features are: multilocular cyst, solid areas, metastases, ascites and bilateral lesions. She has two (multilocular and solid areas), so U = 3. M (menopausal status) is 3 for postmenopausal women and 1 for premenopausal women, so M = 3. RMI = 3 × 3 × 30 = 270. An RMI above 200 is high risk (sensitivity about 87%, specificity about 97% for ovarian cancer in the RACGP summary) and needs urgent referral to a gynaecological oncologist, who will usually arrange CT staging and plan surgery. A normal CA-125 does not exclude ovarian cancer: about half of early-stage cancers have a normal CA-125. Her symptoms (bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency) are also typical of ovarian cancer.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
RMI = U (0/1/3) × M (1 premenopausal, 3 postmenopausal) × CA-125. RMI above 200 = high risk: urgent gynaecological oncology referral. A normal CA-125 does not exclude cancer.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "RACGP (AFP 2015). Investigation and management of an ovarian mass", "url": "https://www.racgp.org.au/afp/2015/january-february/investigation-and-management-of-an-ovarian-mass"}
• {"name": "Cancer Australia. Appropriate referral of women with suspected ovarian cancer (GP card)", "url": "https://www.canceraustralia.gov.au/sites/default/files/migrated-files/publications/appropriate-referral-women-suspected-ovarian-cancer/pdf/ocarw_approp_refferal_gp_card_0.pdf"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: RMI 30 comes from scoring both U and M as 1. She is postmenopausal (M = 3) with two ultrasound features (U = 3).

question_text:
A 57-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Adelaide because she has had two episodes of light vaginal bleeding over the past month. Her last natural period was at 52. Four years ago she had a wide local excision and radiotherapy for an oestrogen receptor-positive left breast cancer. She started an aromatase inhibitor but stopped it after 6 months because of severe joint pain, and has taken tamoxifen 20 mg daily for the past 3 years. She has no other medical history, and her BMI is 29 kg/m². Her cervical screening test 2 years ago was negative.

Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with a small amount of blood from the os. Bimanual examination is normal.

Transvaginal ultrasound: uterus normal size; endometrial thickness 7 mm with multiple small subendometrial cystic spaces, described as 'consistent with tamoxifen effect'; no focal lesion seen; ovaries normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months
Stop tamoxifen and observe for further bleeding
Reassure her that the ultrasound appearance is typical of tamoxifen
Hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy
CA-125 and MRI of the pelvis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy

---

Any postmenopausal bleeding needs investigation for endometrial cancer, and tamoxifen increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, polyps and cancer (a partial oestrogen agonist on the endometrium). In women taking tamoxifen, transvaginal ultrasound is unreliable: tamoxifen causes subendometrial cystic change and apparent thickening that make the endometrial thickness hard to interpret, so a reassuring-looking scan does not exclude pathology. RANZCOG's statement on tamoxifen and the endometrium and Cancer Australia's abnormal vaginal bleeding guide advise that women on tamoxifen with abnormal bleeding should be referred promptly for hysteroscopy and endometrial sampling. Hysteroscopy allows direct visualisation and targeted biopsy of polyps and focal lesions, which blind (Pipelle) sampling can miss. Routine ultrasound screening of asymptomatic women taking tamoxifen is not recommended.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen: ultrasound is unreliable because of tamoxifen-related endometrial changes. Refer for hysteroscopy and directed biopsy.

---

question_text:
A 20-year-old woman sees her general practitioner on the Sunshine Coast, Queensland, for review. Two days ago she presented with 5 days of lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia and spotting after sex. She has had a new male partner for 2 months and they do not use condoms; she takes the combined pill. At that visit her temperature was 37.7°C, and there was cervical motion tenderness, bilateral adnexal tenderness and mucopurulent cervical discharge. A pregnancy test was negative. Swabs were taken, and she was treated with ceftriaxone 500 mg IM and started on oral doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days.

Today her pain is improving and her temperature is 37.1°C. She still has mild adnexal tenderness. She wants to stop the tablets because 'the tests showed I don't have an STI'.

Results:
- Chlamydia trachomatis NAAT (endocervical): not detected
- Neisseria gonorrhoeae NAAT: not detected
- Trichomonas vaginalis NAAT: not detected
- Mycoplasma genitalium NAAT: pending
- Pelvic ultrasound: normal uterus and ovaries, no adnexal collection
- C-reactive protein 24 mg/L (<5); urinalysis normal

Which one of the following is the most accurate interpretation?
options: Negative chlamydia and gonorrhoea tests exclude PID, so antibiotics can be stopped
PID remains the most likely diagnosis; she should complete the 14-day course
A tubo-ovarian abscess is likely and needs drainage
Acute appendicitis is more likely and needs surgical referral
Ectopic pregnancy has not been excluded and needs serial β-hCG
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. PID remains the most likely diagnosis; she should complete the 14-day course

---

PID is a clinical diagnosis. The Australian STI Management Guidelines (ASHM) advise a low threshold for diagnosis and empirical treatment in a sexually active young woman with pelvic pain and cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, because delayed treatment increases the risk of tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are found in only a minority of cases; most PID is polymicrobial (including anaerobes and bacterial vaginosis-associated organisms, and sometimes M. genitalium). Negative NAATs therefore do not exclude PID or justify stopping treatment. She is improving clinically at 48–72 hours, which supports the diagnosis and outpatient management. She should complete the recommended regimen (ceftriaxone plus 14 days of doxycycline and metronidazole), and the pending M. genitalium result may change therapy if positive. Her partner(s) from the past 6 months should be tested and treated empirically, and she should avoid sex until both have finished treatment.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
PID is a clinical diagnosis. Negative chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAATs do not exclude it: complete the full course (ceftriaxone plus 14 days of doxycycline and metronidazole) and treat partners.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ASHM. Australian STI Management Guidelines: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)", "url": "https://sti.guidelines.org.au/syndromes/pelvic-inflammatory-diseases-pid/"}
• {"name": "ASHM. Australasian Contact Tracing Guidelines: PID", "url": "https://contacttracing.ashm.org.au/pelvic-inflammatory-disease-pid/"}

---

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman returns to her general practitioner in Newcastle, New South Wales, because of ongoing bleeding after sex. It started 5 months ago and happens after most episodes of intercourse. Six weeks ago, at her first visit about this, the GP took a clinician-collected cervical sample for a co-test and tested for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Results: oncogenic HPV not detected; liquid-based cytology negative; chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT negative. Her previous routine cervical screening test, 3 years ago, was also negative for HPV. She has one long-term male partner and uses a copper IUD, inserted 2 years ago, and her periods are regular and unchanged. She has no intermenstrual bleeding, pelvic pain or discharge.

Speculum examination today shows IUD threads visible at a cervix that looks normal to the GP, with no ectropion, polyp or contact bleeding seen. Bimanual examination is normal. A urine pregnancy test is negative.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her and return to routine 5-yearly cervical screening
Repeat the co-test in 12 months
Offer a self-collected HPV test in 6 months
Remove the copper IUD and review in 3 months
Refer to a gynaecologist for colposcopy and consider transvaginal ultrasound
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Refer to a gynaecologist for colposcopy and consider transvaginal ultrasound

---

Postcoital bleeding is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and can be caused by cervical or other genital tract cancer. Symptomatic people are managed on a diagnostic pathway, not the screening pathway. The National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines (2025) recommend a clinician-collected co-test (REC 10.1), which she has had. After a SINGLE episode of postcoital bleeding with a normal-looking cervix, a negative co-test means colposcopy is not needed (REC 10.2). But for RECURRENT or PERSISTENT postcoital bleeding, even with HPV not detected and negative cytology, she should be referred to a gynaecologist for assessment including colposcopy, and upper genital tract imaging (usually transvaginal ultrasound) should be considered (REC 10.3). This is because rare cancers (e.g. HPV-independent adenocarcinoma) and non-cervical causes can be missed by HPV testing and cytology.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Postcoital bleeding: clinician-collected co-test. If bleeding is recurrent or persistent, refer to a gynaecologist for colposcopy even when the co-test is negative (NCSP 2025, REC 10.3).

---

question_text:
A 36-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Perth because her periods stopped 7 months ago. Before that her cycles had become irregular over a year. She has hot flushes, night sweats and vaginal dryness. She has one child, aged 6, and she and her partner hoped to have another. She stopped the combined pill 2 years ago. She has had no chemotherapy, radiotherapy or pelvic surgery, and no weight loss, excessive exercise or galactorrhoea. Her mother went through menopause at 41. Her BMI is 23 kg/m² and examination is normal.

Investigations (random day, as she has no cycle):
- Urine and serum β-hCG negative
- FSH 68 IU/L
- Oestradiol 55 pmol/L (low)
- Prolactin and TSH normal

Which one of the following is the most accurate interpretation?
options: This confirms premature ovarian insufficiency; a repeat FSH is not required
Premature ovarian insufficiency cannot be diagnosed until FSH is repeated 4–6 weeks later
Hypothalamic amenorrhoea is the most likely cause
This is early normal perimenopause and no specific follow-up is needed
An AMH level is needed as the primary diagnostic test
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. This confirms premature ovarian insufficiency; a repeat FSH is not required

---

Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is loss of ovarian function before 40. The 2024 ESHRE/ASRM/CRE/IMS international evidence-based guideline (developed with the Australian Centre for Research Excellence in Women's Health in Reproductive Life) changed the diagnostic criteria. POI is now diagnosed by disordered cycles (amenorrhoea or irregular cycles) for at least 4 months plus ONE elevated FSH above 25 IU/L. A repeat FSH after 4–6 weeks is needed only if there is diagnostic uncertainty. The 2015/16 guideline required two elevated FSH levels. She has 7 months of amenorrhoea, oestrogen deficiency symptoms, FSH of 68 IU/L with low oestradiol, and no hormonal contraception confounding the result, so there is no uncertainty. She should be counselled (including about the small chance of spontaneous pregnancy and options such as donor eggs), have karyotype and FMR1 premutation testing (and consider autoimmune screening), baseline bone density, and hormone therapy until at least the average age of menopause, unless contraindicated.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
POI (2024 guideline): at least 4 months of disordered cycles plus a single FSH >25 IU/L. Repeat FSH only if the diagnosis is uncertain. AMH is not the primary test.

---

• {"name": "Evidence-based guideline: premature ovarian insufficiency (Hum Reprod Open / Climacteric 2024; PubMed 39647506)", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39647506/"}
