question_text:
A 32-year-old woman and her partner see their general practitioner in Townsville, Queensland, because they have not conceived after 13 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Her periods have always been regular, every 35 days (range 34–36 days), with 5 days of bleeding. She has no hirsutism, acne, galactorrhoea, pelvic pain or history of pelvic infection. Her BMI is 22 kg/m². Her partner's semen analysis is normal.

The GP requested a 'day 21 progesterone'. Blood was taken on day 21 of her cycle (counting the first day of bleeding as day 1). Her next period started on day 35 as expected.

Investigations:
- Serum progesterone (day 21): 6 nmol/L (a level above about 30 nmol/L in the mid-luteal phase usually indicates ovulation)
- FSH (day 3) 6 IU/L, LH 5 IU/L, TSH and prolactin normal
- Rubella immune, cervical screening up to date

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Anovulatory cycles; start letrozole
Luteal phase defect; start vaginal progesterone after ovulation
The sample was taken too early; repeat progesterone on about day 28
Diminished ovarian reserve; refer urgently for IVF
Hyperprolactinaemia is likely despite a normal prolactin
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. The sample was taken too early; repeat progesterone on about day 28

---

Progesterone should be measured in the mid-luteal phase, about 7 days BEFORE the expected next period. The 'day 21' test only fits a 28-day cycle. In a regular 35-day cycle, ovulation occurs around day 21 (the luteal phase is fairly constant at about 14 days), so a day 21 sample is taken at or before ovulation, when progesterone is expected to be low. The mid-luteal sample for her should be taken around day 28 (35 − 7). Regular cycles of 34–36 days are very likely to be ovulatory, and a single low result at the wrong time does not show anovulation. Repeating a correctly timed progesterone (or using ovulation tracking) avoids unnecessary ovulation induction. Investigation of the couple should continue in parallel (e.g. tubal patency assessment), as they have been trying for more than 12 months.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Measure progesterone 7 days before the expected period, not automatically on day 21. In a 35-day cycle, test around day 28.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "GPnotebook. Progesterone (ovulatory test)", "url": "https://gpnotebook.com/en-GB/pages/gynaecology/progesterone-ovulatory-test"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Her early follicular FSH is normal. Nothing here suggests diminished ovarian reserve, and IVF is not the first step.

question_text:
You are the paediatric registrar at a regional hospital in Rockhampton, Queensland. A midwife asks you to review a male infant who is 2 hours old. He was born at 38 weeks and 3 days by planned caesarean section. His mother has type 2 diabetes that needed insulin from 20 weeks of gestation. Birth weight was 4180 g, and Apgar scores were 8 and 9.

He had his first breastfeed at 40 minutes of age, and a pre-feed heel-prick blood glucose at 2 hours is 2.0 mmol/L. It is 1.9 mmol/L on a repeat sample sent to the laboratory. He is pink and alert, with normal tone. He is not jittery or lethargic and had no apnoea. His temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate 138/min and respiratory rate 44/min. He attaches well at the breast, and his mother is keen to keep breastfeeding and to keep him in the room with her.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give a 10% glucose bolus of 2 mL/kg IV and then start an IV glucose infusion
Reassure that this is normal transition and recheck the glucose before the next feed in 3 hours
Give 40% glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg to the buccal mucosa, feed, and recheck glucose in 30 minutes
Admit him to the special care nursery for continuous IV glucose infusion at 60 mL/kg/day
Give 30 mL/kg of infant formula by bottle instead of breastfeeding and recheck in 1 hour
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Give 40% glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg to the buccal mucosa, feed, and recheck glucose in 30 minutes

---

This infant is at risk of hypoglycaemia: his mother has insulin-treated diabetes and he is macrosomic. He is well, ≥35 weeks, under 48 hours old and feeding, and his blood glucose is 1.5–2.5 mmol/L without symptoms. Queensland Clinical Guidelines recommend 40% glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg (200 mg/kg) massaged into the buccal mucosa, followed by a feed (breastfeed, or expressed breast milk or formula if needed), and a repeat BGL about 30 minutes after the gel. Gel can be repeated (commonly up to a total of about six doses in 48 hours). Escalate to IV glucose if the BGL stays low despite gel and feeds, falls below 1.5 mmol/L, or if he develops symptoms. Gel plus feeding keeps the mother and baby together, supports breastfeeding and reduces NICU admission for hypoglycaemia.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Well at-risk newborn (≥35 wk, <48 h), BGL 1.5–2.5 mmol/L without symptoms: give 40% glucose gel 0.5 mL/kg buccally plus a feed, and recheck in 30 min. Go to IV glucose for symptoms, BGL <1.5, or failure of gel and feeds.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hypoglycaemia/"}

---

question_text:
A 5-day-old girl is brought to the emergency department of a regional hospital in Townsville, Queensland, because she has vomited three times in the last 4 hours. Her mother says the last two vomits were 'bright green'. She was born at term by normal vaginal birth after an uncomplicated pregnancy, passed meconium on day 1 and has been breastfeeding well until today.

She is alert and pink. Her heart rate is 168/min, respiratory rate 40/min, capillary refill time 2 seconds and temperature 36.9 °C. Her abdomen is soft and not distended, and there are no palpable masses. The anus is normally placed, and there is yellow stool in her nappy. A plain abdominal X-ray shows a non-specific bowel gas pattern with some gas in the distal bowel.

A nasogastric tube has been placed on free drainage, IV fluids have been started and she is nil by mouth. The on-call paediatric surgeon has been contacted.

Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate to establish the diagnosis?
options: Urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study
Abdominal ultrasound for pyloric muscle thickness
Contrast enema to look for a microcolon
Repeat abdominal X-ray in 6 hours to look for obstruction
Blood culture, urine culture and lumbar puncture
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study

---

Bilious vomiting in a neonate is due to intestinal obstruction until proven otherwise, and malrotation with midgut volvulus is the diagnosis that must not be missed, because the midgut can become ischaemic within hours. A soft abdomen, a well-looking baby, passed stool and a non-specific X-ray do NOT exclude volvulus; early volvulus often looks exactly like this. The investigation of choice in a stable infant is an urgent upper GI contrast study to show the position of the duodenojejunal flexure (normally left of the spine at the level of the pylorus) and any 'corkscrew' duodenum. If she is unstable or peritonitic, she goes straight to theatre (Ladd procedure) without imaging. The RCH guideline says bilious vomiting needs urgent surgical referral.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Green vomiting in a neonate means malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise: NBM, NG drainage, IV fluids, urgent surgical referral and an urgent upper GI contrast study (straight to theatre if unstable).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Vomiting (last updated Sept 2025)", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vomiting/"}

---

subtopic: Bilious vomiting in a neonate: urgent upper GI contrast for malrotation with volvulus

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Pyloric stenosis causes NON-bilious projectile vomiting, usually at 2–8 weeks of age. Green vomit points to obstruction beyond the ampulla.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A contrast enema helps in distal obstruction (for example Hirschsprung disease or meconium ileus), where there is distension and failure to pass meconium. She has passed stool and her abdomen is not distended.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Waiting for the X-ray to become 'obstructive' risks loss of the midgut. A normal or non-specific film does not exclude volvulus.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Sepsis can cause vomiting in a neonate and can be considered, but bilious vomiting in a well baby needs urgent exclusion of a surgical cause first. A septic screen does not establish that diagnosis.

question_text:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to his general practitioner in Ballarat, Victoria, because his kindergarten teacher has noticed he cannot keep up with other children, falls often and cannot jump with both feet together. He walked independently at 19 months. His speech was a little late, but he now speaks in sentences. He was born at term, and there were no concerns in the neonatal period. His maternal uncle 'had problems with his muscles' and used a wheelchair from his teens, but the family knows few details.

On examination he waddles when he walks and runs awkwardly. When getting up from the floor he rolls prone and pushes on his thighs with his hands to stand. His calves are firm and look bulky. Tone is normal, reflexes are present but reduced at the knees, and sensation appears normal. Hearing and vision were normal at his 4-year health check.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate first investigation?
options: MRI of the brain and whole spine
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography
Thyroid function tests and vitamin D level
Serum creatine kinase level
Quadriceps muscle biopsy for dystrophin staining
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Serum creatine kinase level

---

This boy has a proximal myopathic pattern (waddling gait, Gowers manoeuvre), calf pseudohypertrophy, early motor delay and a family history in a maternal male relative, consistent with X-linked Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The first test is serum creatine kinase, which is markedly raised in DMD (often 10–100 times the upper limit). A high CK leads to genetic testing of the DMD gene (deletion/duplication analysis, then sequencing), which confirms the diagnosis in most boys and usually removes the need for biopsy. Early diagnosis allows referral to a neuromuscular service, genetic counselling for the family (including the mother's carrier status), and timely corticosteroid treatment and cardiac and respiratory surveillance.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Boy with late walking, Gowers sign and calf hypertrophy: check CK first. A markedly raised CK leads to DMD gene testing and neuromuscular referral.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Birnkrant DJ et al. Diagnosis and management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, part 1. Lancet Neurol 2018;17:251\u2013267", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1016/S1474-4422(18)30024-3"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: NCS/EMG can show a myopathic pattern but is uncomfortable, non-specific and is no longer routine in suspected DMD when CK and genetic testing are available.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Hypothyroid myopathy and rickets can cause weakness, but they do not explain calf pseudohypertrophy with a matching family history. They are not the best first test here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Muscle biopsy is invasive and is now reserved for cases where genetic testing is non-diagnostic. It is not the first investigation.

question_text:
A 6-week-old Aboriginal girl is brought by her mother and grandmother to the Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service in Wagga Wagga, New South Wales, for her first scheduled immunisations. She was born at 39 weeks, weighs 4.6 kg and is breastfeeding well. She received hepatitis B vaccine at birth. There is no family history of immune deficiency, and she has no medical conditions. Her mother had dTpa, influenza and RSV vaccines during pregnancy.

Her mother says she wants 'everything she is due', but has heard that 'one of the needles makes babies really hot' and asks whether it should be given on a different day.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate plan for today?
options: Give DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib, 20vPCV and rotavirus today, and give MenB alone at 8 weeks
Give DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib, 20vPCV, rotavirus and MenB today, with paracetamol for 3 doses
Give DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib, 20vPCV, rotavirus and MenB today, with paracetamol if fever develops
Give DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib, 20vPCV and rotavirus today; MenB is not funded without a risk condition
Give DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib, 20vPCV, rotavirus and BCG today, and offer MenB from 6 months of age
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Give DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib, 20vPCV, rotavirus and MenB today, with paracetamol for 3 doses

---

Under the National Immunisation Program, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander infants receive meningococcal B vaccine (Bexsero) at 2 and 4 months, with a booster at 12 months (plus an extra dose at 6 months if they have a specified risk condition). It is given with the routine 2-month vaccines: DTPa-hepB-IPV-Hib, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (20vPCV) and oral rotavirus. The Handbook recommends 20vPCV at 2, 4, 6 and 12 months for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children. MenB commonly causes fever in infants, especially when given with other vaccines, so prophylactic paracetamol (15 mg/kg) is recommended for children under 2 years: the first dose within 30 minutes before vaccination (or as soon as possible after), then two more doses 6 hours apart, whether or not fever develops. MenB can be given on a separate day, but this is not necessary. Co-administration with prophylactic paracetamol is the standard approach and avoids extra visits and delayed protection.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander infants get MenB at 2, 4 and 12 months with the routine vaccines (20vPCV at 2, 4, 6 and 12 months). Give prophylactic paracetamol 15 mg/kg: first dose around vaccination, then 2 more doses 6 h apart, regardless of fever.

---

question_text:
An 18-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department of a metropolitan hospital in Perth, Western Australia, because he felt hot and has been feeding a little less for 6 hours. His 3-year-old brother has had a runny nose and cough for 4 days. He was born at term by vaginal birth. His mother's group B streptococcus screen was negative, and membranes ruptured 2 hours before birth.

His rectal temperature is 38.4 °C, heart rate 164/min, respiratory rate 48/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Capillary refill time is 2 seconds. He is alert, handles well and has a soft anterior fontanelle, clear nasal discharge and no rash. Chest and abdominal examinations are normal.

A rapid nasopharyngeal PCR done at triage is positive for respiratory syncytial virus. His parents ask whether he can go home now that 'they know it is just a virus'.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate approach to investigation?
options: No further tests are needed because RSV explains the fever; arrange review in 24 hours
Bag urine for microscopy and culture, and discharge home if the result is negative
Full blood count, CRP and blood culture, with admission for observation off antibiotics
Chest X-ray and urine by catheter, deferring lumbar puncture unless he becomes unwell
Bloods with blood culture, catheter or suprapubic urine and lumbar puncture, then IV antibiotics
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Bloods with blood culture, catheter or suprapubic urine and lumbar puncture, then IV antibiotics

---

RCH guidance for febrile infants ≤28 days old recommends a full septic work-up and empirical IV antibiotics regardless of how well they appear: FBE, CRP, blood culture, urine by catheter or suprapubic aspirate, and lumbar puncture (chest X-ray if respiratory signs). Clinical appearance and a positive viral test do not reliably exclude serious bacterial infection (bacteraemia, UTI or meningitis) in this age group, and concurrent bacterial infection with RSV is well described in young infants. Empirical treatment at this age covers group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria (for example benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin plus cefotaxime), and aciclovir is added if HSV is possible.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Any febrile infant aged 28 days or less gets a full septic screen (bloods, blood culture, catheter/SPA urine, LP) and empirical IV antibiotics, even if well-appearing and virus-positive.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Febrile_child/"}

---

question_text:
A 4-month-old boy is admitted to the paediatric ward of a regional hospital in Bendigo, Victoria, on day 3 of an illness with rhinorrhoea, cough and increased work of breathing. He was born at term and has no medical history. His 2-year-old sister attends childcare.

He is taking about 40% of his usual breastfeeds, and his mother reports three wet nappies in the past 24 hours. His temperature is 37.8 °C, heart rate 158/min and respiratory rate 58/min, with moderate subcostal recession and widespread fine crackles and wheeze. Oxygen saturation is 91–93% on room air, dipping to 89% for a few seconds during feeds and recovering quickly. He is alert and has no apnoeas. The mucous membranes are slightly dry, and capillary refill time is 2 seconds.

The resident asks what to do about feeding and oxygen.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Start nasal high-flow therapy at 2 L/kg/min and give IV fluids at full maintenance
Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol and continue if his work of breathing improves
Start nasogastric feeds at two-thirds maintenance rate and do not give supplemental oxygen
Give supplemental oxygen to keep saturations above 95% and start nebulised 3% saline
Start IV fluids at two-thirds maintenance and give oxygen by nasal prongs at 1 L/min
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Start nasogastric feeds at two-thirds maintenance rate and do not give supplemental oxygen

---

The RCH Bronchiolitis guideline advises that oxygen is not needed while saturations are persistently 90% or above; brief self-correcting dips during feeds or sleep do not need oxygen. He needs non-oral hydration because he is taking less than 50% of feeds. The nasogastric route is preferred over IV (fewer complications, supports nutrition) and is given at two-thirds of the calculated maintenance, because of the risk of fluid retention from ADH secretion. IV fluids are reserved for infants who cannot tolerate NG feeds, or who are severely ill or approaching respiratory failure. Salbutamol, nebulised hypertonic saline, adrenaline, corticosteroids and antibiotics are not recommended in bronchiolitis, and routine chest X-ray and blood tests are not needed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Bronchiolitis: oxygen only if SpO2 is persistently <90%. If intake is <50%, use NG fluids at two-thirds maintenance (IV only if NG is not possible). No salbutamol, steroids, hypertonic saline or antibiotics.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis (Nov 2023)", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Bronchiolitis/"}

---

subtopic: Bronchiolitis: oxygen threshold and nasogastric hydration

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: High-flow therapy is for infants with hypoxia despite standard oxygen or severe work of breathing, not for this infant. Full maintenance IV fluid is also inappropriate because fluids are restricted to about two-thirds maintenance.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Bronchodilators do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis, and a 'trial' of salbutamol is specifically not recommended under 12 months of age.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Targeting saturations above 95% prolongs admission without benefit; the threshold is persistently below 90%. Hypertonic saline is not recommended.

key_takeaways: Bronchiolitis: oxygen only if SpO2 is persistently <90%. If intake is <50%, use NG fluids at two-thirds maintenance (IV only if NG is not possible). No salbutamol, steroids, hypertonic saline or antibiotics.

question_text:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to a rural emergency department in Dubbo, New South Wales, at 2 am. For 2 days he has had a runny nose and a barking cough, and his general practitioner diagnosed croup yesterday. Tonight he suddenly became much worse, with a temperature of 39.9 °C and noisy breathing. His immunisations are up to date.

He is flushed, looks toxic and is sitting up. There is loud inspiratory and expiratory stridor, marked sternal recession and a harsh cough producing thick yellow secretions. He is not drooling and is able to speak a few words. His heart rate is 178/min, respiratory rate 44/min and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. The front of his neck is tender over the trachea.

He was given oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and two doses of nebulised adrenaline 30 minutes apart. The stridor improved only slightly and briefly each time. The white cell count is 22 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia, and CRP is 168 mg/L (<5).

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute epiglottitis
Bacterial tracheitis
Severe viral laryngotracheobronchitis
Retropharyngeal abscess
Inhaled foreign body in the trachea
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Bacterial tracheitis

---

Bacterial tracheitis (usually Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes or Moraxella) typically follows a viral croup-like prodrome and then deteriorates quickly with high fever, toxicity, a productive cough with thick purulent secretions, tracheal tenderness and poor or short-lived response to nebulised adrenaline. RCH lists these features in its Acute upper airway obstruction guideline. Management is a senior airway response: anaesthetic and ENT involvement, controlled intubation in theatre (secretions and sloughed membrane can block the tube), and IV antibiotics covering S. aureus.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
A 'croup' that turns toxic, with high fever, purulent secretions, tracheal tenderness and poor response to adrenaline, is bacterial tracheitis: get senior airway help and give IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

---

---

question_text:
An 8-year-old girl with known asthma is brought to the emergency department of a metropolitan hospital in Adelaide, South Australia, with 6 hours of worsening wheeze after a cold. She uses an inhaled corticosteroid preventer irregularly.

On arrival she could speak only single words, was using her accessory muscles and had oxygen saturation of 89% on room air. She has had one hour of continuous nebulised salbutamol driven by oxygen, three doses of nebulised ipratropium bromide 20 minutes apart, and oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg.

She is now sitting forward, still speaking in short phrases, with marked subcostal and intercostal recession. Her heart rate is 150/min, respiratory rate 40/min and oxygen saturation 93% on 6 L/min oxygen by mask. There is widespread wheeze with reduced air entry at both bases. She is alert and not drowsy. A capillary blood glucose is 9.4 mmol/L. IV access has been obtained.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes
IV aminophylline loading dose over 1 hour
Chest X-ray before any further treatment is given
Capillary blood gas to guide the need for intubation
IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg in addition to the prednisolone
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes

---

She has severe acute asthma that has not responded to first-line treatment (continuous salbutamol, ipratropium and systemic corticosteroid). The RCH Acute asthma guideline recommends IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (0.2 mmol/kg, maximum 2 g/8 mmol) over 20 minutes as the next add-on, while salbutamol continues and senior help is involved. Further escalation (IV salbutamol, aminophylline, non-invasive ventilation or intubation) is considered after magnesium, with ICU involvement. A chest X-ray and blood gas are not routinely needed and must not delay treatment; a rising CO2, drowsiness or a silent chest are ominous signs.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Severe paediatric asthma not responding to continuous salbutamol, ipratropium and steroid: give IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 min before aminophylline or IV salbutamol. No routine CXR or blood gas.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Acute asthma (Jul 2023)", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_acute/"}

---

subtopic: Acute severe asthma not responding to initial therapy: IV magnesium sulfate

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Aminophylline is a later-line option in critical asthma because it has a narrow therapeutic index and frequent side effects. Magnesium comes first.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A chest X-ray is needed only if pneumothorax, collapse or another diagnosis is suspected. Reduced air entry at both bases is expected in severe asthma and is not an indication.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Blood gases are not routinely needed and should not delay treatment. The decision to intubate is clinical (fatigue, drowsiness, rising CO2 despite maximal therapy).
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: She has already had an adequate systemic corticosteroid. IV hydrocortisone is used if she cannot take oral medicines and gives no additional benefit here.

question_text:
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department in Geelong, Victoria, because she has been pale and very tired for a day and has passed very little urine since yesterday. Seven days ago, two days after the family visited a petting farm during the school holidays, she developed crampy abdominal pain and diarrhoea that became bloody on day 2. The diarrhoea has now settled. She has not had antibiotics.

She is pale and lethargic. Her temperature is 37.2 °C, heart rate 136/min and blood pressure 118/76 mmHg (above the 95th centile for her age and height). There are a few petechiae on her legs and mild periorbital oedema.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 74 g/L (105–135)
- Platelets 38 × 10^9/L (150–400)
- White cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L (5.0–15.0)
- Blood film: numerous fragmented red cells (schistocytes)
- Reticulocytes 6% (0.5–2.5)
- Lactate dehydrogenase 2150 U/L (<500)
- Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test: negative
- Urea 24 mmol/L (2.5–6.0)
- Creatinine 188 µmol/L (20–40)
- Coagulation studies (PT, APTT, fibrinogen): normal
- Urinalysis: blood 3+, protein 2+

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura
Disseminated intravascular coagulation from sepsis
Prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration
Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome

---

She has the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (anaemia, schistocytes, high LDH and reticulocytes, negative Coombs test), thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury about a week after bloody diarrhoea. This is typical of haemolytic uraemic syndrome due to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (e.g. O157), and animal contact at a petting farm is a classic exposure. Normal coagulation studies separate HUS from DIC. Management is supportive: careful fluid balance, avoiding antibiotics and antimotility agents in suspected STEC (they may increase toxin release/HUS risk), avoiding nephrotoxins, managing hypertension and electrolytes, transfusing red cells as needed (platelets only for bleeding or procedures), and early referral to paediatric nephrology for possible dialysis. Send stool for culture/PCR and notify public health.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Bloody diarrhoea followed a week later by MAHA (Coombs-negative, schistocytes), low platelets and AKI with normal coagulation is STEC-HUS. Give supportive care, avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs, and refer to nephrology early.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Gastroenteritis (Aug 2025)", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Gastroenteritis/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome after bloody diarrhoea (STEC)

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal haemoglobin and kidney function. It does not explain the schistocytes or AKI.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: DIC causes prolonged PT/APTT and low fibrinogen. Her coagulation studies are normal, and she is not septic.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Dehydration can raise urea and creatinine, but it does not cause haemolysis, schistocytes and thrombocytopenia. Her hypertension and oedema also argue against volume depletion.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Autoimmune haemolysis is Coombs-positive and does not cause thrombocytopenia with AKI or red cell fragments.

key_takeaways: Bloody diarrhoea followed a week later by MAHA (Coombs-negative, schistocytes), low platelets and AKI with normal coagulation is STEC-HUS. Give supportive care, avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs, and refer to nephrology early.

question_text:
A 4-month-old boy is brought by his father to a general practice in Frankston, Victoria, for a routine visit about eczema. While examining his skin you notice a 1.5 cm purplish bruise over the left cheek and a smaller bruise on the outer ear. The father says the boy's 3-year-old sister 'hit him with a plastic toy' two days ago. The boy cannot roll over yet. He was born at term, is thriving along the 50th centile and has had all his scheduled immunisations.

He is alert and smiles, with a soft anterior fontanelle. There are no other bruises, petechiae or mouth injuries, and his limbs move normally without obvious pain. There is no family history of bleeding disorders. The father is calm and cooperative and says the mother is at work.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Accept the explanation, document the bruise and review the boy in one week
Arrange a full blood count and coagulation studies and review the results tomorrow
Refer to an ophthalmologist as an outpatient to check for retinal haemorrhages
Report to Child Protection and wait for their assessment before any investigations
Arrange same-day hospital assessment including skeletal survey, bloods and a report
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Arrange same-day hospital assessment including skeletal survey, bloods and a report

---

Any bruise in a non-mobile infant (not yet cruising) is a sentinel sign that needs assessment for physical abuse: 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise'. Bruising of the face or ear in an infant is a recognised high-risk pattern (TEN-4-FACESp: torso, ears, neck; frenulum, angle of jaw, cheeks, eyelids, subconjunctivae; or ANY bruise in a child 4 months or younger). The explanation that a toddler caused it is plausible but does not remove the need for work-up. The Victorian Forensic Paediatric Medical Service advises same-day paediatric/forensic assessment with a skeletal survey (particularly for infants under 6 months with suspected physical abuse), FBE and coagulation screen, consideration of neuroimaging and ophthalmology, and a report to Child Protection. Doctors in Victoria are mandatory reporters when they form a belief on reasonable grounds that a child needs protection because of physical injury. Assessment and reporting happen in parallel and are handled non-judgementally with the family.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Any bruise in a non-mobile infant, especially to the face, ears or neck, needs same-day paediatric/forensic assessment: skeletal survey, FBE and coagulation, consideration of neuroimaging, and a child protection report.

---

REFERENCES

• {"name": "Victorian Forensic Paediatric Medical Service (RCH). Fractures guideline", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/vfpms/guidelines/Fractures/"}
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Child abuse", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Child_abuse/"}

question_text:
A 15-year-old girl is brought by her mother to a general practice in Launceston, Tasmania, because of headaches on most days for the past 3 months and missing about two school days a week. The headaches are frontal and band-like, are worse in the afternoon, are not present on waking and are not associated with vomiting or visual symptoms. Paracetamol helps a little. Her mother says she 'spends all night on her phone' and has recently dropped out of her netball team. The girl sits with her arms folded and lets her mother answer most questions.

Her blood pressure is 108/66 mmHg, and her neurological examination, including fundoscopy, is normal. Her height and weight are on the 50th centile. She has no past medical history and takes no regular medicines.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in the assessment?
options: Arrange a CT scan of the brain to reassure the family that there is no tumour
Explain confidentiality and its limits, then talk with her alone using HEEADSSS
Ask the mother to stay so that she can provide the most accurate history
Give her a headache diary and review her in 3 months with her mother
Refer her to a paediatric neurologist for assessment of chronic daily headache
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Explain confidentiality and its limits, then talk with her alone using HEEADSSS

---

Her headaches have features of tension-type headache with no red flags, and her normal neurological examination and fundoscopy make a structural cause unlikely. The school absence, withdrawal from sport, late-night phone use and reluctance to speak suggest a psychosocial driver (for example bullying, low mood, anxiety, family conflict, substance use or abuse) that will be missed if only her mother speaks. The RCH guideline recommends explaining confidentiality (and its limits: risk of serious harm to self or others, or abuse) and completing a HEEADSSS psychosocial assessment (Home, Education/Employment, Eating/Exercise, Activities, Drugs/alcohol, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety) with the adolescent alone for at least part of the consultation.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
With adolescents, explain confidentiality and its limits, then spend time with them alone using HEEADSSS. Psychosocial issues often drive somatic presentations such as headache and school refusal.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient (May 2025)", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Engaging_with_and_assessing_the_adolescent_patient/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Imaging is not indicated without red flags (such as morning vomiting, papilloedema, focal signs or a change in pattern). It exposes her to radiation and does not address the likely cause.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Parents are valuable informants, but adolescents often do not disclose sensitive information in front of them. Time alone is recommended practice.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A diary may help later, but deferring for 3 months misses a chance to identify psychosocial problems or risk now.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Specialist referral is not needed for tension-type headache without red flags. The key next step is a psychosocial assessment.

key_takeaways: With adolescents, explain confidentiality and its limits, then spend time with them alone using HEEADSSS. Psychosocial issues often drive somatic presentations such as headache and school refusal.

question_text:
A 4-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department of a regional hospital in Wagga Wagga, New South Wales, because over the past 6 hours he has become grey, breathless and uninterested in feeds. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy with a normal 20-week morphology scan, and he was discharged home on day 2 after a normal newborn examination.

He is mottled and grey, with a heart rate of 196/min, respiratory rate 72/min and capillary refill time of 5 seconds. Brachial pulses are weak, and femoral pulses cannot be felt. The liver edge is 4 cm below the costal margin. Oxygen saturation is 90% in the right hand and 84% in the foot. There is a soft systolic murmur.

Investigations:
- Venous pH 7.04 (7.35–7.45)
- Lactate 9.2 mmol/L (<2.0)
- Glucose 4.1 mmol/L

A 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride has been given with no improvement. IV access is in place, and the newborn emergency transport service has been called.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Start an IV alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) infusion
Give IV indomethacin to reduce ductal shunting
Give 100% oxygen by mask and further 20 mL/kg saline boluses
Give IV furosemide 1 mg/kg to treat heart failure
Give IV antibiotics and await an urgent echocardiogram
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Start an IV alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) infusion

---

A previously well neonate who collapses in the first days to weeks of life with shock, absent or weak femoral pulses, hepatomegaly, a differential in saturations and severe lactic acidosis most likely has a duct-dependent systemic circulation (for example critical coarctation, interrupted aortic arch or hypoplastic left heart syndrome) with closure of the ductus arteriosus. A normal antenatal scan does not exclude it. The immediate life-saving treatment is an IV prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion to reopen the duct, with the dose set on specialist/retrieval advice (higher starting doses in shock). Be ready to support the airway, because apnoea is a common dose-related adverse effect. Other care runs in parallel: cautious fluids, inotropes, correction of acidosis and glucose, and empirical antibiotics because sepsis cannot be excluded, with urgent echocardiography and retrieval.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Neonate in shock at days 2–14 with poor femoral pulses, hepatomegaly and pre/post-ductal saturation difference: start a prostaglandin E1 infusion empirically (watch for apnoea) while arranging echo and retrieval.

---

REFERENCES

question_text:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department of a regional hospital in Cairns, Queensland, 50 minutes after her father found her chewing a TV remote control with the battery cover open. One 20 mm lithium coin battery is missing and cannot be found in the room. Nobody saw her swallow anything.

She is playing happily and eating a biscuit. She has no drooling, coughing, vomiting, stridor or chest pain. Her heart rate is 118/min, respiratory rate 26/min and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Examination of the mouth, chest and abdomen is normal. She weighs 12 kg and has no allergies. Her father asks whether they can go home and 'watch her nappies'.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with advice to check her stools, because she has no symptoms
Arrange an abdominal X-ray, because most batteries pass beyond the stomach
Arrange an urgent X-ray from neck to abdomen, giving honey while it is organised
Observe her in the department for 6 hours and X-ray her if symptoms develop
Give a nasogastric laxative preparation to hasten passage of the battery
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Arrange an urgent X-ray from neck to abdomen, giving honey while it is organised

---

Any suspected button battery ingestion is an emergency, even when the child is asymptomatic and the ingestion was not witnessed. A lithium coin cell of 20 mm or more can lodge in the oesophagus and cause severe caustic injury within 2 hours (perforation, tracheo-oesophageal or aorto-oesophageal fistula). RCH and Queensland (CHQ) guidelines recommend urgent X-ray covering the neck, chest and abdomen (a battery shows a 'halo'/double-ring sign). A battery in the oesophagus needs endoscopic removal as soon as possible (ideally within 2 hours). For children over 1 year within 12 hours of ingestion, honey 10 mL every 10 minutes (up to 6 doses) can be given while arranging imaging or transfer, but it must not delay them. Batteries beyond the oesophagus are managed according to size, age, symptoms and time, often with repeat imaging. The Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) can advise.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected button battery ingestion: urgent X-ray from neck to abdomen, even if asymptomatic. An oesophageal battery needs emergency removal within 2 h. Honey 10 mL every 10 min (up to 6 doses) if over 12 months and within 12 h, without delaying imaging or transfer.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Foreign body ingestion", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/"}
• {"name": "Children's Health Queensland. Queensland Paediatric Clinical Guideline: Foreign body ingested", "url": "https://www.childrens.health.qld.gov.au/for-health-professionals/queensland-paediatric-emergency-care-qpec/queensland-paediatric-clinical-guidelines/foreign-body-ingested"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: An abdominal film can miss a battery lodged in the upper oesophagus. The film has to include the neck and chest.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Waiting for symptoms delays diagnosis while caustic injury progresses. Imaging is urgent.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Laxatives do not remove an oesophageal battery and delay the key step: urgent imaging to locate it.

key_takeaways: Suspected button battery ingestion: urgent X-ray from neck to abdomen, even if asymptomatic. An oesophageal battery needs emergency removal within 2 h. Honey 10 mL every 10 min (up to 6 doses) if over 12 months and within 12 h, without delaying imaging or transfer.

question_text:
A 10-year-old Torres Strait Islander girl is brought to the primary health care centre on Thursday Island, Queensland, by her mother and grandmother. For 3 weeks her teachers have noticed that her handwriting has become messy, she drops things and she 'can't sit still'. Her mother says she has become tearful and irritable, which is unlike her. She had no sore throat or skin sores that the family can recall in the past 3 months. She is otherwise well, and her immunisations are up to date. The clinic's Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner, who knows the family, is present at their request.

She has irregular, non-rhythmic, jerky movements of her face, hands and feet that are worse when she is anxious. When asked to squeeze the examiner's fingers her grip waxes and wanes, and she cannot keep her tongue protruded for more than a few seconds. She can walk and feed herself, but more slowly than usual. Her temperature is 36.8 °C, and her heart rate is 88/min. There is no murmur, joint swelling or rash. She weighs 31 kg.

Investigations:
- ESR 12 mm/h (<20)
- CRP 3 mg/L (<5)
- Anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B titres: within the normal range for age
- Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, glucose, thyroid function and copper studies: normal
- ECG: normal PR interval

The paediatrician on telehealth has reviewed a video of the movements and agrees they are choreiform. Other causes of chorea have been excluded as far as possible, and no medicines or toxins are involved.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Explain it is not rheumatic fever because the streptococcal titres are normal, and refer to neurology
Start oral haloperidol for the movements and repeat the streptococcal titres in 2 weeks
Treat as a tic disorder with behavioural therapy and review her again in 3 months
Treat as acute rheumatic fever: benzathine benzylpenicillin G, echocardiogram, and consider carbamazepine
Give a 10-day course of oral penicillin and review whether prophylaxis is needed in 1 month
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Treat as acute rheumatic fever: benzathine benzylpenicillin G, echocardiogram, and consider carbamazepine

---

Sydenham chorea is a major manifestation of acute rheumatic fever. It often appears weeks to months after the streptococcal infection, when inflammatory markers and streptococcal serology may already have returned to normal. Under the 2020 Australian guideline (Edition 3.3), Sydenham chorea ALONE is enough to diagnose ARF, provided other causes of chorea are excluded. Other manifestations and evidence of preceding Strep A infection are not required. Management: give benzathine benzylpenicillin G (to treat any residual Strep A and begin secondary prophylaxis; 1,200,000 units for her weight of 20 kg or more), notify and register her with the state RHD program, and arrange echocardiography, which is essential for all patients with chorea because subclinical carditis is common. Her chorea is moderate (motor impersistence, functional slowing, mood change), so the guideline supports an anticonvulsant such as carbamazepine (or sodium valproate if there is no pregnancy risk), with supportive measures and a calm environment. Haloperidol is now largely discouraged. Care is planned with her family and the Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner, including a culturally safe, pain-minimising approach to regular BPG injections.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Sydenham chorea alone (other causes excluded) is enough to diagnose ARF, even with normal ESR/CRP and streptococcal titres. Start BPG secondary prophylaxis, get an echo, notify, and use carbamazepine or valproate for moderate chorea (not haloperidol).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "RHDAustralia. The 2020 Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of ARF and RHD (Edition 3.3, 2025), Key information", "url": "https://rhdaustralia.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Key-Information-2025_August.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Chorea is the one manifestation of ARF that does not need evidence of preceding Strep A infection. Normal titres are expected in late-onset chorea and do not exclude ARF.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Haloperidol is largely discouraged because of sedation and extrapyramidal effects. Delaying the diagnosis and penicillin prophylaxis while waiting for titres is inappropriate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: New-onset chorea with motor impersistence and emotional lability in a child from a high-risk setting is Sydenham chorea until proven otherwise, not a tic disorder. Delay risks missed carditis and recurrence.

question_text:
You are the resident attending an emergency caesarean section at 39 weeks of gestation at a hospital in Mackay, Queensland, for a pathological cardiotocograph. The liquor is clear.

The baby girl is floppy and pale at birth and is placed on the resuscitaire under a radiant warmer. She is dried, the wet towel is removed, and her head is placed in a neutral position. She is gently stimulated. At 30 seconds of age she is still not breathing, and her heart rate by auscultation is 80/min. A pulse oximeter probe is being placed on her right wrist. The neonatal team has been called and is 3 minutes away.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio with ventilation
Give positive-pressure ventilation by mask using air (21% oxygen)
Give positive-pressure ventilation by mask using 100% oxygen
Intubate and suction the trachea before starting any ventilation
Give adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg via an umbilical venous catheter
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Give positive-pressure ventilation by mask using air (21% oxygen)

---

An apnoeic newborn (or one with a heart rate below 100/min) after drying, warming, airway positioning and stimulation needs positive-pressure ventilation by face mask within the first minute. ANZCOR recommends starting resuscitation of infants ≥35 weeks with air (21% oxygen), then titrating oxygen to pre-ductal SpO2 targets. Effective ventilation is the most important intervention in newborn resuscitation; most babies' heart rates rise once the lungs are aerated. Chest compressions (3:1) start only if the heart rate stays below 60/min despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Newborn apnoeic or HR <100 after initial steps: PPV by mask within the first minute, starting with air (21%) at ≥35 weeks. Compressions only if HR stays <60 despite 30 s of effective ventilation.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 13.4: Airway management and mask ventilation of the newborn", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/neonatal-resuscitation/guideline-13-4-airway-management-and-mask-ventilation-of-the-newborn"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Newborn resuscitation: apnoeic term infant with HR <100 after initial steps; PPV in air

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Compressions are indicated for a heart rate below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation, not for 80/min before any ventilation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Starting with 100% oxygen in term or near-term infants is associated with worse outcomes than air. Oxygen is increased if saturations stay below targets or compressions are needed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Routine tracheal suction is not recommended (even with meconium-stained liquor, which is absent here) and delays ventilation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Adrenaline is for a heart rate below 60/min despite effective ventilation and compressions.

key_takeaways: Newborn apnoeic or HR <100 after initial steps: PPV by mask within the first minute, starting with air (21%) at ≥35 weeks. Compressions only if HR stays <60 despite 30 s of effective ventilation.

question_text:
A 6-year-old boy with no previous seizures is brought by ambulance to the emergency department of a hospital in Hobart, Tasmania. His mother found him having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home 25 minutes ago. Paramedics gave intramuscular midazolam 0.15 mg/kg 15 minutes ago with no effect. On arrival he is still having generalised clonic movements.

He weighs 20 kg. His temperature is 38.1 °C, heart rate 150/min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% on 15 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather mask with an airway manoeuvre. Capillary blood glucose is 6.2 mmol/L. IV access is obtained, and he is given IV midazolam 0.15 mg/kg. Five minutes later he is still seizing.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give a third benzodiazepine dose of IV diazepam 0.2 mg/kg
Perform rapid sequence intubation with thiopentone now
Give IV pyridoxine 100 mg for possible pyridoxine dependency
Give rectal paraldehyde 0.4 mL/kg and wait 10 minutes
Give IV levetiracetam 40–60 mg/kg over 5 minutes
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Give IV levetiracetam 40–60 mg/kg over 5 minutes

---

He is in convulsive status epilepticus and has already had two benzodiazepine doses (one pre-hospital, one in hospital). The RCH Seizures – acute management guideline (June 2025) limits benzodiazepines to a MAXIMUM of two doses, including any given pre-hospital, because further doses add respiratory depression with little additional benefit. The next step is a second-line agent: levetiracetam 40–60 mg/kg IV/IO (max 4.5 g) over 5 minutes, or phenytoin 20 mg/kg as an alternative. If seizures continue after the second-line agent, a further second-line drug is given and anaesthetic/ICU help is called for rapid sequence induction. Look for and treat causes in parallel (glucose, electrolytes, infection, head injury).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Paediatric status epilepticus: a maximum of two benzodiazepine doses (count pre-hospital doses), then a second-line agent such as levetiracetam 40–60 mg/kg IV over 5 min (or phenytoin 20 mg/kg). Escalate to RSI if still seizing.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Seizures \u2013 acute management (June 2025)", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Seizures_-_acute_management/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Convulsive status epilepticus after two benzodiazepine doses: second-line levetiracetam

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A third benzodiazepine dose is not recommended. It increases the risk of apnoea and hypotension and rarely stops seizures that have not responded to two doses.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: RSI/anaesthesia is for refractory status after second-line agents, or for airway compromise. He is oxygenating with airway support.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Pyridoxine is considered in infants (typically under 18 months) with refractory seizures. It is not the next step in a 6-year-old.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Paraldehyde is an older option that is not a standard step in current RCH guidance, and waiting prolongs status epilepticus.

key_takeaways: Paediatric status epilepticus: a maximum of two benzodiazepine doses (count pre-hospital doses), then a second-line agent such as levetiracetam 40–60 mg/kg IV over 5 min (or phenytoin 20 mg/kg). Escalate to RSI if still seizing.

question_text:
A 14-year-6-month-old boy is brought by his mother to a general practice in Darwin, Northern Territory, because he is the shortest boy in his year and is being teased. He is otherwise well, plays soccer and is doing well at school. His sense of smell is normal. His father recalls that he 'shot up at 17' and started shaving at university. His mother had her first period at 13.

His height is 148 cm (below the 3rd centile), and his weight is on the 10th centile. His growth record from the school nurse and previous GP visits shows height tracking just below and parallel to the 3rd centile since age 4, with a growth velocity of 4.8 cm in the last year. His mid-parental target height is on the 50th centile. Testicular volumes are 4 mL bilaterally (Tanner stage 2 genitalia), and there is no pubic hair. He has no dysmorphic features, and the rest of the examination is normal.

Investigations:
- Bone age (Greulich and Pyle): 12 years
- TSH 2.1 mU/L (0.5–4.0)
- Free T4 14 pmol/L (10–20)
- Coeliac serology: negative
- Full blood count, ESR, electrolytes and creatinine: normal

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Familial short stature
Growth hormone deficiency
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann syndrome)
Primary hypothyroidism
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

---

Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the most common cause of short stature with late puberty in boys. Features: normal height velocity for bone age, height tracking parallel to a low centile, a delayed bone age (here 2.5 years behind), a family history of late puberty ('late bloomer' father), a normal examination and normal screening tests. Testicular volume of 4 mL shows puberty has only just started at 14.5 years, which argues against hypogonadism. Final adult height is usually close to the genetic target. Management is reassurance and monitoring; a short course of low-dose testosterone can be offered by a paediatric endocrinologist for psychosocial distress.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Short boy growing parallel to a low centile with delayed bone age, late puberty and a 'late bloomer' parent has constitutional delay. Familial short stature has normal bone age; GH deficiency and hypothyroidism cause falling velocity.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Palmert MR, Dunkel L. Delayed puberty. N Engl J Med 2012;366:443\u2013453", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMcp1109290"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Short stature with delayed puberty: constitutional delay of growth and puberty

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: In familial short stature, bone age matches chronological age, puberty occurs at a normal time and parents are short. His mid-parental height is on the 50th centile.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: GH deficiency causes growth velocity that falls away (crossing centiles downwards), often with increased truncal adiposity. He is growing in parallel to the centile at a normal prepubertal velocity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Kallmann syndrome causes absent puberty, often with anosmia. He has a normal sense of smell and 4 mL testes (early puberty), and his father's history suggests constitutional delay.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: His thyroid function is normal. Hypothyroidism also causes falling height velocity and weight gain.

key_takeaways: Short boy growing parallel to a low centile with delayed bone age, late puberty and a 'late bloomer' parent has constitutional delay. Familial short stature has normal bone age; GH deficiency and hypothyroidism cause falling velocity.

question_text:
A 9-year-old girl with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is being treated for severe diabetic ketoacidosis in the emergency department of a regional hospital in Ballarat, Victoria. At presentation her venous pH was 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, sodium 131 mmol/L and urea 11 mmol/L. She is receiving IV 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium at the calculated rate and an insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour, started one hour after fluids.

Four hours into treatment she complains of a severe headache and vomits. She is now confused and opens her eyes only to voice; her GCS has fallen from 15 to 11. Her heart rate has fallen from 124/min to 68/min, and her blood pressure has risen from 104/60 to 132/84 mmHg. Pupils are equal and reactive. Capillary glucose is 17 mmol/L. The paediatric retrieval service has been called.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Give mannitol 0.5 g/kg IV over 20 minutes and reduce the fluid rate by one-third
Arrange an urgent CT scan of the brain and treat if oedema is confirmed
Increase the IV fluid rate, because the bradycardia suggests hypovolaemia
Give sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis more rapidly
Stop the insulin infusion and give a 5 mL/kg bolus of 10% glucose
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Give mannitol 0.5 g/kg IV over 20 minutes and reduce the fluid rate by one-third

---

New headache, vomiting and falling GCS, with bradycardia and rising blood pressure (Cushing response), during DKA treatment strongly suggest DKA-related cerebral injury (cerebral oedema). This is most common in young children with new-onset diabetes and severe acidosis, often 4–12 hours into treatment. The RCH DKA guideline says to treat immediately, without waiting for imaging: hyperosmolar therapy with mannitol 20% 0.5 g/kg IV over 20 minutes OR 3% hypertonic saline 3 mL/kg over 15 minutes, reduce IV fluids by one-third, elevate the head of the bed, and involve ICU/retrieval and senior staff. CT can be done after the child is stabilised, to exclude other causes such as thrombosis or haemorrhage.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
DKA with headache, falling GCS, bradycardia and hypertension is cerebral injury: give mannitol 0.5 g/kg or 3% saline 3 mL/kg now (no CT first), cut fluids by one-third, head up, and call ICU.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne. Clinical Practice Guideline: Diabetic ketoacidosis (Jul 2025)", "url": "https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Diabetic_Ketoacidosis/"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: DKA-related cerebral injury (cerebral oedema): immediate hyperosmolar therapy

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Imaging should not delay treatment. Cerebral injury is a clinical diagnosis, and early CT can be normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Bradycardia with hypertension here reflects raised intracranial pressure, not hypovolaemia. Increasing fluids may worsen the oedema.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Bicarbonate is not recommended in paediatric DKA except in specific life-threatening situations, and it is associated with cerebral injury.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Stopping insulin prolongs ketoacidosis. A glucose of 17 does not call for a glucose bolus; glucose is added to fluids when glucose falls, as per protocol.

key_takeaways: DKA with headache, falling GCS, bradycardia and hypertension is cerebral injury: give mannitol 0.5 g/kg or 3% saline 3 mL/kg now (no CT first), cut fluids by one-third, head up, and call ICU.

question_text:
A 3-month-old girl is brought to a general practice in Hobart, Tasmania, for a routine check. She is the first child of her parents. She was in breech presentation from 34 weeks until birth; an external cephalic version was unsuccessful, and she was born by planned caesarean section at 39 weeks. Her newborn examination and 6-week check both recorded 'hips stable' (negative Barlow and Ortolani tests). No imaging has been done. Her mother has read about 'clicky hips' and asks whether anything else is needed.

The girl is thriving along the 50th centile. On examination, hip abduction is full and symmetrical, leg lengths and thigh skin creases are equal, and Barlow and Ortolani tests are negative. The rest of the examination is normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure the mother, because two normal hip examinations exclude dysplasia
Arrange an anteroposterior X-ray of the pelvis now
Fit a Pavlik harness as a precaution until she is 6 months of age
Arrange an ultrasound of both hips as soon as possible
Repeat the clinical examination at 6 months and image if it is abnormal
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Arrange an ultrasound of both hips as soon as possible

---

Breech presentation in late pregnancy (regardless of mode of birth) is a major risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip, along with family history. Clinical examination can miss dysplasia with a stable but shallow acetabulum. Australian neonatal guidance, including Safer Care Victoria, recommends a targeted hip ultrasound at about 6 weeks of age (generally 6–12 weeks) for infants with risk factors, even when examination is normal. She has missed it, and at 3 months ultrasound is still the best test; the femoral head ossific nucleus is not yet reliably visible on X-ray. If ultrasound shows dysplasia, she is referred to paediatric orthopaedics for treatment such as abduction bracing.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Breech presentation or a family history of DDH: arrange hip ultrasound at about 6 weeks (and up to about 4–6 months), even if the hip examination is normal. After that age, X-ray is preferred.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Safer Care Victoria. Developmental dysplasia of the hip in neonates", "url": "https://www.safercare.vic.gov.au/best-practice-improvement/clinical-guidance/neonatal/developmental-dysplasia-of-the-hip-in-neonates"}
• {"name": "ASUM. Statement on the use of ultrasound in the diagnosis of developmental hip dysplasia and dislocation", "url": "https://www.asum.com.au/files/public/SoP/curver/Paed-Neo/Statement-on-the-Use-of-Ultrasound-in-the-Diagnosis-of-Developmental-Hip-Dysplasia-and-Dislocation.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Breech-born infant with normal hip examination: ultrasound screening for DDH

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A normal Barlow and Ortolani examination does not exclude acetabular dysplasia, which is why at-risk infants have imaging.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Plain X-ray becomes the preferred test from about 4–6 months, when the femoral head ossifies. At 3 months ultrasound is more accurate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Treatment is not started without an imaging diagnosis. Unnecessary bracing has risks (for example avascular necrosis and skin problems).
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Waiting reduces the chance of successful harness treatment, which works best when started early.

key_takeaways: Breech presentation or a family history of DDH: arrange hip ultrasound at about 6 weeks (and up to about 4–6 months), even if the hip examination is normal. After that age, X-ray is preferred.

question_text:
A 27-year-old graphic designer sees a general practitioner in Adelaide, South Australia, with 5 weeks of low mood, loss of interest, sleeping 11 hours a night, increased appetite, poor concentration and feelings of worthlessness. She has no thoughts of self-harm. This is her third episode like this since age 19; the previous two got better after several months, and she was never treated.

On careful questioning, she describes at least three periods, each lasting 5–6 days, when she felt 'switched on': she needed only 4 hours of sleep without feeling tired, talked quickly, started several design projects at once and spent more than usual on clothes. Her colleagues noticed she was 'unusually chatty'. She kept working and was never admitted to hospital, and she never lost touch with reality. She drinks alcohol socially and does not use other drugs. Thyroid function is normal.

Her mother has had treatment for 'depression and mood swings'.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed
Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed
Cyclothymic disorder
Recurrent major depressive disorder with atypical features
Borderline personality disorder
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed

---

She has had recurrent major depressive episodes and at least one hypomanic episode: an elevated mood with decreased need for sleep, pressured speech and increased goal-directed activity lasting at least 4 consecutive days, noticed by others, without marked impairment, hospitalisation or psychosis. Major depression plus hypomania (never mania) is bipolar II disorder. Recognising it matters because antidepressant monotherapy may destabilise mood, and treatment follows bipolar depression guidance (for example quetiapine, lamotrigine or lithium, with psychoeducation), as in the RANZCP mood disorders guideline. Features that should prompt screening for bipolarity in depression include early onset, atypical features (hypersomnia, hyperphagia), recurrence and a family history.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Depression plus at least one hypomanic episode (≥4 days, noticed by others, no marked impairment or psychosis) is bipolar II. Always ask about past elevated mood before starting an antidepressant.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "RANZCP. Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders (Malhi et al., 2020)", "url": "https://www.ranzcp.org/getmedia/a8c79505-c0b5-46b4-9f27-67f79e047674/Mood-disorders-clinical-practice-guideline-2020.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Bipolar I needs at least one MANIC episode (lasting 7 days or needing hospitalisation, or with marked impairment or psychosis). Her episodes did not impair function and had no psychosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Cyclothymia involves 2 years of numerous hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet criteria for a hypomanic or major depressive episode. She has had full major depressive episodes.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: She does have atypical features, but her history of hypomanic episodes rules out unipolar depression.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Mood changes in BPD are brief (hours to days), reactive to interpersonal stress and occur with identity disturbance and impulsivity. Her episodes are sustained, distinct changes from her baseline.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man sees his general practitioner in Perth, Western Australia, for review. Seven months ago he had his first episode of major depression after being made redundant, with low mood, anhedonia, insomnia, weight loss and passive thoughts of death. He started sertraline, increased to 100 mg daily at week 4, and attended six sessions of CBT with a psychologist under a Mental Health Treatment Plan.

He has felt 'completely back to normal' for the past 3 months. He has a new job, is sleeping well, exercises three times a week and has a PHQ-9 score of 3. He has no side effects apart from mildly delayed ejaculation. He has no history of mania, and there is no family history of mood disorder. He asks whether he can stop the tablets now 'because I feel fine'.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop sertraline now, because he has been in remission for 3 months
Reduce sertraline to 50 mg daily as a maintenance dose for 2 years
Taper sertraline over the next 2 weeks and restart it if symptoms recur
Continue sertraline 100 mg daily for a further 3–9 months before a slow taper
Continue sertraline 100 mg daily indefinitely because of the risk of relapse
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Continue sertraline 100 mg daily for a further 3–9 months before a slow taper

---

After a first episode of major depression treated to remission, antidepressants should be continued at the dose that achieved remission for at least 6–12 months after remission, to reduce the high risk of early relapse. The RANZCP mood disorders guideline supports continuing effective treatment beyond remission, then withdrawing gradually (over weeks to months) with monitoring for relapse and discontinuation symptoms. He has been well for 3 months, so a further 3–9 months at the same dose (total 6–12 months) is appropriate. The side effect can be discussed, including strategies such as timing of the dose, rather than stopping early. Longer-term maintenance is considered for recurrent episodes or other risk factors.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
First episode of depression: continue the antidepressant at the full effective dose for 6–12 months after remission, then taper slowly. Do not reduce the dose during continuation.

---

REFERENCES

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Reducing the dose during continuation increases relapse risk. The dose that achieved remission is continued. Two years of maintenance is not routinely needed after a single uncomplicated episode.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A 2-week taper at 3 months of remission is too early and too fast.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Indefinite maintenance is considered for recurrent (for example three or more) episodes or high-risk features, not after a single episode with full remission.

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Mackay, Queensland, 4 months after a crash on the Bruce Highway in which her car was hit by a truck and the other driver died at the scene. Her physical injuries have healed.

Since the crash she has had nightmares about the collision several times a week, intrusive images when she hears truck horns, and she avoids driving, taking a longer bus route to work. She feels 'on edge', startles easily, sleeps 4–5 hours a night and feels guilty that she 'could have swerved'. She has had to reduce her hours at work. She has no thoughts of self-harm, drinks two standard drinks on weekends and does not use drugs. Her PCL-5 score is 52.

She asks what treatment is most likely to help.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Trauma-focused CBT such as cognitive processing therapy
Sertraline 50 mg daily, increasing according to response
Diazepam 5 mg at night for 4 weeks to improve her sleep
A single session of psychological debriefing about the crash
Quetiapine 25 mg at night for nightmares and hyperarousal
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Trauma-focused CBT such as cognitive processing therapy

---

She meets criteria for PTSD more than a month after a traumatic event (intrusions, avoidance, negative changes in mood and cognition such as guilt, and hyperarousal, with functional impairment). The Phoenix Australia Australian PTSD Guidelines (NHMRC-approved) strongly recommend trauma-focused psychological therapies (cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy for PTSD, prolonged exposure, trauma-focused CBT or EMDR) as first-line treatment for adults. Medicines (SSRIs such as sertraline, paroxetine or fluoxetine, or venlafaxine) are recommended when trauma-focused therapy is not available, not preferred or has not helped enough. Benzodiazepines are not recommended. A GP Mental Health Treatment Plan can support referral, and a road-crash compensation scheme may fund treatment in some states.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
PTSD in adults: trauma-focused psychological therapy (CPT, CT-PTSD, PE, TF-CBT, EMDR) is first line. SSRIs or venlafaxine if therapy is unavailable or not preferred. Avoid benzodiazepines and debriefing.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Phoenix Australia. Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, PTSD and Complex PTSD", "url": "https://www.phoenixaustralia.org/australian-guidelines-for-ptsd/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: An SSRI is a reasonable second-line option (or first choice if she prefers medicine or therapy is unavailable), but trauma-focused psychological therapy has stronger evidence and is first line.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Benzodiazepines do not treat PTSD, may interfere with recovery and carry dependence risk. They are not recommended.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Single-session psychological debriefing is not recommended; it does not prevent PTSD and may cause harm. She has established PTSD, which needs treatment.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Antipsychotics are not first-line treatment for PTSD; they are sometimes used as specialist adjuncts.

question_text:
A 34-year-old accountant sees a general practitioner in Canberra, Australian Capital Territory, because for about 9 months she has been worrying 'about everything': her work, her parents' health, money and her children's safety. She finds it hard to stop worrying, feels tense, has neck and shoulder aches, tires easily, has trouble falling asleep and gets irritable with her family. She has had no panic attacks. She drinks one to two glasses of wine most nights 'to switch off' and does not use other drugs. Caffeine intake is two coffees a day.

Physical examination, thyroid function and full blood count are normal. Her GAD-7 score is 15, and her PHQ-9 score is 8, with no thoughts of self-harm. She says a friend 'got Valium and it worked straight away' and asks for the same. She is open to other options and has a smartphone and reliable internet.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Regular diazepam 5 mg three times daily, reviewed in 4 weeks
Low-dose quetiapine 25 mg at night to help her worry and sleep
Cognitive behavioural therapy, face to face or internet-delivered
Regular propranolol 40 mg twice daily for the physical symptoms
Pregabalin 75 mg twice daily as the first-line medicine
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Cognitive behavioural therapy, face to face or internet-delivered

---

She has generalised anxiety disorder (more than 6 months of excessive, hard-to-control worry with muscle tension, fatigue, sleep disturbance and irritability, causing distress). First-line treatment is CBT, which can be delivered face to face (e.g. with a psychologist through a Mental Health Treatment Plan) or through evidence-based internet-delivered programs such as MindSpot (free, national) or THIS WAY UP. If medicine is chosen or therapy is not enough, an SSRI (e.g. escitalopram or sertraline) or an SNRI is the first-line medicine. Benzodiazepines are not recommended for ongoing treatment because of dependence, cognitive effects and interaction with her nightly alcohol use. Her drinking should be discussed as part of the plan.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
GAD: offer CBT first (face to face or internet-delivered, e.g. MindSpot). If medicine is needed, use an SSRI or SNRI. Avoid ongoing benzodiazepines.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Andrews G et al. RANZCP clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of panic disorder, social anxiety disorder and generalised anxiety disorder. Aust N Z J Psychiatry 2018", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1177/0004867418799453"}
• {"name": "MindSpot (free national digital mental health service, Macquarie University)", "url": "https://mindspot.org.au/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Quetiapine has some evidence in GAD but causes metabolic adverse effects and sedation. It is not a first-line option in primary care.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Beta-blockers may reduce tremor or palpitations in performance anxiety but do not treat the worry of GAD.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Pregabalin is a second-line option in some guidelines; it has misuse potential and is not first line ahead of CBT or an SSRI/SNRI.
