question_text:
A 22-year-old university student is brought to the emergency department of a tertiary hospital in Brisbane, Queensland, by her flatmates. Two weeks ago she had a flu-like illness with headache. Over the past 10 days she became anxious, stopped sleeping, and then began saying that her flatmates were 'recording her thoughts'. She has been hearing voices commenting on her actions. She has no previous psychiatric history, does not use drugs according to her flatmates, and her urine drug screen is negative.

In the department she is disorientated, with periods of staring and reduced responsiveness alternating with agitation. She makes repetitive chewing and lip-smacking movements, and her left arm occasionally takes up an abnormal posture. Her temperature is 37.9 °C, heart rate varies between 58 and 132/min and blood pressure between 104/60 and 168/98 mmHg. There is no neck stiffness or rash. Twenty minutes after arrival she has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds.

Full blood count, electrolytes, glucose, calcium, liver function, thyroid function and a CT scan of the brain are normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in establishing the diagnosis?
options: Admit to the mental health unit and start oral olanzapine, reviewing in 1 week
Serum prolactin level to confirm that the seizure was epileptic
Repeat urine drug screen with an extended synthetic cannabinoid panel
HIV and syphilis serology, then outpatient neurology review
MRI brain, EEG, and lumbar puncture with CSF and serum NMDA receptor antibodies
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. MRI brain, EEG, and lumbar puncture with CSF and serum NMDA receptor antibodies

---

A young woman with a viral-like prodrome followed by rapidly progressive psychiatric symptoms, then reduced consciousness, orofacial dyskinesias, abnormal postures, autonomic instability and a seizure, has probable autoimmune encephalitis. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is the most common type in this group. This is not a primary psychotic disorder. Seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability and fluctuating consciousness are 'red flags' for an organic cause of first-episode psychosis. The work-up is MRI brain (often normal or showing medial temporal changes), EEG (slowing, epileptiform activity or 'extreme delta brush'), and lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, HSV PCR (with empirical aciclovir until HSV encephalitis is excluded) and CSF NMDAR antibodies (more sensitive than serum). Screen for an ovarian teratoma (pelvic ultrasound/MRI). Early immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange) and tumour removal improve outcomes. Antipsychotics are poorly tolerated in these patients and may worsen dyskinesias or precipitate an NMS-like state.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
First-episode psychosis with seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability or fluctuating consciousness needs an encephalitis work-up (MRI, EEG, LP with CSF NMDAR antibodies, HSV PCR) and a teratoma screen, not antipsychotics alone.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Graus F et al. A clinical approach to diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391\u2013404", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1016/S1474-4422(15)00401-9"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Suspected autoimmune (anti-NMDA receptor) encephalitis presenting as first-episode psychosis

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Treating this as primary psychosis would miss a treatable encephalitis. These patients are prone to severe antipsychotic adverse effects.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Prolactin testing after a seizure has limited value and does not address the underlying cause.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A negative screen with the neurological signs and autonomic features makes drug-induced psychosis less likely. An extended panel would not explain a seizure with dyskinesia and fluctuating consciousness here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: HIV and syphilis testing is reasonable in first-episode psychosis, but outpatient review is unsafe for a patient with encephalopathy and seizures.

key_takeaways: First-episode psychosis with seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability or fluctuating consciousness needs an encephalitis work-up (MRI, EEG, LP with CSF NMDAR antibodies, HSV PCR) and a teratoma screen, not antipsychotics alone.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man is an inpatient in the acute mental health unit of a hospital in Newcastle, New South Wales, with first-episode schizophrenia. Aripiprazole was started 10 days ago and increased to 15 mg daily 4 days ago. His auditory hallucinations are becoming less intrusive.

Over the past 3 days nursing staff report that he paces the corridor for hours, cannot sit through meals or groups and repeatedly shifts his weight from foot to foot when standing. He says he feels 'like I'm going to jump out of my skin' and that 'my legs won't stop', and he became tearful and said, 'I can't live like this.' The night nurse has asked for PRN olanzapine 'for agitation'.

His temperature is 36.8 °C, heart rate 88/min and blood pressure 124/78 mmHg. There is no rigidity, tremor or abnormal posturing, and his conscious state is normal. He is not responding to hallucinations on the ward. Creatine kinase is 140 U/L (<200).

Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for his current symptoms?
options: Antipsychotic-induced akathisia
Worsening psychotic agitation
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Acute dystonic reaction
Tardive dyskinesia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Antipsychotic-induced akathisia

---

Akathisia is a subjective sense of inner restlessness with objective motor restlessness (pacing, rocking, shifting weight, inability to sit). It usually appears days to weeks after starting or increasing an antipsychotic. Aripiprazole is a common cause despite its otherwise favourable side-effect profile. It is often mistaken for psychotic agitation or anxiety, which leads to more antipsychotic and worse symptoms. It is distressing and associated with suicidal thoughts and impulsivity, so his comment needs a risk assessment. Management: reduce the dose or switch to an antipsychotic less likely to cause akathisia, and consider propranolol (low dose, titrated) or a short benzodiazepine course, while avoiding extra antipsychotic PRNs.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Inner restlessness, pacing and inability to sit days after starting or increasing an antipsychotic is akathisia, not agitation. Reduce or switch the drug, consider propranolol, and assess suicide risk.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Family Physician (RACGP), May 2017. Beyond anxiety and agitation: a clinical approach to akathisia", "url": "https://www.racgp.org.au/afp/2017/may/beyond-anxiety-and-agitation-a-clinical-approach-t"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: New restlessness after starting aripiprazole: akathisia mistaken for agitation

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: His psychotic symptoms are improving, and his restlessness is focused on the legs and inner tension, not on psychotic experiences. Giving more antipsychotic would likely worsen akathisia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: NMS causes fever, rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability and a raised CK. None of these are present.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Acute dystonia is a sustained involuntary muscle contraction (e.g. torticollis, oculogyric crisis), usually within the first days, not motor restlessness.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Tardive dyskinesia appears after months to years of treatment, with involuntary choreiform or orofacial movements. The patient is often unaware of it and does not feel restless.

key_takeaways: Inner restlessness, pacing and inability to sit days after starting or increasing an antipsychotic is akathisia, not agitation. Reduce or switch the drug, consider propranolol, and assess suicide risk.

question_text:
A 52-year-old sheep farmer from near Horsham in western Victoria sees a general practitioner at the local clinic because his wife made the appointment for 'his sleep'. After three years of drought he has sold most of his flock, and his bank has refused to extend his loan. His wife has recently moved to their daughter's house in Ballarat.

He says he has been waking at 3 am, has lost 6 kg, has stopped going to the football club and is drinking four to six beers most nights. He says he feels 'useless' and adds, 'Everyone would be better off without me around; the insurance would at least clear the debt.' He denies having made any attempt. He has no previous psychiatric history. He is calm and makes limited eye contact, and there is no evidence of psychosis.

He agrees to keep talking but says he needs to be home before dark to feed the dogs.

Which one of the following is the most important question to ask him next?
options: Whether anyone in his family has a history of depression
How many hours of sleep he is getting each night
Whether he has thought about how he would end his life and has access to firearms
His score on a structured suicide risk scale such as SAD PERSONS
Whether he would accept a referral to a psychologist in the next month
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Whether he has thought about how he would end his life and has access to firearms

---

He has disclosed suicidal thinking with a possible motive (insurance), multiple risk factors (male, middle-aged, rural, financial loss, relationship separation, social withdrawal, increasing alcohol use, depressive symptoms) and likely access to lethal means: firearms are common on farms and are a leading method of suicide in rural men. The priority is to ask directly and specifically about suicidal intent, plans, preparations and access to means, especially firearms. Asking about suicide does not increase risk. This leads to a collaborative safety plan: means restriction (for example firearms stored off-site with a trusted person or the police, with his agreement), reducing alcohol, involving supports with consent, and a same-day or next-day review or urgent mental health triage depending on intent. The RANZCP recommends against using risk-scoring tools to classify people as low or high risk; assessment should be a comprehensive, needs-based clinical formulation.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
When someone discloses suicidal thoughts, ask directly about intent, plans, preparations and access to means (especially firearms in rural men), then make a collaborative safety plan. Do not rely on risk-scoring tools.

---

REFERENCES

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Sleep is part of the depression assessment but does not address immediate safety.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Risk scales such as SAD PERSONS have poor predictive value and are not recommended for deciding care. They should not replace a direct inquiry about intent, plans and means.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Referral is part of management, but a routine referral within a month does not address immediate risk. Safety assessment and planning come first.

question_text:
A 15-year-old girl is brought by her parents to the emergency department of a children's hospital in Perth, Western Australia, after she fainted at school. Over the past 8 months she has lost 11 kg (2 kg in the last 2 weeks) by restricting food and running for 2 hours a day. Her periods stopped 5 months ago. She says she 'feels fat' and is frightened of gaining weight. She denies vomiting or laxative use.

Her weight is 38 kg and height 163 cm (BMI 14.3 kg/m², about 70% of the median BMI for her age and sex). Her tympanic temperature is 35.4 °C. Heart rate is 44/min lying (awake) and 98/min standing. Blood pressure is 86/52 mmHg lying and 64/40 mmHg standing. Her hands and feet are cold, with lanugo hair on her arms.

Investigations:
- Sodium 136 mmol/L (135–145)
- Potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5–5.0)
- Phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.0–1.8)
- Magnesium 0.72 mmol/L (0.7–1.0)
- Glucose 3.6 mmol/L
- ECG: sinus bradycardia 44/min, QTc 440 ms

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Discharge with urgent family-based treatment in the community and weekly GP weighing
Admit to a paediatric medical ward for monitoring and supervised nutritional rehabilitation
Admit to an adult mental health unit under the Mental Health Act for psychiatric treatment
Start olanzapine 2.5 mg daily to reduce her fear of weight gain before any refeeding
Give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 10% glucose and then discharge her once the heart rate is above 50
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Admit to a paediatric medical ward for monitoring and supervised nutritional rehabilitation

---

She meets several criteria for medical instability that require admission in the RCH emergency department eating disorder guideline: awake heart rate below 50/min, postural heart rate rise above 30–50/min (here 54), systolic BP below 80 (standing) and a postural drop above 20 mmHg, temperature below 35.5 °C, BMI about 70% of median, rapid weight loss (more than 1 kg/week), low phosphate and syncope. She needs admission to a paediatric medical bed (with mental health and dietetic input) for cardiac monitoring, electrolyte monitoring and a structured refeeding plan. Nutrition is started early with close monitoring for refeeding syndrome: phosphate, potassium and magnesium are checked and replaced, and thiamine is given. Family-based treatment remains the main evidence-based therapy once she is medically stable.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Adolescent anorexia nervosa with awake HR <50, postural instability, hypothermia, low phosphate, syncope or rapid weight loss needs admission to a paediatric medical bed for monitoring and supervised refeeding (with phosphate and thiamine).

question_text:
A 34-year-old man attends a community drug and alcohol clinic in Parramatta, New South Wales, asking to start opioid treatment. He has injected heroin daily for 3 years, about 0.5 g a day, and last injected 4 hours ago, before catching the train to the clinic. He has not used methadone or other opioids in the past month. He also drinks 2–3 standard drinks a day and uses cannabis occasionally. He wants to start buprenorphine today because he 'can't keep doing this'.

He is alert and cooperative, with a heart rate of 84/min and blood pressure 126/80 mmHg. His pupils are 3 mm. There is no yawning, sweating, rhinorrhoea, piloerection or tremor, and he feels 'okay for now'. There are healed injection sites on both forearms. The nurse practitioner has prepared a sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone 8 mg/2 mg film.

Before the first dose of buprenorphine is given, which one of the following assessments is most important?
options: A urine drug screen confirming opioid use
Liver function tests and hepatitis C serology
A 12-lead ECG to measure the corrected QT interval
Objective withdrawal severity using a scale such as COWS
A breath alcohol reading below 0.05%
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Objective withdrawal severity using a scale such as COWS

---

Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist. If it is given while a full agonist such as heroin still occupies the receptors, it displaces the heroin and causes precipitated withdrawal, which is severe and discourages patients from continuing treatment. NSW guidelines advise waiting until the patient has objective signs of at least moderate withdrawal before the first dose, measured with a validated scale such as the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS), commonly a score of 8 to 12 or more. This is typically at least 8–12 hours after short-acting opioids such as heroin (longer after methadone). He used 4 hours ago and has no withdrawal signs, so dosing now risks precipitated withdrawal. He can wait in the clinic or return later, or a low-dose ('micro-dosing') induction can be considered under specialist guidance. Once withdrawal is confirmed, a typical first dose is 2–4 mg, then further doses are titrated.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Start buprenorphine only when objective opioid withdrawal is at least moderate (e.g. COWS ≥8–12; usually ≥8–12 h after heroin). Dosing too early causes precipitated withdrawal.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NSW Health. NSW Clinical Guidelines: Treatment of Opioid Dependence (GL2018_018)", "url": "https://www1.health.nsw.gov.au/pds/ActivePDSDocuments/GL2018_018.pdf"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Baseline LFTs and blood-borne virus screening are part of comprehensive assessment but do not determine the timing of the first dose.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: ECG monitoring for QT prolongation matters more for methadone; buprenorphine has minimal QT effect.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Intoxication with alcohol or sedatives is a reason to delay dosing, but his reported intake is modest and he is not intoxicated. The key issue is opioid withdrawal status.

question_text:
A 48-year-old man is brought to the emergency department of a regional hospital in Mildura, Victoria, by a friend who found him confused at home. He has drunk about 1.5 litres of wine a day for years and has eaten very little for the past month. His last drink was the previous evening.

He is disorientated to time and place and cannot recall why he is in hospital, but he is not hallucinating and not agitated. His temperature is 36.6 °C, heart rate 92/min and blood pressure 128/80 mmHg. He is not sweating, and there is no tremor. He has horizontal nystagmus and cannot fully abduct his right eye. When he tries to walk he has a wide-based, unsteady gait and needs support. There is no asterixis, jaundice or ascites. He has reduced vibration sense in both feet.

Investigations:
- Capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L
- Sodium 136 mmol/L (135–145)
- Bilirubin 18 µmol/L (<20)
- ALT 64 U/L (<40)
- GGT 280 U/L (<60)
- Albumin 34 g/L (35–50)
- INR 1.1
- CT brain: mild generalised atrophy, no bleed

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Korsakoff syndrome
Delirium tremens
Hepatic encephalopathy
Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration
Wernicke encephalopathy
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Wernicke encephalopathy

---

He has acute confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus and ataxia in the setting of long-term heavy drinking and poor nutrition. This is Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. The full triad is present in only a minority, so any one feature in an at-risk person should prompt treatment. Treatment is urgent high-dose parenteral thiamine (Australian alcohol guidelines recommend doses such as 300–500 mg IV three times daily for suspected WE), given before or with glucose-containing fluids but without delaying treatment of hypoglycaemia. Magnesium is corrected too. Without adequate treatment it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome (permanent amnesia with confabulation).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus or ataxia in a person with alcohol dependence or malnutrition is Wernicke encephalopathy until proven otherwise: give high-dose parenteral thiamine immediately.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Government Department of Health. Quick reference guide to the treatment of alcohol problems (companion to the 2021 Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems)", "url": "https://www.health.gov.au/sites/default/files/quick-reference-guide-to-the-treatment-of-alcohol-problems_0.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in alcohol dependence: Wernicke encephalopathy

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Korsakoff syndrome is a chronic amnestic state with confabulation and a relatively clear sensorium, usually after WE. It does not explain the acute eye signs and ataxia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Delirium tremens occurs 48–72 hours after the last drink, with agitation, hallucinations, tremor, fever and autonomic hyperactivity. He last drank the previous evening and is calm, afebrile and not tremulous.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Hepatic encephalopathy causes confusion with asterixis, usually with signs of liver failure (jaundice, ascites, raised INR). His liver synthetic function is preserved.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration causes chronic truncal and gait ataxia but not acute confusion or ophthalmoplegia.

key_takeaways: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus or ataxia in a person with alcohol dependence or malnutrition is Wernicke encephalopathy until proven otherwise: give high-dose parenteral thiamine immediately.

question_text:
A 31-year-old woman brings her 3-week-old son to a general practice in Toowoomba, Queensland, for a weight check. She had an emergency caesarean section after a long labour, and breastfeeding has been difficult. Her partner went back to work, driving trucks, a week after the birth. As part of routine postnatal care, the practice nurse asked her to complete the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale in the waiting room.

Her total EPDS score is 11. For question 10 ('The thought of harming myself has occurred to me') she ticked 'Sometimes'. In the consultation she is tired but engages well and smiles at her baby. She says she is 'just exhausted, like every new mum'. The baby is gaining weight appropriately.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ask her directly about thoughts of self-harm or suicide and assess her safety today
Repeat the EPDS in 2–4 weeks, because her total score is below 13
Reassure her that this is likely to be the 'baby blues' and review at the 6-week check
Start sertraline 50 mg daily, because it is compatible with breastfeeding
Give her a referral to a perinatal psychologist with a routine appointment
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Ask her directly about thoughts of self-harm or suicide and assess her safety today

---

Any positive response to EPDS item 10 (thoughts of self-harm) needs an immediate, direct assessment of risk, regardless of the total score. The COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline (2023) uses a total of 13 or more to prompt further assessment and 10–12 for monitoring and repeat screening, but item 10 is the exception. The GP should ask about the nature, frequency and intent of the thoughts, any plans, thoughts of harm to the baby, psychotic symptoms and supports, then make a collaborative safety plan and arrange referral (e.g. perinatal mental health service, or urgent mental health triage if risk is high). The 'baby blues' peak at days 3–5 and settle by about 2 weeks. Symptoms continuing at 3 weeks, with self-harm thoughts, need assessment for perinatal depression.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
EPDS: ≥13 = further assessment, 10–12 = monitor and repeat, BUT any positive answer to item 10 needs an immediate direct risk assessment regardless of the total.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "COPE (Centre of Perinatal Excellence). Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period: Australian Clinical Practice Guideline (2023)", "url": "https://www.cope.org.au/uploads/images/Health-professionals/COPE_2023_Perinatal_Mental_Health_Practice_Guideline.pdf"}

---

subtopic: Postnatal EPDS below the cut-off but with a positive self-harm item: immediate risk assessment

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Baby blues settle within about 2 weeks and do not include thoughts of self-harm. Waiting 3 weeks risks missing serious illness.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Sertraline is compatible with breastfeeding and may be appropriate after assessment, but medicine is not started before the risk and diagnosis are assessed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Referral may be appropriate, but a routine appointment does not address the possible immediate risk, which must be assessed first.

question_text:
A 16-year-old boy is reviewed by his general practitioner in Wollongong, New South Wales, with his consent and his mother present for part of the visit. For 4 months he has had low mood, irritability, loss of interest in basketball and gaming, poor sleep, falling school grades and social withdrawal.

Over the past 10 weeks he has attended eight sessions of CBT at a headspace centre and has engaged well. His sleep has improved slightly, but he still feels 'flat most days', has stopped seeing friends and scores 18 on the PHQ-A. He has passive thoughts that 'it wouldn't matter if I didn't wake up', but no plans or intent and no self-harm. He does not use alcohol or other drugs. There is no personal or family history of bipolar disorder. He and his mother would like to discuss medicine, and his psychologist agrees.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop CBT and start venlafaxine, because a dual-action drug will work faster
Continue CBT and start sertraline 100 mg daily, reviewing in 8 weeks
Continue CBT and add fluoxetine 10 mg daily, with weekly review early on
Continue CBT and add paroxetine 10 mg daily, with monthly review
Continue CBT alone for another 6 months before considering any medicine
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Continue CBT and add fluoxetine 10 mg daily, with weekly review early on

---

He has moderate-to-severe depression with only a partial response to an adequate trial of psychological therapy. Adding an antidepressant alongside continued therapy is appropriate. In young people, fluoxetine has the best evidence of benefit and is the first-choice antidepressant (its use under 18 years is off-label in Australia). It is started at a low dose (e.g. 10 mg, increasing to 20 mg after 1–2 weeks if tolerated). Because antidepressants can increase suicidal thinking and agitation in people under 25, especially in the first weeks, close monitoring (about weekly for the first 4 weeks), a safety plan, and involving family with his consent are recommended. Psychological therapy continues.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Adolescent depression: psychological therapy first. If moderate-to-severe or only partly responding, add fluoxetine (off-label, start low) with weekly monitoring for the first 4 weeks for suicidality. Avoid paroxetine and venlafaxine.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Antidepressants in adolescence", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/antidepressants-in-adolescence.html"}
• {"name": "RANZCP. Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders (Malhi et al., 2020)", "url": "https://www.ranzcp.org/getmedia/a8c79505-c0b5-46b4-9f27-67f79e047674/Mood-disorders-clinical-practice-guideline-2020.pdf"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Sertraline (or escitalopram) is a second-line alternative if fluoxetine is unsuitable. Starting at 100 mg and waiting 8 weeks to review is too high and too slow.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Paroxetine is not recommended in adolescents (poor efficacy and higher suicidality risk), and monthly review is not close enough early on.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: With moderate-to-severe depression and only partial response after an adequate CBT trial, waiting 6 more months prolongs illness and risk.

question_text:
An 83-year-old woman living in a residential aged care facility in Toowoomba, Queensland, is reviewed by her general practitioner because staff say she has been 'not herself' for 3 days. She has mild Alzheimer disease (MMSE 24/30 six months ago), osteoarthritis and hypertension. Five days ago she was started on trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection and on oxycodone 5 mg twice daily for knee pain.

Staff report that she is staying in bed, eating little, dozing through meals and has stopped joining activities. Her daughter thinks she is 'depressed because her friend in the next room died last month'. When examined she is drowsy but rousable, gives short answers and drifts off mid-sentence. She cannot say the months of the year backwards and is unsure where she is. Staff say she was 'much brighter' yesterday afternoon. Her temperature is 37.4 °C, heart rate 90/min, blood pressure 118/64 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. There are no focal neurological signs, and her bladder is not palpable. Her 4AT score is 7.

Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for her change?
options: Major depressive episode triggered by bereavement
Progression of her Alzheimer disease
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Hypoactive delirium
Late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Hypoactive delirium

---

She has an acute onset (days) of fluctuating inattention (cannot do the months backwards, drifts off mid-sentence), altered alertness and disorientation, with likely precipitants: infection, a new opioid and underlying dementia. This is hypoactive delirium. A 4AT score of 4 or more suggests delirium. The hypoactive form is the most commonly missed and is often mistaken for depression or 'tiredness', and it has a worse prognosis. The ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard asks for early identification using a validated tool, a search for and treatment of causes (here: review the oxycodone, check bowel and bladder function, reassess the infection, bloods), non-drug strategies, and involving the family. Antipsychotics are not first line.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
An acute, fluctuating change in attention and alertness in an older person, especially with new drugs or infection, is delirium (often hypoactive). Screen with the 4AT and find and treat the cause.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care. Delirium Clinical Care Standard (2021)", "url": "https://www.safetyandquality.gov.au/standards/clinical-care-standards/delirium-clinical-care-standard"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Older person withdrawn and drowsy after a UTI and new opioid: hypoactive delirium, not depression

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Depression develops over weeks, with low mood; it does not usually cause fluctuating attention and drowsiness. Bereavement is a distractor here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Alzheimer disease progresses gradually over months to years. A change over 3 days with fluctuating alertness suggests delirium superimposed on dementia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: DLB causes fluctuating cognition, but over a longer course with visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder. This acute change after new precipitants is delirium.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: There are no hallucinations or delusions, and the presentation is acute with impaired attention and alertness, which points to delirium.

key_takeaways: An acute, fluctuating change in attention and alertness in an older person, especially with new drugs or infection, is delirium (often hypoactive). Screen with the 4AT and find and treat the cause.

question_text:
A 74-year-old retired electrician was admitted to a hospital in Launceston, Tasmania, 3 days ago with a urinary tract infection. On the first night he was frightened and trying to leave, saying there were 'children standing at the end of the bed'. He was given haloperidol 1 mg orally twice.

The next day he became very stiff, fell twice and was much more confused and drowsy. He is afebrile, and his creatine kinase is normal. The UTI has been treated.

His wife says that for about a year before admission his memory and concentration have 'come and gone': some days he is almost normal, and on others he stares into space for long periods. He often sees small children or animals in the house and is not frightened by them. For several years he has shouted and punched out in his sleep, 'acting out his dreams'. In the past 6 months he has become slower and shuffles when he walks. On examination (off haloperidol for 48 hours) he has symmetrical bradykinesia and mild rigidity, and no tremor. His MoCA is 17/30, with marked impairment of attention and visuospatial function and relatively preserved recall.

Which one of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Alzheimer disease
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Parkinson disease dementia
Vascular dementia
Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Dementia with Lewy bodies

---

He has the core clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies: fluctuating cognition and alertness, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism. Cognitive testing shows the typical profile of attention, executive and visuospatial deficits with relatively preserved memory early on. Severe sensitivity to antipsychotics (marked worsening of parkinsonism, confusion and falls after haloperidol) is a supportive feature and a major safety issue. Haloperidol and other D2 blockers should be avoided. Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. rivastigmine or donepezil) can help cognition and hallucinations. By the '1-year rule', dementia starting before or within a year of parkinsonism is called DLB; dementia arising in established Parkinson disease is PDD.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism suggest dementia with Lewy bodies. These patients can react severely to antipsychotics, so avoid haloperidol.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of dementia with Lewy bodies: fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium. Neurology 2017;89:88\u2013100", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.0000000000004058"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Severe reaction to haloperidol with fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations: dementia with Lewy bodies

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Alzheimer disease typically begins with prominent episodic memory loss. Early visual hallucinations, RBD, fluctuations and parkinsonism point to DLB.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: PDD is diagnosed when dementia develops in the context of well-established Parkinson disease (more than 1 year of motor symptoms first). His cognitive fluctuations and hallucinations came before the parkinsonism.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Vascular dementia usually has a stepwise course with focal neurological signs and vascular risk factors, not RBD and well-formed hallucinations.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: bvFTD presents with early disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and compulsive behaviour, usually in younger people, without RBD or visual hallucinations.

key_takeaways: Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism suggest dementia with Lewy bodies. These patients can react severely to antipsychotics, so avoid haloperidol.

question_text:
A 23-year-old hospitality worker sees her general practitioner in Hobart, Tasmania, a week after an emergency department visit for superficial cuts to her forearms after an argument with her partner. She has self-harmed by cutting at times of distress since age 15. She describes intense, rapidly changing emotions that last hours, chronic feelings of emptiness, a strong fear of being abandoned, a series of intense but unstable relationships, and impulsive spending and binge drinking. She has had two brief overdoses of paracetamol in the past 3 years, both after relationship break-ups.

She has previously been prescribed sertraline, quetiapine and diazepam by different doctors, 'none of which helped'. She is not psychotic, and she has no current plan or intent to end her life. She has agreed a safety plan with the ED mental health team. She asks, 'Is there anything that actually works for people like me?'

Which one of the following is the most appropriate longer-term management?
options: Start lamotrigine as a mood stabiliser and titrate over 6 weeks
Restart quetiapine at 100 mg at night to reduce emotional instability
Arrange a planned 4-week inpatient psychiatric admission for stabilisation
Prescribe regular diazepam for use at times of intense distress
Refer for a structured therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Refer for a structured therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy

---

She meets criteria for borderline personality disorder (affective instability, fear of abandonment, unstable relationships, identity disturbance and emptiness, impulsivity, recurrent self-harm). The NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of BPD (2012) recommends structured psychological therapies designed for BPD (for example DBT or mentalisation-based therapy) as the main treatment. Medicines are NOT recommended as primary therapy because they do not change the course of the disorder. They may be used short term as adjuncts for specific symptoms, with attention to overdose risk. The GP's role includes giving a diagnosis with hope (many people improve substantially), a consistent treating relationship, crisis/safety planning, and managing comorbidities such as alcohol use.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
BPD: structured, BPD-specific psychotherapy (e.g. DBT, MBT) is the main treatment. Medicines are adjuncts only (not primary), benzodiazepines are best avoided, and admissions should be brief and goal-directed.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NHMRC. Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder (2012)", "url": "https://www.nhmrc.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-10/mh25-bpd-guideline.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Borderline personality disorder: structured psychotherapy as the main treatment

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Mood stabilisers have not been shown to change the overall course of BPD and are not recommended as primary treatment. Lamotrigine also has serious rash risks.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Antipsychotics are not recommended as primary therapy in BPD. They add metabolic risk and overdose potential.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Long admissions can reinforce dependence and self-harm. The guideline supports only brief admissions for crisis with clear, agreed goals.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Benzodiazepines increase disinhibition, impulsivity and overdose risk in BPD and should be avoided.

key_takeaways: BPD: structured, BPD-specific psychotherapy (e.g. DBT, MBT) is the main treatment. Medicines are adjuncts only (not primary), benzodiazepines are best avoided, and admissions should be brief and goal-directed.

question_text:
A 29-year-old man is brought to a general practice in Bendigo, Victoria, by his parents, with whom he lives. Over 3 weeks he has stopped sleeping, barricaded his bedroom window and says that neighbours are 'pumping gas through the vents' to kill him. Two days ago he threatened a neighbour with a garden spade. He has a history of schizophrenia and stopped his depot antipsychotic 4 months ago. He is not currently under a treatment order.

The general practitioner examines him now. He is suspicious and guarded, describes persecutory delusions and hears voices telling him to 'defend the house'. He has no insight and refuses any treatment or referral, saying 'there's nothing wrong with me'. He is not intoxicated and is physically well. The local area mental health service cannot send a community team to assess him today, and his parents are frightened to take him home.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate action for the general practitioner?
options: Make a temporary treatment order so that he can be given his depot injection today
Apply to the Mental Health Tribunal for an order requiring him to be assessed
Make an inpatient assessment order and arrange his transport to a designated service
Ask his parents to take him home and phone police if he becomes violent again
Arrange two medical recommendations so he can be detained under the Act
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Make an inpatient assessment order and arrange his transport to a designated service

---

Under the Victorian Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022, a registered medical practitioner (including a GP) who has examined the person may make an assessment order if the criteria appear to be met: the person appears to have mental illness; because of it, needs immediate treatment to prevent serious deterioration in mental or physical health or serious harm to themselves or another person; an assessment order would enable an assessment; and there is no less restrictive means reasonably available. An inpatient assessment order is made only if the assessment cannot occur in the community, which is the case here. It allows the person to be taken to (and detained in) a designated mental health service for examination by an authorised psychiatrist, who decides whether to make a temporary treatment order. Only an authorised psychiatrist can make a temporary treatment order. Transport can be arranged under the Act (ambulance and/or police). The GP should explain the order and his rights to him and give him the statement of rights.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Victoria (MHW Act 2022): a GP who has examined the person can make an assessment order (inpatient if community assessment is not possible). Only an authorised psychiatrist can make a temporary treatment order.

question_text:
A 70-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, stable for 15 years on lithium carbonate 750 mg daily, is brought to the emergency department of a hospital in Hobart, Tasmania, by her husband. Three weeks ago her GP started ramipril for hypertension, and she has been taking ibuprofen for a painful shoulder. For 4 days she has had diarrhoea and vomiting and has been eating and drinking little.

She is drowsy, opening her eyes to voice, and confused (GCS 12). She has a coarse tremor of both hands, multifocal myoclonic jerks, dysarthria and ataxia. Her temperature is 37.1 °C, heart rate 64/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. There is no evidence of an overdose, and her husband keeps her tablets in a dosette box.

Investigations:
- Serum lithium 2.4 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6–1.0); sample taken 12 hours after her last dose, which she took the evening before admission
- Sodium 138 mmol/L (135–145)
- Potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.2)
- Creatinine 196 µmol/L (45–90; baseline 88 three months ago)
- eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²
- ECG: sinus rhythm 64/min, QTc 470 ms, T-wave flattening

In addition to stopping lithium, ramipril and ibuprofen, which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: IV 0.9% sodium chloride and urgent haemodialysis
IV 0.9% sodium chloride and repeat the lithium level in 6 hours
Activated charcoal 50 g orally, with IV fluids
Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol, with IV fluids
IV furosemide with IV fluids to increase lithium excretion
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. IV 0.9% sodium chloride and urgent haemodialysis

---

She has chronic lithium toxicity, precipitated by dehydration, an ACE inhibitor and an NSAID (all reduce renal lithium clearance), with acute kidney injury. In chronic toxicity, neurological toxicity correlates poorly with the serum level; a level of 2.4 mmol/L with a reduced level of consciousness is serious. The EXTRIP workgroup recommends extracorporeal treatment (haemodialysis) in lithium poisoning when there is a decreased level of consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmias IRRESPECTIVE of the lithium concentration, or when the level is above 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidney function. It also suggests dialysis when the level is above 5.0, with significant confusion, or when the expected time to reach a level below 1.0 mmol/L with optimal management is more than 36 hours. She meets the 'recommended' criterion (reduced consciousness), and her AKI will also slow elimination. IV isotonic saline to restore volume is given too. Discuss early with a clinical toxicologist (Poisons Information Centre 13 11 26) and nephrology.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Lithium toxicity: reduced consciousness, seizures or dysrhythmia means haemodialysis regardless of the level (EXTRIP). So does a level >4.0 with impaired kidney function. Charcoal does not bind lithium.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Decker BS et al. Extracorporeal treatment for lithium poisoning: systematic review and recommendations from the EXTRIP workgroup. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015;10:875\u2013887", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4422246/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Fluids alone might be adequate in mild chronic toxicity with normal consciousness, but with reduced GCS and AKI, delaying dialysis risks permanent neurological injury (SILENT syndrome).
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium (or other metal ions) and is not indicated.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Whole bowel irrigation is considered only after a large ingestion of a sustained-release lithium preparation. This is chronic toxicity without an overdose.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Forced diuresis with loop diuretics does not increase lithium clearance meaningfully and worsens volume depletion and kidney function.

key_takeaways: Lithium toxicity: reduced consciousness, seizures or dysrhythmia means haemodialysis regardless of the level (EXTRIP). So does a level >4.0 with impaired kidney function. Charcoal does not bind lithium.

question_text:
A 26-year-old woman with schizophrenia sees her general practitioner in Geraldton, Western Australia, for review. Her illness has been stable for 6 months on risperidone 4 mg daily, prescribed through her community mental health team. She says her periods, which used to be regular, stopped 3 months ago, and she has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples. She has a new partner and says they 'mostly' use condoms. She has no headaches or visual symptoms. She takes no other medicines.

Her BMI is 29 kg/m², up from 26 a year ago. Blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg. Visual fields are full to confrontation. Expressible milky discharge is noted from both breasts, with no breast lumps. She is worried that 'the tablets have ruined my fertility' and wants to stop them.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
options: Serum prolactin level
MRI of the pituitary gland
Thyroid-stimulating hormone
Serum or urine β-hCG
Serum FSH, LH and oestradiol
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Serum or urine β-hCG

---

Risperidone is one of the antipsychotics most likely to raise prolactin, and amenorrhoea with galactorrhoea is a typical adverse effect. However, pregnancy is the commonest cause of secondary amenorrhoea in a sexually active woman, and it also raises prolactin and can cause breast secretion. Her contraception is inconsistent, so a pregnancy test is the first investigation. It changes management immediately (antenatal care, medication review and planning with her psychiatrist) and must be known before interpreting a prolactin level or arranging imaging. If she is not pregnant, check prolactin (plus TSH and renal function), then consider switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic or adding aripiprazole in liaison with her mental health team. She should not stop risperidone abruptly because of relapse risk. Discuss reliable contraception, because fertility may return when prolactin falls.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Amenorrhoea in a woman taking a prolactin-raising antipsychotic: do a pregnancy test first, then prolactin. Manage hyperprolactinaemia with her psychiatrist (switch or add aripiprazole) and discuss contraception.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Galletly C et al. RANZCP clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia and related disorders (2016), MJA summary", "url": "https://cdn.craft.cloud/019efd17-dcc2-707f-8e07-011d00d1146a/assets/issues/10.5694mja16.01159.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Prolactin is very likely raised and will be checked, but pregnancy also raises prolactin and must be excluded first.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Pituitary imaging is considered only if prolactin is markedly raised without another explanation, or if there are headaches or visual field defects. It is not the first step.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Hypothyroidism can raise prolactin and is part of the work-up, but pregnancy is far more likely and more urgent to exclude.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Gonadotropins help classify amenorrhoea after pregnancy and hyperprolactinaemia have been assessed. They are not the first test.

key_takeaways: Amenorrhoea in a woman taking a prolactin-raising antipsychotic: do a pregnancy test first, then prolactin. Manage hyperprolactinaemia with her psychiatrist (switch or add aripiprazole) and discuss contraception.

question_text:
A 52-year-old man is admitted to the medical ward of a regional hospital in Bunbury, Western Australia, with community-acquired pneumonia. He expects to stay in hospital for at least 4 days. He tells the admitting resident that he drinks 'a fair bit': about 10–12 standard drinks every day, mostly beer, for the past 15 years. His last drink was 3 hours ago.

He currently feels well apart from his cough. His temperature is 38.0 °C, heart rate 98/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% on room air. He is not tremulous or sweaty, and he is fully orientated. Blood tests show a GGT of 240 U/L (<60), MCV of 102 fL (80–100), platelets 168 × 10^9/L (150–400), potassium 3.8 mmol/L and a normal INR.

The resident is planning alcohol withdrawal monitoring with a withdrawal scale and wants to know how likely he is to develop severe or complicated withdrawal.

Which one of the following additional pieces of history is most important to obtain to anticipate complicated withdrawal?
options: The age at which he first started drinking alcohol
Whether he has had withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens before
Whether he prefers beer, wine or spirits
Whether he has a family history of alcohol dependence
Whether he has ever attended Alcoholics Anonymous
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Whether he has had withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens before

---

The strongest clinical predictor of severe or complicated alcohol withdrawal (seizures, delirium tremens) is a past history of these complications. Other predictors include heavy daily consumption, concurrent medical illness (such as his pneumonia), older age, other substance dependence (especially benzodiazepines), and markers such as thrombocytopenia, hypokalaemia and a high initial withdrawal score. NSW Health withdrawal guidance identifies a history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens as high risk, which should prompt early prophylactic benzodiazepine dosing (typically diazepam, with dose adjusted for liver function), close monitoring and thiamine, rather than symptom-triggered treatment alone. All patients with heavy alcohol use should receive thiamine, and withdrawal is monitored with a validated scale (e.g. AWS or CIWA-Ar).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
A past history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens is the strongest predictor of complicated alcohol withdrawal; it calls for prophylactic benzodiazepines, close monitoring and thiamine.

---

• {"name": "Goodson CM et al. Predictors of severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2014", "url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25346507/"}

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The type of drink matters less than the quantity (standard drinks per day) and past withdrawal history.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Family history contributes to the risk of developing alcohol use disorder but does not predict the severity of withdrawal in this admission.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Past engagement with mutual-help groups is useful for planning long-term recovery support but does not predict withdrawal severity.

question_text:
A 63-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Wollongong, New South Wales, after seeing an advertisement for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program. She asks for 'the free lung scan'.

She smoked 15 cigarettes a day from age 18 until she quit at age 54, 9 years ago. She has not smoked since and does not vape. She has no cough, haemoptysis, breathlessness, weight loss or chest pain. She had a normal chest X-ray 2 years ago for a pre-operative assessment before a knee replacement. She has hypertension treated with perindopril. Her father died of lung cancer at 70. Her examination is normal, and her oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate response to her request?
options: Refer her for a low-dose CT scan through the national program now
Enrol her in the program once she reaches 65 years of age
Arrange a chest X-ray now and repeat it every two years
Explain that she does not meet the program's smoking-history criterion
Refer her through the program after spirometry confirms COPD
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Explain that she does not meet the program's smoking-history criterion

---

The National Lung Cancer Screening Program (started 1 July 2025) offers low-dose CT every 2 years to people who are aged 50–70 years, have no signs or symptoms suggesting lung cancer, currently smoke or quit within the past 10 years, and have at least a 30 pack-year smoking history. Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked = (15 ÷ 20) × 36 = 27 pack-years. She meets the age, symptom and quit-time criteria (quit 9 years ago) but not the 30 pack-year threshold, so she is not eligible. The GP should explain this, discuss her risk honestly (family history is not an eligibility criterion), reinforce that she should present promptly with any symptoms, and continue other preventive care. A chest X-ray is not a screening test for lung cancer.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
NLCSP: age 50–70, asymptomatic, currently smoking or quit within 10 years, and ≥30 pack-years (cigarettes/day ÷ 20 × years) means 2-yearly low-dose CT. Calculate pack-years carefully.

---

question_text:
A randomised controlled trial in Queensland assigned 40 000 adults aged 55–74 years to annual screening with a new blood test for a particular cancer or to usual care, and followed them for 12 years.

Results:
- Cumulative incidence of the cancer: 1.9% in the screened group and 1.8% in the usual-care group
- Proportion diagnosed at an early stage: 58% screened vs 31% usual care
- 5-year survival from the date of diagnosis: 71% screened vs 49% usual care
- Mean age at diagnosis: 66.1 years screened vs 68.3 years usual care
- Mean age at death from the cancer: 72.4 years screened vs 72.5 years usual care
- Cancer-specific mortality: 41 per 100 000 person-years in both groups

A newspaper headline reports that 'the new test improves cancer survival by 45%'.

Which one of the following best explains the difference in 5-year survival between the groups?
options: Length-time bias
Lead-time bias
Overdiagnosis
Healthy volunteer (selection) bias
Recall bias
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Lead-time bias

---

Lead-time bias occurs when screening moves the date of diagnosis earlier without delaying death. Survival measured from diagnosis looks longer even though patients do not live any longer. Here screening brought diagnosis forward by about 2 years (mean age 66.1 vs 68.3), but age at death (72.4 vs 72.5) and cancer-specific mortality were unchanged. The apparent survival gain is therefore an artefact of the earlier start. Randomisation makes selection bias unlikely, and similar cumulative incidence argues against substantial overdiagnosis. The valid measure of screening benefit is a reduction in disease-specific (and ideally all-cause) mortality in a randomised comparison, not survival from diagnosis.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Longer survival from diagnosis with unchanged mortality and age at death means lead-time bias. Judge screening by mortality reduction in randomised trials.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Government Department of Health. Population Based Screening Framework (2018)", "url": "https://www.health.gov.au/resources/publications/population-based-screening-framework"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Improved survival from diagnosis without reduced mortality in a screening trial: lead-time bias

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Length-time bias arises because screening preferentially detects slow-growing tumours with a better prognosis. It is a concern when comparing screen-detected with symptomatic cancers, but here the key finding is an earlier diagnosis with unchanged age at death.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Overdiagnosis (detecting cancers that would never cause harm) would usually increase incidence in the screened group. Incidence was almost the same.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Healthy volunteer bias affects observational comparisons of people who choose screening. This was a randomised trial.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Recall bias affects case-control studies that rely on participants' memory of exposures. It does not apply to survival data.

key_takeaways: Longer survival from diagnosis with unchanged mortality and age at death means lead-time bias. Judge screening by mortality reduction in randomised trials.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Government Department of Health. Population Based Screening Framework (2018)", "url": "https://www.health.gov.au/resources/publications/population-based-screening-framework"}

question_text:
A youth health service in regional South Australia is considering a new point-of-care test for chlamydia for asymptomatic 16–29-year-olds attending for other reasons. In this population the prevalence of chlamydia is estimated at 2%. The manufacturer reports that the test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 95% compared with nucleic acid amplification testing.

The service director asks you to estimate, for a young person in this setting who tests positive on the new test, how likely it is that they actually have chlamydia.

Which one of the following is closest to the probability that a person with a positive result has chlamydia?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. 27%

---

This is the positive predictive value (PPV), which depends on prevalence as well as on test accuracy. Take 10 000 people: 200 have chlamydia (2%) and 9800 do not. True positives = 90% of 200 = 180. False positives = 5% of 9800 = 490. PPV = 180 ÷ (180 + 490) = 180 ÷ 670 ≈ 27%. So about three in four positive results would be false positives. In a low-prevalence population even a fairly specific test gives a low PPV, which is why confirmatory NAAT testing (or a more specific test) would be needed before treatment and partner notification. The negative predictive value is very high: 9310 ÷ 9330 ≈ 99.8%.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
PPV falls as prevalence falls. At 2% prevalence, a test with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity has a PPV of only about 27%, so confirm positives with a more specific test.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Government Department of Health. Population Based Screening Framework (2018)", "url": "https://www.health.gov.au/resources/publications/population-based-screening-framework"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Positive predictive value of a screening test in a low-prevalence population

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 90% is the sensitivity: the proportion of people WITH chlamydia who test positive. It is not the probability of disease given a positive test.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 95% is the specificity: the proportion of people WITHOUT chlamydia who test negative.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 50% has no basis in these figures. PPV has to be calculated from prevalence, sensitivity and specificity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 99.8% is the negative predictive value (the probability of NOT having chlamydia after a negative result).

key_takeaways: PPV falls as prevalence falls. At 2% prevalence, a test with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity has a PPV of only about 27%, so confirm positives with a more specific test.

question_text:
A general practitioner in Brisbane is reviewing a randomised, placebo-controlled trial of a new once-yearly injection to prevent hip fracture in community-dwelling women aged over 70 years with osteopenia. The trial enrolled 8000 women and followed them for 3 years.

Results:
- Hip fracture over 3 years: 4.0% in the placebo group and 2.5% in the treatment group
- The difference was statistically significant (p = 0.002)
- Serious adverse events: similar in both groups

A patient asks how many women like her would need to have the injection for one of them to avoid a hip fracture.

Which one of the following is the number needed to treat for 3 years to prevent one hip fracture?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. 67

---

Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = 4.0% − 2.5% = 1.5% (0.015) over 3 years. NNT = 1 ÷ ARR = 1 ÷ 0.015 ≈ 66.7, which rounds UP to 67 women treated for 3 years to prevent one hip fracture. The relative risk reduction (RRR) is 1.5 ÷ 4.0 = 37.5%, which sounds much more impressive. Presenting absolute rather than relative effects, with the time frame, helps patients make informed decisions. The NNT depends on baseline risk: the same RRR gives a smaller NNT in higher-risk women.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction (round up) and always has a time frame. Here ARR 1.5% gives NNT 67 over 3 years, while the RRR is 37.5%.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Interpreting risks and ratios in therapy trials", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/interpreting-risks-and-ratios-in-therapy-trials.html"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Number needed to treat from absolute risk reduction in a fracture-prevention trial

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 3 is roughly 1 ÷ RRR (1 ÷ 0.375). Using the relative risk reduction instead of the absolute risk reduction is a common error.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 25 is 1 ÷ 0.04, the reciprocal of the placebo event rate, not of the risk difference.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 40 is 1 ÷ 0.025, the reciprocal of the treatment event rate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: 150 comes from a decimal error (treating 1.5% as 0.0067 or similar). The correct ARR is 0.015.

key_takeaways: NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction (round up) and always has a time frame. Here ARR 1.5% gives NNT 67 over 3 years, while the RRR is 37.5%.

question_text:
Clinicians at a tertiary maternity and neonatal service in Melbourne have noticed several infants born with a rare abdominal wall defect (about 1 in 3000 births) whose mothers reported using a particular over-the-counter decongestant in early pregnancy. The state health department wants to know, within about 12 months and with a limited budget, whether there is an association between early-pregnancy use of the decongestant and the defect.

State perinatal data collections can identify all affected infants born over the past 8 years, and a random sample of unaffected births from the same hospitals and years can be selected. Mothers can be interviewed, and pharmacy records are available for some.

Which one of the following study designs is most appropriate to answer this question?
options: Prospective cohort study of women exposed and unexposed in pregnancy
Randomised controlled trial of the decongestant in early pregnancy
Case-control study comparing past exposure in cases and controls
Cross-sectional survey of current decongestant use among pregnant women
Ecological study correlating sales data with birth defect rates
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Case-control study comparing past exposure in cases and controls

---

For a rare outcome, a case-control study is the most efficient design: start with people who have the outcome (cases) and a comparable group without it (controls), then compare how often each group was exposed. It can be done quickly and cheaply using existing records and interviews, and it gives an odds ratio. Its main weaknesses are recall bias (mothers of affected infants may remember exposures more thoroughly; pharmacy records help) and selection of appropriate controls. Confounders such as maternal age, smoking and fever should be measured and adjusted for.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Rare outcome with a suspected earlier exposure: use a case-control study (efficient, quick, gives an odds ratio; watch for recall and selection bias). Cohorts suit rare exposures or common outcomes.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NHMRC. Guidelines for Guidelines handbook (evidence and study design)", "url": "https://www.nhmrc.gov.au/guidelinesforguidelines"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Choosing a study design for a rare outcome and a suspected earlier exposure: case-control study

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A prospective cohort would need to follow tens of thousands of pregnancies to observe enough cases of a 1-in-3000 outcome, and would take years. It is best suited to common outcomes or rare exposures.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Randomly assigning pregnant women to a drug suspected of causing birth defects would be unethical, and an RCT would be enormous and slow for a rare outcome.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at one time. It cannot establish that the exposure came before the outcome, and it would capture very few cases.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Ecological studies use group-level data and are prone to the ecological fallacy. They can generate hypotheses but cannot link exposure to outcome in individuals.

key_takeaways: Rare outcome with a suspected earlier exposure: use a case-control study (efficient, quick, gives an odds ratio; watch for recall and selection bias). Cohorts suit rare exposures or common outcomes.

question_text:
A 26-year-old cook at a busy café in Hobart, Tasmania, sees his general practitioner with 5 days of fatigue, nausea, anorexia and dark urine, and yellow eyes that he noticed 2 days ago. He returned from a 3-week trip to South-East Asia a month ago and had not been vaccinated against hepatitis A. He lives with his partner and has worked shifts preparing food, including salads and sandwiches, up until yesterday.

He is jaundiced and has mild tender hepatomegaly. He is alert, with no asterixis.

Investigations:
- ALT 2140 U/L (<40)
- Bilirubin 96 µmol/L (<20)
- INR 1.1
- Hepatitis A IgM antibody: positive
- HBsAg: negative; HCV antibody: negative

He asks when he can return to work, because he cannot afford to take much time off.

In addition to notifying the public health unit, which one of the following is the most appropriate advice about work?
options: He can return to work as soon as he feels well enough, with careful hand hygiene
Exclude him from food handling until 7 days after the onset of jaundice
Exclude him from food handling until his liver function tests are normal
Exclude him from food handling until 2 weeks after his last day of work
Exclude him from food handling until his hepatitis A IgM is negative
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Exclude him from food handling until 7 days after the onset of jaundice

---

Hepatitis A is notifiable in all Australian jurisdictions, and a food handler with hepatitis A is a public health priority because of the risk of foodborne outbreaks. People with hepatitis A are most infectious in the 2 weeks before symptoms start, and infectivity falls quickly after jaundice appears. The CDNA national guidelines and state control guidelines recommend that food handlers are excluded from work until at least 7 days after the onset of jaundice (or 2 weeks after the onset of first symptoms if there is no jaundice). The public health unit will assess the risk to café patrons and co-workers. Close contacts (such as his partner) should be offered post-exposure prophylaxis (hepatitis A vaccine, or normal human immunoglobulin for some groups) as soon as possible and within 2 weeks of last exposure.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Hepatitis A in a food handler: notify, and exclude from food handling until 7 days after jaundice onset (or 2 weeks after first symptoms if no jaundice). Offer contacts vaccine or NHIG within 2 weeks of exposure.

---

question_text:
A 19-year-old university student in Perth, Western Australia, was admitted to hospital this morning with invasive meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis confirmed on blood PCR). His symptoms began yesterday afternoon, and he received IV ceftriaxone on arrival in the emergency department. The public health unit asks the treating team to help identify contacts. The following people are identified:

- A lecturer who taught him in a 150-seat lecture theatre 3 days ago
- His flatmate, who has been overseas for the past 10 days
- The emergency department nurse who took his blood samples while wearing a surgical mask
- His girlfriend, who kissed him and stayed at his flat 2 nights before his symptoms began
- The rideshare driver who drove him to hospital, a 20-minute trip

Which one of the following people should be offered clearance antibiotics?
options: The lecturer
The flatmate
The emergency department nurse
The girlfriend
The rideshare driver
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. The girlfriend

---

Clearance antibiotics are for close contacts: people who had close, prolonged contact with the case during the 7 days before symptom onset, until 24 hours after the case started effective antibiotics. This includes household or household-like contacts (e.g. staying overnight), intimate (kissing) contacts, childcare contacts with household-equivalent exposure, healthcare workers with unprotected close airway exposure (e.g. intubation or suctioning without a mask), and passengers seated next to the case for more than 8 hours. His girlfriend had intimate contact and stayed overnight within the 7-day window. Options are single-dose ciprofloxacin (ceftriaxone in pregnancy; rifampicin is contraindicated in pregnancy), given as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of the diagnosis. The case also needs clearance if the treatment antibiotic does not eliminate carriage (ceftriaxone does). Close contacts are offered vaccination if the serogroup is vaccine-preventable.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
IMD clearance antibiotics: household or household-like, intimate (kissing), childcare-equivalent, unprotected airway-exposed HCWs, and adjacent passengers >8 h, within 7 days before onset. Ciprofloxacin single dose (ceftriaxone in pregnancy).

---

---

question_text:
A 30-year-old woman in her second pregnancy moves from overseas to Melbourne, Victoria, and attends her first antenatal visit at a general practice at 37 weeks and 2 days of gestation. The pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She had an influenza vaccine through her workplace in April this year, before she became aware of the pregnancy's dates. She has not had any other vaccines during this pregnancy. Her first child, now 3, is fully immunised.

She has read about whooping cough and RSV and asks whether it is 'too late' for any vaccines. She has no allergies and is well today.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?
options: Give RSV vaccine and dTpa today; the baby needs nirsevimab if born within 2 weeks
Give dTpa today; RSV vaccine is not recommended after 36 weeks of gestation
Give no vaccines now; plan nirsevimab for the baby and give her dTpa after birth
Give RSV vaccine today and dTpa in 2 weeks, as the two should be spaced apart
Give dTpa today and give the RSV vaccine to her in the first week after birth
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Give RSV vaccine and dTpa today; the baby needs nirsevimab if born within 2 weeks

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) in each pregnancy from 28 weeks' gestation. A woman who has not been vaccinated by 36 weeks should receive it as soon as possible. Antibody transfer needs at least 2 weeks before birth for adequate protection, so if the baby is born less than 2 weeks after maternal vaccination, the infant is recommended to receive nirsevimab. Pertussis vaccine (dTpa) is recommended in every pregnancy, ideally at 20–32 weeks, but if it was missed it should be given as soon as possible, at any time up to delivery. RSV vaccine can be given at the same visit as dTpa, influenza or COVID-19 vaccines. Her influenza vaccine this year covers the current season.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Maternal RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) is recommended from 28 weeks; if missed, give it as soon as possible (no 36-week cut-off). Infants born <2 weeks after maternal vaccination get nirsevimab. dTpa is ideally given at 20–32 weeks but can be given up to delivery, and can be co-administered.

---

question_text:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and long-standing schizophrenia is an inpatient at a hospital in Newcastle, New South Wales, with a spreading infection and wet gangrene of his right forefoot. The vascular surgeon recommends a below-knee amputation within 24 hours and explains that without it he will probably develop worsening sepsis and may die. He refuses, saying, 'I've had this leg for 58 years and I'm going out with it. I know I might die.'

His schizophrenia has been stable for 10 years on a monthly depot antipsychotic. He lives alone in a public housing unit, manages his own finances and attends his community mental health appointments. He is not delirious. He has no current hallucinations and expresses no delusions about his leg or the surgery. His sister, who is his closest relative, strongly wants the surgery to go ahead. A nurse suggests that 'he can't consent because he has schizophrenia'.

Which one of the following is most important to establish before accepting or overriding his refusal?
options: Whether he currently meets diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia
Whether his score on a cognitive screening test is in the normal range
Whether his family members agree with the decision he has made
Whether his decision is one most people in his situation would make
Whether he can understand, weigh and communicate this specific decision
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Whether he can understand, weigh and communicate this specific decision

---

Adults are presumed to have capacity. Capacity is decision-specific and is assessed functionally: can the person understand the information relevant to the decision (including the consequences of refusing), retain it long enough, use or weigh it to reach a decision, and communicate that decision? A diagnosis of mental illness does not in itself mean that a person lacks capacity, and an unwise or unusual decision does not prove incapacity. If he has capacity, his refusal must be respected even if it leads to death. The team should explore his reasons, correct misunderstandings, offer alternatives and support, involve his treating psychiatrist and document carefully. If he lacks capacity for this decision, NSW law provides for substitute decision-making (a person responsible or guardian under the Guardianship Act 1987, or the Tribunal), guided by his known wishes; emergency treatment provisions apply if needed to save life.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Capacity is presumed, decision-specific and functional (understand, retain, weigh, communicate). Mental illness or an unwise choice does not by itself mean incapacity.

---

REFERENCES

---

question_text:
A 44-year-old interstate B-double truck driver from Shepparton, Victoria, sees his general practitioner for a repeat prescription of levetiracetam. A neurologist diagnosed epilepsy 2 months ago after two generalised seizures in 6 weeks, one of them at a truck stop. He had a further seizure at home 10 days ago. The neurologist and the GP have both told him that he is not fit to drive any vehicle and that he must tell VicRoads. His letter from the neurologist confirms this advice.

He says he has not told VicRoads or his employer and is still driving his usual Melbourne–Brisbane route 'because I'll lose my job and the house'. He becomes angry when the GP raises it again and says, 'What I tell you is confidential.' He leaves for a run to Brisbane tomorrow. The GP has discussed the risks with him, offered a letter to support a change of duties, and documented the advice.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step for the GP?
options: Maintain confidentiality, because telling VicRoads is legally his duty alone
Notify his employer directly so he can be taken off driving duties
Tell him that you intend to notify VicRoads, and then notify VicRoads
Notify VicRoads, because Victorian law makes medical reporting mandatory
Report him to Victoria Police so that his licence is cancelled at once
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Tell him that you intend to notify VicRoads, and then notify VicRoads

---

Under Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive, drivers are legally responsible for reporting conditions that affect their driving to the licensing authority. Health professionals advise patients about their fitness to drive and document it. If a patient continues to drive despite advice and poses a risk to public safety, a health professional may report directly to the driver licensing authority. In most jurisdictions, including Victoria, this is voluntary (not mandatory), and doctors who report in good faith are protected. Only South Australia and the Northern Territory have mandatory reporting by health professionals. Confidentiality is not absolute. Disclosure is justified here because the risk of serious harm to the public (a heavy vehicle driver with recent seizures) outweighs his privacy, and the Medical Board code supports disclosure when there is a serious risk to others. Good practice is to tell the patient of the intention to report (unless this would increase risk), report to VicRoads with the minimum necessary information, and document everything.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Fitness to drive: the patient must self-report. If a patient keeps driving unsafely, a doctor may report to the licensing authority (voluntary and legally protected in most states; mandatory in SA and NT). Tell the patient and document.

---

• {"name": "Medical Board of Australia. Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia", "url": "https://www.medicalboard.gov.au/Codes-Guidelines-Policies/Code-of-conduct.aspx"}
