question_text:
A 76-year-old woman is an inpatient on a medical ward at a hospital in Townsville, Queensland, after an elective knee replacement. Her creatinine clearance is 25 mL/min. Because of a prescribing error, she was given enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily (a treatment dose not adjusted for her kidney function) instead of the intended prophylactic dose for 3 days. Last night she developed a large thigh haematoma and a haemoglobin drop from 118 to 76 g/L, needing a two-unit red cell transfusion. She is now stable.

The error was identified this morning and has been entered into the hospital's incident management system. The consultant has asked you, the ward resident who is part of the treating team, to help plan what to tell the patient and her son, who is asking 'what went wrong'.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate approach?
options: Wait until the incident review is complete so that accurate information can be given
Meet them soon, say sorry, explain the known facts and outline the next steps
Explain what happened but avoid the word 'sorry', as it could be an admission of liability
Ask the nurse who gave the doses to explain the error to the family on her own
Contact the hospital's medical indemnity insurer before speaking to the family
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Meet them soon, say sorry, explain the known facts and outline the next steps

---

The Australian Open Disclosure Framework (ACSQHC) requires timely, open communication with patients and their support people when an adverse event causes harm. Key elements: an apology or expression of regret that includes the words 'I am sorry' or 'we are sorry'; a factual explanation of what is known (without speculation or blame); the opportunity for the patient and family to tell their story and ask questions; an explanation of the steps being taken to manage the event and prevent recurrence; and a plan for ongoing communication and support. Disclosure starts early (ideally within 24 hours) and continues as the review progresses; it is led by a senior clinician, with other team members as appropriate. All Australian jurisdictions have apology provisions protecting an expression of regret from being treated as an admission of liability.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Open disclosure: prompt, senior-led, includes saying 'sorry', gives the known facts without speculation or blame, listens to the patient and family, and explains the next steps and follow-up. Apology laws protect expressions of regret.

---

question_text:
An 81-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 28% predicted, home oxygen) is admitted to a hospital in Geelong, Victoria, with pneumonia and hypercapnic respiratory failure. He is on non-invasive ventilation and IV antibiotics. Over the past 6 hours he has become drowsy and no longer has capacity to make treatment decisions.

A year ago, after an ICU admission, he completed an advance care directive with his GP. It is signed and properly witnessed. Its instructional directive states: 'I refuse intubation and mechanical ventilation and I refuse CPR. I consent to antibiotics, oxygen and mask ventilation (NIV) for a chest infection.' His values directive says that being 'kept alive on machines' is unacceptable to him. His daughter is his appointed medical treatment decision maker. She is distressed and asks the ICU registrar to intubate him, saying 'he didn't really mean it, and I'm the one who decides now'. The ICU consultant agrees that intubation is a clinically reasonable option.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Intubate him, because his appointed decision maker has consented to it
Apply to VCAT and intubate him while waiting for its decision
Intubate him for a 48-hour time-limited trial, then review the directive
Follow the instructional directive: continue NIV and antibiotics without intubation
Intubate him, because the directive was made before this illness began
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Follow the instructional directive: continue NIV and antibiotics without intubation

---

Under the Victorian Medical Treatment Planning and Decisions Act 2016, an instructional directive is a legally binding statement of consent to, or refusal of, specified future medical treatment. It takes effect as if the person had made the decision themselves when they lack capacity. A medical treatment decision maker cannot override a relevant instructional directive; their role applies to decisions the directive does not cover, guided by the person's values and preferences. His directive explicitly refuses intubation in exactly the kind of situation he anticipated (a chest infection with COPD). Health practitioners should therefore continue the treatments he consented to (NIV, antibiotics, oxygen) and provide comfort-focused care, while supporting his daughter compassionately. The Act allows a practitioner to not follow an instructional directive only in narrow circumstances (e.g. circumstances have changed so much that the person would not have wanted it to apply), and then an application can be made to VCAT. Those circumstances do not apply here.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Victoria: a valid instructional directive is legally binding; the medical treatment decision maker cannot override it. They decide only matters the directive does not cover, guided by the person's values.

---

---

question_text:
A general practice in Adelaide, South Australia, is reviewing why very few of its patients are recorded as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, even though the local population includes a sizeable Aboriginal community. The audit finds that the Indigenous status field is blank for 38% of patients. Reception staff explain that they 'only ask people who look Aboriginal', because they worry that asking everyone might offend people. One of the GPs says she usually works it out from a patient's surname, family connections or appearance, and records it herself.

As a result, eligible patients are missing out on annual Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health assessments, follow-up services and other programs linked to Indigenous status. The practice manager asks you, the GP registrar, to recommend a change to practice.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate way for the practice to collect this information?
options: Ask every patient the standard Indigenous status question and record the answer they give
Ask the question of patients whose appearance or surname suggests an Aboriginal background
Have the GP record Indigenous status from family knowledge, to avoid offending patients
Ask for a confirmation of Aboriginality letter before recording a patient as Aboriginal
Record Indigenous status as 'not stated' unless the patient raises it themselves
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Ask every patient the standard Indigenous status question and record the answer they give

---

The AIHW National best practice guidelines for collecting Indigenous status in health data sets recommend that ALL patients are asked the standard question, 'Are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin?', with the response options No / Yes, Aboriginal / Yes, Torres Strait Islander / Yes, both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander. Staff should never guess or assume based on appearance, surname, country of birth or family knowledge. Self-identification is what is recorded, and people can choose not to answer. Explaining why the question is asked (to provide appropriate care and access to services) makes it more acceptable. Accurate identification improves access to culturally appropriate care, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health assessments and follow-up, and improves population health data for planning. It is part of culturally safe practice under the Medical Board code and the RACGP/NACCHO National Guide.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Ask every patient 'Are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin?' and record their self-identified answer. Never assume from appearance or surname.

---

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman sees her general practitioner in Orange, New South Wales, with bruising on her upper arms and neck. After gentle questioning she says that her partner 'grabbed me by the throat and squeezed until I nearly blacked out' during an argument 4 days ago. Their children, aged 4 and 7, were in the room and screamed at him to stop. She says he has pushed her before, has been drinking more since losing his job, and last night threatened that she would 'never see the kids again' if she left.

She does not want the police involved and asks the GP not to tell anyone, because she fears it will 'make things worse'. She plans to stay with her sister for a few nights. The children are at school today. The GP has assessed her injuries, documented them and discussed safety options and 1800RESPECT.

Which one of the following best describes the GP's obligation regarding the children?
options: Keep the disclosure confidential, because the adult victim has refused consent to share it
Notify police rather than child protection, because the violence was directed at her
Report to the Child Protection Helpline if the Mandatory Reporter Guide indicates risk of significant harm
Report to child protection if she gives written consent, because otherwise it breaches her privacy
Advise her to leave the relationship and review the children at the next scheduled visit
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Report to the Child Protection Helpline if the Mandatory Reporter Guide indicates risk of significant harm

---

In NSW, doctors are mandatory reporters under the Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998. They must report to the Child Protection Helpline (13 21 11), or through the online ChildStory Reporter, when they have reasonable grounds to suspect a child is at risk of significant harm (ROSH). Exposure to domestic and family violence that causes or is likely to cause serious physical or psychological harm is one of the ROSH circumstances. The Mandatory Reporter Guide helps decide whether the threshold is met and what to do if it is not (e.g. referral to a Child Wellbeing Unit or support services). Non-fatal strangulation is a strong predictor of future lethal violence, the children witnessed it, and there are escalating threats, so a report is very likely to be required. Consent is not needed for a mandatory report. Where it is safe, the GP should tell her about the report and involve her in safety planning, and should call police (000) if anyone is in immediate danger.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
NSW: doctors must report reasonable suspicion of risk of significant harm (including DFV exposure) to the Child Protection Helpline (13 21 11); use the Mandatory Reporter Guide. Consent is not required; strangulation is a major lethality red flag.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "NSW Department of Communities and Justice. Mandatory reporting (NSW Interagency Guidelines)", "url": "https://dcj.nsw.gov.au/service-providers/deliver-services-to-children-and-families/nsw-interagency-guidelines-for-practitioners/reporting-responding-wellbeing-and-safety-concerns/mandatory-reporting.html"}
• {"name": "Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 (NSW)", "url": "https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/whole/html/inforce/current/act-1998-157"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The mother's wishes carry weight, but they do not override the mandatory reporting obligation for children at ROSH. Confidentiality is legally limited here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Police may need to be involved if there is immediate danger, but the obligation regarding the children is a report to child protection. Children exposed to DFV are themselves at risk of harm.

question_text:
A 36-year-old single general practitioner works in one of two practices in Esperance, Western Australia. For 2 years she has treated a 38-year-old man, also single, for depression and anxiety, including regular reviews under a Mental Health Treatment Plan. His mood has been stable for 6 months. At the end of his latest review he thanks her for 'getting him through the worst year of his life' and asks whether she would like to go out for dinner. She finds him attractive and has run into him socially at community events.

She is unsure how to respond.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept, because they are consenting adults in a small town who meet socially anyway
Transfer his care to the other practice first, and then accept the invitation
Accept once 6 months have passed since his last consultation with her
Continue as his GP and see him socially, keeping it separate from his care
Decline kindly, keep the professional relationship, and document and seek advice
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Decline kindly, keep the professional relationship, and document and seek advice

---

The Medical Board of Australia's guidelines 'Sexual boundaries in the doctor–patient relationship' state that it is never appropriate for a doctor to engage in a sexual relationship with a current patient. Ending the professional relationship in order to start a relationship is not acceptable. For former patients, a relationship may still be unethical depending on the power imbalance, the patient's vulnerability, the nature and length of care, and the use of knowledge gained in the doctor–patient relationship. Long-term psychological care creates a lasting power imbalance, so a future relationship would be very likely to breach the guidelines. She should decline kindly and clearly, maintain professional care if it remains appropriate, document the interaction, and seek advice from a colleague or her medical defence organisation. She should consider transferring his care if she cannot keep objectivity. Small rural communities need extra attention to boundaries, but the obligations are the same.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Sexual relationships with current patients are prohibited. Ending care to start a relationship is not acceptable. Relationships with former patients (especially after psychological care) are often unethical, because of lasting power imbalance.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Medical Board of Australia. Guidelines: Sexual boundaries in the doctor-patient relationship (2018)", "url": "https://www.medicalboard.gov.au/Codes-Guidelines-Policies/Sexual-boundaries-guidelines"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Current patient asks his GP on a date: sexual boundaries (Medical Board guidelines)

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A relationship with a current patient is prohibited regardless of consent or community size.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Ending care in order to start a relationship is specifically identified as inappropriate. The power imbalance from 2 years of mental health care persists.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: There is no 'safe' waiting period. Time alone does not remove the power imbalance, especially after psychological care.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A romantic relationship alongside ongoing care is a clear boundary violation.

key_takeaways: Sexual relationships with current patients are prohibited. Ending care to start a relationship is not acceptable. Relationships with former patients (especially after psychological care) are often unethical, because of lasting power imbalance.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Medical Board of Australia. Guidelines: Sexual boundaries in the doctor-patient relationship (2018)", "url": "https://www.medicalboard.gov.au/Codes-Guidelines-Policies/Sexual-boundaries-guidelines"}

question_text:
Dr Tran is a general practitioner in Brisbane, Queensland. During a busy month the following situations arise:

- His brother, who lives nearby, asks him for a repeat prescription for temazepam because he 'can't get in to see his own GP'.
- At a family picnic in a park, his 9-year-old niece, who has a known peanut allergy, develops lip swelling, wheeze and hypotension after eating a biscuit. Her parents are frozen, and the ambulance is 15 minutes away.
- He notices he feels tired, orders his own thyroid function tests through his practice, and increases his own thyroxine dose.
- His wife asks him to excise a changing mole from her back in his rooms after hours to save her a wait.
- His 24-year-old son asks for a medical certificate to cover two days off work for 'a bad cold'.

Which one of the following actions is consistent with the Medical Board of Australia's code of conduct?
options: Writing a repeat temazepam prescription for his brother
Giving his niece her adrenaline autoinjector and starting first aid
Ordering his own thyroid tests and adjusting his own thyroxine
Excising the mole from his wife's back in his rooms after hours
Writing a medical certificate for his son's sick leave
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Giving his niece her adrenaline autoinjector and starting first aid

---

'Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia' advises doctors to avoid providing medical care to themselves and to anyone with whom they have a close personal relationship. Exceptions are minor or emergency situations where no other care is available, and then care should be handed to another practitioner as soon as possible. The code specifically says doctors should not prescribe Schedule 8, psychotropic and/or drugs of dependence, or perform elective surgery, for themselves or people close to them. Giving adrenaline to a child with anaphylaxis while awaiting an ambulance is emergency care where no other practitioner is available, and it is expected of any doctor. Doctors should also have their own GP rather than self-treat, and certificates for family members compromise objectivity.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
MBA code: avoid treating yourself and people close to you. Never prescribe S8/psychotropic drugs or do elective procedures for them. Emergency care when no one else is available is the exception.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Medical Board of Australia. Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia (2020)", "url": "https://www.medicalboard.gov.au/Codes-Guidelines-Policies/Code-of-conduct.aspx"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Medical Board code: treating family members and oneself; the emergency exception

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Temazepam is a psychotropic drug of dependence. The code advises against prescribing such drugs for people in a close personal relationship.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Self-treatment, including ordering one's own tests and adjusting one's own medicines, is discouraged. Doctors should have their own independent GP.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Elective procedures on close family members are specifically discouraged. Objectivity, consent and follow-up are compromised.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Certifying a family member's illness lacks objectivity and is inappropriate. His son should see his own doctor.

key_takeaways: MBA code: avoid treating yourself and people close to you. Never prescribe S8/psychotropic drugs or do elective procedures for them. Emergency care when no one else is available is the exception.

question_text:
Researchers in New South Wales conducted a case-control study of solarium (sunbed) use and melanoma in adults aged 18–40 years. They recruited 200 people with newly diagnosed melanoma from the state cancer registry and 400 controls without melanoma, frequency-matched for age and sex, from the electoral roll. Participants completed a telephone interview about past sunbed use.

Results:
- Cases: 80 of 200 (40%) reported ever using a sunbed
- Controls: 80 of 400 (20%) reported ever using a sunbed
- Crude odds ratio 2.67 (95% confidence interval 1.83–3.88)

The analysis was not adjusted for skin type, number of naevi or history of sunburn.

Which one of the following is the most accurate interpretation of these results?
options: The odds of sunbed use were about 2.7 times higher in cases; confounding is possible
Sunbed use causes melanoma, because the confidence interval does not include 1
The result is not statistically significant, because the confidence interval is wide
The incidence of melanoma among sunbed users in this study was 40%
The relative risk of melanoma calculated directly from these data is 2.0
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. The odds of sunbed use were about 2.7 times higher in cases; confounding is possible

---

OR = (80 × 320) ÷ (120 × 80) = 25 600 ÷ 9600 ≈ 2.67. In a case-control study the odds ratio compares the odds of exposure in cases with the odds in controls; mathematically this equals the odds ratio for disease. Because melanoma is relatively rare, it approximates the relative risk. The 95% CI (1.83–3.88) excludes 1, so the association is statistically significant at the 5% level. However, an association does not prove causation. This crude estimate was not adjusted for important potential confounders (fair skin, naevi, sunburn history, which are linked to both sunbed use and melanoma), and case-control studies are prone to recall and selection bias. Incidence and relative risk cannot be calculated directly from a case-control design, because the investigators fixed the numbers of cases and controls.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Case-control studies give odds ratios (≈ RR if the disease is rare), not incidence or RR. A CI excluding 1 means statistical significance, not causation; consider confounding and bias.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Interpreting risks and ratios in therapy trials", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/interpreting-risks-and-ratios-in-therapy-trials.html"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Interpreting an odds ratio and confidence interval from a case-control study

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Statistical significance shows the association is unlikely to be due to chance alone; it does not establish causation, particularly with unadjusted confounding and possible recall bias.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The CI excludes 1, so the result is statistically significant. Width reflects precision, not significance.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 40% is the proportion of CASES who used sunbeds, not the incidence of melanoma among users. Incidence cannot be derived from a case-control study.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Risks are not directly calculable in case-control studies. 2.0 is just the ratio of the exposure proportions (40% ÷ 20%), not a relative risk of disease.

key_takeaways: Case-control studies give odds ratios (≈ RR if the disease is rare), not incidence or RR. A CI excluding 1 means statistical significance, not causation; consider confounding and bias.

question_text:
A 29-year-old registered nurse at a hospital in Darwin, Northern Territory, sustains a deep needlestick injury with a hollow-bore needle while taking blood from a patient known to have chronic hepatitis B (HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative). The source patient is HIV and hepatitis C antibody negative on testing done this week. She washed the site immediately with soap and water and reported to the staff health service within 30 minutes.

Her staff health record shows she completed a three-dose hepatitis B vaccine course 9 years ago as a nursing student, and her anti-HBs level measured 6 weeks after the third dose was 184 mIU/mL. A rapid anti-HBs test done today is below 10 mIU/mL. She is well, is not pregnant and has no other medical conditions. She is anxious and asks whether she needs 'the injection and another vaccine'.

Which one of the following best interprets her hepatitis B immune status and need for prophylaxis?
options: Immunity has been lost; she needs immunoglobulin and a booster dose
She is partially immune; she needs a booster dose but no immunoglobulin
She is immune; no immunoglobulin or booster dose is needed
She is a vaccine non-responder; she needs a repeat full vaccine course
Her status is uncertain until anti-HBs is rechecked in 1 month
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. She is immune; no immunoglobulin or booster dose is needed

---

According to the Australian Immunisation Handbook, a person who has had a documented anti-HBs level of 10 mIU/mL or more at any time after completing a primary hepatitis B vaccine course is considered immune and does not need hepatitis B immunoglobulin, booster doses or further hepatitis B testing after an exposure, even if the current anti-HBs level has fallen below 10. Immune memory persists and gives protection despite waning antibody levels. She had a documented response (184 mIU/mL), so no hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis is needed. The rest of the occupational exposure pathway continues: baseline testing, counselling, and assessment for HIV and HCV risk according to the local protocol (here the source is negative for both), incident reporting and follow-up.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Hepatitis B exposure: a documented anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL at any time after a primary course means immune, so no HBIG, booster or HBV testing is needed, even if the current level is low.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Immunisation Handbook. Hepatitis B", "url": "https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/hepatitis-b"}
• {"name": "Queensland Health. Management of occupational exposure to blood and body fluids (guideline)", "url": "https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0032/1398191/occ-exposure-blood-body-fluids.pdf"}

---

EDITED BY HEISENBERG
subtopic: Needlestick from an HBsAg-positive source: known vaccine responder needs no hepatitis B prophylaxis

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A fall in anti-HBs below 10 years after a documented response does not mean lost immunity; immune memory persists. HBIG plus vaccine is for people who are non-immune or whose response is unknown.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: There is no 'partial immunity' category requiring a booster after a documented response. Boosters are not recommended for documented responders.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A non-responder is someone whose anti-HBs was <10 mIU/mL after a primary course. She had 184 mIU/mL, so she is a responder.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Her documented post-vaccination response already establishes immunity. Rechecking anti-HBs adds nothing and would not change management.

key_takeaways: Hepatitis B exposure: a documented anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL at any time after a primary course means immune, so no HBIG, booster or HBV testing is needed, even if the current level is low.
